World.title: NFIU, patners seek financial intelligence sharing collaboration framework
World.content:
The Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) is planning a new framework for intelligence sharing collaboration, a move aimed at enhancing the integrity and resilence of the nation’s financial system.

Representatives of finacial system actors and regulators met at a “high-level engagment” in Abuja on Wednesday to co-design the proposed Joint Financial Intelligence Collaboration (JFIC).

The meeting organised by the NFIU under the auspices of the British High Commission in Nigeria and the Convention for Business Integrity (CBi), brought together representatives of regulators, banks, insurance companies, fintech companies, Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), technology firms and other stakeholders to work out the JFIC framework.

NFIU Chief Executive Officer, Hafsat Bakari, said in a statement on Thursday that “the collaboration will help identify emerging threats, disrupt illicit financial networks and strengthen the integrity of Nigeria’s financial system.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The initiative seeks to create a trusted platform through which public and private-sector institutions can work together more effectively,” she wrote.

During the meeting, NFIU’s General Counsel, Felix Obiamalu, who represented Mrs Bakari at the event, said the process had moved beyond discussions about the proposed partnership.

“We have moved from dialogue to design, to commitment and implementation,” Mr Obiamalu declared.

He added that the focus was now on determining what the partnership would look like, how it would operate and the value it would create for participating institutions.

Delivering the keynote presentation, Xolisile Khanyile, former Chairperson of the Egmont Group and former Director of South Africa’s Financial Intelligence Centre, described private-sector participation as a national responsibility.

Ms Khanyile urged Nigeria to adopt a practical and phased approach to implementing the proposed partnership.

She said trust, shared ownership and collaboration “are the foundations of every successful public-private partnership.”

She also described the initiative as timely and necessary, given Nigeria’s importance within the global anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing framework.

Stakeholders seek stronger cooperation

Speaking on behalf of the British High Commission, Jehanzeb Khan, an Illicit Financial Flows Officer at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), stressed the need for “stronger public-private collaboration in tackling illicit financial flows.”

Also, the Managing Director of the Convention for Business Integrity, Olusoji Apampa, said the process was deliberately designed to place the private sector “at the centre of decision-making.”

According to him, this will ensure that the emerging framework reflects the “operational realities” of private-sector institutions and enjoys broad stakeholder ownership.

The NFIU said the engagement ended with “strong stakeholder support for the proposed framework” and “a shared commitment” to advancing a partnership capable of strengthening financial intelligence and improving threat detection.

It said the partnership would also enhance Nigeria’s response to “increasingly sophisticated forms of financial activity.”

“For many participants, the message was clear: no single institution can combat today’s financial crimes alone,” the statement said.

It added: “Effective action requires government and industry working together, sharing insights, identifying risks early and building collective resilience against illicit financial activity.”

About NFIU

The NFIU is Nigeria’s central agency for receiving, analysing and disseminating financial intelligence linked to money laundering, terrorism financing and other financial crimes.

READ ALSO: VP Shettima to unveil biography of late Brigadier Musa Usman

The unit receives suspicious and threshold-based transaction reports from financial institutions and other reporting entities. It analyses the information and shares relevant intelligence with law enforcement, security, intelligence, regulatory and supervisory agencies for further investigation and prosecution.

It also researches emerging financial crime threats and works with domestic and international partners to strengthen Nigeria’s anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing systems.

It was established in 2004 and became operational in 2005 as a unit of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC). The NFIU Act 2018 later granted it autonomy and independence.

The NFIU serves as Nigeria’s central coordinating body for anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and counter-proliferation financing efforts.

World.title: Abia’s Positive Ranking: How fiscal discipline, visionary leadership put Abia on top, By Ferdinand Ekeoma
World.content:
In less than three years, Abia State was moved from the margins of national conversations to the very centre. The reason is simple: results.

The recently released “BudgIT 2026 State of States Report”, placed Abia among Nigeria’s top-performing states across fiscal performance, health, education, infrastructure, and governance. The numbers are not just impressive. They are historic.

The Numbers That Tell the Story

BudgIT’s data shows Abia leading on the metrics that matter most to development:

– 1st in total expenditure growth

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

– 1st in capital expenditure growth

– 1st in personnel expenditure growth

– 2nd in aggregate revenue growth

Earlier in the year, a separate BudgIT analysis ranked Abia number one in Nigeria for capital expenditure per resident, with ₦137,253 spent per person on infrastructure and development projects. That means more roads, more hospitals, more schools, and more jobs— per Abian.

The wins didn’t stop at spreadsheets. A few months ago, Abia emerged as the best-performing state in the South-east zone and clinched $500,000 USD at the 2025 Nigeria Governors’ Forum Primary Healthcare Leadership Challenge. That prize is a direct reward for visible improvements in primary healthcare delivery, immunisation coverage, and facility upgrades across the 17 LGAs.

The Otti Doctrine: Economics meets empathy

None of this happened by accident. At the heart of Abia’s turnaround is the Governor of Abia State, Dr. Alex Otti, OFR.

His pedigree matters. As a renowned economist, former group managing director of a bank, and one of Nigeria’s most respected financial minds, Governor Otti came into office with a clear understanding of two things: how money works, and how to make it work for people.

His vision has been consistent from day one: “A New Abia” — a state where government is efficient, transparent, and delivers tangible value to citizens.

That vision translated into three core pillars:

1. Fiscal responsibility

By blocking leakages, prioritising IGR, and aligning expenditure with impact, Abia moved from borrowing to build, to building from earnings. The result: top rankings in expenditure growth and revenue growth. Capital projects were no longer abandoned. Personnel were paid on time. The books were opened.

2. Infrastructure as an economic engine

From the reconstruction of strategic roads like Port Harcourt Road, Ohanku Road, Umuahia-Uzuakoli-Abiriba-Ohafia Road etc. to rural road networks, the administration treats infrastructure as more than concrete. It is commerce, jobs, and dignity. Spending ₦137,253 per resident on capital projects is the clearest proof that Abia is building for the next 50 years, not just the next election.

3. Human capital investment

The NGF $500,000 healthcare prize reflects deliberate investment in PHCs, health worker training, and drug supply chains. In education, there’s renewed focus on teacher recruitment and welfare, school rehabilitation, and skills acquisition to prepare Abia’s young people for a digital economy.

These achievements do more than win awards. They change perception.

For decades, Abia in national discourse was associated with decay in Aba, unpaid salaries, unhygienic environment, and infrastructural deficit. Today, “Abia” is associated with reform, growth, and possibility.

1. Investor confidence: When a state ranks 1st in capital expenditure and 2nd in revenue growth, investors pay attention. Businesses are more willing to site factories, shops, and tech hubs in Aba and Umuahia.

2. Diaspora pride: Millions of Abians at home and abroad now have a government they can point to with pride. That pride translates to remittances, partnerships, and advocacy.

3. Better services: Fiscal discipline means doctors are equipped, teachers are paid, and roads are motorable. Governance stops being an abstract idea and becomes water, streetlights, and classrooms.

The case for greater support

Giant strides require sustained momentum. Governor Otti’s economic background gave Abia the technical competence to reset its finances. But technical competence alone cannot finish the job.

Aba’s roads need to be protected from destruction. New PHCs need communities to use them and hold them accountable. Revenue targets need citizens and businesses to pay taxes willingly because they see what the money is doing.

This is the moment for Abians to double down.

Support the tax reforms. Support the ongoing audits. Support the contractors delivering quality work. Support the health and education policies, even when they demand patience.

When a government proves, with data, that it can spend ₦137,253 per person on development and still grow revenue, the rational response is not skepticism. It is partnership.

Governor Otti has shown that a banker’s discipline and an economist’s vision can be fused with a servant’s heart. Abia is no longer waiting to be discovered. Abia is leading.

The BudgIT 2026 report is not the finish line. It is the scoreboard at half-time.

If Abians intensify their support, hold the government accountable, and keep faith with the “New Abia” agenda, the next report will not just rank us first in growth. It will rank us first in prosperity.

A New Abia is here.

Ferdinand Ekeoma is Governor Alex Otti’s Special Adviser of Media and Publicity

World.title: Jigawa sets up task force to crack down on substandard private health institutions
World.content:
The Jigawa State Ministry of Health have launched a crackdown on illegal and substandard private health institutions across the state, warning that unaccredited institutions pose a direct threat to public safety.

Speaking at a stakeholders’ meeting with provosts of health training institutions in Dutse, the Chairman of the North-West Health Commissioners’ Forum and Jigawa State Commissioner of Health, Abdullahi Kainuwa, announced the inauguration of a specialised Taskforce Committee on Private Health Institutions.

Mr Kainuwa said the mandate of the committee is to enforce regulatory compliance and shut down any institution failing to meet established legal standards.

“The forum is well aware of the illegal operations and substandard conditions in many private health institutions, and this will no longer be tolerated,” Mr Kainuwa, a medical doctor, stated.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Adding that “any school that fails to meet the set standards will be closed down by the committee. This enforcement exercise would be executed concurrently across all seven North-West states, warning that any proprietor (s) leaving Jigawa to neighbouring states to set up the institutions will not be spared.”

The Commissioner expressed alarm over the egregious conditions observed in several unaccredited schools, noting that some operate without permanent structures, qualified full-time faculty, proper laboratories, or basic clinical training equipment.

While acknowledging the vital role of private enterprise in supplementing public educational capacity, Mr Kainuwa stated that academic and professional rigour cannot be compromised when human lives are at stake.

“We recognise that the government alone cannot absorb every candidate, and there is a legitimate need for private institutions. However, any institution operating as a health school must truly earn that title,” he remarked.

Mr Kainuwa announced that sanctions would extend beyond the schools to corrupt or negligent regulators.

“We will query any regulatory agency that grants approvals without verifying facilities, faculty, and equipment on the ground. Anyone found culpable in issuing compromised licenses will lose their job.”

The surge of unregulated Health Institutions in Nigeria

Mr Kainuwa acknowledged that tens of thousands of secondary school graduates compete annually for limited slots in accredited public universities, nursing schools, and colleges of health technology.

This deficit has fueled a rapid proliferation of private health training facilities—many operating as unregistered, commercial enterprises lacking affiliation with regulatory bodies like the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN) or the Community Health Practitioners Registration Board of Nigeria (CHPRBN).

He said unregulated schools produced inadequately trained health workers, who are subsequently deployed into clinics, maternity homes, and pharmacies, directly contributing to misdiagnoses, medical errors, and compromised patient outcomes.

He said the northeastern states under the North-West Health Commissioners’ Forum task force represent a unified policy shift toward systemic oversight and public safety.

In his remarks, the chairperson of the Taskforce and technical adviser to the governor on health, Isa Surajo, announced the government’s pre-notice regarding the assignment and strategy for implementing the Taskforce’s activities.

This approach ensures that justice and fairness are upheld not only for schools, but also for parents and the wider community.

“As the guardian of the people, the government is committed to safeguarding dignity, maintaining trust, and ensuring fairness across all stakeholders in Jigawa State’s healthcare sector”, Mr Surajo said.

World.title: Amokachi, Adepoju lead legends as Afreximbank, TopTier unveil initiative to celebrate Nigeria’s golden generation
World.content:
The African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), through its Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) programme, and TopTier Sports Management have announced plans for a landmark Legends Football Match to celebrate Nigeria’s celebrated mid-1990s football generation.

The match, scheduled for 8 November at the Mobolaji Johnson Arena, Onikan Lagos, will form part of the CANEX WKND 2026 programme and bring together football icons from Nigeria, Africa and beyond.

The event will mark 30 years since Nigeria’s historic 1996 Atlanta Olympic triumph, while also celebrating the generation that won the 1994 Africa Cup of Nations and represented Nigeria at the 1994 FIFA World Cup.

Temwa Gondwe, Director of Creatives and Diaspora at Afreximbank, said the initiative was designed to celebrate the achievements of a generation that helped reshape perceptions of African football while creating new conversations around the future of sports and the creative economy.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The 1996 Super Eagles did more than win Olympic gold; they re-wrote the global narrative, proving to the world that African talent is an unstoppable force,” Mr Gondwe said.

He said the Legends Game would demonstrate the connection between sports, entertainment and culture while providing “a strategic and formidable platform to discuss the future commercialisation and empowerment of African athletes and creatives globally.”

Chichi Nwoko, Founder and CEO of TopTier Sports Management and What Media Group, said the initiative was both a tribute to the players and an opportunity to examine how athletes can be better supported during and after their careers.

“Thirty years ago, a generation of Nigerian footballers showed the world what African talent was capable of. The Legends Football Game is our way of saying thank you to them, and our chance to ask harder questions: what are we building for this generation and the next?” Ms Nwoko said.

“We want to build the infrastructure that lets African athletes turn a playing career into a lasting one, on and off the field; this is a huge gap that must be addressed. That’s what this partnership with Afreximbank seeks to achieve.”

Amokachi seeks stronger welfare for legends

The significance of the initiative was echoed by former Super Eagles striker Daniel Amokachi, one of the players who featured prominently for Nigeria during the period being celebrated.

Speaking after the unveiling at the Lagos Continental Hotel, Amokachi said the Legends Game would celebrate the 1994-96 generation and provide an opportunity to reflect on the contributions of players who helped put Nigerian football on the global map.

“Afreximbank and TopTier Sports Management have come up with a Legends Game to celebrate the 1994-96 generation of footballers in Nigeria and across the continent,” he said.

But for Amokachi, the occasion should go beyond nostalgia.

He appealed to corporate organisations to use their corporate social responsibility programmes to establish sustainable welfare initiatives for former footballers and other athletes.

“The corporate social responsibility of having a pension scheme for footballers, not only footballers but athletes generally, is something that is done everywhere in the world,” he said.

“Ninety-nine per cent of my colleagues from my generation are struggling. Only a few of us are doing a bit well, and if we had that kind of support, it would definitely go a long way.”

Amokachi said the support of the media, corporate bodies and sponsors would be crucial to making the November event successful.

“There are a lot of faces missing today because this is a Nigerian and African legends’ event. We need everybody to come on board to help make this a very memorable first week of November,” he said.

Emotional reunion for golden generation

The announcement produced a memorable reunion at the Lagos Continental Hotel, where Amokachi was joined by several other members of Nigeria’s celebrated football generation, including Mutiu Adepoju, Garba Lawal, Alloy Agu, Ben Iroha, Finidi George and Victor Ikpeba.

The gathering quickly turned into an emotional trip down memory lane as the former internationals exchanged stories, laughed over old dressing-room experiences and remembered the teams and moments that defined one of the most successful periods in Nigerian football.

The 1994 team won Nigeria’s second Africa Cup of Nations title in Tunisia before reaching the round of 16 at the 1994 FIFA World Cup in the United States.

Two years later, Nigeria’s Olympic team, built around many of the same players, stunned the football world in Atlanta by winning the men’s football gold medal after defeating Mexico, Brazil and Argentina during the knockout stages.

The former players at the Lagos gathering commended the initiative and emphasised the need for more programmes that recognise their generation and provide meaningful support for Nigeria’s sporting legends.

Bet9ja named headline sponsor

Bet9ja has been unveiled as the headline sponsor of the Legends Football Match, while the organisers have called on more corporate bodies to come on board and support the initiative.

The organisers said the match would form part of CANEX WKND 2026, Afreximbank’s platform for advancing Africa’s creative and cultural industries.

They added that the event would help position Lagos as a leading destination for sports, entertainment and creative activities while attracting football fans, creatives, media organisations and international visitors.

World.title: 2027: Obi supporters won’t trust INEC with votes —  Aisha Yesufu
World.content:
By Sekinat Osundiji

Political activist and Nigeria Democratic Congress member, Aisha Yesufu, has said supporters of the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, will not rely solely on electoral institutions to protect their votes in the 2027 presidential election.

Yesufu said Obi’s supporters would deploy representatives to polling units and monitor the movement of election materials and results from polling units through the various collation centres to Abuja.

She stated this during an interview on Arise News, where she discussed Obi’s chances in the 2027 presidential election and lessons from the 2023 election.

According to her, the experience of the 2023 election had made it necessary for voters and political groups to take a more active role in protecting their votes.

“Yes, we are going to have people at every polling unit to protect the votes,” Yesufu said.

She said the plan was to monitor the results at every stage of the collation process, from the polling unit to the ward, local government and state levels, until the final declaration in Abuja.

“No result sheet will leave our sight. We will follow the results from the polling units all the way to Abuja,” she said.

Yesufu said the strategy was aimed at ensuring that the results eventually declared reflected the votes cast by Nigerians.

She further stated that she had “zero trust” in INEC, security agencies and the judiciary, insisting that citizens could not afford to leave the protection of their votes entirely to institutions.

According to her, the 2027 election would therefore require greater grassroots mobilisation, with supporters concentrating on polling units rather than relying only on political rallies and campaigns.

Speaking on the recent incident in Benue State, where Obi’s movement was reportedly obstructed, Yesufu defended the former Anambra State governor’s decision not to engage those who blocked his convoy.

She argued that Obi had other engagements to attend that day and should not allow what she described as “miscreants” to dictate his movements.

Yesufu also expressed confidence that Obi could win the 2027 election, saying Nigerians were now more concerned about the impact of economic hardship and insecurity on their daily lives.

She criticised the administration of President Bola Tinubu, describing it as a “colossal failure” and arguing that the government’s claims about improved macroeconomic indicators had not translated into better living conditions for ordinary Nigerians.

According to her, Nigerians were dealing with rising costs, insecurity and declining purchasing power, adding that economic policies should ultimately be measured by their impact on citizens.

Yesufu said she believed Obi had an advantage because, in her view, voters were increasingly focused on competence, character and capacity rather than religious considerations.

She also expressed confidence that Obi would win Lagos again in 2027 and make significant gains across other parts of the country.

Yesufu, who said she was not seeking an elective position, stated that her focus was on mobilising supporters for the 2027 presidential election and ensuring that votes were protected.

She said the experience of 2023 had shown that supporters needed to be more organised at the grassroots if they wanted the votes of Nigerians to determine the final outcome of the election.

World.title: Dangote Refinery IPO: Global leaders rally behind plan to democratise Africa’s industrial wealth
World.content:
Aliko Dangote

By Udeme Akpan, Energy Editor

The proposed initial public offering of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has drawn strong backing from prominent African and international leaders, who say opening the industrial giant to wider ownership could mark a new phase in African wealth creation, industrialisation and economic sovereignty.

The leaders, speaking at the 2026 ADF Africa Diaspora Leadership Programme Young Global Leaders Convening in Lagos, yesterday, said the refinery had already demonstrated Africa’s capacity to build at global scale, while its proposed IPO could allow ordinary Africans, pension funds, institutional investors and the diaspora to participate directly in the wealth created by one of the continent’s biggest industrial investments. President and Chief Executive, Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, said the philosophy behind the IPO was to extend the prosperity created by the refinery beyond its promoters and give ordinary Africans an opportunity to become owners.

“I want drivers, cooks, the woman selling food on the streets of Ghana, Rwanda and South Africa to invest so they can share in this prosperity. We are doing the IPO to pass this prosperity to Africans,” Dangote said during a fireside chat. “I am wealthy, not rich. A wealthy man creates wealth, while a rich man makes money and keeps it for himself. “What keeps me going is that we must industrialise Africa. There is no amount of hurdle that will stop us. If you put a brick wall in front of me, I will make a hole and pass through.” He expressed confidence that the refinery could eventually become Africa’s largest company by size and profitability, drawing parallels with global corporations such as Amazon, Microsoft, Tesla and Alibaba, which grew substantially after entering the public markets.

“By the grace of God, this refinery will be the largest company in Africa by size and profitability,” he said. “Our job is to derisk Africa, encourage more investors, create jobs and create more opportunities. That is how we will transform Africa,” Dangote said. Former United States Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs and CoChair of The Africa Center, Amb. Jendayi Frazer, said: “The refinery connects us all through the proposed IPO that creates broader ownership. “It can broaden participation in the value created by African industry. It can connect investment with African production to scale with African institutions, pension funds, savers, individual investors, including the African diaspora coming into this, owning a stake in Africa’s growth.” Frazer said the refinery had already “changed the equation” for Africa, with implications extending far beyond petroleum production into the continent’s geopolitical standing.

“Economic power is not only what a country possesses, it’s what it can create, process, finance, transport and sell. Supply chains, energy systems and capital markets shape sovereignty,” she said. Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu of Lagos State, similarly called for a new model of African industrial ownership in which ordinary citizens, institutional investors and diaspora capital hold stakes in the continent’s strategic assets.

“The next frontier of African scale is not another giant. It is a thousand ordinary owners: the teacher in Enugu, the nurse in New Jersey and the pension fund in Nairobi, each holding a piece of the strategic assets of their own continent. “Mr Dangote did not build a refinery. He built a country around a refinery, and then he built the refinery. There was no port that could receive the equipment, so he built a jetty. There was not enough power, so he built a power plant.”

Noting that the project survived enormous construction challenges, the COVID 19 pandemic and severe currency depreciation, Sanwo Olu recalled predictions that it would never become operational. World.title: The 9/11 that never happened: What Britain saved the world from
World.content:
…and What Nigeria Must Learn

By Jide Ajani

TWENTY-FIVE years after the planes struck America, the most frightening part of 9/11 may not be what the terrorists achieved, but what they originally intended to achieve – and what intelligence agencies have since learned to prevent. Twenty-five years ago, the world watched in disbelief as four commercial aircraft became weapons of mass destruction. Two disappeared into the towers of the World Trade Centre. Another tore into the Pentagon.

The fourth came down in a Pennsylvania field after its passengers fought back. Nearly 3,000 people died. But that was not the end of the story. In some ways, it was not even the most frightening part. Because the 9/11 that happened was, in important respects, a reduced version of the 9/11 that Khalid Sheikh Mohammed (KSM) and his associates had imagined. Evil reigned in their hearts.

The plot was much bigger

When Vanguard wrote about 9/11 fifteen years ago, to mark the tenth anniversary, what was most fascinating was the audacity of the original conspiracy. The 9/11 Commission documented how KSM’s thinking had evolved from the earlier Bojinka Plot, in which his nephew, Ramzi Yousef, and others had contemplated the destruction of multiple aircraft. The idea that eventually emerged was chilling in its simplicity: if an aircraft could be turned into a bomb, why bother planting a bomb inside it? Hijack the aircraft. Control the aircraft.

Fly the aircraft into the target. The terrorists’ imagination had moved from destroying an aeroplane to weaponising it. And KSM’s original vision went considerably beyond the four aircraft eventually hijacked on September 11. The intended targets included, but were never limited to multiple American landmarks and institutions. The plan envisaged simultaneous attacks on an extraordinary scale. The point is worth remembering in 2026 because terrorism rarely begins with the operation that eventually reaches the headlines.Terrorists experiment. They test vulnerabilities. They study security. They improvise. They learn from failure. And they try again. The Director General of Nigeria’s Department of State Services (DSS), Tosin Ajayi insists that “is why intelligence matters.” The plots we never heard about There is another side to the 9/11 story that deserves greater attention on its 25th anniversary. The attacks we remember are the attacks that succeeded. But the history of counterterrorism is also a history of attacks that never happened. In Nigeria, for instance, the DSS continues to intercept communications and foil plots that would have been very devastating to the peace of the country.

But the reports that grab the headlines are always about the terrorists who succeed. The greatest success can produce the least visible evidence.

There is no memorial to a passenger who was never killed. There is no photograph of the aircraft that never exploded. There is no anniversary for the family that was never bereaved. That is the strange mathematics of intelligence. The greatest success can produce the least visible evidence. The 2006 liquid-bomb plot in Britain is one of the clearest examples. British intelligence and law-enforcement agencies, working closely with American counterparts, uncovered an al-Qaedalinked conspiracy to destroy several transatlantic passenger aircraft with liquid explosives. The plot was sufficiently advanced to demonstrate the terrifying vulnerability of civil aviation. The arrests in Britain prevented the conspirators from carrying out what could have become one of the worst aviation atrocities since 9/11. And here lies the point that should never be lost in the history. Thousands of people may have lived because intelligence officers connected pieces of information before the terrorists could connect the pieces of their own plan.

That is intelligence at its finest: Not revenge. Not retaliation. Prevention. (Vanguard will provide details of that security intervention next week)

The liquid that changed aviation

The legacy of that plot remains visible every time an airline passenger is forced to think twice about carrying a bottle of liquid through airport security. What passengers sometimes regard as an annoying restriction has its roots in a very real vulnerability exposed by the 2006 conspiracy. The lesson was brutally simple: terrorists had moved beyond conventional explosives and were looking for ways to disguise components of a weapon as ordinary objects. Security consequently had to move ahead of the threat. That principle is as relevant today as it was then. Because the terrorist who can exploit yesterday’s security system is already planning tomorrow’s attack.

The British lesson

The British success was not simply about having clever intelligence officers. It was about a system capable of turning fragments into a picture. It involved surveillance. Human intelligence. Communications intelligence. International cooperation. Police work. Analysis. And, crucially, information-sharing. The Americans had pieces of the puzzle. The British had pieces. The threat crossed the Atlantic. So did the intelligence. This is perhaps the most important lesson for Nigeria.

Nigeria must learn before the next attack

Nigeria has its own long and painful counterterrorism experience. Boko Haram has been followed by ISWAP’s evolution into a sophisticated regional threat. Kidnapping networks, bandit groups, arms traffickers and terrorist organisations increasingly exploit the same porous spaces, criminal economies and communication technologies. The threat is no longer confined neatly to one forest, one state or one national border.

A recent UN assessment noted that ISWAP has expanded its use of drones and exploited commercial channels to acquire components, while terrorist logistics continue to exploit routes running through Libya, Sudan, Chad, Cameroon, Niger and Nigeria. That should worry every intelligence professional. Because the next great terrorist vulnerability may not look like the last one.

The war must move from reaction to anticipation

Nigeria has made progress in this direction. In 2026, the Federal Government said its security response increasingly rests on intelligence gathering, surveillance, community engagement and inter-agency coordination. It has also strengthened its counterterrorism relationship with the United States, including intelligence-sharing and capacity-building. That is encouraging. But the test is whether the intelligence architecture can consistently anticipate rather than merely react.

World.title: Ndigbo are very nice people — Tinubu’s wife
World.content:
Remi Tinubu

By Nwabueze Okonkwo

Nigeria’s first lady and wife of President Bola Tinubu, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, has identified Ndigbo as very nice set of people worthy of partnering with in all it’s ramifications.

Mrs. Tinubu who made the observation at Dr. Alex Ekwueme Square in Awka, Anambra State capital during her one-day official visit to the state and civic reception, shortly after she was conferred with a Chieftaincy title of “Ugoeze Anambra” (Royal Eagle), by the state council of traditional rules led by its Chairman, Igwe Chidubem Iweka III of Obosi Kingdom, said she was highly impressed with the warm reception accorded her by Anambra people and disclosed that she would come back to the state to show her appreciation in due course.

Mrs. Tinubu who had earlier commissioned a Technological Centre at the Federal Polytechnic, Oko in Orumba South Local Government Area of the state, described Governor Chukwuma Soludo’s administration as very superb, adding that he has done so much so that he has become the talk of the country in terms of his quality leadership.

She also praised Soludo’s wife, Nonye for empowering as much as 5,000 indigents in the state, adding that she would give N100,000 to each of the beneficiaries to augment Mrs. Soludo’s empowerment scheme.

According to her, “I didn’t come here for campaign but as a Nigerian. I will come back in due course because Ndigbo are very nice people and trustworthy”.

She disclosed that she was in Anambra State and other states in the South-East not for political campaigns but as a Nigerian, stressing that she would return to the region for campaign when the time comes.

She said the visit was aimed at fostering unity among Nigerians and supporting citizens, regardless of their political affiliations or geographical locations.

“I am not in the state for political campaign but as a united country, men and women, the citizens must be their brothers’ keepers wherever they are,” she stated.

World.title: Kidney crisis: Rising cases, crushing treatment costs threaten Nigerians
World.content:
By Chioma Obinna

FOR more than 150 kidney patients gathered under canopies in Enugu, and thousands of others across the country, the struggle goes beyond the pain of a failing organ. It is a daily battle to raise the money needed to stay alive. Recently, videos and pictures of some of the patients in Enugu surfaced on social media, drawing.

Recently, videos and pictures of some of the patients in Enugu surfaced on social media, drawing public attention to their plight. Many reportedly arrived in wheelchairs, while others were visibly weakened, with swollen legs, faces and abdomens.

Many of the patients are living with end-stage kidney disease, a stage at which kidney replacement therapy, including dialysis or transplantation, may be required to sustain life. But how many of them can afford the lifesaving treatment? Sadly, kidney disease respects neither age nor social status. Adults and children were among those waiting for assistance to continue treatment.

According to Consultant Nephrologist, Dr Abdulwasiu Busari, about 90 per cent of Nigerian patients discontinue dialysis within one year, largely because of the cost. Their plight puts a human face on Nigeria’s kidney-care crisis, as experts raise concerns about severe kidney disease affecting Nigerians during their productive years, while the cost of treatment leaves many unable to sustain care. The true scale of kidney disease in Nigeria remains difficult to quantify because the country has no current, nationally representative data establishing the overall burden of kidney disease. Available Nigerian studies have produced widely varying prevalence estimates because of differences in populations, locations and diagnostic methods.

A 2025 review reported chronic kidney disease estimates generally ranging from 10 to 19 per cent among adults across studies, while an earlier systematic review found estimates ranging from 2.5 to 26 per cent. These figures should not be interpreted as a definitive national prevalence.

Globally, the World Health Organisation estimates that 674 million people are living with chronic kidney disease, with most affected people in low- and middle-income countries. But behind the statistics are patients whose survival may depend on whether they can raise enough money for their next dialysis session. One of those trying to keep them alive is Emmanuel Onyeka Okoh, popularly known as “Okwulora”, a philanthropist who has been supporting kidney patients in Enugu. In one of the widely circulated videos, Okoh said: “It is sad. Look at them. They are hopeless and helpless and some of them, if they don’t get dialysis, might not even see the next day.”

He said he had sold personal property to support patients and had spent about N15 million at Park Lane Hospital, Enugu, this year alone, to settle bills and help patients continue treatment. A ccording to him, some patients wait for months, and in some cases up to a year, for assistance, while others die because they cannot raise enough money to continue dialysis. H e said his intervention usually covers dialysis for one or two months, after which patients are again left to find money for treatment. “My greatest worry was the number of children in the age bracket of eight to 10 years that have been brought down by kidney problems,” Okoh said. “These children of six to 10 years have not taken alcohol before. They have not smoked before. Yet, their future is hanging and bleak due to this illness.” He said the increasing number of patients needing assistance had become emotionally and financially exhausting. “I’m already tired,” he said, reflecting the enormous burden of trying to keep vulnerable patients on treatment through personal fundraising.

Kidney disease now attacking productive Nigerians

A Consultant Nephrologist at the Federal Medical Centre, Ebute Metta, Dr Danladi Nmadu, said most Nigerian patients with severe kidney impairment or those receiving dialysis are between 40 and 60 years old. “In most developed countries, kidney disease tends to accumulate in people in their 60s and above, while in Nigeria most patients that we have on dialysis or have severe kidney impairment are between the ages of 40 and 60,” he said. According to Nmadu, the pattern has serious economic consequences because the disease is affecting Nigerians during their productive years. One reason for the late presentation, he said, is that kidney disease can remain silent for a long time. “The kidneys are very resilient organs. They don’t show signs until they are almost completely shut down,” he explained. As a result, many Nigerians only seek medical attention when their kidney function has fallen drastically. “If we catch them early, there are things we can do to stop or slow down the progression such that these patients do not develop kidney failure,” Nmadu said. He blamed poor health-seeking behaviour partly for the late presentation, noting that many Nigerians consider themselves healthy simply because they do not feel sick. “Most young people don’t think they should go to the hospital. A lot of times when they present, it’s too late,” he said.

N150,000 weekly dialysis burden

For those who develop end-stage kidney disease, dialysis can become an unbearable financial burden. Nmadu said dialysis typically costs about N50,000 per session, while many patients require two or three sessions every week. “That means N150,000 every week. Most individuals cannot afford that,” he said. Busari said the financial burden becomes even greater when the additional costs associated with dialysis are taken into account. According to him, apart from the dialysis session itself, patients also have to pay for investigations, erythropoietin and iron treatment, among other services. “The average cost of a single session of haemodialysis now is N50,000. A patient will need two or three sessions per week. But apart from dialysis itself, there are other things that may cost money, such as investigations, erythropoietin and iron treatment,” Busari explained. He estimated that the overall cost could amount to about N600,000 monthly for a patient receiving regular dialysis.

The consequences can be fatal

Nmadu said findings from their practice suggest that more than 70 per cent of patients requiring dialysis die within two years, stressing that inability to afford regular treatment is a major contributor to poor survival. Busari, in a chat with Vanguard, said the financial burden also explains why many patients are unable to remain on dialysis for long.

World.title: Presidency, APC battle Obi over 2023 victory claim
World.content:
***Obi’s fat on ambition, drunk on political arrogance — PRESIDENCY

***He has reached the end, should prepare for another loss — APC

***None of Tinubu’s challengers has 10% of his qualities — YARI

By Clifford Ndujihe, Henry Umoru Johnbosco Agbakwuru Ayobami Okerinde & Olayinka Ajayi

LAGOS — The ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, yesterday, took the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Mr. Peter Obi to task over his claim that he won the 2023 presidential poll and will only concede in 2027 if the exercise was credible.

Obi, in an interview on Arise News where he unveiled a radical governance blueprint aimed at rescuing the nation from economic drift, infrastructural decay, and systemic insecurity, slammed President Bola Tinubu over handling of N16 trillion fuel savings, describing his fiscal spending as “reckless” and completely out of touch with the agonising realities of everyday Nigerians.

Obi ran the 2023 presidential contest on the platform of the Labour Party, LP, and came third behind Tinubu and Atiku Abubakar, according to official results declared by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC.

Answering a question on the 2023 election, the former Anambra State governor maintained that he won the poll, saying those who conducted the poll knew what happened.

His words: “I did, and I will maintain that as long as I live that I won the 2023 election. Those who conducted it know the records; they know why there was a glitch and what happened.”

Obi has reached the end, should prepare for another loss — APC

Picking holes in Obi’s claims, National Chairman of the APC, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, who spoke through his Special Adviser on Media and Information Strategy, Abimbola Tooki, said there was no way Obi could have won the 2023 election.

His words: “How can he say that he won the 2023 poll? How did he win it? Where is the result? He had no agents in many states of the North. Why didn’t the INEC declare him as winner? He should go and prepare for another imminent loss in 2027.”

On Obi’s questioning of the impact of N16 trillion fuel subsidy savings, Tooki said: “He should ask state governors what they were getting as federal allocation before President Tinubu came and what they are getting now. He should check the last time we had fuel queues in Nigeria. When was the last time we had a strike? He should check if students in tertiary institutions are not receiving their NELFUND loans. Does he want the N16 trillion to be transported to his bedroom?”

Obi’s fat on ambition, drunk on political arrogance — Presidency

In like manner, the Presidency accused Obi of hallucinating and wallowing in a political fantasy land.

Reacting to Obi’s 2023 victory claims, the Presidency, through the Special Adviser to President Tinubu on Media and Public Communications, Mr. Sunday Dare said: “Mr. Obi is fat on ambition but drunk on political arrogance.

“Peter Obi wallows freely in a political fantasy land. To still insist he won the presidential election after the country’s highest court, the Supreme Court, delivered a final judgment is clear hallucination.

“Who imbued him with the power to concede or not? He lacks such power. Only the Nigerian people have the power of the votes. And in 2027, they will deliver their votes massively for President Tinubu, leaving no room for the kind of antics Obi is already front-loading.”

None of Tinubu’s challengers has 10% of his qualities — Yari

This was as Senator Abdulaziz Yari, Director-Deneral (DG) of the APC presidential campaign council, said none of those contesting against President Tinubu in the 2027 election matches him in terms of quality and competence.

The senator representing Zamfara west spoke on Wednesday while addressing members of the Nigerian Union of Road Transport Workers, NURTW, in Gusau, Zamfara State capital, where he canvassed support for Tinubu’s re-election bid.

Addressing the NURTW members, the senator said the other presidential candidates could not match Tinubu.

“That is how politics is. When you put all the aspirants contesting against Bola Tinubu on a scale, I don’t think the scale would even accept them,” said Yari, who spoke in Hausa.

“We all know that none of the aspirants contesting against him are on his level when it comes to merit and quality; we don’t think any of them have even 10 per cent of what Bola Tinubu possesses.”

The senator acknowledged that the presidential candidates had the right to contest but said the APC will work to secure victory in 2027.

No proxy rule, 4 years enough for total reform — Obi

In the hard-hitting interview, Obi, who said he did not reject an offer to serve as running mate to Atiku Abubakar, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, in the 2027 elections because no such proposal was made, set a sharp contrast to conventional governance in Nigeria.

He declared that his administration would be characterized by direct presidential accountability, promising to take personal responsibility for the success or failure of his cabinet. He emphasized that he would dismantle the culture of running the presidency through influential cliques or undeclared power brokers.

“I will be in charge and I will not run the government by proxy. I will be answerable to the people,” Obi vowed.

Dismissing the familiar political narrative that a single four-year term is insufficient to fix Nigeria’s multi-layered woes, the NDC candidate insisted he would not seek an extra day in office beyond his first mandate. He argued that focus and structural clarity are what the nation lacks, rather than time.

“I will not spend one extra day. Four years is enough to engender change and I did it as Governor of Anambra State,” he said. He added that the key to achieving results within a single term would be the selection of priorities, appointment of qualified and credible officials, and effective teamwork.

On the economic policies of President Tinubu, he mounted a fierce critique of the current administration’s removal of the fuel subsidy. While agreeing that the old subsidy regime was riddled with corruption, he slammed the government for borrowing more money while failing to show any tangible relief from the trillions saved from the policy.

The NDC presidential candidate insisted that the core problem was not necessarily removal of the subsidy itself, but rather the total failure to deploy the resulting savings productively. He noted that the Federal Government itself disclosed that the removal of subsidy generated about N15.8 trillion, a figure he said informed his repeated reference to approximately N16 trillion.

“The subsidy regime in Nigeria was enmeshed with corruption and criminality. I have said clearly that I will remove subsidy and fight corruption and criminality. It is only when you remove it that you will know exactly whether we have a subsidy or not. I believe that if you remove corruption, there might not be subsidy. That’s my belief,” Obi stated.

He further lamented the high cost of living triggered by premium motor spirit pricing, noting that domestic refining should protect citizens from international market shocks. “I believe that the price of petroleum products today is high. We are an oil-producing country, which means that if we can do regular supply of crude to our local refineries, working with them competitively to refine for domestic consumption, the prices can come down.”

Obi explained that global economic leaders use targeted subsidies to stimulate wealth rather than consumption, drawing a direct parallel with Asian economic policies.

“There are things you give subsidies for. I’ll give you an example. This is why I always compare countries. When I do, people say, ‘Oh, it’s another country’. We only go to school to learn. You go to those who have done it well to learn. If you go to Indonesia today, the interest rate is about 15 per cent. But the interest rate to SMEs, small businesses, is between three and five per cent. Maximum of six per cent. That’s subsidy. You’re giving it to where it is productive, not where it’s not productive. We’re going to make sure that we do the right thing that will make the country productive and create wealth, opportunities and employment, a win-win. But what we’re having today is that we’ve impoverished ourselves because we removed subsidy and no gain is seen. Because the money we say we have borrowed, we borrowed more.”

Defending his claims regarding the N16 trillion savings, Obi challenged the presidency to provide a transparent audit of the funds. “It’s actually the government who said that the subsidy they removed produced N15.8 trillion. Can you look at that and show the effect of this?”

He argued that these resources could have been deployed to address critical deficiencies in healthcare and other vital social sectors, citing the nation’s severe lack of oncological infrastructure as an example of misplaced national priorities.

“When I talk about waste, people say, ‘Ah, we have a problem now with the issue of explosion in cancer.’ People are dying of cancer. To do a cancer centre will cost you about N4 billion to N5 billion. We have less than 10 cancer centres. And to add just 25, you need to spend about N100 billion. That’s what our president used to buy a plane. A jet. And we saved N16 trillion,” Obi said.

Speaking on the contentious debate over subsidy restoration, where other opposition front-runners like Atiku Abubakar, have promised to restore the subsidy regime, Obi maintained that his approach would be fundamentally different. He stated that he would not return to the old corrupt framework but would instead redirect those funds into localized agricultural and industrial subsidies that would directly transform the northern region.

“I know the problems in the northern part. I will deal with the issue of poverty the way it has not been dealt with before, and in a non-corrupt way, where they will see it. The North has an asset. Nobody in this country, none of us, none of the areas, can say they have what the North has. I will deal with that asset, and that asset is agriculture. We’ll invest in it. We’ll give the subsidy to it. We will ensure that it will take all those poor people, almajirai, back to education, support them in different areas.”

He promised to resuscitate the collapsed industrial sectors of northern commercial hubs to curb rising unemployment and insecurity. “We will make sure we invest in health, in skills, and support them. I’ll make sure that I bring back all those manufacturing activities that have been lost. Today, if you go to Kano, there are factories that are gone. I will deal with the North in such a way that they will see it. And this fuel you’re talking about, we will moderate the price all over Nigeria. It’s not only affecting them.”

On President Tinubu’s administration so far, Obi noted that government had failed to meet the expectations of Nigerians, describing its leadership and expenditure as reckless. “I think you should ask the people. But if you ask me, they’ve not done well. They’ve been a bit reckless in what they’re doing.”

Asked whether he believed President Tinubu was fully in charge of the day-to-day running of the state, Obi replied: “At times, I believe he’s not in charge. Because if he’s in charge, he will even be explaining to the people. That’s what I’m talking about, which is capacity. I will be in charge. Nobody will talk for Peter. Because I’m the one that’s elected. I’ll be answerable to the people. And for every penny, I’ll be answerable to the people.”

Obi also promised a shift in infrastructural strategy by halting what he described as unnecessary new government construction projects, focusing instead on fixing existing, dilapidated national assets. “We will not build new roads until we fix the existing ones,” he maintained.

On national security, the NDC candidate took a hardline stance against the rising wave of kidnapping and banditry across the country. To break the economic life cycle of organized crime, Obi categorically rejected the payment of ransoms to criminal groups, promising instead to aggressively bolster state tactical intelligence, improve security welfare, and ensure decisive military responses.

Addressing potential post-election outcomes and electoral integrity, Obi reiterated his firm stance that he won the controversial 2023 presidential election. While expressing a willingness to accept the outcome of the upcoming January ballot, he stated that his compliance is strictly dependent on transparency, revealing an independent plan to deploy cutting-edge technology to prevent systemic manipulation.

“I will concede defeat if the process is free, fair and credible,” Obi asserted. He disclosed that his campaign organization is establishing an independent, parallel electoral result transmission network that will ensure polling-unit results are sent in real time directly to a central citizen-led Situation Room, bypassing potential institutional bottlenecks

Obi also highlighted his educational background, listing Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Columbia and Kellogg among institutions he had attended.

“You can look at our qualification in terms of training. I’ve been to the best schools from all over the world, from Oxford to Cambridge, Harvard, Columbia, and Kellogg, and I’ve been everywhere, and every certificate I’m showing you is the way it is. If they find anyone wrong, I will drop from the race,” he said.

He also criticised the lack of youth representation in Nigeria’s presidency, noting that no person born after 1960 had served as president since independence.

“Since 1960, nobody born outside 1960 has been president of Nigeria. This is 66 years of independence; no other country in the world has had this happen to, and they tell youths they’re the leaders of tomorrow,” Obi said.

Asked whether he would step down for Atiku or accept the vice-presidential slot if an alliance was reached, Obi said the discussion had gone beyond individual candidates.

“I’m a candidate, yes. So, my leader, Atiku, is candidate of another party. I am a candidate for another party. So, you are talking about two parties coming together; it is no longer him or me,” Obi said.

Obi said any potential alliance must involve the political parties rather than be reduced to negotiations between individuals.

“All those parties have candidates. So, it is a discussion. It is no longer me, as Peter is talking. It is like a situation where two corporations are trying to come together. It is no longer something the two CEOs go to a drink and say we are going to work together. They need to look at how to bring these two corporations together,” he said.

When told he had previously said he would not accept the vice-presidential position from any candidate, Obi denied rejecting any such offer.

“I don’t know where that was said. I wasn’t even in a position where that was being offered, and I refused,” he said.

Obi was Atiku’s running mate in the 2019 presidential election. However, they contested the 2023 election on different party platforms, with Obi running on the LP platform and Atiku on the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP platform.

I’ll retain Tinubu’s naira float policy if I’m elected

However, Obi said he would retain the free floating exchange rate policy of theTinubu administration, if elected

A free-floating exchange rate occurs when a government allows the exchange rate to be determined purely by market forces and there is no attempt to ask the central bank to influence the external value of the exchange rate.

Asked to name one policy of the Tinubu administration he would keep if he became president, he said: “Yes. One. It’s floating of the naira. I’m not going to defend it, but I’m going to put productivity to work to make it more valuable to the people,” he said.

The Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, introduced a “willing buyer, willing seller” model on June 14, 2023, in a major reform that unified the country’s multiple foreign exchange market segments.

The naira depreciated sharply following the reform, with the exchange rate at the investors’ and exporters’ window closing at N770.88 kobo per dollar at the end of June 2023, compared with N460 at the end of December 2022, according to CBN data and currently hovering at N1385 to N1407 per dollar.

World.title: Self-care key to curbing Nigeria’s rising disease burden — Experts
World.content:
… Say hospitals can’t cope if Nigerians ignore prevention, rational drug use

By Chioma Obinna

As Nigeria battles a growing burden of chronic and non-communicable diseases, health experts have called for an urgent shift from hospital-centred healthcare to preventive self-care, warning that the country’s health system and household finances cannot withstand the rising cost of treating preventable illnesses.

The wellness experts spoke at the third edition of the D’Bio Wellness and Self-Care Summit in Lagos, where stakeholders stressed that individuals, families, pharmacists, healthcare professionals, communities and policymakers must work together to prevent disease and reduce pressure on hospitals.

Delivering the keynote address, Pharm. Olayinka Subair said the country must move from sickness care to self-care, arguing that many health outcomes are determined long before a patient reaches the consulting room.

According to him, self-care rests on five foundations, nutrition, physical activity, mental health, rational use of medicines and risk avoidance. “What you eat, how you move, how you manage stress, how you use drugs, supplements and services wisely, and how you avoid risks like smoking, unsafe practices or skipping screening” are central to health, he said.

Subair warned that failure to prioritise prevention would continue to expose Nigerians to avoidable illnesses and enormous treatment costs.

He said: “An approach that empowers people, reduces preventable complications and eases the burden on healthcare services is critical. When we support self-care intelligently, we improve outcomes, reduce the cost of treatment and strengthen the community.”

He noted that Nigeria’s primary healthcare system was already under pressure while many patients struggle to access care and afford prescribed treatment. “We are going to flip the discussion today from the hospital to you, to me, and focus on how we help ourselves,” he said.

Subair also urged policymakers to make healthy living more affordable through measures including taxation of sugary products and subsidies for fruits and vegetables.

“Let’s begin to tax sugar, increase the tax of sugar so that people will be forced to use less of it. Subsidise fruits and vegetables for people,” he said.

He challenged Nigerians to make physical activity part of everyday life, recommending at least 30 minutes of movement five days a week.

The pharmacist further called for mental health to be integrated into school and workplace programmes, describing a healthy mind as “the engine of all other self-care.”

He urged communities and faith leaders to stop treating mental health problems solely as spiritual issues and to encourage affected persons to seek appropriate medical care.

“Stress is a major cause of disease and sicknesses,” he said, adding that policymakers must take mental health seriously.

Subair said pharmacists, in particular, should take their counselling role seriously, helping patients use medicines rationally, avoid antibiotic misuse and monitor basic health indicators such as blood pressure and blood glucose.

“Clinical care has a place, but not the centre. Your role as healthcare professional is to enable self-care.”

He added that pharmacists could serve as an accessible first point of contact within primary healthcare, while community health workers should support education, follow-up and referral.

Subair said the ultimate objective was to build communities where prevention becomes the first line of defence.

“Hospitals will become for emergency and the community will be for prevention,” he said.

Speaking, the convener of the summit, Dr. Monica Hemben Eimunjeze, said self-care should be viewed as a deliberate investment in better health outcomes rather than an act of selfishness.

“Self-care is important for everybody. It helps us to prevent disease, to promote wellness and to make sure that we intentionally do those things that will help us have positive health outcomes,” she said.

Eimunjeze noted that non-communicable diseases, including hypertension, diabetes and high cholesterol, had assumed epidemic proportions, stressing that lifestyle choices could play a major role in prevention.

She said: “You have to be intentional. You have to be deliberate. You have to embrace those things that will help you — what you eat, how much you eat, whether you are exercising and whether you are compliant with your medications.”

Meanwhile, President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria, PSN, Pharm. Tanko Ayuba, warned Nigerians against fake medicines and misleading health claims circulating on social media.

Ayuba said many counterfeit products were difficult for ordinary consumers to identify, stressing the importance of a reliable medicine distribution system.

“They clone them. But if we get our distribution system right, you can pick it from the point where you are buying the drug,” he said.

He particularly warned against online testimonials promoting purported medicines and treatments.

“Most of the social media products are misleading. Very misleading,” Ayuba said, alleging that artificial intelligence was being used to create fake endorsements involving prominent Nigerians.

“What they do, the dangerous thing is that they will get a prominent Nigerian and use AI to put words in his mouth,” he said.

He urged Nigerians not to be gullible when confronted with extraordinary health claims online.

“We should all be alert. And whenever you see something, we should not be gullible. There are some things we say: if it’s too good to be true, then it is too good to be true,” Ayuba said.

He clarified that the PSN was a professional body rather than a regulator, noting that the Pharmacy Council of Nigeria, PCN, remained the regulatory authority responsible for enforcing the law.

The experts also called for stronger collaboration among doctors, nurses, pharmacists, community health workers, families and policymakers.

World.title: Obi’s Benue blockade: NDC never told me to transmit letter to go, I only provided security – CP
World.content:
By Luminous Jannamike and John Alechenu

As reactions continue to trail the blocking of Nigerian Democratic Congress, NDC, presidential candidate, Mr. Peter Obi during his visit to Benue State on Tuesday, the state Commissioner of Police, Mr. Cletus Nwadiogbu, has said the party (NDC), never asked him to transmit a letter notifying him of Obi’s visit to the state to Governor Hyacinth Alia.

Meanwhile, the Inter Party Advisory Council, IPAC, has condemned the attack, alleging that youths were sponsored to block and attack him, as the council said it was an invitation to anarchy.

This came as Labour Party condemned the alleged blockade of Obi, saying if the alleged miscreants who blocked Obi were sponsored by the state government, then it was frightening, as it called on President Bola Tinubu to call the governor under his party, the All Progressives Congress, APC, to order.

Also, the South East Amalgamated Markets Traders Association, SEMATA, condemned the attack on Obi, in Benue State, describing it as an act of impunity and brigandage.

Nwadiogbu said the letter was presented to him by members of the NDC, who visited his office to inform the police command about Obi’s planned arrival in the state, adding that the information was primarily for security arrangements.

The commissioner spoke on Channels Television’s Lunch Time Politics programme, yesterday, while explaining the events leading up to the disruption of Obi’s movement in Benue State on Tuesday.

According to him, members of the NDC initially informed his Police Public Relations Officer, PPRO, saying, “On that very day, my PRO came to me and said members of NDC said they were paying me a visit. I said, well, I am currently in the office, and the PRO said they are coming by 3 p.m. I said ‘Okay.

It’s an invitation

to anarchy —IPAC

IPAC said the police had been notified of the visit, warning that preventing a presidential candidate from entering a state was an ‘invitation to anarchy’ as the country heads into an electoral season.

In a statement by its National Publicity Secretary, Egbeola Martins, the council said the action also violated Obi’s constitutional right to freedom of movement.

“Restricting a citizen from entering a state is a flagrant violation of the 1999 Constitution as amended,” IPAC said.

The council said the alleged attack was particularly troubling given Benue’s worsening security situation.

“Benue State is already bleeding over constant terrorists’ attacks, sponsoring youths to block and attack Obi’s convoy is a misplaced aggression and height of rascality,” it said.

IPAC commended the police for arresting 46 suspects and urged a thorough investigation to identify the perpetrators and their alleged sponsors.

It said the incident must not be allowed to undermine democratic participation, stressing its commitment to a just democracy.

Labour Party asks Tinubu to rein in governors

Labour Party in a statement by its National Publicity Secretary, Ken Asogwa, described the incident as shameful, calling on President Tinubu to rein the governors.

The party further alleged that miscreants who blocked Obi were sponsored by the state government, an allegation it said, if true, is frightening.

“If a Reverend Father who mounts the pulpit to teach morals could descend to this level of violence, what should Nigerians expect from more indecorous politicians and governors, like the one in Edo?

“It is particularly concerning that a governor who, as the Chief Security Officer of Benue State, has never been able to arrest and prosecute the criminals ravaging his state could instead be feasting on a man who was embarking on a humanitarian mission.”

“The sanctity of our democracy depends on the ability of every citizen to move freely, express political opinions and participate in public life without fear of harassment or attack,” it stated.

SEMATA condemns attack

SEMATA in a statement by its President-General, Chief Emeka Emechebe, and Secretary-General, Chief Chima Eruchalu, after an emergency executive meeting in Onitsha, warned that such conduct could undermine peaceful elections in 2027.

SEMATA, which represents traders of South-East extraction across Nigeria and the diaspora, urged youths in Benue and other parts of the country not to repeat the incident, stressing that all presidential candidates have a constitutional right to freedom of movement and peaceful assembly, regardless of political affiliation.

It warned that no individual or group has a monopoly on violence, stressing that SEMATA would neither tolerate nor support acts of lawlessness.

“We are a nation of laws where the rule of law prevails at all times,” the association said, adding that Nigeria must not allow political violence and turbulence to threaten democracy.”

World.title: Obi: In 2023 We Took Things for Granted, Believed INEC, But Not Again
World.content:
• Says Tinubu not in charge, hasn’t spent 3 nights in any state

•Faults president for spending holidays abroad

• Promises decisive action against insecurity

•Rules out oil subsidy return

•Vows to set up independent system to monitor 2027 results

Chuks Okocha, Sunday Aborisade in Abuja and Sunday Ehigiator in Lagos





The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr. Peter Obi, yesterday said the 2027 elections would be very different from the 2023 experience, because he and his team took things for granted in the last election, believing the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) would walk its talk.

Obi, who spoke during an exclusive interview on Arise Television, said confidently that he had proof that the Mahmood Yakubu-led INEC worked for the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) in 2023 and was not going to sit back and take things for granted again in 2027.

Speaking on the proposed opposition coalition and the allegation that he would never take the vice-presidential slot in the new alliance talks, Obi said he had never told anyone such and that the offer had not even been made in the first place.

Obi also questioned the continued insecurity in Nigeria, arguing that modern technology should enable the government to locate people and respond effectively to criminal activities.

He said this while responding to questions on how his administration would handle kidnappings and ransom demands and other issues.

According to Obi, Yakubu had convinced Nigerians and the international community that INEC would conduct the election fairly, but he alleged that the commission chairman was, in reality, working for the opposition.

“In 2023, we took things for granted. We believed INEC. We believed what they said they would do. The INEC Chairman convinced the world that he would do the right thing, when in fact he was working for the opposition. This time, we will only trust them by doing the right thing ourselves,” Obi said.

Obi also promised to establish an independent system for monitoring election results from polling units in 2027, saying the arrangement would enable his political organisation to receive results directly from polling units and compare them with figures eventually collated and announced by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

He stressed that the proposed arrangement would not constitute a parallel electoral commission.

“We must make sure that every polling unit, the votes are counted, the votes are recorded properly, the votes are transmitted properly. And we will even have a dual transmission so that as it’s going to the proper, designated INEC portal, it’s also being transmitted where the people can see it,” he said.

Asked whether the arrangement amounted to establishing a parallel INEC, Obi said: “Not at all. All we are saying is that this time around, we will make sure that in every polling unit, we must have a system that transmits to our own situation room the correct results.

“And I’m sure there’s so many other agencies that intend to do the same thing. So we are not going to have a situation where somebody just pronounces something that didn’t emanate from the polling unit. Our task is to make sure that the right things are done.”

The former Anambra State governor said the 2023 presidential election had demonstrated the need for political parties and candidates to independently monitor the electoral process.

He maintained that he won the 2023 election despite INEC’s declaration of Tinubu as the winner, but said he had decided to focus on the 2027 contest.

“As long as I live, I will maintain that I won the 2023 presidential election. Because they know, those who conducted it, know the records. They know why there was a glitch. They know what happened and everything. But I said, ‘I leave it to the past,’” Obi said.

On his statement in Port Harcourt that he was prepared to “die” for his votes, Obi said the comment was symbolic and was made in response to supporters who had pledged to defend their votes.

“What I did in Port Harcourt is more of listening to the people. It wasn’t me talking. They were asking questions. And one of them said, we are prepared to die this time to defend our votes.

And I said to encourage them that I’m prepared to die with them. It’s symbolic. What we are saying is that we are prepared to ensure that our vote counts and it must count.”

Besides, Obi questioned President Bola Tinubu’s leadership of the country, alleging that the president had not spent three consecutive nights in any state outside Lagos and Abuja since assuming office.

The politician cum businessman faulted Tinubu for spending holidays abroad, saying a Nigerian president should use such periods to visit and engage communities within the country, particularly areas affected by insecurity.

He stated if elected president in 2027, he would personally take charge of the fight against insecurity, visit affected areas and appoint competent heads of security agencies with clear instructions to end the menace.

On the Tinubu administration, Obi said the government had not performed well and had been “a bit reckless” in its management of public resources. Asked whether he believed Tinubu was in charge of the government, Obi said: “At times, I believe he’s not in charge.”

He explained that the president must be directly accountable to Nigerians for decisions taken by his administration.

“Because if he’s in charge, he will even be explaining to the people. That’s what I’m talking about, which is capacity. I will be in charge. Nobody, all decisions you see, the President is talking. Nobody will talk for Peter. Because I’m the one that’s elected. I’ll be answerable to the people. And for every penny, I’ll be answerable to the people,” he assured.

He added: “President Tinubu has not slept three nights anywhere in Nigeria. He went to Jos. Stayed at the airport to see people who’ve lost their loved ones. He went to Benue. Did the same thing. He said there was no road. The road they are supposed to build to go to see people who have lost their loved ones,” he said.

Obi argued that the president should spend longer periods in states affected by insecurity and engage directly with stakeholders. “When he should go to Benue and say I’m here. For the next 30 days, I want to see the stakeholders in the state. Let’s discuss these killings,” he added.

Obi also addressed the possibility of an opposition alliance ahead of the 2027 election, refusing to say whether he would step down for former Vice President Atiku Abubakar or accept the position of running mate.

He said any such decision would have to be taken through consultations within the political parties involved, rather than by individual politicians.

“It’s no longer me as Peter talking. It’s like a situation where you have two corporations trying to come together. It’s no longer something the two CEOs go to a drink and say, we’re going to work together. They need to look at how we bring these two corporations together,” he said.

Obi said the NDC had candidates contesting various elective positions and that he could not unilaterally commit the party to an alliance. “For me, it would be irresponsible for anybody to stand before the viewers on television and say, yes, I know. No, because you’re dealing with an institution,” he said.

Obi also criticised Tinubu’s foreign holidays, insisting that the Nigerian president should spend his vacations in the country.

“The Nigerian President must spend his vacation in Nigeria. We cannot continue with this nonsense. As President of Nigeria, I’ll visit other countries, but I’ll not take my holidays in other countries. The holiday is here,” he said.

On insecurity, Obi said the problem would be his first priority if elected, promising to personally take charge of the response. He added: “Insecurity today is making it impossible for farmers to go to farm. It’s making it impossible for produce to be moved around. It’s making it impossible for manufacturers to move their goods. It’s making it impossible even for human movements. So you need to deal with it decisively.”

He said his first week in office would involve appointing competent security chiefs and giving them clear instructions to tackle insecurity.

“In the first week, it’s for me to appoint competent heads in our security agencies with a decisive instruction. We must deal with this. Tell me what will stop us from achieving this,” he said.

He also promised to visit areas affected by insecurity rather than directing the response solely from Abuja.

“I’m not going to sit in Abuja if there’s a problem in Zamfara. We’ll call the people in Zamfara and see what this problem is. And deal with it decisively. And I’m not going to do it from Abuja, I’m going to visit Zamfara. And the same thing will happen in many other areas. I will not be in Abuja when there’s a problem in Nigeria. We will go there, we must tell us how we can solve it.”

Obi said he supported state police and rejected ransom payments to kidnappers. Asked whether he believed in paying ransom, he answered: “No.”

He said the government should use available technology and security resources to locate criminals and rescue victims.

“I’ll take decisive action. There might be casualties. It doesn’t matter who that is, me. But we will deal with it decisively. I’m not going to stay in Abuja when 600 people are kidnapped and in the bush. And that bush is in Nigeria. That bush, people will enter. Our forces will enter it.”
