Kenya’s Konza Technopolis was meant to be Africa’s “Silicon Savannah,” a 2,024-hectare smart city rising from the plains south of Nairobi. Nearly two decades after its 2008 launch, the project has become a case study in how smart cities are financed, and who holds the power.

A flagship project with a US$14.5 billion price tag

Konza Technopolis is a Kenya Vision 2030 flagship, planned as a hub for technology, research and digital government. The estimated total project cost is about US$14.5 billion, a figure that dwarfs Kenya’s annual infrastructure budgets.

Phase 1 horizontal infrastructure began in June 2017 under an Engineering, Procurement, Construction and Financing agreement with Italy’s UniCredit SpA. That contract was valued at roughly KSh 50.4 billion (about US$391 million).

The Italian financing covered the physical groundwork: roads, drainage, water and power corridors. It signalled that European capital still had a role in Africa’s urban future, even as other players moved in.

Chinese credit and the Digital Silk Road

The smart-city core systems tell a different story. The National Cloud Data Centre, smart ICT network, public “safe city” surveillance, smart traffic and government cloud were contracted to Huawei in 2017.

Funding came from a China Eximbank concessional loan of RMB 1.225 billion, signed on 26 April 2019. At the time, that was roughly KSh 17 billion, or about US$172–175 million.

The loan terms are generous but binding: 2% interest, a 19.5-year maturity to 21 September 2038, a 7-year grace period and a 0.5% commitment fee. By 2022, disbursements had exceeded RMB 470 million, with an outstanding balance above RMB 600 million.

China also finances the 400kV Konza substation to guarantee power for the technopolis. This places Konza firmly inside Beijing’s Digital Silk Road, where smart-city systems and surveillance platforms are exported via Huawei and other state-owned enterprises.

The shift to public-private partnerships and local capital

From 2025–26, Kenya’s Treasury began turning to public-private partnerships and domestic capital to ease fiscal pressure. In the 2025–26 financial year, KSh 3.1 billion (about US$24 million) was budgeted for smart cities and the existing data-centre footprint.

In December 2025, the PPP Unit approved a Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer expansion model for the Konza cloud and smart-city facilities. Requests for proposals issued in March–April 2026 explicitly seek local debt and equity, alongside “optional stapled-financing structures.”

Core infrastructure remains in state ownership under the PPP Act 2021 and the Public Finance Management Act 2012. The goal is to blend Chinese concessional credit, Western and multilateral funding, PPPs and local capital markets without surrendering digital sovereignty to any single external power.

Guodong Network and the next phase

In August 2026, Konza signed a framework with China’s Guodong Network. The proposed programme is valued at KSh 38.8 billion, or about US$300 million, covering towers, smart cities, data centres, fibre and cloud.

Kenya has also discussed hosting Guodong’s Africa headquarters. That would deepen the Chinese footprint in Kenya’s digital backbone, even as Nairobi courts European and domestic investors.

The Guodong deal shows how smart-city finance is becoming more layered. A single project now mixes Italian engineering, Chinese concessional loans, PPP structures and potential green bonds.

What smarter finance actually means

For Africa’s smart cities, smarter finance means blending Chinese concessional credit, Western and multilateral funding, PPPs, local capital markets and strong governance. The alternative is fiscal strain and digital dependence on one external power.

Kenya’s experience at Konza is a warning and a template. Low-conditionality Chinese loans and bundled technology give Beijing sway over data, security and standards.

Italy’s UniCredit and the new PPP structures signal European and domestic attempts to rebalance the financial centre of gravity. Whether that rebalancing succeeds will shape not just Konza, but every smart city planned across the continent.

The broader contest for Africa’s digital infrastructure is part of the story covered in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The next test is whether the Guodong Network framework translates into signed contracts and disbursed capital. Kenya’s Treasury will also need to show that PPP-driven expansion can attract local debt and equity without stalling.

Investors should watch the China Eximbank repayment schedule, which runs to 21 September 2038. Every disbursement deepens Kenya’s exposure, while every PPP approval tests whether domestic capital can share the load.

The lesson from Konza is already clear: smart cities are not just engineering projects. They are financial and geopolitical bets, and the terms of those bets will determine who controls Africa’s urban data.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Konza Technopolis? Konza Technopolis is a 2,024-hectare smart city in Kenya, launched in 2008 as a Kenya Vision 2030 flagship. It is planned as an “African Silicon Savannah” with an estimated total project cost of about US$14.5 billion. Who is financing Kenya’s Konza smart city? Phase 1 infrastructure was financed by Italy’s UniCredit SpA at roughly KSh 50.4 billion (about US$391 million). Core smart-city systems were built by Huawei under a China Eximbank loan of RMB 1.225 billion (about US$172 million) signed on 26 April 2019. What is Kenya doing to reduce reliance on Chinese loans for Konza? Kenya’s PPP Unit approved a Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer expansion model in December 2025. Requests for proposals issued in March–April 2026 seek local debt and equity, while core infrastructure remains in state ownership.

World.title: Senator Wade defends vote on MCC compact bills
World.content:
Senator Wade defends vote on MCC compact bills

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Senator Louis Wade Jr. has publicly defended his vote in favour of the legislation tied to Belize’s Millennium Challenge Corporation compact.

In a social media post, Wade said the United States is providing US$125 million to Belize in exchange for several legislative commitments.

Those include raising the school leaving age from 14 to 16, introducing national assessment so student performance can be tracked, and restructuring vocational and technical schools to create a standardised qualification for people who study trades.

On the electricity side, Wade said the compact would fund a cable connecting San Pedro, which generates the most expensive electricity in the country, to the cheaper mainland supply.

“In MY OPINION no one needed to pay us to do what is in OUR BEST INTEREST,” he wrote. “So you would really vote against all that?”

Wade said he voted yes alongside all PUP and all UDP senators, while his fellow independent senators chose to abstain.

He added that he and other church leaders negotiated commitments to changes in the Education and TVET bills.

“We love sensational news, without a love for facts,” his post concludes.

World.title: Shyne and 50 Cent bury old feud as rapper turned politician earns public praise
World.content:
Shyne and 50 Cent bury old feud as rapper turned politician earns public praise

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Shyne Barrow’s return to the United States continues to generate attention, this time after a surprise reunion with longtime rival 50 Cent in Miami.

The encounter took place at Serafina, where both men were dining separately before being introduced again.

50 Cent later praised Shyne publicly, saying he was impressed by his growth and referring to him as a “world leader.”

The comments stand in sharp contrast to the pair’s history.

Their feud dates back to the early 2000s, when 50 Cent took aim at Shyne while he was incarcerated. Shyne later responded with the track “For the Record,” and the tension continued for years.

Now, the tone is completely different.

Shyne said he views himself as an elder statesman and believes his role should be about bringing people together rather than carrying old grudges.

He said he has offered olive branches to former rivals and described the reunion with 50 Cent as a sign of maturity and evolution within hip hop.

The meeting also comes as Shyne continues to straddle two worlds, music and politics, with his Belizean leadership role now forming a major part of his international identity.

What was once a feud has now turned into a public show of respect.

World.title: 50 Cent says he wants to visit Belize after making peace with Shyne
World.content:
50 Cent says he wants to visit Belize after making peace with Shyne

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): American rap superstar 50 Cent could be heading to Belize after publicly expressing interest in visiting the country following his reconciliation with former rival Shyne Barrow.

50 Cent made the comment on Instagram while reacting to Shyne discussing their recent reunion and the end of their decades old feud.

The G Unit frontman praised Shyne’s transformation over the years, writing that the Belizean politician had impressed him.

“I’m not gonna front shyne impresses me,” 50 Cent wrote. “world leader, he shown nothing but growth.”

But it was what came next that could generate even more attention in Belize.

“When I get some free time I’ll come to your country,” 50 Cent added.

The comments follow a chance reunion between the two former rivals in Miami, where they reportedly crossed paths while dining at Serafina.

Shyne has since described the encounter as an example of his effort to extend olive branches to people with whom he previously had disagreements.

The relationship between Shyne and 50 Cent was once very different. Their feud stretched back to the early 2000s, when the two exchanged lyrical attacks and public jabs.

More than two decades later, 50 Cent is now publicly praising Shyne and talking about coming to Belize.

No date or formal plans for a Belize visit have been announced, and 50 Cent’s Instagram comment does not confirm that a trip has been scheduled.

Still, the possibility of one of hip hop’s biggest stars visiting Belize following the reconciliation is likely to generate plenty of attention locally.

World.title: Armed robbers hit San Roman Shopping Mall and escape in white SUV
World.content:
Armed robbers hit San Roman Shopping Mall and escape in white SUV

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police are investigating an armed robbery at the San Roman Shopping Mall in the Stann Creek District where two masked men reportedly held up the store owner at gunpoint.

According to police information, officers responded to the business at around 11:35 a.m. on Thursday, September 10, after receiving reports of an armed robbery.

The store owner told police that at approximately 11:15 a.m., two masked men armed with pistol type firearms entered the establishment and held him at gunpoint.

The men then reportedly took an undisclosed amount of cash from the register.

They also stole a black iPhone 16 Pro Max valued at $2,500.

Police say the robbers fled the area in a white Nissan SUV.

No one was injured during the incident.

Investigators visited and processed the scene and reviewed surveillance footage from the area.

Police are continuing their investigation.

World.title: The most consequential election for Belize this year is one no Belizean can vote in
World.content:
The most consequential election for Belize this year is one no Belizean can vote in

By Horace Palacio:

Eight weeks from now, on November 3, an election will be held that will help decide your grocery bill, your light of employment in tourism, and the remittance envelope your family receives from abroad.

You are not invited.

Americans will elect a new Congress that day, every House seat, a third of the Senate, and this newspaper’s news pages have laid out the four channels through which their choice reaches Belizean kitchens, the tourists, the imports, the remittances, the aid. Read that piece for the machinery. This column is here for the meaning, because there is a lesson inside November 3 that stings more than any tariff.

Here it is. Measure how much a foreign election matters to your household, and you have measured, to the decimal point, how sovereign your country actually is.

Call it the exposure index. A fully sovereign nation reads foreign elections the way it reads foreign weather reports, with interest, not anxiety. A dependent nation reads them the way a tenant reads the landlord’s moods. So take Belize’s reading honestly. Seven of every ten visitors who fund our biggest industry carry American passports. More than four of every ten dollars of goods on our shelves arrive from American suppliers. Our families’ lifeline flows from American cities, and our own budget speech already recorded remittances dipping as American migration politics shifted. And beneath it all, our very dollar is the American dollar’s shadow, pegged two to one, importing their inflation without a customs check.

Add it up and face the conclusion like adults. The American voter, a stranger in Ohio who has never heard of Belize and could not place us on a map, sits, functionally, on every Belizean household’s budget committee for the next two years. Unelected by us. Unremovable by us. Deciding, in aggregate, more about the price of our month than most decisions taken in Belmopan.

I wrote a column asking Belizeans to count the kings who actually rule us. Add one more to the census, the American electorate. It reigns over a corner of every Belizean ledger, and on November 3 it holds court.

Now, before anyone reaches for anger, aim it correctly, because there is no villain in Washington here. Americans voting their own interests in their own election owe Belize nothing. That is what elections are for. The wire that runs from their ballot box to your kitchen was not laid by them.

It was laid by us. Wire by wire, decade by decade. Every year we chose imports over production, we laid wire. Every season we marketed to one tourist and ignored the world’s other calendars, we laid wire. Every megawatt we failed to build at home, every export we never shipped, every skill we never trained, wire, wire, wire. Dependence is never an event, my friends. It is an accumulation of small, comfortable choices, and November 3 is simply the day the accumulated wiring hums loud enough to hear.

So what does a serious small nation do with a foreign election it cannot vote in? Three things.

First, watch it like a farmer, not a fan. The farmer does not cheer for rain or curse the drought. He reads the sky and moves early. Whatever November produces, a Congress that squeezes American wallets, a trade fight that lifts prices, an enforcement wave that thins remittances, the Belizean response is the same hedging this column has preached all year. The second tourism market courted now. The export push now. The food grown here now. Every one of those is a levee, and levees are built before the water rises.

Second, run the same audit at home. The household exposed to one employer, one income, one customer, lives at the mercy of moods it cannot vote on, exactly like the nation. The ownership gospel, the skill, the side trade, the titled lot, the shares, is how a family lowers its personal exposure index. Sovereignty, it turns out, is fractal. It is built at the kitchen table with the same materials as at the treasury.

And third, give the country its number. Publish the exposure index alongside the national scorecard this column has demanded, the share of visitors from our top market, the share of imports from our top supplier, the share of household income arriving as remittances. Three numbers, tracked yearly. Not to shame the present, but to steer the decade, because a dependence you measure is a dependence you can shrink, and one you refuse to measure is one you have chosen to keep.

Here, then, is the finish line, and I want every reader to memorize it, because it is the most precise definition of national success this column can offer.

Belize will know it has arrived on the day an American midterm election becomes merely interesting to us instead of consequential. The day we read their results over coffee the way a well-built house hears a storm, aware, unafraid, dry. That day is not granted by anyone. It is constructed, export by export, megawatt by megawatt, market by market, skill by skill.

Americans vote on November 3, once, for their future.

Belize votes every single day, in what it builds or fails to build, for whether their future keeps writing ours.

They will count their ballots in one night.

Ours are counted over a generation. Cast today’s well.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: International News: US Secretary of State ends Latin America tour with push for stronger Regional Security
World.content:
International News: US Secretary of State ends Latin America tour with push for stronger Regional Security

By Zoila Palma: Today, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is wrapping up his South America tour in Peru where he is expected to hold security talks with President Keiko Fujimori as Washington seeks stronger cooperation with conservative governments in the region and intensifies efforts to combat drug trafficking and organized crime.

Rubio arrived in Lima on September 9 following visits to Colombia and Ecuador, where he promoted closer coordination against criminal gangs that the United States has designated or plans to designate as terrorist organizations.

Peru recently joined the “Shield of the Americas,” a US-led coalition promoted by President Donald Trump to combat drug trafficking and organized crime.

Peru, one of the world’s largest cocaine producers, has also experienced a significant deterioration in public security, with homicides rising sharply since 2018, AFP reports.

Peruvian Foreign Minister Carlos Espa said security and preparations for the El Niño weather phenomenon are the country’s two main priorities for Rubio’s visit.

During his stop in Ecuador, Rubio announced that Los Tiguerones, one of the country’s most powerful criminal gangs, would be designated a terrorist organization by Washington. Similar measures have already been taken against other Ecuadorian gangs, Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua and Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel.

Rubio’s regional tour also highlights Washington’s efforts to strengthen its influence in Latin America and counter growing ties between countries in the region and China, Russia and Iran.

World.title: Ministry of Health expands youth outreach on tobacco and alcohol prevention
World.content:
Ministry of Health expands youth outreach on tobacco and alcohol prevention

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Health and Wellness, through the National Drug Abuse Control Council (NDACC), is continuing its nationwide efforts to prevent tobacco and alcohol use among young people and promote healthier communities, in partnership with the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO).

The initiative recently reached the Cayo District, where Youth Forums were held in Belmopan and San Ignacio, along with a Community Sensitization Session.

The engagements provided young people, community members and other stakeholders with information on the risks associated with vaping, tobacco and alcohol use, while creating opportunities to share experiences and discuss practical approaches to strengthening prevention efforts.

The Ministry said the nationwide initiative will continue with upcoming activities in Belize City South Side, Dangriga in the Stann Creek District, and Punta Gorda in the Toledo District.

The sessions form part of ongoing efforts to engage youth, community leaders, educators, parents and other stakeholders in addressing substance use and its impact on communities.

The Ministry said the initiative is focused on empowering young people, strengthening community action and increasing awareness while supporting the development of healthier, tobacco- and alcohol-free environments across Belize.

World.title: Prime Minister wishes Belizeans Happy St. George’s Caye Day!
World.content:
Prime Minister wishes Belizeans Happy St. George’s Caye Day!

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister of Belize John Briceño has extended St. George’s Caye Day greetings to Belizeans at home and abroad, calling on the nation to reflect on its history and celebrate the identity that has emerged from it.

The Prime Minister encouraged Belizeans to recognize the country’s history in its entirety, including its complexities and the experiences that have shaped the nation over generations.

“As we celebrate St. George’s Caye Day, may we embrace our history in all its complexity and celebrate the Belizean identity forged through it,” Prime Minister Briceño said.

“Happy St. George’s Caye Day, Belize!”

World.title: Stalled by squatters
World.content:
FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Squatters have taken over hundreds of acres of privately owned land across this parish, with approximately 58 acres of a 147.48-acre property at Flamingo Beach already illegally occupied, threatening to derail a major development for which a plan has been submitted to the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC).

Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager, who on Thursday raised the alarm during the corporation’s regular monthly meeting, said the growing problem has resulted in the TMC being inundated with complaints from frustrated landowners.

“We have had a number of landowners coming to the corporation to report instances where individuals have occupied and begun developing their properties without the owners’ permission,” Gager said.

He warned that the scale of the illegal occupation is undermining the development of the parish he described as having significant potential for growth.

Gager said the situation at Flamingo Beach was particularly concerning.

“There is a submitted plan here for that property that will help to build Trelawny, but we cannot proceed because there is this problem of squatting,” he bemoaned.

“Approximately 58 acres of [well-known attorney] Gordon Brown’s property has been illegally occupied,” Gager added.

Efforts to get a comment from Brown were unsuccessful as, up to press time he did not return the phone call as promised.

Meanwhile, according to the mayor, at another property in Flamingo Beach, 11 acres of a 57.6-acre parcel have also been informally settled.

Explaining the extent of the problem, he pointed to Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny — which recently made news headlines following the early-morning demolition of about 20 structures — where approximately 12 acres of the property have been informally occupied.

Gager also referenced significant squatting on sections of 344.5 acres of land in an area called Tilston; Hague, where one acre has been informally settled; and Hague Cave Island, where four acres of the property have similarly been occupied.

Gager, who is also chairman of the TMC, said squatters are relying on claims of adverse possession which, for privately owned land, is based on undisturbed occupation of at least 12 years.

“Once they get a little cut on it they try to say that they have been there for over 12 years, when in fact they weren’t there,” he said.

“We find that the law-abiding citizen who pays their taxes, buy their land for maybe later on in their years when things get bad and they want to protect their future, they are now met with a problem that they might have to… find extra money to take it to the Supreme Court level,” the mayor added.

Gager pushed back against criticism of the TMC and the Government over the squatting crisis, insisting that the authorities have been taking steps within their remit.

“We must do all that we can and, as the municipality, I must note that we have been serving our notices on those that occupy the lands,” he said, adding that notices have also been served on landowners to facilitate court action.

He said the TMC is frequently contacted by property owners seeking help, but its ability to resolve disputes is ultimately limited when matters enter the judicial system.

“All we can do sometimes is have a discussion and try to guide them into the right process where they are going,” said Gager.

Pointing to the substantial structures being erected in some of the settlements, he questioned whether everyone occupying the properties could legitimately be regarded as people without the means to legitimately acquire property.

The mayor said he has seen two- and three-storey houses, split-level structures and buildings apparently configured to accommodate renters and commercial activity.

“I can see houses that are really arranged for business, so that renters can accommodate. How can we be so lawless?” he asked.

Gager urged politicians, members of the police force, social workers, and ordinary citizens not to facilitate or encourage illegal occupation, warning that continued squatting could tarnish Trelawny’s development prospects.

“This cannot continue in a growing parish. The future of this parish is great; let us not mar the beauty of this parish by encouraging squatting,” he urged.

World.title: $6.8-m payout for unjust redundancy
World.content:
The Industrial Disputes Tribunal.

THE Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) has ordered Spectrum Insurance Brokers to pay a former employee $6.8 million after it found that his dismissal by way of redundancy in 2019 was “unjustifiable”.

In a ruling handed down on Tuesday the IDT rejected the company’s arguments that it was facing financial challenges at the time it decided to make the position of Claims Manager Laurel Smith redundant.

Initially, lawyers representing the company had argued that the IDT lacked the jurisdiction to hear matters regarding redundancies after the Ministry of Labour sent the dispute for its hearing in 2021.

Lawyers representing Spectrum took the matter to the Supreme Court seeking to challenge the authority of the IDT, but in a 2023 ruling the court said there was no legal basis for it to grant a stay of the judicial review proceedings.

When the matter finally started before the IDT in January 2025 the company argued that Smith’s post was made redundant as it was experiencing financial difficulties in 2019 and it was agreed that his position of claims manager would be absorbed into the operations manager position for the purpose of greater efficiency.

The company, however, admitted that Smith’s post was the only one made redundant and argued that he was offered a new post of recovery officer but he did not express an interest in that job.

It was also confirmed that there was no issue with Smith’s performance and no disciplinary matter pending against him.

Witnesses who testified on Smith’s behalf pointed out that he was a good manager and claimed that “he would be ranked among the best in the industry”.

In his testimony Smith claimed to have had a problem with how a senior manager — who was employed by the company five years after him — spoke to the staff and, after he tackled her about this, his department was faced with significant attacks, until it was indicated that his post would be made redundant.

According to Smith, he was embarrassed and traumatised by the redundancy, which affected him financially with his house being put on the market for sale.

In its ruling the IDT said despite the company’s claims of facing increasing financial challenges, the records show that its operating profit moved from approximately $17.3 million in 2018 to approximately $20.2 million in 2019, with its total revenue climbing to $19.3 million compared to a budgeted 16.5 million.

“Based on the evidence before us, we are able to make specific findings of fact that the company’s case suffered from a number of infirmities and fallacies. When weighted against the provisions… governing redundancy, their contentions, (which are more asserted that demonstrated) that this was a genuine redundancy, could not pass muster,” said the IDT panel chaired by Donald Roberts.

“The redundancy exercise fell afoul of the requirements… as the process did not satisfy the standards of fairness and the company did not show that it engaged in meaningful consultation, that it made reasonable attempts to avoid redundancy, and that it assisted Mr Smith in finding alternative employment,” the IDT added as it made the award to Smith.

World.title: Skatta upbeat as Coolie Dance rhythm takes flight, again
World.content:
BURRELL... I’m always happy whenever a new interest comes to fruition and a great song is released with the sample.

THE success of the Coolie dance rhythm sampled hit Bby WOW by Karol G, featuring Judeline and rusowsky, has once again propelled the enigmatic Cordell “Skatta” Burrell-produced beat into the spotlight.

Bby WOW is the biggest song globally at present, topping both Billboard’s Global 200 and Global 200 Excluding US charts. It is also #1 on Billboard’s Hot Latin Songs, and Hot Latin Rhythm Songs charts.

Outside of the United States, the song has so far hit #1 in Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Peru and in Spain.

Created in early 2004, the initial Coolie Dance rhythm featured more than 70 songs. Among the hits at the time were songs by dancehall acts Guinness by Jagwa, Yuh Gaawn by Bounty Killer, Geenie Dance by Elephant Man, Head Gaawn by Elephant Man, Do it To Me Baby by Ce’Cile, Gal Dem Way by TOK,

Tell Me Why by Frisco Kid, Please Mr Please by Vybz Kartel and Feel Alright by Sean Paul.

Mr Vegas’ Pull Up and Jook Gal (Wine Wine) by Elephant Man, Kiprich, Twista and YoungBloodz were Billboard chart-hitters, so too Culo by Pitbull and Nina Sky’s Move Your Body, both of which hit the Billboard Hot 100 charts in late 2004, and most recently After Hours by R&B singer Kehlani.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer on Thursday, Burrell who is also a former judge on the television reality series Magnum Kings and Queens of Dancehall, spoke about the renewed interest in the beat which he created 22 years ago.

“I’m always happy whenever a new interest comes to fruition and a great song is released with the sample,” said Burrell. “It reminds me that the riddim is timeless and has the ability to connect with generations of music lovers. I think the continued interest from international acts in sampling the rhythm has a lot to do with the original approach I made when I sat down to create it. I took a more artistic approach than musical, meaning mostly drums and percussions slightly aggressive but still groovy enough to make you feel the movement between each sound. Less sometimes means more so not crowded. My dancehall influences along with the Indian samples all together made it not only appealing to my culture but straight across the globe.”

According to Burrell, the latest sampling of the beat was brought to his attention by his publishing company.

“My publishing company was contacted after the song’s release, and we did what we could and ensured that we covered all the necessary areas that suited all parties. I think they did a great job on the production because the first thing that stood out was the beautiful synth melodies and vocal samples that played alongside the lead vocals and even though its in Spanish, the sound is captivating enough and is still enjoyed and appreciated,” said Burrell.

Unlike most of his projects, the beat for the Coolie Dance rhythm was not created in a recording studio. Burrell shared that he envisioned the production would have been a hit.

“The rhythm itself was not created in a studio. I was in New York at the time and was by a friend’s house. I purchased a sample CD at a place called Samash music somewhere in Queens I think and was eager to sit with it and get creative. The first opportunity I got was in my friend’s living room. I plugged in my drum machine and put my headphones on and got to work. The process was about an hour because from listening to the samples in the car, I knew exactly how I wanted to interpret and build around it. I knew it was different and had extreme potential so when I had an offer of purchase from another producer, I made the decision not to sell it and instead use it for my own label and the minute I played it for Bounty Killer, he also gave me the nod that it was a hit,” Burrell recalled.

Though not 100 per cent sure, Burrell recalled that budding artiste at the time Jagwa may have recorded the first song on the Coolie Dance rhythm.

Prior to venturing into music production, Burrell tried his hand at becoming a recording artiste, but that didn’t work out.

“I got into music while attending The United Pentecostal Church on Grant’s Pen Road where at a very young age, I used to sit at the front bench and mimic Clevie the drummer as he played. I eventually got the opportunity to play the drums after some time and that’s where my passion grew. From beating the desk at Calabar High school classrooms to building beats and recording demos in my friend Benzly Hype’s home studio on Hillary Avenue. I was rejected as an artiste at Celestial Sound because my voice wasn’t good enough, so I decided to learn the 56 Channel Amek Hendricks Mixing Console at the first digital studio owned by Steven Ventura,” he shared.

“He gave me the opportunity to be a fly on the wall to watch and learn until I started recording and mixing. Iley Dread, however, gave me the biggest support by giving me his label, Kings Of Kings, to run for almost two years and that’s where I homed in on my passion and worked with many artistes, musicians and producers. Norris Man gave me my very first hit song and Ce’Cile and I did our very first dancehall juggling that propelled me to the mainstream lanes from which I was able to navigate my success,” the producer reminisced.

World.title: INVESTORS SNAP UP JAMAICA BOND
World.content:
NEARLY 10 months after Hurricane Melissa inflicted an estimated US$8.8 billion in damage across Jamaica, international investors have turned out strongly for the Government’s latest US$1-billion bond, allowing the country to borrow at a lower rate than initially indicated.

The bond was heavily oversubscribed after Jamaica returned to the international capital markets last week to raise funds for both debt management and general budgetary needs.

Before the offer was formally launched, investors were initially being guided to an interest rate of about 6.50 per cent. Strong demand subsequently allowed the Government to offer the bond at 6.25 per cent, according to market sources.

In simple terms, investors wanted more of the bond than Jamaica was seeking to sell, giving the Government room to offer a lower return and still attract sufficient buyers.

The strong reception is particularly notable given Jamaica’s return to the market less than a year after Hurricane Melissa caused widespread damage and disrupted economic activity.

Of the US$1 billion being raised, approximately US$600 million was earmarked to help repurchase portions of three older Government of Jamaica global bonds, while the remaining US$400 million, or about $63 billion, was intended for general budgetary purposes.

The transaction forms part of the Government’s wider liability management strategy, under which it is seeking to replace portions of older, more expensive debt with new borrowing while pushing some repayments further into the future.

At the same time that the new bond was being marketed, the Government invited holders of its 6.75 per cent notes due in 2028, 8.50 per cent notes due in 2036, and 8.00 per cent notes due in 2039 to sell some of those securities back to Jamaica.

By the time that tender offer closed on September 9, investors had submitted approximately US$476.62 million in bonds for repurchase.

After adjusting for the amortisation of the 2028 notes, the amount represented approximately US$392.23 million.

The Government is expected to determine how much of those tendered notes it will accept, with settlement scheduled for September 17. The official tender documents confirm that completion of the buyback is tied to the closing of the new international bond transaction.

“Jamaica intends to apply a portion of the net proceeds of its new notes offering announced on Wednesday, September 2, 2026 to purchase the Old Notes accepted pursuant to the Invitation at the applicable Total Purchase Price,” the Government said in its release.

The repurchase is expected to lower the Government’s annual interest bill by approximately US$3.5 million while moving part of its external debt obligations further into the future.

Beyond the savings, however, the reception to the new bond provides another test of how international investors now view Jamaica’s creditworthiness.

That assessment has changed significantly over the past decade.

When Jamaica raised US$2.05 billion on the international market in July 2015, its April 2028 bond carried an interest rate of 6.75 per cent while its July 2045 bond carried a rate of 7.875 per cent.

At the time, Jamaica was rated B by S&P Global, B– by Fitch Ratings, and Caa2 by Moody’s.

Today, the country carries a BB rating from S&P Global with a stable outlook, BB– from Fitch with a stable outlook, and Ba3 from Moody’s with a stable outlook.

The improvement has accompanied a steep reduction in public debt, with Jamaica’s debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio falling from approximately 116 per cent in 2015 to about 68 per cent today.

The ratings have also been maintained despite the economic damage caused by Hurricane Melissa.

Investor demand for the latest bond therefore provides another indication that international markets continue to place weight on Jamaica’s fiscal management and debt reduction record, even as the country faces significant reconstruction costs.

The comparison is even more striking against the backdrop of rising US interest rates.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year United States Treasury has recently moved close to five per cent amid a global bond sell-off. On Wednesday it was trading at approximately 4.8 per cent.

At a 6.25 per cent rate, Jamaica would, therefore, be borrowing at roughly 1.4 percentage points above the yield available on US Government debt.

That margin, known in the market as the spread, represents the additional return investors demand for taking the greater risk associated with lending to Jamaica instead of the United States.

The narrower that gap, generally, the more favourably investors are assessing Jamaica’s risk.

A comparison with Trinidad and Tobago provides some regional context.

Trinidad and Tobago, which carries stronger credit ratings than Jamaica, issued a 10-year US$1-billion bond earlier this year at 6.50 per cent and later raised another US$800 million through a 12-year bond at 6.20 per cent.

When Trinidad issued the January bond, its borrowing rate was roughly 2.27 percentage points above the US 10-year Treasury yield prevailing at the time.

Jamaica’s latest transaction, despite its lower sovereign credit rating, appears to have been priced at a smaller premium above US Treasuries.

That does not mean Jamaica is viewed as less risky than Trinidad across the board, since bond pricing is also affected by market conditions, maturity, and investor demand at the time of issuance.

It nevertheless points to strong appetite for Jamaican debt during the latest transaction.

The new unsecured bond is expected to mature in 2037, giving it an 11-year tenure.

Citigroup Global Markets Inc and Scotia Capital (USA) Inc acted as deal managers and joint lead underwriters. Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP and Patterson Mair Hamilton advised the managers, while the Government was advised by Paul Hastings LLP and the Attorney General’s Chambers.

World.title: IT WILL BE GREAT!
World.content:
Oblique Seville celebrates winning the men’s 100m final during the World Athletics Diamond League athletics meeting in Belgium on September 4, 2026. He is set to compete in the Ultimate Championships in Hungary. (Photo: AFP)

Despite several of Jamaica’s top athletes set to compete, retired Jamaican-born Olympic and world champion Donovan Bailey admits the World Athletics Ultimate Championships could lose some of its appeal with several of the sport’s biggest stars, including American Noah Lyles, set to miss the event.

The inaugural three-day invitational meet, which gets underway on Friday in Budapest, will feature the world’s top 16 athletes in individual track events and the top eight competitors in field events. Gold medallists from the 2024 Paris Olympics, 2025 Tokyo World Championships and this year’s Diamond League final winners earned automatic qualification while the remaining entrants were determined by the World Athletics Ranking for the period from last September to the start of this September.

However, reigning Olympic Games 100m champion and 200m world champion Lyles will be absent due to injury.

American star 400m and 400m hurdles star Sydney McLaughlin Levrone, America’s Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall, Kenyan middle-distance star Faith Kipyegon, Kenya’s 800m world champion Lilian Odira, and reigning Olympic and World Champion in the 5000m Faith Kipyegon will also be missing from the championships for different reasons.

Former world record holder Bailey, who won 100m gold for Canada at the 1996 Olympics and the 1995 World Championships, says World Athletics will miss the star power but believes it will still be a great event.

“I think that anytime that you’re having major championships and this is the ultimate championship [in] it’s first year, the big stars that are missing, it does dampen it a little bit,” he said on CBC Sports. “I think that in any sport, you want to have the greatest people of that time, appealing to the fans, catering to the crowd and breaking world records and winning stuff.”

“But I also think that there are some incredible stars that are established now and there are some really, really talented young athletes that’s going to establish themselves. I’m looking forward to it, I’m sorry for the athletes that are injured or season’s done or whatever but there’s going to be some great competition.”

With the Ultimate Championships being the first of its kind, it’s not yet viewed as a major championship on the level of the Olympics and World Championships.

However, Bailey believes it gives athletes another opportunity to compete for additional prize money as well as securing bragging rights.

“I think that championships matter, consistency matters, delivering messages matter, being confident, being injury-free matters,” he said. “We look at the Commonwealth Games or PanAm Games, some sort of regional championships — to me, the Ultimate Championships now is like a regional championships. If you win, you win and you’re going to get paid. Does it matter? Yes, it matters for the person that wins.”

“Also, it matters for everyone that competes there because they’re going to have money. If you win, it’s incredible because it’s a title and what this does next year going into, uh, 2027 [with the] World Championships and when you’re on a Diamond League starting line, the Ultimate Championship champion is another title that gets added and maybe you can demand a little bit more cash.”

Each competitor at the Ultimate Championships is guaranteed at least US$2,000 with the winner set to earn US$150,000.

Reigning 100m world and Diamond League champion Seville heads the list of 27 Jamaicans set to compete at the event.

Jamaica’s long-serving technical leader Maurice Wilson and former Olympic and world champion Michael Frater will be Jamaica’s two-man delegation in charge of the relay teams.

Men: Oblique Seville, Ackeem Blake, Christopher Taylor, Navasky Anderson, Orlando Bennett, Romaine Beckford, Bryan Levell, Tyler Mason, Demario Prince.

Women: Tina Clayton, Ackera Nugent, Danielle Williams, Lamara Distin, Nickisha Pryce, Brianna Lyston, Rushell Clayton, Shiann Salmon, Jonielle Smith, Ashanti Moore, Ackelia Smith, Demisha Roswell, Megan Simmonds, Sanique Walker, Jodean Williams, Lavanya Williams.

World.title: Ottey cleaves through dexterity competition
World.content:
Cleve Ottey bested all others by a two-second margin in what was an exciting run to the finish.

Cleve Ottey was the winner at the third round of the Point 2 Point Time Attack dexterity series, held on Saturday, August 22, at Overton Plaza, Montego Bay.

“It feels good to win. It’s been a while since I’ve had to put down such a spectacular drive, but it was great,” Ottey told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

And spectacular it was as Ottey held off rivals during the two-lap championship runs, after trading close times all event from said opposition. His Toyota Starlet took blows from familiar names like Maurice Whittingham, Christopher Addison, and Zachary Isaacs. He even had to fend off front-wheel drive charges from Kai Chuck-Dixon and Daren Givans, but in the end Ottey managed to pull out a two-second lead to seal the deal at the end of the night.

“I just settled down, kept my composure, and tried to point and shoot the car. That’s how I got the time,” said Ottey.

Running in reverse order for the championship runs, it was Givans who first did the unthinkable, posting both the fastest front-wheel drive run of the section and the fastest time until then. Once done, the massive crowd was on the edge of their seats to see if the 1:15.307 time could be beaten. It took the might of Whittingham to best the simple Corolla, with an anti-lag snorting 1:13.894. Isaacs, who had been the fastest in the main event by a 10th of a second over Ottey, lowered it even further after a 1:11.919 run. Both men would finish third and second, respectively, as Ottey continued the two-second margin trend, winning overall after completing a 1:09.916.

Givans would head back to Kingston with a class win for front-wheel drive and the respect of the Montegonian fans. Chuck-Dixon claimed the front-wheel drive with limited slip differential class in his Honda Civic. The rear-wheel drive with limited slip differential class went to Isaacs, a small consolation prize for almost winning the event.

“It was a magnificent event for all involved. The runs were superb. The drivers were excellent,” Stephen Mahoney, event organiser, said.

The series heads for conclusion in October.

World.title: ‘Total Fabrication’: TikToker threatened with lawsuit over claims about Dervan Malcolm’s widow
World.content:
At left, late broadcaster Dervan Malcolm and wife Patrice on their wedding day. At right, Milton Wray.

Lawyers representing the widow of late broadcaster Dervan Malcolm have threatened legal action against blogger Milton Wray, otherwise known as “119”, over alleged false and defamatory remarks he made about her on social media in connection with the death of her husband.

The legal team of Patrice Hussey Malcolm says the remarks, published on platforms such as TikTok and Youtube, have caused “significant distress, embarrassment, humiliation and reputational injury” to its client.

“Your statements were not merely criticism or commentary. They constituted a sustained and deliberate campaign of public vilification, harassment, intimidation, bullying and degradation directed at our client,” wrote senior counsel Anthony Williams, managing partner of USIM, Williams and Company Attorneys-At –Law, in a letter to Wray and shared with Observer Online.

Williams noted that the firm has been instructed that “there are ongoing issues and disagreements” within the family of the late Dervan Malcolm, and that an alleged incident was “fabricated and circulated by several persons in an attempt to cause strife with our client and discredit her in the eyes of the public. Our client maintains that these accounts are untrue, misleading, and have no factual basis.”

“It’s a total fabrication and propaganda by the blogger,” Williams claimed in an interview with Observer Online.

In the meantime, the law firm is demanding that Wray immediately seize and desist from “publishing, republishing, repeating or communicating” the allegations against Hussey Malcolm and “immediately remove” the “offending videos” from Tiktok, Youtube and other social media platforms.

Wray is also being demanded to produce a written and verbal apology to Hussey Malcolm and enter into negotiations to pay compensation for the alleged defamation of her, as well as her legal costs, by noon Friday, September 11, 2026.

According to the firm, failure to comply with its demands will result in the company commencing legal proceedings against Wray in the Supreme Court.

World.title: ‘His heart was broken’
World.content:
File photo Aston Coke, father of 10-year-old Shani Coke, speaking with journalists in Troy, Trelawny. (Photo: Kasey Williams)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Aston Coke, the father of slain 10-year-old Shani Coke, died Thursday morning at the Percy Junor Hospital after suffering from a prolonged illness.

It comes just under two weeks after his daughter was laid to rest.

Her partially nude body was found with her throat slashed on July 21. Her murder rocked the usually quiet community of Tyre in Troy, Trelawny.

“He was already gravely ill, and then when his daughter was murdered he took down worse. He was in hospital shortly after the incident and didn’t even get to go to her funeral two weeks ago. His heart was broken,” a family friend told Observer Online.

In a July 22 interview, Aaron Coke said his daughter was well loved and admired by many in her community.

“Her grandmother sent her to the shop, and she did not make it back home. Someone stopped her on the street and disturbed her somehow and slashed her throat… She was loving and caring in the community growing up. Everybody knows her. She knows everyone. She can see you and call you by your full name. She had a sense of humour. She was doing well in school, and she got a lot of academic awards,” said the heartbroken father.

“She decided that she wanted to make something out of herself growing up, because we were driving that into her head, but things just happened overnight,” added Coke, as he alleged that the man believed to have killed his daughter was a habitual offender.

Her alleged killer, Delroy Coke, was mobbed to death while his father was injured during an attack by residents.

World.title: Is Europe winning the ‘fight’? Von der Leyen’s SOTEU, one year on
World.content:
When Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivered her State of the European Union speech last year, the backdrop was chaotic.

Russian drones had just crossed into Polish airspace, Donald Trump was casting doubt on America’s commitment to NATO, and the Commission president herself was facing votes of no confidence. Her answer to this disarray? Europe, she said, was in a fight — and this was its “independence moment.”

A year later, can we say that Europe met that moment? And is it winning the fight or losing it?

To take stock of what the EU has achieved — and where it has fallen short — host Sarah Wheaton is joined by Senior EU policy editor Joanna Roberts, deputy tech editor Laurens Cerulus and Nick Vinocur, our chief foreign affairs correspondent.

Plus, we want to hear from you! We have a survey out and would love to know what you like about the podcast and what we could do differently. The survey will take max five minutes — you can access it here.

Otherwise, you can contact us as always via WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: Everyone wants a line in the State of the European Union speech
World.content:
Some are taking the conventional approach. Last month, almost 200 industry associations and national groups signed a letter addressed to von der Leyen demanding she use her speech to commission an expansive, Mario Draghi-style report into the bloc’s appetite for fossil fuels.

Others are a little more in-your-face. Alcohol lobby group SpiritsEurope has set up shop at Place du Luxembourg, where it has organized four days’ worth of events and — naturally — drinks receptions. It also conducted a competitiveness “temperature check” among its members to see how they are feeling, and to hammer home the point that the Commission could be listening more to the demands of an industry that feels somewhat overlooked.

Von der Leyen “can bend the system to her will,” said SpiritsEurope Director General Mark Titterington. “That’s why we take the speech so seriously.”

“It sets the direction, sets the tempo and helps to condition the environment,” he added. “The words that are in there are pored over for meaning.”

Yet it’s not just the words in the speech that lobbyists and advocates are interested in — it’s the broader message.

“We’re not looking for the president simply to say the word ‘health’,” said Milka Sokolović, director general at EPHA, an EU-wide public health NGO.

World.title: Inside Nigel Farage’s battle to get Reform election-ready
World.content:
Recruiters are also searching for hundreds of prospective peers, which the party believes it might need to prevent the unelected House of Lords from blocking its program for government if Farage does enter Downing Street.

What was always going to be a rush to get battle-ready is taking place under greater urgency amid speculation Andy Burnham, the new Labour prime minister, could trigger an early election, though one is not due until 2029.

Ready or not, here we come

It was late in June that Richard Tice stood on Westminster’s College Green confidently calling for a general election as it became clear that Keir Starmer would be replaced by Burnham.

“Bring it on — the sooner the better,” the deputy Reform leader said, signaling the party was raring to go. That’s not how everyone felt.

“I was sitting there saying no, we’re not,” said one official working on efforts to get election-ready, grimacing and adopting a high-pitched tone to stress just how far from reality this was. They, like others in this piece, were granted anonymity to discuss internal matters.

Those who have participated in the party’s nationwide recruitment tour describe the boot camp-like grillings taking place under a “semi-omerta.”

World.title: EU in space: Going boldly where plenty of people have gone before
World.content:
Just yesterday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen publicly endorsed a proposed space project between Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, with the three satellite makers looking to create a rival to tech trillionaire Elon Musk’s Starlink. It might not be as good, but at least it won’t be owned by a man who names his children by smashing his face into a keyboard.

Alas, the name for the proposed European firms’ space venture is Bromo, which sounds like being told to wait a minute by a man who’s really into crypto.

Von der Leyen was speaking at the International Space Summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron, who wants Europe to develop a crewed (as opposed to crude) spaceflight program within a decade. It’s a bold move, even if rather unlikely given the speed with which things move in Europe.

But let’s say it happens and in 2036, Europeans are regularly flying into space for their holidays to escape what’s become the commonplace searing 45-degree August heat in northern Scandinavia (alas, the Schuman roundabout still isn’t finished in 2036 and can’t be used as a launchpad, so the EU has paved over Luxembourg instead).

What happens if they encounter alien life? Which language will be used to communicate with extraterrestrials? I’m going with German, as it’s direct and intimidating. And what if these visitors from deep space want to invade and have their eye (singular) on Europe? I’m just not sure that Frontex, the EU’s border control agency, has the resources to cope with an alien invasion unless there’s a massive increase in funding in the 2034-2041 Multiannual Financial Framework.

Of course it’s increasingly difficult to know what the EU will look like by the end of 2027, let alone 2036. I’m going with a surprising amount of continuity, as even the far-right governments that have taken over the bloc have found dismantling the bureaucracy far too tiresome and have just left it alone.

World.title: A new path to power for the far right: Don’t moderate. Stay radical.
World.content:
The AfD has moved in the opposite direction, doubling down on anti-immigration, anti-Islam rhetoric and its pro-Russian stance — and still surging at the ballot box.

With the far right polling strongly ahead of major elections expected this year and next in Sweden, France, Spain, Poland and Italy, the AfD’s breakthrough is reverberating far beyond eastern Germany. It raises a more troubling possibility for Europe’s establishment: that the next wave of populist challengers may see less reason to emulate Meloni or Le Pen — and more incentive to copy the AfD.

The election results in Saxony-Anhalt are proof that “nationalist and identitarian policies” are “exactly the kind of policy we need to win elections and save our countries,” Afonso Gonçalves, the leader of the ultranationalist Portuguese movement Reconquista, said.

The Italian former general Roberto Vannacci, who is challenging Meloni from the far-right flank she used to occupy, also cheered the win. “Now, keep calling us extremists,” he posted on X. “If half the population stands with AfD, the accusations of extremism, by definition, evaporate and vanish.”

Roberto Vannacci gives a press briefing in Rome on June 13, 2026. | Filippo Monteforte/AFP via Getty Images

From across the Atlantic, U.S. President Donald Trump weighed in on his social media platform Truth Social: “Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night. They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations, which have hurt Germany so badly. THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore! MGGA!!!”

Meanwhile, in Italy and France, Le Pen and Meloni have abstained from commenting.

World.title: Ireland aims to avoid the rough with golf-mad Trump
World.content:
The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the behind-the-scenes preparations for a trip that has been on Ireland’s radar since St. Patrick’s Day nearly six months ago. When Taoiseach Micheál Martin visited the White House, he agreed with Trump that he probably should visit his County Clare resort in remote Doonbeg this weekend as it hosts the country’s premier golf tournament.

Once Trump’s Qatari-donated Air Force One lands at Dublin Airport, he’s expected to be flown by Marine One helicopter into Phoenix Park, a vast urban oasis that was once the hunting grounds for the British ruling elite — and today provides an ideal one-stop shop for diplomacy behind easily secured walls.

Confining Trump to the Phoenix Park has meant shutting down one of the biggest urban parks in Europe, including one of Dublin’s top tourist attractions, the zoo, since Thursday night.

But it also sidestepped the U.S. government’s initial wish to have the center of Dublin shut down so Trump could visit the future site of a new American embassy. That had been the hope of Trump’s ambassador to Ireland, a New Jersey property developer and avid golfer named Edward Walsh.

“A groundbreaking ceremony in the middle of the capital would have been a security and logistical nightmare,” the Irish official said.

It’s still going to take an estimated 4,000 security personnel — including a reported 1,000 U.S. Secret Service agents and other American security staff operating anti-drone weaponry — to keep protesters and any would-be assassins out of range when Trump meets Irish leaders in Phoenix Park before flying across to Doonbeg.

World.title: Tusk warns of future attacks after ‘direct threat’ averted at Poland-Ukraine border
World.content:
Tusk did not provide any further details about the nature of the threat or which of the 18 border crossings between Poland and Ukraine was affected.

The prime minister added that the incident was just a taste of what is to come and noted he had received a “fairly precise report” from the CIA regarding possible events in the coming months.

“We must anticipate various scenarios; both Poland and all of Europe need to ⁠be ​prepared for different possibilities concerning the ​situation not only on the Russian-Ukrainian front but also along the EU’s eastern ​flank.”

The incident at the border crossing between Moldova and Ukraine’s Odesa region left two people dead, causing President Maia Sandu to call for further European air defense support for Ukraine.

Russia also struck a Moldova-Ukraine border crossing in August.

“As you know, Russia has already resorted to provocative attacks on border crossings—for instance, in Moldova. We expect similar actions targeting border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” said Tusk.

World.title: 25 years on, 9/11 continues to cast a long shadow over the US
World.content:
A quarter of a century after hijacked planes struck New York, Washington and Pennsylvania, the attacks of 11 September 2001 remain lodged in the American psyche more firmly than almost any other event of the past 25 years.

 

A new Ipsos poll finds that roughly half of US adults, unprompted, name 9/11 among the most significant events of their lifetime — ahead of the Covid-19 pandemic, the elections of Barack Obama and Donald Trump, and Hurricane Katrina of 2005.

Nine in ten say the attacks changed the country "a great deal" or "quite a bit," and most Americans can still recall exactly where they were when they heard the news.

Yet despite that lasting wound, only around one in ten plan to actively mark Friday's anniversary - for those that do a moment of silence and the flying of the flag are the most common gestures.

Two planes flew into the World Trade Center in New York on 9/11 killing 2,977 people. 11 September, 2001. Chao Soi Cheong/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Confidence in the government's ability to prevent another attack has also declined steadily since the record highs recorded in the days after 2001.

What's planned for the 25th anniversary?

Commemorations will unfold across the three sites. In New York, victims' relatives will gather on the Memorial plaza to read aloud the names of those killed, punctuated by seven moments of silence — one more than in previous years, added to honour those who have since died of 9/11-related illnesses.

Ceremonies will also take place at the Pentagon in Arlington and at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

People were forced to flee as the streets around lower Manhattan were covered in a thick ash after the twin towers collapsed. 11 September, 2001. SUZANNE PLUNKETT/2001 AP

Trump will not attend the New York ceremony this year, opting to speak at the Pentagon instead.

Vice President JD Vance will go to Ground Zero - the area where the first search for survivors in began - while former presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama, Bill Clinton and George W. Bush are also expected to attend the New York event.

Why is it called 9/11?

For some, the shorthand can seem puzzling. The date was the eleventh day of the ninth month but the American convention of writing dates with the month-first leads to "9/11" which also mirrors how the emergency number 911 is dialled in the US.

How many Europeans died in 9/11?

While nearly 3,000 Americans died in the event, hundreds of foreign nationals were also among the dead. Estimates place the number of non-American victims at roughly 372, drawn from around 60 countries.

Britain suffered the heaviest toll of any country besides the US, with 67 nationals killed. Germany, Italy, Ireland and other European states also lost citizens, many of them financial workers employed at or visiting the World Trade Center.

Over 2,600 pieces of the World Trade Center were distributed across the US and 11 other countries including this display in London. FILE AP Photo

American financial services firm Cantor Fitzgerald occupied floors 101 through 105 of the World Trade Center's North Tower, directly above the impact zone of American Airlines Flight 11.

The company employed a number of Europeans and in total 658 employees were killed that day - the largest loss of life of any individual firm.

Number of Europeans killed in 9/11 attacks:

United Kingdom — 67

Germany — 11

Italy — 10

Ireland — 6

Poland — 6

Portugal — 5

France — 4

Romania — 4

FR Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) — 2

Sweden — 2

Switzerland — 2

Belarus, Belgium, Lithuania, Moldova, Netherlands, Russia, Spain, Ukraine - 1 per country

What happened to the perpetrators?

All 19 hijackers died carrying out the attacks - 15 were Saudi nationals, two from the United Arab Emirates, and one from Egypt and one from Lebanon.

Behind them stood the wider terrorist al-Qaeda network who claimed direct responsibility for the attacks. Osama bin Laden, the group's leader, evaded capture for almost a decade before being killed by US special forces in Pakistan in 2011.

His eventual successor, Ayman al-Zawahiri, was killed in a drone strike in Kabul in 2022.

The self-described "mastermind" of the plot, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, was captured in Pakistan in 2003 and has been held at Guantánamo Bay since 2006 charged with the first-degree murder of 2,977 people.

A US military judge has now set his long-delayed trial to begin in June 2028, alongside several alleged co-conspirators, following a collapsed 2024 plea deal that would have seen the men admit guilt in exchange for the death penalty being removed from sentencing options.

Proceedings have dragged for over two decades amid disputes over evidence obtained through the use of torture, including waterboarding, at secret CIA sites.

World.title: Can the ECB rate hike stop an inflation shock driven by energy costs?
World.content:
Europe is facing a squeeze from two directions: more expensive energy and higher borrowing costs intended to contain the inflation that the same energy shock created.

 

The European Central Bank raised its key three interest rates by 0.25% on Thursday, bringing the deposit rate to 2.5%.

It is the second rate hike in three months, and the reason is visible on every forecourt in Europe.

Brent crude climbed back above $100 a barrel on Wednesday as the conflict between the United States and Iran continued to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

The pressure is arguably sharper in gas, where the Dutch TTF benchmark, the reference price for the European market, has rallied by 190% since the start of the year.

Eurozone inflation accelerated to 3.3% in August from 2.9% in July, with energy prices rising 14.3% over the year against 10.3% a month earlier.

Which raises the question that hangs over the whole decision.

Interest rates do not produce barrels of oil or cubic metres of gas. So what exactly is a higher deposit rate meant to achieve?

What higher rates can and cannot reach

Christine Lagarde described the decision as a "no-brainer".

In her press conference she said that "the conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period."

A central bank cannot reopen a shipping lane. It cannot refill a gas storage facility before winter.

What it can do is cool demand at home, so that an imported price shock does not turn into a domestic one. The evidence so far suggests the shock has not yet made that jump.

Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, actually edged down in August to 2.4% from 2.5%.

Services inflation, the measure the ECB watches most closely for signs of domestic overheating, eased to 3.0% from 3.3%.

"Wages do not show a material response to the energy shock at this stage," Lagarde said.

The ECB is not responding to what has happened. It is responding to what it fears will happen next.

"While more restrictive monetary policy is not an effective response to short term, supply driven inflation shocks, the ECB is moving in this direction to combat inflation that is becoming more structural," Emeritus Professor Joe Nellis, head of economic research at the accountancy and advisory firm MHA, said in a note.

What began in the spring as a war premium on crude has now lasted long enough to work its way into contracts, transport costs, insurance and household expectations.

The real target is expectations

Headline inflation is still seen at 3.0% this year, but the forecasts for 2027 and 2028 were both revised upwards, to 2.5% and 2.1% respectively.

Neither headline nor core inflation returns cleanly to 2% by the end of the horizon.

"The energy shock could intensify further, and its effect on other prices and wages could be stronger than currently expected," Lagarde said, adding that "gas prices, in particular, could increase in the event of further supply disruptions or an unusually cold winter coinciding with low storage levels."

The ECB's own wage tracker already points to negotiated wage growth ticking up to 2.7% in the first half of 2027.

That is the mechanism the Bank is trying to interrupt. If workers expect prices to keep rising and employers expect to be able to pass costs on, the oil shock stops being an oil shock and becomes an inflation regime.

"Inflation should remain well above target into next year, as higher gas and food prices put additional upward pressure on the index," said Leo Barincou, senior economist at Oxford Economics.

Could ECB interest rates hit 3%?

The most consequential part of Thursday was arguably what Lagarde did not say.

She declined to push back against market pricing for further tightening, noting only that the council had not debated the path ahead and that markets were doing "their job" while the ECB did its own.

Claus Vistesen, chief eurozone economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, treated that silence as a hawkish signal.

"We now think the ECB will shift its policy rate more decisively into restrictive territory over the next six months, with a rate hike in December followed by another in February, taking the deposit rate to 3.00%," he said.

Oliver Rakau, chief Germany economist at Oxford Economics, drew a similar conclusion.

"The bigger take away from today was how low the bar to further tightening is," he wrote, while noting that "contained underlying inflation pressures continue to favour a reactive or data dependent approach to policy setting from the ECB".

Can Europe afford the squeeze?

The cost of preventing persistent inflation is that higher rates also restrain activity already burdened by expensive energy.

Further interest rate increases could squeeze indebted households, weaken housing markets and make business investment more expensive.

Small companies could delay or abandon projects as financing costs rise.

Yet, the ECB has upgraded its growth outlook for this year and next.

Technology-related business activity and German fiscal support offer positive impacts on growth. That gives policymakers room to act, although it does not eliminate the pressure on borrowers.

The question is therefore not simply whether the ECB raises rates again, but how long higher rates remain necessary. Monetary policy can limit inflation’s spread.

Whether it succeeds without damaging growth will depend heavily on how quickly Europe’s energy pressures ease.

World.title: Moonlight, phone screens and standby LEDs: Is your bedroom too bright?
World.content:
Light pollution during night sleep — as little as moonlight or light coming through a door gap — takes a toll on human hearts, according to a new study published in the European Heart Journal.

 

“Exposure to higher levels of light at nighttime is linked to cardiac remodelling,” Lu Qi from Tulane University, New Orleans, USA, who led the research, said in a press release. “This is where the structure and function of the heart changes and we typically see it in response to chronic stress or injury to the heart.”

While that’s how the human body adapts to that stress, “ultimately it weakens the heart and can lead to heart failure,” he said.

Therefore, keeping bedrooms as dark as possible “should be considered as one of the potential strategies for preventing heart disease by clinicians and policy makers,” Qi said.

The study included 11,071 people who were exposed to different levels of light overnight for a week, from near total darkness to varying levels of light up to light equivalent to a phone screen at low brightness on light coming through a cracked door.

Three years later, participants were given a cardiovascular magnetic resonance scan to examine any potential changes to the structure and function of their hearts.

The results showed that participants who were exposed to the highest levels of nighttime light saw the walls of the left chamber of their heart thicken, reducing the space inside the ventricle. There were also signs that the heart’s ability to flex during a heartbeat was reduced — an early indication of heart dysfunction.

“Darkness deserves recognition as a vital sign, as essential to cardiovascular health as blood pressure control and clean air,” an accompanying editorial professor, Thomas Münzel, from University Medical Center Mainz, Germany and colleagues said.

They turned to clinicians, urging them to ask about sleep environment: “how dark the bedroom is, whether the patient works night shifts, and how much screen use occurs after sunset,” they said, advising using blackout curtains, warm-coloured bedside lighting, and covering the small standby LEDs on household electronics.

Municipalities also have a role to play, with light pollution being “one of the few environmental hazards that cities can control directly and affordably,” they said, listing shielded fixtures, warm-spectrum bulbs, and dimming or motion-activated streetlights as “energy-efficient, and climate-friendly” ways to reduce light exposure.

World.title: From Galápagos penguins to giant daisy trees: Powerful El Niño could decimate rare wildlife
World.content:
The prediction that this season’s El Niño phenomenon will be stronger than normal has alarmed the Ecuadorian scientific community, which has warned of its impact on the flora and fauna of the Galápagos Islands.

 

Home to the highest concentration of species not found elsewhere on Earth, the archipelago is made up of more than 230 islands, of which only four are inhabited. It is located in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, 1,000 kilometres off the coast of Ecuador.

The climatic phenomenon occurs periodically and in the equatorial Pacific is characterised by an increase in sea temperature and intense rainfall. Its strength is determined by measuring the water temperature in that area and comparing it to the normal average. If it is 2 degrees Celsius above normal, it is considered “very strong”.

The sea temperature will be about 2.2°C above normal, according to the latest projection from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), which means that “the impact will be significant”, says Franklin Ormaza, a professor and researcher at the Faculty of Maritime Engineering and Marine Sciences of the Higher Polytechnic School of the Coast (ESPOL).

Will El Niño put Galápagos wildlife at risk?

Animals and fish will be at risk because as the water temperature rises, “plankton, algae, and smaller fish species, which are food for larger marine animals, practically disappear,” explains Washington Tapia, director of Biodiversa Ecuador, a conservation organisation in the archipelago.

He specifies that the species most at risk are the iconic Galápagos penguins, blue-footed boobies, petrels, flightless cormorants, albatrosses, and even sea lions. Coral colonies could also be seriously affected, as could tuna fishing.

In the absence of food, “animal colonies stop reproducing”, disperse in search of food, and die of starvation in the process, explains scientist Gustavo Jiménez, from the Charles Darwin Foundation.

FILE - Saltwater succulents grow by the water on Bartolome Island, Ecuador in the Galapagos on June 7, 2024. AP Photo/Alie Skowronski, File

If the phenomenon occurs with the expected magnitude, the archipelago’s vertebrate population could decrease by at least 20 per cent this year, Jiménez adds.

One of the most closely monitored species in the islands, the Galápagos penguins, serves as a marker of the impact of this climate phenomenon on the archipelago’s fauna.

According to data from the Charles Darwin Foundation, after the 1998 El Niño – one of the most powerful and destructive cycles – only 400 of the 1,300 existing Galápagos penguins remained.

Effects of El Niño on Galápagos flora

If El Niño strikes with the expected force, the last three remaining Scalesia forests – dominated by 20-metre-tall giant daisy trees – could be at risk of disappearing, scientist Heinke Jager of the Charles Darwin Foundation says.

Opuntia cacti, which grow along the seashore, would also be threatened.

These plants, found only in the Galápagos Islands, support various ecosystems of insects, birds and other smaller plants that are part of the archipelago’s unique biodiversity.

Jager explains that “these species need human support” because the heavy rains brought by El Niño will cause the territory they occupy to be overrun by invasive plants, such as blackberries, which have shorter reproductive cycles.

Therefore, they have organised a plan that includes the eradication of invasive plants, the collection of seeds and the creation of nurseries to conserve threatened species. The Ecuadorian government, foundations, and nongovernmental organisations working in the archipelago are participating in the program.

The Galápagos Islands were declared a Natural World Heritage Site in 1978 for their unique animal and plant species, which served as the basis for the English scientist Charles Darwin to develop his theory of evolution.
