World.title: Leaf-peeping in Europe: The best destinations for autumn colours
World.content:
The northeastern United States might get most of the attention when autumn arrives, but Europe can certainly rival it as a destination for "leaf peeping".

 

While the famous fall colours of New England can be spectacular, the window to see them is notoriously short and unpredictable. Europe, meanwhile, has the advantage of everything from high Alpine peaks and deep river valleys to vast forests, meaning autumn arrives at different times across the continent.

The result? If you know where to look, you can chase fiery reds, golden yellows and burnt oranges for weeks – and sometimes months – rather than gambling on one perfect weekend.

Here are 10 of the best places in Europe to see autumn foliage this year.

Lake Bled, Slovenia

Lake Bled is one of Slovenia’s most popular destinations – and for good reason. It offers some of the most spectacular scenery in the whole country and is also home to the nation’s only natural island.

It can be very busy in the summer, so autumn is an ideal time to visit. While the water will likely be too chilly for casual swimmers in the "-ber" months, it’s possible to hire a rowing boat and admire the richly-coloured leaves around the lake.

If you’re more of a walker, you can circumnavigate the lake in about an hour and a half, while stopping to snap pictures of the stunning foliage, of course.

Bavarian Alps, Germany

The Bavarian Alps are beautiful all year round, and tourists flock every season to see the majestic Neuschwanstein Castle.

It’s a fantastic spot for an autumn break, especially, though, not because of the varied elevation here.

Autumn colours start as early as September, high near the Zugspitze summit, before heading down the mountainsides to the lower valleys, which still boast red and orange hues into November.

Stay in the town of Füssen if you can, as it’s an ideal access point to the many trails which crisscross the mountains here.

Bavaria comes into its own in the autumn, and Neuschwanstein Castle is perhaps even more impressive than usual Ilia Bronskiy/Unsplash

Lake District, England

Although it’s only been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017, England's Lake District has been inspiring visitors for centuries, including Romantic poets like Samuel Taylor Coleridge to William Wordsworth.

Buttermere is a particularly beautiful spot in autumn. Arrive early for a walk around the lake, when the water is often calm enough to reflect the surrounding hills and foliage.

Coniston Water is another autumn highlight, with woodland trails, mountain views and a mixture of evergreen and deciduous trees providing plenty of rich colour.

Transylvania, Romania

There’s more to Transylvania than vampires – and autumn is the ideal time to discover that for yourself.

As well as the must-do of visiting Bran Castle – also known as Dracula’s Castle – in spooky season, the trees across the Carpathian Mountains turn exquisite hues as autumn progresses, and the varying altitude here means the colours last a long time.

Stay in Brașov, the ideal place to soak in the atmosphere after exploring the mountains. Plenty of restaurants set up heaters outside and offer guests blankets so you can warm up while making the most of the crisp autumnal air.

Perthshire, Scotland

Think of autumn colours, and Scotland will probably come to mind.

If it’s on your list for an autumn trip, head to Perthshire, which has one foot in the Highlands and one in the Lowlands.

Not only is it home to the Meikleour Beech Hedge, officially the tallest hedge in the world, which turns red and orange in the autumn, but there’s also the National Trust-owned The Hermitage, a beautiful, colourful stretch of forest with waterfalls and ruins which has to be seen to be believed.

Families will enjoy a visit to the Enchanted Forest in Pitlochry. From early October to the start of November, the spectacle of light and sound brings added magic to the region’s autumnal woodlands.

The Dolomites are particularly beautiful in the autumn due to a multitude of larch trees which turn golden as the season progresses Federica Galli/Unsplash

The Dolomites, Italy

The Dolomites are on many a hiker’s bucket list, but they also make for an excellent autumn destination come September.

As well as spotting the larch trees, which turn a glowing golden colour from October until the heavy snow starts in November, be sure to gaze at the autumn light hitting the dramatic rock faces.

The season’s long shadows also cast an otherworldly glow at sunset, while the majestic foliage is reflected in Lago di Sorapis and Lago di Braies, both well worth a visit.

Loire Valley, France

World-renowned for its wine, the Loire Valley is particularly beautiful in autumn. As well as sampling the region’s famous vintages, you can admire the vineyards as their leaves turn rich shades of red, orange and purple, especially around the valley’s many grand châteaux.

Château de Chaumont-sur-Loire is a particular favourite in autumn, when its grounds are decorated with pumpkins and squash, adding a wonderfully seasonal touch to the already spectacular gardens and historic setting.

Lapland, Finland

Many tourists associate Lapland with all things Christmas, but it’s also a fabulous place for an autumn break.

While Rovaniemi, the region’s capital, is packed full of strikingly coloured trees, the Northern Lights are actually particularly strong in the fall. You might even get the chance to see the aurora borealis reflected off Lapland’s many lakes, which are flanked by autumnal foliage.

While it’s definitely not as cold here as in the dead of winter, it can get to below freezing, so be sure to pack clothes for winter and not just one or two extra layers.

Douro Valley, Portugal

Most people associate fall foliage with dense forests, but Portugal’s famous wine region offers a different kind of autumn spectacle, with miles of terraced vineyards turning fiery shades of red, orange and yellow after the harvest.

The Douro’s mild climate means the colours can linger well into November, making it one of Europe’s longest autumn displays.

Base yourself in Porto for day trips or stay at a local quinta – or wine estate – then take a river cruise through the valley. From the water, the vast, flame-coloured terraces are particularly spectacular.

Croatia is perhaps best known as a summer destination, but the Plitvice Lakes National Park is stunning in the autumn Joshua Humpfer/Unsplash

Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia

Croatia might be best known for its summer beaches and sailing, but head inland in autumn, and Plitvice Lakes offers a completely different side of the country.

The national park’s 16 turquoise lakes tumble into one another through a series of waterfalls, surrounded by dense beech and oak forests that turn brilliant shades of yellow, orange and red. Because the lakes sit at different elevations, the colours appear progressively, helping to stretch the autumn season.

Stay in a guesthouse near one of the park entrances and visit in late October or early November, when the summer crowds have disappeared, and the whole park feels significantly more peaceful.

World.title: Anthropic says AI could bring both 15% growth and mass unemployment by 2030
World.content:
The company behind Claude has put numbers on its own disruption.

 

Anthropic's economics team released a technical paper and an interactive tool on Wednesday, modelling the economy as bundles of tasks that AI can leave alone, assist with, automate outright or create anew, then tracing what different rates of capability and adoption would mean for growth, wages and jobs in the US.

The authors are explicit that these are not forecasts as the paper reads "the scenarios are not predictions and we attach no probabilities to them."

In the modest scenario, AI turns out to be a minor technology.

GDP in 2030 sits 1.6% above where it would be without AI, growth reaches 2.4% a year, and cognitive employment, meaning management, professional, sales and office work, falls half a percent. Unemployment barely moves.

The substantial scenario doubles the economy's normal growth rate to 5.4% as AI becomes capable of half of all knowledge work, though most tasks are still done without its assistance.

GDP lands 8.3% higher, cognitive employment falls 3.9% and unemployment among office workers rises to 4.5%. Wages diverge as cognitive pay dips slightly while everyone else gains nearly 6%.

The extreme scenario has no precedent.

Annual growth hits 15.4%, GDP finishes 32.4% above the no-AI path and the economy would double roughly every four and a half years.

However, cognitive employment collapses by 21.5%, unemployment among those workers reaches 17.9% and joblessness across the whole workforce hits 11.9%, worse than a typical recession. Office wages fall 11.5% while other wages jump 33.6%.

The starkest number is who collects the proceeds.

Labour's share of national income drops from 60% to 45.2%, with capital income rising more than 80%.

The machines would make the economy vastly richer while shifting the gains decisively from workers to asset owners.

What the public thinks and what the boss said

Anthropic paired the model with a Morning Consult survey of US adults fielded in August.

According to the paper, the median respondent's expectations map onto the substantial scenario, implying GDP roughly 8% higher by 2030 and cognitive employment down about 4%.

That leaves the company's own CEO as an outlier given that Dario Amodei warned in May 2025 that up to half of entry-level office jobs could disappear within five years, with unemployment reaching 10% to 20%, figures that sit squarely in the extreme scenario rather than the middle one.

Adoption, not capability, may prove decisive.

"If AI can do amazing things but nobody uses it, then it's not going to have an economic impact," said Anton Korinek, who leads Anthropic's transformative AI economic studies.

Co-founder Jack Clark expects rapid technical progress but slower uptake, telling NPR that "diffusion of the technology will likely be more challenging than people think."

The scenario that is not there

What the economic model does not include has drawn attention of its own.

Every path assumes an economy that still functions, with no scenario for AI going badly wrong in the ways the industry itself keeps warning about.

That gap looked pointed this week as Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned on Tuesday and published a thread explaining why.

"Neither company is acting responsibly," Coxon wrote, adding that "they are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence."

He also claimed colleagues privately believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade" while executives soften their language publicly, and described the industry's approach as "a hubristic gamble that should not be launched from a private company's Slack."

Anthropic has itself disclosed that Claude models gained unauthorised access to the real systems of three organisations this year. Whether that belongs in an economic model is a fair question.

When asked, Claude's own answer is that it does not.

World.title: Japanese company unveils 'robot ambulance' for on-site humanoid repairs
World.content:
Tokyo’s streets could soon see a new kind of ambulance, one built not for humans but for humanoid robots.

 

Japanese IT giant GMO Internet Group revealed a van designed to carry engineers, repair equipment, replacement parts and a spare humanoid robot to a site.

The company says it is the first in Japan designed specifically for humanoid robot maintenance.

“The humanoid 'ambulance' carries the replacement humanoid to the site and replaces it with the damaged humanoid,” said Shota Takizawa, an engineer at GMO Air.

If repairs cannot be completed there, the damaged robot can be taken back to a repair base while the replacement takes its place.

GMO AIR said it developed the service after experiencing disruptions when damaged humanoids had to be sent away for repair.

“Learning from that experience, we came up with the idea of providing replacement humanoids,” Tomohiro Uchida, CEO of GMO Air, said.

Despite its ambulance-style markings and purple roof lights, the vehicle is effectively a mobile repair workshop. Its interior has space for robots, laptops and maintenance equipment.

There is currently one vehicle based at GMO’s Tokyo headquarters, but the company says it could add more vehicles and bases if demand increases.

“When humanoids become more popular, this kind of service will be needed,” Takizawa said.

Japan in the global humanoid robot race

The launch comes as competition over humanoid robots intensifies, particularly between China and the United States.

China has built a large humanoid manufacturing industry backed by government investment and domestic supply chains, while US companies are competing strongly in AI and advanced robotics.

McKinsey estimates the market for general-purpose robotics could reach about $370 billion (€315bn) by 2040.

Japan, long a major industrial robotics producer, is now trying to strengthen its position in AI-powered robotics.

In June, the Japanese government set a target of introducing around 10 million robots by 2040 and expanding their deployment across 18 sectors, including healthcare, food services and manufacturing.

For more on this story, watch the video in the media player above.

World.title: Podcast: Eco-anger, France in space, world's first photograph
World.content:
A climate expert experiences eco-anxiety firsthand after living through France's hottest summer on record. France tries to find its place in the new space race. And the story of the earliest known photograph still visible today.

Advertising

Eco-anxiety is on the rise in France after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves led to wildfires, scorched crops and the deaths of at least 7,000 people as well as livestock and birds. Juliette Decq, a climate adaptation consultant, says fear is a normal response to the reality people are now facing. A mother of two young children, she experienced that reality firsthand when her own home became unsafe. She talks about her anger over France’s lack of preparedness, not least in schools, but also about the solidarity she witnessed in her local community as they helped people protect themselves. Eco-anger, she says, can be a force for change. (Listen @0')

Historically a leader in Europe’s space programme, France is reassessing its role in space. Although French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on the International Space Station, France’s space ambitions haven’t focused on human space flight. But as the US and China ramp up their Moon missions and space becomes increasingly industrialised, France is looking to find its place. Space policy analyst Xavier Pasco explains how Europe is positioning itself as a regulator in a rapidly changing sector that has, until now, remained largely unchecked. (Listen @20'10'')

French inventor Nicéphore Niépce took the earliest surviving photograph in July 1827: a scene from a window that might have taken days to make. He fell into obscurity, and the photo itself was lost. Now it's returning to France, as part of a celebration of 200 years of photography in his honour. (Listen @14'15'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Why are European banks moving their gold out of the US?
World.content:
The Netherlands and France have moved their gold out of US vaults. Part of the reason is fear over US reliability, but equally important is the need to have their gold closer to home in the event of a crisis.

Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where around half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security.

To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the US as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane.

The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move some 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis.

The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness".

France also removed all its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although the Bank of France governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time it was not politically motivated.

The Dutch have moved their gold to the Bank of England Image: Peter Nicholls/REUTERS

Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns over the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy towards the EU, including threats to annex part of its territory in Greenland.

The gold rush

Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, says that for European central banks, outright seizure of their assets is an "extremely remote risk". However, he says there are growing concerns over ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty.

"The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he told DW.

Krishnan Gopau from the World Gold Council says that in general, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs.

A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-ton average over the preceding decade.

Gopau says that because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset.

"As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he says.

The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the US and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held, so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis.

Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location.

"Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximise resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," says Tillett.

Gopaul says reserve management has become "incredibly important" and that while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub which moves fast.

He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the UK is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market."

"The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he says. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold."

The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion).

The US question

While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making.

Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries.

That decision seems to be driven by concern over US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors.

Tillett says gold remains sensitive to decisions by the US federal reserve and that general concern over US financial markets means gold holders are looking to move their assets.

As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric around Greenland and continued veiled threats towards the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around.

US President Trump's threats against Greenland alarmed EU leaders Image: Federico Parra/Odd Andersen/AFP

Yet the US, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved around 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017, it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the US.

Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves."

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

World.title: Spanish lawmakers back citizenship for Sahrawis
World.content:
Spanish lawmakers approved a bill that could give citizenship to tens of thousands of Sahrawis and their descendants, amid tense ties with Morocco. The legislation must now pass the senate.

Spanish lawmakers on Thursday voted to grant citizenship to people born in Western Sahara under Spanish colonization — a region now that is now largely controlled by Morocco.

The move could test Madrid's already delicate relations with Rabat, especially after the border crisis in Ceuta.

The lower house approved the bill by:

In favor: 168

Against: 31

Abstentions: 145

The legislation would grant Spanish nationality to Sahrawis born before September 29, 1977, and allow their descendants to obtain citizenship through naturalization.

Estimates of those eligible range from around 70,000 to more than 100,000.

The legislation must now pass the senate to become law.

Many Sahrawis live in refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, or elsewhere abroad [FILE: February 25, 2025] Image: Juan Carlos Rojas/picture alliance

Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara

Spain's ruling Socialist Party and its left-wing coalition partner Sumar supported the measure, while the conservative People's Party abstained and far-right Vox opposed it.

Sumar lawmaker Tesh Sidi, the first woman of Sahrawi origin to serve in parliament, said the legislation restores the "Spanish national identity card to those Sahrawis who once held ​and from whom this state took it away."

Spain controlled Western Sahara until 1976. Morocco claims sovereignty over the territory, while an indigenous resistance group, the Polisario Front, seeks independence.

Morocco occupies almost all of the territory. Meanwhile, the Polisario Front across the border in the Algerian town of Tindouf, where tens of thousands of displaced Saharawi people live in refugee camps.

The region remains on the United Nations' list of non-self-governing territories.

How the Ceuta influx raised tensions

The vote comes amid renewed tensions between Madrid and Rabat following a large influx of migrants into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta in July.

Scores of migrants died in their attempt to reach EU territory, most by drowning.

Western Sahara dispute: Morocco's gamble won global support To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Although most of those who breached Ceuta's borders have returned, thousands remain, many of them unaccompanied minors living in dire conditions.

The incident caused a major rift among EU member states, most publicly between Spain's left-wing government and Italy's far-right leadership.

World.title: Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with UAE
World.content:
Algeria said that it was closing its airspace and severing ties with the United Arab Emirates. Algiers accuses Abu Dhabi of destabilizing countries such as Libya, Sudan and Mali.

Algeria severed diplomatic ties with the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, citing what it described as "provocative and hostile acts."

The Algerian Defense Ministry said the country would close its airspace to the UAE beginning on Friday.

However, commercial flights to and from Algiers will be allowed to continue until the end of 2026.

Relations between the two countries have been strained for years over the UAE's expanding influence in northern and western Africa.

What did Algeria and the UAE say about the decision?

The Algerian Foreign Ministry said that it had made the decision "after exhausting all avenues to preserve bilateral relations" with the Gulf country.

It added that the UAE had "persisted in its actions, reaching a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable."

Algiers said it had given the UAE's ambassador 48 hours to comply with the decision to cut ties.

The Emirati Foreign Ministry said that it hoped that the decision would be temporary.

"The UAE expresses hope that this decision will be temporary, in a manner that preserves the fraternal ties between the two brotherly peoples," the ministry said in a statement.

It said that it "affirms the UAE's appreciation for the brotherly Algerian people and its pride in the bonds ​that unite the two peoples, particularly through the Algerian community residing in the UAE and Algerian visitors."

Following the announcement, Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic advisor to UAE leader Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, said that diplomatic relations should be based on "rationality, communication and clarity of interests" rather than "riddles and signals that require decoding."

He did not explicitly mention Algeria in his post on X.

Algerian President Abdelmajid Tebboune has accused the UAE of contributing to armed conflicts in the region [FILE: 18 August, 2024] Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What are the tensions between Algeria and the UAE?

Algeria has in the past accused Abu Dhabi of working to destabilize countries in northern Africa and the Sahel such as Libya, Mali, and Sudan.

The UAE has been accused of supporting the RSF paramilitary in Sudan's civil war, a charge it denies.

It also backs former warlord Khalifa Haftar's Tobruk-based administration in eastern Libya, a rival to the UN-recognized government in Tripoli.

In July, Algerian President Abdelmajid Tebboune harshly criticized the UAE for its influence in other countries, saying "wherever they set foot, blood flows."

"We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country."

Algeria also severed its diplomatic ties with neighboring Morocco in 2021, accusing Rabat of supporting Amazigh separatists in the coastal Kabylia region and amid longstanding tensions over the territory of Western Sahara.

World.title: Several killed in coach crash in eastern Switzerland
World.content:
Several people were killed and others injured in a tourist bush crash near the alpine village of Susch in Switzerland's eastern canton of Graubünden.

Several people were killed and others injured in a tourist bush crash near the alpine village of Susch in Switzerland's eastern canton of Graubünden, police said on Thursday.

Local police said that emergency response teams had been dispatched to the site of the crash.



Dutch media reported that the bus was carrying tourists from the Netherlands.

"These ​are Dutch ‌customers of [Dutch tour operator] OAD. We cannot yet say how many ​people ⁠have been killed or injured," a spokeswoman for Dutch travel association ANVR told the newspaper De Telegraaf.

De Telegraaf reported that 48 people were aboard the bus. The number has not been confirmed by police.

The crash occurred on the road between Susch and the nearby village of Zernez, where the bus collided with a guardrail around 4:45 p.m. local time (1445 UTC), according to Swiss broadcaster SRF.

The broadcaster reported that multiple helicopters were deployed as part of rescue operations.

Swiss President Guy Parmelin expressed his condolences in a post on X.

"I am deeply shocked and dismayed by today’s tragic accident involving a Dutch coach in Graubünden," he said. "I offer my sincere condolences to the families of those who lost their lives."

"The relevant Swiss authorities will ensure that a comprehensive and thorough investigation is carried out to establish all the circumstances surrounding this accident."

More to come…

World.title: Digital data leeches: Trading on our profiles
World.content:
US tech companies gather, link, and sell more and more information about their users. The scandal involving the dating app Grindr shows how easy it is for highly sensitive data to fall into the wrong hands.

Everyone has secrets. Things they wouldn't tell just anyone – except, perhaps, their dating app. What sort of partner they're looking for. Where they go to look for them. Their sexual preferences, maybe, or details about their health.

This information is meant to help the app find suitable matches. Selling the details on to other companies is not in the users' interest.

But this is what allegedly happened with Grindr, a dating app explicitly aimed at the LGBTQ+ community. Around 12,000 app users in Britain sued the company, which they said had shared highly sensitive personal information with advertisers — even, in some cases, a user's HIV status.

The lawsuit, filed in 2024, was settled earlier this week. Grindr has agreed to pay the claimants a total of 26 million pounds (€30 million; $35 million) – but stresses that this is not an admission of liability. Grindr continues to dispute the allegations, there has been no legal judgement.

Grindr, a dating platform aimed at (mostly men in) the LGBTQ+ community, is alleged to have passed on sensitive personal data Image: Andre M. Chang/ZUMAPRESS.com/picture alliance

What happens to the data you entrust to apps?

This latest case is just one of many that raise the bigger question of what actually happens to the information we entrust to our apps on a daily basis.

For users, an app is primarily just a helpful product. But they are often supported by cloud services, analysis tools, advertising networks and other service providers. They save and transfer data, link and analyse it — often contrary to our interest.

Jan Penfrat, a digital policy expert, says that many of the big tech companies want to "make it as difficult as possible for users and regulatory authorities to understand what data is gathered on our devices by which players, and for what purpose."

Penfrat works for European Digital Rights (EDRi), a European network of NGOs and experts that campaigns to defend fundamental rights and freedoms in the digital realm.

We all know what it's like: An app, a messenger service, for example, is quickly installed, and when it asks if it has permission to use personal data, users will often just click "yes."

Phone numbers are stored on servers — without approval

But the devil is in the detail. When you install WhatsApp, for example, you give it access to all the contacts in your smartphone. The phone numbers are transferred to the server — including those of people who don't use WhatsApp themselves, and who have not given permission for their contact details to be passed on.

"All of this flows into an enormous profile," says Penfrat.

Designed to fail: What dating apps really want from you To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Companies like Google then offer so-called "targeting" products based on this data.

"This means a car or clothes manufacturer can say: I'd like to address these target groups, and I want my advertising to appear in their Google search, Google Mail, or any of the hundreds of millions of third-party websites with integrated Google advertising," Penfrat explains.

Selling data profiles

Google is just one of many companies that offer data profiles. Two types of data feed into these profiles. One is the data that every user voluntarily discloses when they state something in their profile, or upload private photos.

But in addition, many big tech companies have for years now made assumptions based on the data they receive.

"If they have access to my location data and know where I usually am at night, they can assume that this is my home address," Penfrat says.

Who is in control of your data? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"If, for example, it's in a very expensive part of town, they can immediately make assumptions about my income. If they see: Oh, he has geolocation switched on and he regularly goes to a gay club, then he's probably a member of the LGBTQ community. And all this goes straight into the profile."

Strict regulation in Europe

The EU already has one of the strictest data protection regulations in the world. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) aims to protect people's personal data and privacy.

Other EU digital laws such as the Digital Markets Act or the Digital Services Act are intended to prevent big tech companies misusing their power over businesses and users. US businesses also have to abide by these laws if they offer their services to people in Europe, or observe their behavior.

The EU Commission has imposed numerous fines as punishment for violations of these regulations. In 2025, it fined Apple €500 million euros ($580 million). Meta, the company that operates Facebook, was fined another €200 million ($232 million).

EU Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier in July 2026, announcing that the EU would fine Google 890 million euros Image: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Google had to pay €890 million ($1.03 billion) in fines this year. That sounds like a lot — but a look at the net profit of the Google corporation Alphabet puts it into perspective. In 2025, Alphabet's net profit was around €117 billion ($136 billion).

"So these are sums that a company like Google or Amazon will make in just a few days," says Penfrat. "They just include it in their budget."

Dependency on US digital services

As a result, it is not that easy for the EU to implement truly effective controls. The tech giants have global infrastructures, huge financial resources, and complex business models. European agencies first have to get past these.

Europe's quest for digital independence To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Added to this is Europe's dependency on cloud services, operating systems, platforms and increasingly also AI infrastructure that, at least to date, have been provided in large part by US companies.

Penfrat criticizes Brussels for lacking the political will needed to take firmer action against these companies, and to better equip European data protection authorities.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Canada, Ukraine pledge 100-year partnership
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Canada would provide Ukraine with a "very important" air defense package.

Canada and Ukraine on Thursday signed a declaration vowing to keep a 100-year partnership between the two countries.

It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visits the country for talks with Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian officials.

Zelenskyy and Carney said that Canada had pledged to help shore up Ukraine's air defense.

"Earlier today, Canada and Ukraine finalized an agreement to deliver critical air defense interceptors (through) the United States Jumpstart mechanism," Carney said.

He said that the package would amount to some 350 million Canadian dollars ($260 million, €218 million).

The prime minister said that Canada had provided the equivalent of 26 billion Canadian dollars ($19 billion, €16 billion) in support for Ukraine.

"We've provided support for the energy systems and beyond. We'll provide more support," he said.

Zelenskyy expressed his graitude for what he described as a "very important" air defense package.

"I'm so thankful," Zelenskyy said. "This is very important package of air defense and this is crucial."

Speaking ahead of his meeting with Zelenskyy, Carney also emphasized Ukrainians' historical role in contributing to European settlement in the prairies of Canada's western provinces.

"Ukrainians help build ​this province, ⁠this country. Canada will help rebuild Ukraine when peace comes," he said, referring to Alberta, of which Calgary is the largest city.

Canada is home to over a million people of Ukrainian descent.

Zelenskyy and his wife Olena arrived in Canada late on Wednesday Image: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Zelenskyy visits Canada after Norway

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Calgary late on Wednesday for "important meetings ​and agreements" with Canadian officials.

His visit comes on the heels of his attendance at King Harald V's funeral in Norway, where his plane had been delayed by a drone incursion.

The Ukrainian leader is in the middle of a flurry of trips and meetings to shore up his country's defenses for the cold winter months.

"The main focus will be on supporting Ukraine in protecting our skies and preparing for the winter," Zelenskyy said in a social media post before leaving.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that the visit "will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defense, economic, and energy cooperation."

Carney's statement added Canada "remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine's defense, recovery, and reconstruction."

Zelenskyy had also signaled a desire to meet with US President Donald Trump on the matter before the end of September.

Since Russia's invasion in 2022, Moscow has consistently increased attacks on fuel and heating infrastructure in Ukraine in the autumn and winter.

What is happening on the battlefield?

Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region overnight, as well as a seaport in Dagestan, Zelenskyy said. He added that other unnamed sited critical to Russia's war industry had also been hit.

Alexander Gusev, governor of Russia's Voronezh region, said that one woman in the town of Borisoglebsk had been killed by falling drone debris overnight and that at least 19 drones had been destroyed while flying over the region.

The Russian Defense Ministry said a total of 448 Ukrainian drones were shot down overnight.

In Ukraine, Russian attacks hit buildings owned by a major food producer in Dnipro, killing at least two according to local officials.

Two Azerbaijani crew members were killed in a drone attack on a cargo ship in the Ukrainian region of Odesa, Ukraine's infrastructure ministry said.

Azerbaijan's foreign ministry also confirmed the information, adding that two further members of the crew were taken to hospital in Chornomorsk, Ukraine.

While Baku did not mention who was responsible for the attack, Ukraine blamed Russia for the drone strike.
