World.title: 25 years after 9/11: Al-Qaeda weakened but not gone
World.content:
25 years after 9/11, the terrorist group al-Qaeda is no longer the global terrorist organization it once was. Its central leadership has been weakened, but offshoots remain strong across Africa and Asia.

The extremist preacher Abdullah al-Muhaysini no longer has to worry about US sanctions. In late August 2026, the US Department of the Treasury removed the former jihadist from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list, or SDN List . It includes individuals and organizations whose assets are frozen in the US and with whom US citizens are generally not allowed to do business.

After Syria's civil war broke out in 2011, al-Muhaysini recruited fighters and helped establish a governing structure shaped by the Nusra Front, which emerged from al-Qaeda.

His removal from the list is linked to the new US government policy on Syria: Washington also removed the Nusra Front and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) from the SDN List.

25 years after the September 11 attacks, this is a remarkable snapshot. Al-Qaeda — which means "the base" in Arabic — has neither disappeared nor remained the same organization: Its core has weakened, but its regional branches have remained strong across parts of Africa and Asia, observers agree.

25 years on, what has the war on terror actually achieved? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regional offshoots in the Sahel, Yemen and Afghanistan

Only, al-Qaeda itself is operating less and less under its own name.

"This is largely due to the successful counterterrorism efforts following 2001," Lars Berger, professor of terrorism studies at the German Federal University of Administrative Sciences, told DW.

The military campaign in Afghanistan, along with cooperation between intelligence agencies and police, has significantly weakened the group.

"From this perspective, the September 11 attacks were a major strategic failure for al-Qaeda," Berger said.

The hoped-for radicalization of the Arab world and the overthrow of its regimes failed to materialize. About ten years after the attacks in New York and Washington, al-Qaeda's most famous figure, Osama bin Laden, was killed in May 2011.

As a result, al-Qaeda reorganized itself.

"The militia sought out areas where it could establish a permanent foothold, for example in parts of Africa or Yemen," Berger said, adding that "countries with weak state structures, overwhelmed security forces and unresolved local conflicts are particularly favorable."

"Today, this is particularly true of Africa," Rüdiger Lohlker, professor emeritus of Islamic studies at the University of Vienna, notes.

Fighters of the al-Qaeda offshoot al-Shabab are gaining a foothold in the Sahel region Image: Badri Media/dpa/picture alliance

In the Sahel, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM, has emerged as a powerful al-Qaeda offshoot, he said.

An analysis by the think tank Critical Threats Project uses Niger as an example to show how JNIM and the Islamic State's Sahel Province (ISSP) compete for territory, fighters and resources. In June 2026, JNIM claimed responsibility for an attack on the international airport in Niger's capital, Niamey.

In Somalia, al-Shabab — a group closely linked to al-Qaeda — is strong, and in Yemen, al-Qaeda is present in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP). Afghanistan also remains a safe haven for the terrorist organization.

However, the success of these offshoots cannot be explained solely by jihadist ideology, Lohlker added.

Rather, it often coincides with a kind of "economy of violence," he said, noting that "violence including kidnappings, smuggling and looting has long been an economic factor for terrorism."

He also said that there are veritable "markets for violence:" Where money can be made through violence, jihadist organizations can also recruit and retain followers.

"We fundamentally need to move away from a Eurocentric perspective," Lohlker further points out.

In his view, al-Qaeda and other jihadist groups have always been far more present outside Europe and the US than it has appeared from a Western perspective.

Al-Qaeda's regional involvement

However, over the years, the offshoots' strategies have undergone a change. According to Lars Berger, there has been a "strategic shift" away from direct attacks on the "distant enemy" and toward the establishment of local structures.

"We are now seeing an attempt to proceed in an alternative and gradual manner, namely instead of spectacular acts of violence ordered from the highest levels, there are smaller-scale actions that are more grassroots in nature," he said.

In the Sahel, this entails forming local alliances, gaining influence in communities, and controlling territories. The Critical Threats Project describes this development as "localization."

Al-Qaeda is thus surviving precisely through this differentiation. JNIM capitalizes on ethnic and social conflicts in the Sahel, while al-Shabaab exploits conflicts within Somali clan structures. The global jihadist goal remains as an ideological framework, but the actual fighting takes place on the ground.

Ten years after the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden was killed. Since then, the group has lost visibility but not regional influence through their proxies (file photo from 2001) Image: AFP/Getty Images

Al-Qaeda competes with the "Islamic State"

In the competition for public attention, however, al-Qaeda faces a superior rival: the so-called "Islamic State," or IS.

"Ultimately, younger jihadists tend to be more drawn to the 'Islamic State,'" terrorism expert Behnam Heidenreuter-Said, head of the research center for Strategic Police Research at the Hamburg Police Academy, told DW.

IS has carried out "more spectacular" and media-effective terrorist attacks, he said, highlighting that "al-Qaeda has taken a more long-term approach."

Heidenreuter-Said, who published a comprehensive history of al-Qaeda in 2018, added that "IS wanted to make a splash and demonstrate successes as quickly as possible in order to grow explosively."

However, IS's expansion was followed by its collapse, he said. Al-Qaeda, on the other hand, continues to exist, albeit under changed circumstances.

Shortage of al-Qaeda updates

The terrorist group meanwhile faces the question of whether it can replace its aging fighters. Although this is conceivable, al-Qaeda as a brand is visibly fading, Heidenreuter-Said observed. In Europe in particular, militant jihadism has become less attractive. However, jihadist ideas have not disappeared, al-Qaeda has simply lost its former ability to mobilize large numbers of young people, he said.

It is hard to say just how dangerous the organization actually still is, Behnam Heidenreuter-Said points out.

"Everyone agrees that there is currently virtually no information about al-Qaeda and we simply don't know what it is doing right now," he said.

Furthermore, since the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, it has been striking how little al-Qaeda has been visible in the major regional conflicts, he said. In his view, Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran have dominated the political and military stage.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
World.content:
The German government wants to follow other EU countries and take more decisive action against Russia's shadow fleet, accusing it of helping Moscow evade sanctions and carry out acts of sabotage.

On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures.

Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions.

But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping.

"The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. "What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities, including acts of sabotage, espionage and possibly drone operations and related disruptions."

Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party.

In a recent interview with DW, she complained, "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet."

Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table."

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

She accuses the German government of failing to take action. "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea, but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong."

Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet

By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel.

Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior."

In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety or violate environmental regulations.

Russia's threats: just a bluff?

It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint aims to avoid escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war."

Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded.

"Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened," Peters said.

"Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely avoided confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels."

After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it."

Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through."

Why did Norway seize a Russian ship for Ukraine? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Armed Russian crews on board

Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk.

"Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board," Pawlak said. "Those are risks that must be factored into the equation."

Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way.

"It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel."

Explained: How Germany will expand intel powers, and why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inspections would raise costs for Russia

While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions.

"We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone," he said. "Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it."

He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy."

This article has been translated from German.

What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast.

World.title: No puedo hacer frente a la derrama para la instalación del ascensor. ¿Pueden embargar mi casa? ¿Podría no usarlo para no pagar?
World.content:
Pregunta. En el edificio donde vivo la comunidad de propietarios ha decidido la instalación de un ascensor, pero me encuentro en la situación de no tener recursos para hacer frente a la derrama. ¿Pueden embargar mi vivienda? ¿Puedo solicitar que no me den acceso al ascensor a cambio de no pagar? C. Manuel F.

Respuesta. Los acuerdos válidamente adoptados por la junta de vecinos son obligatorios para todos los propietarios, tal y como establece el artículo 17.9 de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal.

En el caso de aprobarse la instalación de un ascensor, el pago de las cantidades correspondientes deberá realizarse en los términos acordados por la junta y reflejados en el acta. Asimismo, la comunidad de propietarios puede reclamar judicialmente el abono de las cantidades pendientes, ya sean gastos ordinarios o extraordinarios. Para ello, puede acudir al procedimiento monitorio y, si no logra cobrar la deuda mediante cuentas bancarias u otros bienes del deudor, podría solicitar el embargo de la vivienda y, en último término, su subasta para satisfacer el importe adeudado.

Este es el marco legal aplicable. No obstante, la ley no impide que los propietarios alcancen acuerdos específicos. Como hemos indicado, las cantidades deben abonarse conforme a lo acordado por la junta y recogido en el acta. Por ello, es perfectamente posible que la propia junta apruebe un calendario de pagos distinto, más amplio o flexible, para aquellos propietarios que no puedan asumir las cuotas en las mismas condiciones que el resto.

En cuanto a la posibilidad de eximir a un propietario del pago de la instalación del ascensor a cambio de limitar su uso, la ley tampoco prohíbe expresamente este tipo de acuerdos. Sin embargo, su redacción y ejecución exigen una especial precisión. En ese caso, el acuerdo debería reflejarse de forma detallada en el acta, recogiendo tanto la aprobación de la instalación como la excepción aplicable al propietario afectado y las condiciones concretas de dicha limitación. Por ejemplo, debería especificarse si el ascensor no tendrá parada en una determinada planta, si no se facilitará llave o sistema de acceso al propietario excluido, si la limitación podrá levantarse mediante el pago de determinadas cantidades o cualquier otra circunstancia necesaria para evitar interpretaciones o conflictos futuros.

Este tipo de acuerdo sería válido en el ámbito interno de la comunidad de propietarios. No obstante, para que pueda producir efectos frente a futuros adquirentes de la vivienda es necesario acceder al Registro de la Propiedad.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Un arcoíris de sal en el corazón de Cabo de Gata
World.content:
Una visita guiada por las salinas de este parque natural en Almería permite conocer la cosecha del mineral y, de paso, adentrarse en un entorno con una biodiversidad impresionante y en paisajes desérticos

La magia se produce al caer la noche. El agua del mar, embalsada durante días y calentada por el sol, disminuye entonces su temperatura con rapidez. Sobre su superficie, cuando todos duermen, nace una fina lámina salada que se cosecha con delicadeza al amanecer. Nace así la flor de sal, una exquisitez por su valor gastronómico y organoléptico. La llamativa transformación ocurre en paisajes sorprendentes como las salinas de Cabo de Gata, una extensión de 400 hectáreas de terrenos inundables junto al desierto de Almería que, desde la primavera de 2025, se puede visitar. Además de conocer la extracción de este mineral e incluso recogerlo, la ruta permite disfrutar de la elegancia de los flamencos y adentrarse, acompañados de la singular salicornia, en la historia de uno de los parques naturales más asombrosos de la geografía ibérica. “Es un lugar increíble”, confirma Arantxa Roldán, guía en este territorio marciano.

Para llegar hasta las salinas hay que atravesar, primero, un bosque de pitas y ramblas donde un puñado de heroicos árboles resisten en una tierra seca que parece gritar por una gota más, un último sorbito para sobrevivir a la sequía y el calor. Son las condiciones a las que se adapta el azufaifo, joya botánica “fácil de ver gracias a los senderos públicos cercanos al centro de visitantes de Las Almoladeras”, cuenta el director del parque natural Cabo de Gata-Níjar, Salvador Parra, quien recomienda allí una parada para hacerse una idea sobre el ecosistema formado por la Sierra de Gata y su orla costera de charcos salinos. Desde ellos llegan los ecos de los flamencos rosados que se pueden avistar desde el mirador junto al pueblo de El Cabo, donde arranca una línea de mar totalmente recta que, más de seis kilómetros después, llega hasta el Arrecife de las Sirenas y sus curiosas formaciones volcánicas.

Vista de las salinas de Cabo de Gata, una extensión de 400 hectáreas de terrenos inundables. Nacho Sánchez

El paisaje huele al salitre que llega con la brisa marina. En las dunas crece la siempre viva, el narciso marítimo y un insólito azafrán local de llamativa floración invernal a ras de suelo. Es un terreno plano, donde solo levantan las viejas sierras volcánicas de color oscuro, pero también una enorme y blanca pirámide. Es una garbera, una forma de almacenar la sal al aire libre. En este rincón almeriense espera a su exportación, por barco, al norte de Europa, donde se usa para quitar el hielo de las carreteras. Es el principal destino de las alrededor de 40.000 toneladas anuales —sin tratar— que se extraen en estas salinas, aunque también se utilizan para piscinas, salazones cárnicos y consumo humano. De flor de sal, su mejor versión, son unas 17 toneladas al mes. De cerca, brilla. “Y parece más salada”, dice, entre risas, José Luis Díaz Segovia, uno de los visitantes. Tiene razón, porque por estructura y pureza, tiene un sabor más intenso.

De los romanos al cine

El poblado para trabajadores de las salinas que hay junto a la playa. Nacho Sánchez

“Este humedal tiene más de 2,6 millones de años de historia, pero la explotación salina no arrancó hasta la época romana”, relata Roldán en los primeros minutos de la visita. Fueron ellos quienes, según subraya la guía, construyeron los casi seis kilómetros de canales que permiten que el agua del mar se concentre en más de un centenar de balsas. A principios del siglo XX, una familia catalana, Costa, se hizo cargo de la explotación y construyó el pequeño poblado que hay junto a la playa, con una treintena de viviendas donde residían los salineros y hoy lo hacen sus descendientes. En él destaca, alta y de perfil erosionado, la iglesia de San Miguel de las Salinas y el antiguo cine, que ocupaba un sencillo edificio de madera. En los años noventa, la salina pasó a manos del Grupo Molins, de capital francés, que tiene instalaciones similares en el Puerto de Santa María y Torrevieja. Y que en abril de 2025 decidió impulsar las visitas guiadas a pie por este entorno salado.

Arantxa Roldán, guía en las salinas del Cabo de Gata, en un momento de la visita. Nacho Sánchez

El agua va y viene por los canales al dictado de los técnicos de la compañía: gracias a las esclusas, mueven miles de litros a su antojo con facilidad. La cosecha de sal se realiza entre mayo y septiembre por un equipo de una treintena de empleados que cubren cada centímetro de su piel para evitar el impacto del sol. Ya no lo hacen a mano y con bueyes, sino con herramientas y camiones. Da igual. Las balsas de evaporación siguen hipnotizando con sus colores. Desde los tonos azulados clásicos de las zonas con menos concentración salina hasta las tonalidades moradas y lilas gracias a bacterias y microalgas. Son más llamativas en los cristalizadores, esteros más pequeños donde hay hasta 300 gramos por litro. El arcoíris se completa con el verde de la salicornia, especie vegetal apreciada en gastronomía que aquí se deja en paz. Más allá, los prismáticos permiten ver las tonalidades rosas de los portentosos flamencos y unas pequeñas cigüeñuelas que aletean a toda velocidad.

Un visitante en las salinas de Cago de Gata. Nacho Sánchez

La ruta a pie dura alrededor de una hora. La versión más sencilla cuesta 10 euros, pero hay otras opciones que permiten desde recolectar flor de sal (45 euros) hasta vivir experiencias gastronómicas o celebrar catas durante la caída del sol. Es un atardecer que el fotógrafo almeriense Javier Lozano conoce bien porque lleva disfrutándolo, a pie de playa, desde su infancia. “Pasar la tarde en esa zona del Cabo de Gata es único” reconoce este enamorado de las salinas y de todo el parque natural. “Hay pocos sitios en el Mediterráneo donde mires a tu lado y no veas edificios. Y este es uno de ellos”, afirma quien también celebra la luz, azulada en las mañanas, cálida en las tardes, única cuando hay calima. “Hay un toque africano muy especial. Entiendes que estás viendo algo distinto y no sabes ni qué es, pero se nota en cómo se refleja en el mar, en los edificios. Por eso el cine ha venido tanto a Almería”, destaca quien celebra el agua cristalina y de gran salinidad que hay en este litoral. En el entorno de las salinas, de hecho, se han rodado series recientes como Entre Tierras o La Casa de Papel, ficciones que intentan, sin éxito, superar esta realidad.

World.title: Por qué hay que visitar Enciña da Lastra: no parece Galicia, pero lo es
World.content:
Una encina gigante da nombre al parque natural más desconocido y sorprendente de la comunidad, de clima y paisaje mediterráneos. Es la puerta de entrada a la comarca de Valdeorras, donde se hacen excelentes mieles, vinos y aceites

Si uno se duerme yendo a Galicia por la autovía A-6 a la altura de Ponferrada (León) y el que conduce se desvía sin previo aviso por la carretera N-120 y lo despierta solo un cuarto de hora después en el mirador de Cobas (Ourense), creerá que está en el cielo, porque lo que ve es paradisíaco: un ancho río que no sospecha que es el Sil represado en el embalse de Peñarrubia, en cuya tersa superficie se refleja como sobre un espejo el sol naciente y un cañón bordado de árboles majestuosos y riscos dorados. Lo que no creerá, desde luego, es que está ya en Galicia, porque los árboles no son eucaliptos, sino encinas. Los riscos no son de granito o de pizarra —lo habitual allí—, sino de roca caliza. Y aquel alimoche común que sobrevuela este idílico panorama es tan poco gallego como una tortilla de patata con cebolla, muy hecha y sin sal.

Lo que descubre el viajero desde el mirador de Cobas no parece Galicia. Pero lo es. Es Enciña da Lastra, el parque natural más desconocido de la región, de clima mediterráneo y sustrato calizo, un paraíso de las orquídeas —hay 25 especies— y una puerta de entrada magnífica a la comarca de Valdeorras. Parque y comarca son el extremo oriente de Galicia, donde Ourense linda con León y Zamora. Tan extremo oriente es que se parece más a Castilla y León que a la propia Galicia. Al mejor amigo del hombre, los valdeorreses le dicen perro, no can. A la ventana, ventana, no fiestra. Al vino sí lo llaman viño, pero para conservarlo tienen tropecientas bodegas subterráneas, como si esto fuera la Ribera del Duero. Y lo dicho: en lugar de eucaliptos, que no hay monte en Galicia sin ellos, lo que uno encuentra al entrar en Valdeorras son majestuosas encinas, las que dan nombre al parque natural.

La guardiana de un tesoro oculto

Poco más abajo del mirador de Cobas —o de Covas, pues de las dos formas se escribe—, en la última curva que hace la carretera antes de entrar en la aldea del mismo nombre, proyecta su sombra de 25,60 metros de diámetro una encina monstruosa de 16,90 de altura y con un perímetro de 8,80 en la base de su tronco trifurcado. Es la Aciñeira de Covas o Enciño de Fontenouva, el único ejemplar de Quercus ilex reconocido y protegido por la Xunta de Galicia como árbol singular, y eso que hay 151 catalogados de otras especies. Esta encina de edad incalculable —entre 200 y 500 años— es la guardiana de la aldea, del parque natural y de la comarca. Y, según dicen, también de un tesoro oculto entre las rocas calizas donde hunde sus raíces. Allí, cuentan, lo escondieron o dejaron olvidado los mouros, seres fantásticos de la mitología gallega que habitaban bajo tierra rodeados de riquezas antes de que llegaran los humanos.

La encina centenaria que da nombre al parque de Enciña da Lastra. Andrés Campos

En Cobas se puede bajar paseando en 10 minutos a la orilla del embalse para refrescarse en las aguas del Sil y para ver somormujos lavancos, garzas reales y, en septiembre y octubre, cuando pasan camino de sus cuarteles de invierno andaluces y africanos, águilas pescadoras. O bien echarse a andar por la pista forestal que es prolongación de la calle principal y que va ganando suavemente altura, a unos 200 metros sobre la superficie del embalse, hasta Vilardesilva. Son unas tres horas de camino, siguiendo una ruta circular sencilla de 11 kilómetros.

Si somos más de ir observando la flora y la fauna que de andar por andar, con llegar hasta un antiguo horno de cal que hay a media hora del inicio ya está bien. Por el camino y al pie mismo del calero, florecen en primavera la orquídea araña (Ophrys sphegodes) y la piramidal (Anacamptis pyramidalis), dos de las especies más llamativas de este orquidario natural, y en un escarpe calizo que hay poco antes de cruzar el arroyo de Pereda y de avistar la enorme mole troncocónica del viejo horno, arraigan plantas como la Armeria rothmaleri y la Petrocoptis grandiflora, que no lo hacen en ningún otro lugar del planeta.

El antiguo horno de cal en el parque natural Enciña da Lastra. Andrés Campos

Hay que acercarse también al centro de visitantes del parque natural, en Biobra, donde se informa con detalle de cuanto hay en él y de las rutas más curiosas, como la de Tras os Penedos —la mejor para observar mariposas— o la de As Dúas Vertentes. Recorriendo esta última, se ven en lontananza las minas romanas de Las Médulas y, en el cielo, el alimoche común, que en Galicia es un ave muy poco común, valga la redundancia. Si se viaja en un grupo de al menos ocho personas, se puede hacer las rutas acompañados por un guía del centro de visitantes sin pagar nada, solo escribiendo con antelación a su correo electrónico (servizo.conservacion.natureza.ourense@xunta.gal). Pero hay que tener en cuenta que el centro solo abre de jueves a domingo y que echa el cierre desde mediados de septiembre hasta Semana Santa. Así no es de extrañar que este sea uno de los parques naturales más desconocidos de España.

Dos pueblos ‘enxebres’: Vilardesilva y Pardollán

Además de la naturaleza inaudita de Enciña da Lastra, en el centro aconsejan visitar Vilardesilva y Pardollán, dos de los pueblos más enxebres, más auténticos, con más encanto del parque y de Valdeorras, una región donde el desarrollismo y los marmolistas han causado estragos. El feísmo apenas ha hecho mella en ellos.

Una de las calles del pueblo de Vilardesilva. Andrés Campos

En Vilardesilva abundan las casas de piedra caliza bien labrada, con galerías de madera hermosamente tallada y con buenas historias a sus espaldas. Historias como la que fue propiedad de Paco González, que emigró con sus padres a Alemania, donde fue fontanero y luego payaso —el primero titulado de Europa—, y que volvió regularmente en verano a esta aldea de su Valdeorras natal para hacer un alojamiento rural —Chao do Prao— y dar cursos de clown. Así, hasta que Paco murió en 2017 y su casa rural y su escuela se perdieron. El cercano mirador da Cruz es un buen lugar para olvidarse del triste final del sueño de verano de Paco, admirando el paisajazo —el espolón calizo de Peñarrubia aflorando de las aguas quietas del Sil como la aleta dorsal de los peces acorazados que poblaban este rincón de Galicia hace 400 millones de años, cuando era un cálido mar tropical— y oliendo a tomillo salsero, una planta tan exótica en Ourense como un clown valdeorrés en Alemania.

Pardollán, por su parte, tiene un lugar especialmente cuidado, que justifica por sí solo la visita: la céntrica plaza donde todos los vecinos —43; 10 más que Vilardesilva— beben y llenan sus regaderas en una preciosa fuente de tres caños, rodeada de macetas floridas, pinturas murales y casas con galerías azules. Este colorido rincón, más que de una aldea del interior de Galicia, diríase de un pueblo marinero de las Rías Altas.

El pueblo gallego de Pardollán. Andrés Campos

La ‘alvariza’ que surgió del fuego

En el centro de visitantes del parque también recomiendan, si se va a pasar más de un día en la zona, acercarse a conocer la empresa apícola familiar O Marquesado, en O Porto. “Apicultores desde 1896”, reza un cartel en la fachada de la casa-taller, pero enseguida se da uno cuenta, viendo y oyendo a los dueños, Antonia Franco y Jens Kleinwächter, de que no llevan tanto tiempo en esto y tampoco en Valdeorras. Antonia, hija de emigrantes gallegos en Alemania­ —y prima de Paco, el clown—, volvió hace 12 años a la tierra de su padre con su marido y ambos decidieron seguir el dulce oficio del tío de ella, que iba a retirarse.

Antonia Franco en el taller de miel de O Marquesado, en O Porto. Andrés Campos

El caso es que hacen lo mismo que otras cuatro generaciones de apicultores de su familia —una miel con un sabor especial, gracias al microclima mediterráneo de este rincón de Ourense—, pero con una técnica y una precisión alemanas, como se ve en la limpieza y el orden del taller, de la tienda y de la sala de catas. “En Alemania”, explica Jens, “aprendimos a trabajar con la dócil abeja cárnica y aquí tuvimos que aprender de nuevo con la negra ibérica, que es mucho más nerviosa, más defensiva, más brava”. Una abeja a la que no tranquiliza y vuelve más manejable y productiva el cambio climático y tampoco los graves incendios que sufrió la comarca en 2020 y 2025. “Mi tío”, explica ahora Antonia, “producía siete toneladas al año con 150 colmenas. Nosotros, con el doble, solo cuatro”.

Para compensar, y porque no saben parar, estos emprendedores de cabeza alemana y corazón español llevan a los visitantes que lo desean a hacer de apicultores por un día en alguno de los terrenos donde tienen sus 300 colmenas. Por el camino, van parando aquí y allá para admirar los soutos, montes de castaños productivos que han sido estos últimos años eficacísimos cortafuegos. En una ladera no tan limpia, la maleza ardió como la yesca en agosto de 2025, durante el incendio más grande registrado hasta entonces en España, y entonces apareció una alvariza, una muralla circular que se usaba hace más de un siglo para defender las colmenas de los osos. “Un convenio entre la Xunta y la Fundación Reina Sofía”, informa Jens, “va a permitir recuperar en breve esta estructura patrimonial: nosotros la devolveremos a la vida, llenándola de colmenas. Ya solo queda abrir un camino para poder llegar en un 4x4 allá arriba”. Mientras tanto, Jens lleva a los apituristas al pie del monte donde reapareció la alvariza, en Oulego, y la observa de lejos con la mano en el corazón.

Jens Kleinwächter, frente a la 'alvariza' de Oulego. Andrés Campos

Beber en una cueva y comer en otra

Otra cosa que se hacía en Valdeorras desde siempre, además de miel, es vino, pero poca gente de fuera se fijaba en esta denominación de origen hasta que uno de Rafael Palacios, Sorte O Soro 2020, obtuvo 100 puntos en la guía Robert Parker Wine Advocate. Ahora todo el mundo vuelve los ojos y los paladares hacia esta comarca y alucina con sus montes llenos de vides de Godello —la uva autóctona, la más apreciada, con la que se elaboran vinos frescos, afrutados y elegantes, que se beben solos— y de cuevas. Se decía que había muchas, más de mil cuevas, y un reciente estudio de Carina Rodríguez y Cristina de la Torre, As covas de Valdeorras, ha confirmado que no es una exageración: han catalogado 1.103.

Una cueva bien conservada, que da gusto visitar, es la de Adega Melillas, una bodega familiar creada a principios de siglo por emigrantes retornados de Suiza a su pueblo natal, A Rúa. ¿Y por qué se llama Melillas? Pues porque así llamaba al abuelo de Sonia Prada —copropietaria, gerente y quien explica la saga a los enoturistas—, que hizo la mili en Melilla. Arriba se degustan y se compran los vinos —el mejor, el Lagar do Cigur Godello 2025— y abajo se entra casi a tientas en la cueva, que no es de clara roca caliza, sino de negra pizarra. Cuando los ojos se acostumbran a la oscuridad, se descubre una de las cuevas más altas de Valdeorras, con techos de más de cuatro metros, donde antiguamente el vino se conservaba bien en los veranos de clima tan poco gallego de esta comarca, igual que en una vinoteca.

Sonia Prada en la cueva de bodega Melillas, en A Rúa. Andrés Campos

Mayor aún es una cueva de Seadur, la segunda que vale la pena visitar: tan grande es, que cabe en ella un restaurante, Cova da Xabreira, con 42 comensales dando cuenta en sus mesas de las berenjenas con queso de O Cebreiro y miel de O Marquesado, el chuletón de vaca madurada Simmental y cuanto va saliendo de las brasas. Para beber, nada como el rosado Viñas de Seadur As Fontelas que elabora la misma propiedad con la autóctona y muy escasa uva brancellao. Y para elucubrar en la sobremesa: ¿cómo abrirían semejante boquete en la roca madre del monte? Porque es puro granito. No hay huellas de barrenos. Fue a pico.

Dormir a orillas del Bibei y del Sil

Después de mucho comer y elucubrar, no es mala idea dirigirse a As Ermidas, en O Bolo, para dar una cabezada en la playa fluvial del río Bibei, el principal afluente del Sil por su orilla izquierda, o un paseo por los alrededores, viendo cómo Diego de la Torre cuida los viejos olivos que se retuercen en las escarpadas márgenes, muchos de los cuales debieron de ser plantados en 1624, cuando se creó el santuario barroco de As Ermitas que hay en lo alto. Con las aceitunas que con arduos trabajos obtiene de estos y otros olivos centenarios de Valdeorras, Diego produce con cuentagotas el AOVE Terras Gigurras, que sale a 56 euros el litro y se agota en un amén. Ahora mismo hay que esperar dos meses a que los olivos y este oleicultor heroico hagan más.

Quien quiera algo más que una siesta en bañador —una con pijama—, puede volver a Seadur y alojarse en A Rectoral, la casona de 1783 donde vivía y prácticamente teletrabajaba el cura de la localidad: solo tenía que levantar la voz para decir misa en la vecina iglesia. El lugar, que tenía también algo de cueva, con sillares ciclópeos y rincones sombríos por doquier, ha sido reformado a fondo y decorado alegremente por sus propietarios, Isabel Val y Lucas Presedo, que han tenido el acierto de colgar en casi todas las habitaciones y apartamentos lienzos de la artista de A Rúa Carina Rodríguez, que evocan las máscaras y los trajes del Entroido orensano. Otro acierto: el apartamento A Lareira, con la moderna cocina y un antiguo escaño con mesa abatible integrados a modo de office dentro de la monumental campana de la vieja chimenea.

Una buena opción también para alojarse y para poner a esta ruta punto final —o aparte, porque hay que volver para seguir explorando el extremo oriente de Galicia— es el hotel rural A Pontevella, en Sobradelo. Está en un lugar difícil de creer: a orillas del Sil, junto a un puente seiscentista de 90 metros cuyos siete ojos han visto cosas tremendas —como la crecida de 2010 o como la francesada, que para detenerla se derribó su arco central en 1810—. Soraya Docampo, su propietaria, levantó con sus propias manos este hotel boutique de acabados impecables, como solo puede hacerlo alguien que antes se dedicó a la construcción. Además de buena obrera, es buena cocinera y amena anfitriona.

El puente sobre el río Sil, en Sobradelo. Andrés Campos

Mientras los huéspedes se chupan los dedos —muy ricas, las croquetas de cecina artesanal y la lubina al horno con vino Godello—, les cuenta cosas maravillosas de este pueblo que es la capital de uno de los municipios más ricos de Galicia, Carballeda de Valdeorras, el mayor productor mundial de pizarra. Las piscinas naturales de Sobradelo tienen playa de arena fina, mucha pizarra —¡claro!— y hasta hidromasaje. Mañana habrá que ir a probarlas.

World.title: Four people with long Covid euthanised in NL last year
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Four people died by euthanasia last year after suffering with long Covid, according to the Dutch regional euthanasia review committee.

The youngest patient was 51-years-old, the other three were over 65. In another six cases, long Covid played a role in the decision to end their lives but was not the primary factor.

An estimated 400,000 people in the Netherlands currently suffer from long Covid, many of them have severe symptoms that stop them working or being able to enjoy basic everyday activities.

The Dutch Health Council this year urged the government to give more clarity around the situation with long Covid and do more to help treat those suffering from it.

Last month, a national research and investigation centre was launched by the Long-Covid Foundation, to help prolong work into treating the illness.

Government funding of €40 million dried up, so the foundation raised €500,000 to give to seven scientists to keep researching possible treatments.

World.title: Roof of PM’s office is original 16th-century flat-plack
World.content:
The roof of the Torentje, or Little Tower, at the Binnenhof in The Hague was built in 1547 as a construction kit and has been largely untouched since, broadcaster NOS reported on Thursday.

The research on the eight-metre-high spire above the office of the prime minister was carried out by the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf, the government’s property agency, during the ongoing renovation of the complex.

The ceiling was opened last year to check the area for asbestos, which was found, revealing the oak roof structure behind it.

The wooden construction has needed practically no repair work in 478 years.

An inspection revealed that the beams were sawn by hand, typical in the days before the widespread use of sawmills. The wood came from an oak tree felled in southern Sweden around 1546.

Roman numerals are also chiselled into the beams, indicating that the roof was built in a workshop, taken apart and transported to the building site. The numerals show which parts belong together, like the instructions for a piece of Ikea furniture.

The tower itself is older: the earliest records date from 1497, and Emperor Charles V had it completely rebuilt in 1547, when the spire was added.

The renovation of the Binnenhof began in 2021. The work was initially expected to take five years and cost €475 million, but the bill has since risen to at least €2.7 billion and completion has been postponed until 2031.

Earlier this year, archaeologists found an early 14th-century city gate at the site.

World.title: Parents as “customers” fuelling school disputes, council says
World.content:
Parents are falling out with schools and turning to dispute committees to settle grievances, according to the the government’s independent education council. This is happening partly because parents are being turned into “customers” of the education system, where they can publicly compare and select schools.

The council was asked to look into the problem by the former education minister and sent its findings on Thursday.

Tension between parents and schools is usually blamed on social media, polarisation and a more individualistic society, it said, but that explanation leaves out the part played by law and policy in setting the two sides against each other.

Policy changes, such as the 2014 passend onderwijs reform, which leaves parents and schools to agree between themselves when a child qualifies for additional support, have raised tensions. Previously, an outside committee would make these decisions.

Websites allowing parents to compare schools on performance data, such as exam pass rates and the share of pupils recommended for pre-university education, have also created a customer and provider dynamic, the report said.

Disputes taken to the national dispute committees for schools rose steadily until 2024, with a slight dip last year. The number of secondary teachers who say dealing with parents is giving them stress is rising, and in primary schools a third of all teachers say the same.

The council’s two main recommendations are that ministers should consider what a policy will do to the relationship between parents and schools before introducing it, and that parents should be given more say collectively rather than only as individuals with a complaint.

World.title: Calves shipped from Ireland go 50 hours without milk, NVWA says
World.content:
The Dutch food and product safety authority NVWA is taking enforcement action against four Irish livestock transporters over the treatment of very young calves shipped to the Netherlands, broadcaster NOS reported on Thursday.

The calves are given almost nothing to drink during a journey of at least 50 hours, which breaches EU animal welfare rules, the NVWA said. The transporters have been given a year to change their working methods or face financial penalties.

The animals, mostly bull calves under two months old, are loaded onto trucks in Ireland and put on a ferry to France. After a 19-hour crossing they are unloaded to rest and drink, then driven on to the Netherlands.

EU rules say animals must be fed during transport where “necessary”, which the European Commission and the NVWA interpret as at least every 12 hours. The Irish authorities disagree and have not intervened.

According to the NVWA, the trucks have no drinking systems suitable for milk, and calves of this age have to be helped to drink. The Irish government has itself said that is “practically impossible” on the ferry.

“That means the animals can no longer go directly from Ireland via France to the Netherlands in one go,” NVWA inspector Annebeth van Aartsen told NOS. “The transport would have to be organised differently.”

The Dutch veal sector said earlier it wanted to stop the Irish imports in 2026 because of the suffering involved, but a NOS investigation this year found the transports were still going on.

The NVWA had previously said it could not act because most of the violations take place at sea, outside Dutch jurisdiction. The action follows an enforcement request by animal welfare groups Eyes on Animals and Dier&Recht.

World.title: Amsterdam fails to get EU backing to limit Airbnb rules
World.content:
Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has failed to persuade the European Commission to help crack down on people renting out their own homes to tourists.

Halsema travelled to Brussels in the spring with the mayors of other big European cities that struggle with mass tourism – like Barcelona and Paris – to lobby for tougher powers to regulate holiday rentals through sites like Airbnb.

But the EU Affordable Housing Act, presented on Wednesday, would not ban or limit holiday lets but instead establishes a standard for when an area is under “housing stress” – defined as one where house prices are at least eight times per capita disposable income and have risen over the past decade.

It then gives local authorities a legal basis to restrict commercial short-term rentals and second-home purchases in those areas.

Combating local damage

Amsterdam had asked the commission for two things, according to the Telegraaf: more powers to act against people letting out the home they live in, and for the right to intervene once an area’s liveability has been damaged by tourist rentals.

The commission seemingly dismissed both requests. The text of the act explicitly excludes a host’s primary residence from any restriction, on the grounds that renting out your own home does not take housing off the market. It also only covers measures justified by affordability and availability, not neighbourhood nuisance.

“It is questionable whether this proposal is going to help us,” Amsterdam housing alderman Zita Pels told the paper. Dirk Gotink, an MEP for the centre-right NSC, also told the Telegraaf: “we don’t need a European law to solve local problems.”

Amsterdam already restricts renting your own home through sites like Airbnb to 30 nights per year but has tried to go further in the past. In July 2020 the council banned holiday rentals outright in the red light district and part of the canal ring.

The Amsterdam district court overturned that ban in 2021, and the Council of State, the highest administrative court, upheld the ruling in 2023, saying a total ban was disproportionate and the city should first have tested less drastic measures, such as a lower night limit.

For people in the Netherlands with a second home in Spain, Portugal or France, nothing will change for now. The law would allow local authorities in stressed areas to restrict purchases of homes not used as a primary residence, but only for property bought after the measure takes effect.

The proposal must first be negotiated by the European Parliament and member states, a process likely to take a year or more.

World.title: Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
World.content:
Exports from the Netherlands to the United States fell by 25% in the first half of this year, knocking the US out of the top five destinations for Dutch goods.

Dutch companies sold €13 billion worth of goods to the US between January and June, €4.3 billion less than in the same period last year, figures from national statistics office CBS show. The decline began after the Trump administration imposed a general import tariff of 15% on goods from the EU in August last year.

Almost every type of product was affected. Machinery and transport equipment, the biggest category of Dutch exports to the US, accounted for nearly half the fall. Sales of medicines and other chemical products dropped by more than 30%, and manufactured goods such as medical instruments fell by almost a quarter.

As a result, the US now takes 4% of Dutch goods exports, down from 5.5% a year earlier. Italy has overtaken it as the fifth-biggest market, with Spain also catching up. Exports to Belgium, Germany, France, Spain and Italy all rose over the same period.

Trade in the other direction has grown – imports from the US were up 19% to €27.6 billion, although most of that increase was oil and other fuels, which have become more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East. Other kinds of imports rose by 6.7%.

The tariffs have been costly for the US as well. The country’s Supreme Court ruled in February that most of the levies Donald Trump introduced last year were illegal, and Dutch companies are now claiming back more than €1 billion in duties.

Philips has already received €186 million, and Heineken and Ahold Delhaize are expected to recover hundreds of millions between them.

In 2024, before the tariffs were introduced, the Netherlands exported more than €38 billion worth of goods to the US, nearly 6% of all its exports.

World.title: Library membership tops 3.8 million as more adults sign up
World.content:

More than 3.8 million people were members of public libraries in the Netherlands in 2025, a 3% increase over the year before according to new numbers by national statistics office CBS.

The number of adult library members rose by 46,000 to nearly 1.4 million.

In particular, an increasing number of younger adults, those between the ages of 18 and 30, are joining libraries.

In total, 9% of adults are library members. That statistic is dwarfed by the number of children who are library members. Nearly two-thirds of kids, 74%, are members of a library.

The number of children joining a library has also increased in 2025. Last year saw a rise of 2.4%, or over 57,000 more kids with a library card.

The Netherlands had 802 library locations in 2025, an increase of 35 on the year before. This is due to an increase in funding from the national government, according to CBS.

The number of physical books checked out by patrons has remained stable but the number of e-book loans rose. Nearly 6 million e-books were borrowed via the online library, 3% more than in 2024, and audiobook loans rose 11% to 2.9 million.

Divers have recovered the body of a man who fell out of a boat in the IJ in Amsterdam on Wednesday.

The 47-year old went overboard near the Schellingwouderbrug, which connects Amsterdam East and Amsterdam Noord, at around 12:30PM, the regional safety board reported.

Multiple diving teams and rescue boats were dispatched as well as a helicopter equipped with a thermal camera.

After an hour of searching, the operation was scaled back as it was unlikely the man would be found alive.

Divers found his body late Wednesday evening.

It is not clear how the man ended up in the water. The police are investigating.

Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment

Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation was in Poland this week to visit potential locations for the base and discuss the issue further. World.title: “We remember where Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” says Polish FM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
