World.title: Anthropic disrupts Russian, Chinese AI campaigns targeting its Claude models
World.content:
ANTHROPIC. The Anthropic logo is seen in this illustration taken June 11, 2026.

Anthropic says cybercriminals and state-backed hackers were increasingly using AI not just to assist with tasks but to orchestrate and execute large portions of cyberattacks

Anthropic on Thursday, September 10, said it had disrupted several allegedly malicious uses of its Claude models over the past eight months, including a suspected Russia-linked cyber espionage campaign and efforts by Chinese AI firms it accused of trying to extract and replicate Claude’s capabilities.

Cybercriminals and state-backed hackers were increasingly using AI not just to assist with tasks but to orchestrate and execute large portions of cyberattacks, Anthropic said in its latest Threat Intelligence report. It added that humans were often overseers rather than hands-on operators.

“The use of AI went beyond simple questions and responses from a chatbot but rather involved the use of multi-agent frameworks executing” tasks, Anthropic said.

Anthropic said it had disrupted attacks from seven China-based labs during that period. Among the labs Anthropic named were tech giant Alibaba, Moonshot, DeepSeek, and Xiaomi.

Operators it linked to Alibaba ran what Anthropic called the largest “illicit distillation” attack, allegedly aimed at extracting capabilities of Claude models and using them to improve the Chinese tech firm’s Qwen models, the company said. Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Anthropic said it observed more than 151 million exchanges it attributed to Alibaba between May and July 2026, peaking at nearly 3 million per day from more than 3,500 accounts it described as fraudulent.

Distillation refers to the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive models in a bid to lower the costs of training a new AI tool.

Rather than running bulk queries, Kimi chatbot creator Moonshot and DeepSeek allegedly routed live customer conversations, which sometimes included sensitive information, through Claude and used its responses as training data, Anthropic alleged.

A hacking group whose tradecraft was consistent with Russia-based threat actor Midnight Blizzard allegedly ran phishing, hotel Wi-Fi hijacking and WhatsApp-takeover operations against targets in the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic sectors, using AI at nearly every stage, Anthropic said.

The US government has previously linked Midnight Blizzard, a tracking term coined by Microsoft, to Russia’s SVR foreign intelligence service. The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The group allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defenses and rewrote the code until it evaded detection again.

Anthropic also identified what it called “new categories of threat actors” misusing Claude, including those using the platform to “develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them.” The report detailed incidents of operators using Claude to develop software for weapons design and development, or to support intelligence gathering and procurement related to weapons programs, in China, Russia, and Yemen.

The company said that it detected and disrupted activity linked to affiliates of the ShinyHunters cybercrime collective, one of the most prolific cybercrime enterprises in recent months linked to attacks on major corporations around the world.

Jacob Klein, head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, said in an interview that models have become more capable over the last year, raising new risks. “A year ago, let’s say you wanted to optimize a drone or optimize the software on a missile, the models just wouldn’t be as good at that task as they are now,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: COA finds irregularities in TUPAD payouts in 2025
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit (COA) has found that thousands of Department of Labor and Employment’s (DOLE) Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD) beneficiaries in 2025 either received cash assistance despite submitting incomplete documents or got excess cash assistance.

State auditors said 2,731 beneficiaries were still paid even though they failed to comply with the eligibility documents set under Section 8 of Department Order No. 239, Series of 2023, including submission of valid government-issued ID cards.

Among the areas where these cases were found were:

Eastern Visayas Region with 1,093 beneficiaries

Davao Region with 1,091 beneficiaries

Soccskargen with 523 beneficiaries

Caraga Region with 24 beneficiaries

Auditors also said 2,781 senior citizens received TUPAD funds even though the medical certificates they submitted did not come from a licensed physician.

The questionable payouts cost the DOLE P18.18 million which, COA said, should have gone to legitimate beneficiaries.

It said: “In the absence of such documentation, the audit team could not sufficiently determine whether the beneficiaries were indeed medically fit to perform the assigned work or whether the contracted services were actually rendered.”

The concerned DOLE regional offices, in response to COA’s audit findings, agreed to strictly enforce beneficiary validation and verification procedures to ensure that only those who fully meet eligibility requirements are granted assistance.

Auditors also found 1,275 individuals in the Zamboanga Peninsula region were paid more than the amount they were meant to receive under the TUPAD program.

“Audit of disbursements of TUPAD showed that there were excessive payments to 1,275 beneficiaries totaling P6,463,150 due to lapses in the maintenance of the database,” the COA said.

In Soccskargen, in particular, 330 persons collected TUPAD assistance twice, 57 were paid three times, and 132 got the cash assistance four times, according to COA.

The multiple collection was attributed to “inadvertent” inclusion of certain beneficiaries to the TUPAD Program which was traced to submission of different lists or inconsistencies in the identification details.

State auditors recommended that the COA regional offices implement measures to recover the excess payments. – Rappler.com

World.title: [The Wide Shot] The test that only you can grade
World.content:
A letter to my journalism students as we hold yet another online class

Dear Class,

Reminder: Please strive to be honest.

Honesty is the true test of a journalist. In online assessments where I cannot check if you are cheating or not, another type of assessment is at work. It is an assessment of character, a test that only you can grade.

I hope you excel.

If you pass the test of honesty, you will pass the test of life. If you don’t, you will have small wins now — but trust me, you are doomed to fail in the end. Strive to build your skills through honesty and hard work, and God will reward you with the fullness of life.

Please stay honest in our online quizzes. If you cheat, you win some points now. But eventually, you lose your moral fiber, disintegrate, and become a monster unrecognized even by your own parents. We have been discussing corrupt politicians in class. You will be like them — reviled by the nation, abhorred even by children. Corrupt politicians started by cheating in class.

Please also stay honest in our online writing exercises. I designed these writing exercises to help you practice for our major assessments. I also want to identify the students who need extra help, so that I can meet them where they are. It is useless to cheat in online writing exercises because I do not grade these articles for quality, only for effort. If you cheat in online exercises, you cheat only yourselves.

Please do not mistake good writing for good journalism.

A good journalist is not just a good writer. A good journalist is a truth-teller.

I hope you can see the big picture: Our ultimate goal is not to ensure that you excel in school assessments. Our ultimate goal is to help each of you become a good person.

Be good!

And if you failed this test of life today, there is always tomorrow. There is hope.

Paterno

– Rappler.com

Paterno R. Esmaquel II is a journalist specializing in religion and public life. A former Rappler reporter and news editor, he now writes for international Catholic news outlets, teaches journalism at the University of Santo Tomas, and runs a YouTube channel called The Religion Reporter.

The author originally posted this to Facebook on September 10, 2026.

World.title: Sara Duterte’s arraignment for grave threats case deferred
World.content:
AT COURT. Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on September 11, 2026, for her arraignment for her grave threats case on September 11, 2026,.

(1st UPDATE) It's still unclear what type of motion the Vice President's camp has filed with the court. Even the justice department did not disclose the nature of the motion that triggered the deferment.

MANILA, Philippines – Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 98 has deferred the arraignment of Vice President Sara Duterte for her grave threats case originally scheduled on Friday, September 11.

Duterte’s lawyer, Paul Lawrence Lim, said they filed a motion with the court that prompted the tribunal to defer the Vice President’s arraignment. Duterte made a personal appearance before the court.

“Ito’y pinagbigyan ng korte at pinapa-comment niya, pinapa-submit niya ng comment ang DOJ (Department of Justice), prosecution within a certain period. Tapos maaari rin kami sumagot kung sakali na kailangan, and then saka niya dedesisyunan ito, ‘yong aming motion,” Lim told reporters outside the court.

“Ngayon, pansamantala habang ito’y pinag-iisipan pa niya ‘yong aming motion, hindi muna matutuloy ‘yong arraignment, so suspended muna,” he added.

(The court acknowledged our motion and asked the DOJ, the prosecution, to comment within a certain period. And we can reply to that if ever, and then the judge will decide on our motion. For now, while the court is deliberating on our motion, the arraignment has been deferred, suspended for the meantime.)

Duterte arrived at around 8:30 am with her legal counsel and brother, Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte.

Prior to that, some of her supporters gathered outside the court and staged a rally to call for her protection and the resignation of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr..

Vice presidential spokesperson Paolo Panelo confirmed Duterte’s attendance ahead of her arrival. Following her exit from the court, she thanked her supporters and the members of the media

“Nagpapasalamat ako sa mga kababayan natin. Ang sabi ng ating mga abogado as long as nasa labas ako at nakikita ako ng taumbayan at nandyan ang kanilang cellphone at camera na nagre-record sa atin, mas protektado ako,” Duterte said.

(I thank our fellow Filipinos. My lawyers advised me that as long as the supporters are there and their phones are recording, then I will be more protected.)

Arraignment is the phase in criminal proceedings that happens after the arrest or surrender.

This is when the court reads the accused the case, and asks them either for a guilty or not-guilty plea. If the accused entered a guilty plea, then the case will immediately move to conviction, usually with a lower sentence. If the plea is not guilty, then the case moves to trial.

It’s unclear what type of motion the defense has filed with the court. Even the DOJ did not disclose the nature of the motion.

“The DOJ respects the Court’s decision to defer the arraignment pending resolution of the motion filed by the defense. We will allow the judicial process to take its course. At this point, the prosecution will reserve further comment until the motion has been resolved,” DOJ spokesperson Raphael Martinez told reporters in a message.

“Beyond what has already been stated, we would rather not further characterize or discuss the contents of the pending motion. At least not yet,” he added.

Under Section 11 of the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure, a party may seek a suspension of arraignment on the following grounds:

The accused appears to be suffering from an unsound mental condition that effectively renders him/her to fully understand his/her case.

There is a prejudicial question

A petition for review of the resolution is pending either with the DOJ or Office of the President

So far, the only pending petition sought by the Duterte camp is a petition for review filed with the Supreme Court.

“We confirm that the Vice President has filed a petition, followed by an amended petition for certiorari and prohibition with application for TRO and/or Writ of Preliminary Mandatory Injunction with the Supreme Court a few days ago. The amended petition challenges the DOJ and Quezon City Regional Trial Court’s jurisdiction to prosecute her as an incumbent impeachable officer,” Lim had said on Thursday.

Play Video

What is Duterte being accused of?

Duterte, who was once allied with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., was charged with grave threats by the Department of Justice in August, in relation to her alleged assassination threats against Marcos, his wife Liza, and cousin, former House speaker Martin Romualdez.

It was the National Bureau of Investigation which initiated the criminal proceedings against Duterte after her infamous midnight press conference on November 23, 2024. In response to a supporter’s question, she assured them not to worry about her safety, adding that she had already “talked to someone” who would assassinate Marcos, the First Lady, and Romualdez if she were killed.

The grave threats allegation also formed part of one of the articles of impeachment in Duterte’s Senate impeachment trial.

On September 4, the Quezon City RTC Branch 98 ordered Duterte’s arrest after it found that there was probable cause – or enough evidence – to believe that the Vice President committed the crime. Duterte posted bail the following day, where she dropped her now-controversial line about “not feeling safe.”

“I do not feel safe. I do not feel safe anywhere. Pumunta lang ako [rito] kasi sabi ninyo pupunta ako sa court (I only went here because you told me I needed to appear in court),” Duterte said on Saturday, September 5.

Before the court issued the warrant, Duterte’s camp had filed a motion to defer it. They had sought oral hearings as they they argued that Duterte cannot face a criminal case because she is an impeachable official.

But the court denied the motion to defer and proceeded to order Duterte’s arrest. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: News of 39 soldiers held by MILF is from 2023, not recent
World.content:
The viral Facebook post was likely referring to a 2023 incident in Lanao del Sur that has been falsely presented as a recent development ahead of the BARMM polls on September 14

Claim: Members of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) blocked 39 soldiers from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and confiscated their firearms in Lanao del Sur on September 9.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A September 9 Facebook post published by the page “Kakatoh Trending” claims: “Breaking news! Hinarang ng MILF ang 39 na sundalo ng AFP na dumaan sa kanilang kampo sa Lanao del Sur at pinadeposito pa ang kanilang mga baril, ano ito? Bawian na sila?”

(Breaking news! The MILF intercepted 39 AFP soldiers passing through their camp in Lanao del Sur and even forced them to surrender their firearms, what is this? Is this a case of getting even?)

As of writing, the post has garnered over 859 reactions, 281 comments, and 70 shares. The page itself has more than 21,000 followers.

The post received several comments, most of which backed up the claim, with one comment adding, “Nakita ko na sa balita totoo ‘yan (I already saw that in the news, that is true).”

Another post uploaded on September 9 features an excerpt of a news report regarding the incident. As of writing, it has 7,800 reactions, 528 comments, 874 shares, and 314,000 views.

The posts began spreading ahead of the first-ever Bangsomoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary elections on September 14.

The facts: The false claim is likely referring to a real incident in February 2023, when 39 soldiers belonging to the 1st Special Forces Battalion were held and later released by the MILF after they strayed close to the Front’s 103 Base Camp in Barangay Delimbayan in Maguing town, Lanao del Sur.

The accounts that posted the false claim have been reposting the GMA News report of the incident without saying that it is a 2023 report. The post by the page “Kakatoh Trending” added a “breaking news” label, falsely implying that the incident happened recently.

According to Rappler’s 2023 report, officials said the incident stemmed from a lack of coordination between the Army’s Special Forces and the MILF — though the MILF claimed the soldiers in custody were only “requested” to surrender their firearms rather than being “disarmed.” The soldiers were later released following negotiations.

Commander Bravo’s “off-limits declaration”: The false claims began spreading after MILF leader Abdullah “Commander Bravo” Macapaar declared MILF communities in Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte as “off-limits” to government forces. His statement came after a large MILF convoy was intercepted on September 2 by soldiers and police in Lanao del Norte due to concerns over travel coordination.

These genuine media reports only mention an off-limits declaration, but do not confirm any actual blocking or disarming of soldiers.

In a September 9 Facebook post debunking Kakatoh Trending’s Facebook post, election monitor Independent Election Monitoring Center (IEMC) – BARMM said that following its initial checks with local military contacts, there was “no indication of a blockade, confrontation, or confiscation of firearms involving AFP and MILF personnel in Lanao del Sur.”

The IEMC – BARMM is a coalition of watchdog groups, including the Institute of Autonomy and Governance, National Citizens’ Movement for Free Elections, and Parish Pastoral Council Responsible for Voting, accredited by the Commission on Elections to monitor the BARMM polls.

BARMM parliamentary elections: The upcoming polls represent the Bangsamoro’s third attempt at establishing regional governance, following four postponements from the original 2022 election schedule through March 2026.

The BARMM’s parliamentary elections serve as a milestone in the region’s decades-long journey to peace following the MILF and the Philippine government’s historic peace agreement in 2014. The elections come amid persistence of violence and heightened security concerns, with 108 areas classified as election areas of concern, particularly in Lanao del Sur. (LIVE UPDATES: First BARMM parliamentary elections)

Debunked: In its post debunking the false claim, the IEMC – BARMM also warned against claims involving AFP–MILF security coordination, since unverified reports about such movements or security incidents can heighten tensions.

Rappler has previously debunked claims related to the BARMM and its upcoming elections:

– John Jerome Santos/Rappler.com

John Jerome Santos is a research and data volunteer writer at Rappler. He is a fourth year Bachelor of Science in Accountancy student at the Dr. Gloria Lacson Foundation Colleges of Cabanatuan City.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Trump’s Iran campaign echoes the post-9/11 ‘forever wars’
World.content:
TRUMP BILLBOARD. A woman walks near a billboard depicting US President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran, Iran, July 27, 2026.

Critics say Trump has ignored key lessons from previous post-9/11 wars, including the risks of long-term engagements and the importance of international support, leading to a conflict that lacks public backing and has strained relations with allies

WASHINGTON, USA – When Donald Trump campaigned for a second term in the White House, he promised to be a “president of peace” who would stop foreign wars, not start them.

Now, a quarter-century after the September 11, 2001, attacks that triggered America’s global “war on terror,” he is entangled in an unpopular conflict of his own making that analysts say risks becoming his version of a “forever war.”

With the 9/11 anniversary at hand, Trump’s war against Iran is drawing comparisons in foreign policy circles to the long, divisive conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq that preceded it.

It is also prompting questions about whether the US has again failed to learn the lessons of past conflicts or prepare a clear exit strategy.

“Trump has broken an important post-Iraq and Afghanistan constraint in Washington against launching another major, open-ended war in the Middle East,” said Sina Toossi of the Center for International Policy, a Washington think tank. “That could leave his successor inheriting … an entrenched US-Iran confrontation.”

Administration officials have said the war against Iran is nothing like the protracted post-9/11 engagements.

During the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, the US removed hostile governments, committed thousands of ground troops who took and held territory, suffered and inflicted much higher casualties and struggled to instill Western-style governance.

This time, the US is relying mainly on air and naval power, operations that have damaged Iran militarily and economically but have not defeated it or spurred Iranians to overthrow their rulers as Trump initially urged.

But after six months of war, the United States is mired in a battle of attrition punctuated by bursts of hostilities – exemplified by this week’s exchange of attacks on oil tankers – while Trump tries to tighten the economic noose around Tehran.

Analysts warn it is likely to drag on well past the US midterm elections in November, when voters’ opposition to the war could threaten Trump’s Republican Party’s chances of keeping control of Congress.

And, much like those earlier conflicts, there is no obvious exit even as the economic costs weigh on US consumers.

Tehran’s disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has pushed US gasoline prices higher. The war has weakened Trump’s approval ratings and undermined Washington’s international standing, which was also one of the repercussions from the Iraq and Afghan wars.

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said Trump alone had “possessed the courage” to confront Iran over its nuclear program, that he had achieved all of his objectives and Iran’s economy was being crippled by stepped-up sanctions and a US maritime blockade.

She did not respond directly to Reuters’ questions on how the Iran conflict fits into America’s legacy of post-9/11 wars.

Lessons ignored?

Analysts say Trump has failed to heed the central lessons of the post-9/11 era, which began after al Qaeda militants crashed planes into New York’s World Trade Center and the Pentagon outside Washington, killing nearly 3,000 people.

Those include the steep political downsides of long wars and the dangers posed by an entrenched foe fighting for its survival.

The attacks led to decades of conflict, starting with the invasion of Afghanistan, where al Qaeda leaders were sheltering, and followed by the 2003 invasion of Iraq, based on what turned out to be faulty intelligence that it was developing weapons of mass destruction.

The twin wars undertaken by President George W. Bush overstretched the US military and destabilized the Middle East.

The resulting US public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, and he won a second term in 2024 vowing to avoid military adventurism and focus on Americans’ economic concerns.

But similar to how the Bush administration underestimated the insurgencies the US would face in Iraq and Afghanistan, Trump and his aides have miscalculated Iran’s resiliency and ability to throttle a fifth of the world’s energy shipments, analysts say.

Notably, Trump’s “Operation Epic Fury” launched alongside Israel on February 28 was not precipitated by a 9/11-type national trauma but was deemed by critics to be a war of choice.

Experts have disputed Trump’s claims that Tehran’s nuclear program posed an imminent threat to the US.

Iran may be taking a page from Afghanistan’s Taliban, who returned to power five years ago after a chaotic US withdrawal, that a determined foe can outlast Washington’s superior firepower while domestic pressure erodes its resolve.

The Iran conflict has also illustrated the cost of going to war with few allies on board.

Bush secured significant international support before launching his Iraq and Afghan campaigns, though that backing waned over time.

By contrast, Trump attacked Iran with little prior consultation or explanation and has found European and Asian leaders mostly resistant to his demands for assistance.

Relations with Trump had already been strained by his threat to seize Greenland, his questioning of NATO’s utility, his reduction of weapons supplies to Ukraine and his sweeping tariffs on trade partners.

High cost for allies

The conflict has also mirrored the Iraq invasion in terms of a regional spillover that seemed to catch Washington off-guard, in this case Tehran’s retaliation against US Gulf allies.

With Iran’s neighbors quietly seeking to de-escalate a conflict they never wanted, a Gulf official lamented that the administration might be making some of the same errors of the post-9/11 wars.

“What was the (US) strategy here?” asked the official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Saudi analyst Aziz Alghashian described “a sense of limitation and helplessness in the Gulf about the wars that are taking place due to the whims of the United States.”

The war’s shockwaves expanded on Thursday, September 10, with Yemeni government military sources saying Iran-aligned Houthis had seized control of the Yemeni port city of Mocha and gained further leverage over an important Red Sea oil-shipping route.

While the Iraq and Afghan wars ended as unpopular conflicts, both started with solid support at home.

Trump’s war enjoyed no such honeymoon in public opinion.

Most Americans were against it from the outset, and he has even drawn criticism from prominent figures associated with his “America First” movement.

Trump had initially expected to replicate his quick win from a January 3 raid that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.

But the Iran campaign instead has hardened into an uneasy stalemate that has not achieved most of Trump’s shifting objectives, including shutting down its nuclear program, and has depleted the Pentagon’s missile stockpiles.

Still, Trump is not without defenders.

Mark Dubowitz, head of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank that takes a hard line against Iran’s rulers, denied Trump had plunged the US into an endless war and insisted he had scored successes that would eventually bring victory.

“It’s been a 47-year war waged by the Islamic Republic against America,” Dubowitz said. “And now we’ve struck back.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Romualdez needs 4-6 weeks before hospital transfer, doctor says
World.content:
Former House Speaker and Leyte 1st District Rep. Martin Romualdez at the Cardinal Santos Hospital. INQUIRER.net / JASON SIGALES

MANILA, Philippines — Four to six weeks are needed before former House Speaker Martin Romualdez could be safely transferred to another facility, his cardiologist told the Sandiganbayan on Friday.

Dr. Rody Sy, a cardiologist at Cardinal Santos Medical Center, gave the assessment during clarificatory questions from Associate Justice Ronald Moreno at the hearing on Romualdez’s plea to remain confined at the private hospital.

Moreno asked if he would allow Romualdez to be transferred to another facility, and Sy said it is possible.

Article continues after this 

READ: ‘Big risk’ to transferRomualdez to another hospital, says witness

Asked by Moreno how long it would take before Romualdez’s symptoms would improve enough for a transfer, Sy said, “Around four to six weeks.”

During cross-examination by Deputy Special Prosecutor Omar Sagadal, Sy reiterated that transferring Romualdez at this time is not “appropriate”.

“It will not be ideal because there should be continuity of care,” Sy also said.

READ: Romualdez under BJMP, but transfer on hold

Article continues after this 

Romualdez was admitted to the private hospital on Monday due to chest pain, the same day when a warrant for his arrest came out.

Moreno asked if the arrest warrant could have caused the chest pain, and Sy said: “I think so. That is a big factor.”

Article continues after this 

In his motion filed on Monday, Romualdez said he is suffering from Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, primary hypothyroidism and other illnesses.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued the arrest warrant against Romualdez, former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co and two others on Monday, hours after the Office of the Ombudsman filed plunder charges against them involving alleged kickbacks worth P7.44 billion.

World.title: Tacloban university suspends uniform policy amid extreme heat
World.content:
The Eastern Visayas State University (EVSU) in Tacloban City temporarily suspended the mandatory wearing of prescribed school uniforms from Sept. 10 to Oct. 2, 2026, as a heat-safety measure amid extreme heat conditions. (Photo from EVSU Facebook page)

TACLOBAN CITY — The Eastern Visayas State University (EVSU) temporarily suspended the mandatory uniform policy as a heat-safety measure, while the mayor of Carigara, Leyte, redirected part of his office’s travel and seminar funds to provide air-coolers for the campus classrooms.

Under Memorandum No. 09-06-2026 issued through the Office of the University President, the wearing of prescribed university uniforms is suspended from Sept. 10 to Oct. 2, 2026, citing prevailing extreme heat index conditions and the health and safety of students and employees.

During the suspension, students and employees may wear comfortable, modest, weather-appropriate clothing, provided these remain consistent with university policies on propriety and decorum.

Article continues after this 

READ: Extreme heat raises concerns in some Agusan del Sur schools

EVSU also reminded everyone to wear their official university identification cards at all times while inside university premises.

The directive covers all EVSU offices, schools, and campuses.

In Carigara, Mayor Eduard “Ed” Ong Jr. said he chose to prioritize the comfort of students by using funds originally intended for his office’s travel and seminars to purchase air-coolers for classrooms at the EVSU-Carigara Campus.

“Instead of traveling or spending on seminars, I chose to have air-coolers distributed to all classrooms of the Eastern Visayas State University-Carigara Campus,” Ong said.

Article continues after this 

He said the funds used to purchase the air-coolers came from his office’s travel and seminar budget.

“Students’ comfort is more important than personal travel,” Ong said.

Article continues after this 

READ: 2 Eastern Visayas universities drop uniform rule as heat index soars

The move comes as schools across Eastern Visayas continue to deal with high heat conditions, which can affect students’ concentration, comfort, and health, particularly in classrooms with limited ventilation.

EVSU is the region’s state university, with its main campus in Tacloban City and five campuses outside the city—in Burauen, Carigara, Ormoc, Tanauan and Dulag. The university has more than 20,000 students, based on its reported second-semester enrollment for School Year 2025-2026.

The temporary uniform suspension allows students to wear lighter and more comfortable clothing while the university and its campuses implement measures to address the effects of extreme heat.

University officials also directed all offices, schools, campuses, and personnel to ensure the memorandum is properly disseminated and strictly observed./coa

World.title: MTRCB ready to regulate online platforms if Congress allows
World.content:
Diorella Maria “Lala” Sotto-Antonio, chairperson of the Movie and Television Review and Classification Board (MTRCB) speaks during a budget hearing in this file photo taken on September 27, 2023. (Voltaire F. Domingo/Senate PRIB)

MANILA, Philippines – Movie and Television Review and Classification (MTRCB) Chairperson Diorella Maria “Lala” Sotto-Antonio said the agency can regulate online services, streaming platforms, and subscription video on-demand services if mandated by Congress.

Sotto-Antonio gave the assurance on Friday after Sen. Erwin Tulfo asked during a Senate hearing about the agency’s preparedness should Congress expand its mandate to cover online platforms.

READ: MTRCB says it only eyes online content, not regulation of websites

Article continues after this 

Tulfo presided over the Senate subcommittee on finance’s discussion on the MTRCB’s proposed P49.99 million budget this year.

“First, Mr. Chairman, I would like to emphasize that the MTRCB is not for prohibition but for regulation. We will accept the challenge if the legislators would include the said online services, streaming platforms, the subscription video on-demand services in our jurisdiction or our purview,” Sotto- Antonio said.

“However, it would entail a lot of coordination with the said stakeholders such as the OTTs or the over-the-top, and the online streaming services,” she added.

Tulfo lamented in particular the lack of restrictions on subscription services, recalling an incident when a naked woman suddenly appeared on screen while he was watching a movie.

“And I didn’t know that a young man, my son, behind me was that looking also. So, I don’t know. Kung nangyari nga sa akin, maybe sa ibang mga household, wala naman kasing restriction when you turn on, dahil subscription po yun,” the senator said.

Article continues after this 

(And I didn’t know that a young man, my son, was behind me also watching. So, I don’t know. If this happened to me, maybe it’s also happening in other households. There’s really no restriction when you turn it on because it’s a subscription service.

He then pressed the MTRCB on whether it could address the problem once there is a law allowing it to regulate these online platforms.

Article continues after this 

“Yes, it would be feasible. Yes, the MTRCB can do it,” Sotto-Antonio said. “But I would like to reiterate that it is only the regulation that we can do.”

The MTRCB chief also clarified that movies shown on online streaming platforms “do not need to go through prior constraints,” but stressed that there should be an effective feedback mechanism that can respond quickly to complaints.

According to her, the MTRCB is currently working with Netflix, HBO and Disney, which she said have been very cooperative with them.

World.title: Marcos recalls lessons on leadership on father’s 109th birthday
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. leads the wreath-laying ceremony at the Marcos Monument in Batac City, Ilocos Norte, on Sept. 11, 2026, marking the 109th birth anniversary of his late father, former President Ferdinand E. Marcos Sr. (screen grab from RTVM)

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — “Spending time with him – (and) I never knew it – but he was already teaching me. He was already training me,” President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said as he recalled his late father, former President Ferdinand Edralin Marcos Sr.

The President marked his father’s 109th birthday in Ilocos Norte’s Batac City, where the latter was raised.

Marcos said good leadership requires sacrifice and doing what is right even when it is difficult, as he led the celebration at the Bannawag Shrine in Batac. The province of Ilocos Norte observed Friday as a special nonworking day to mark the memorial for the late president

Article continues after this 

READ: Sept. 11 a holiday in Ilocos Norte for Marcos Sr.’s birth anniversary

He said his father’s lessons were not about becoming an important public figure or reaching the heights of political leadership.

Rather, he said, his father taught him values that he would carry into public service.

“Nothing worthwhile is achieved without sacrifice,” Marcos Jr. recalled his father telling him.

“Do not take whatever is the easy way out. Do what is right, no matter how difficult it may be,” the President said as he recounted his father’s words, adding, “The most important lesson is about your country and your countrymen. “

Article continues after this 

The President led a wreath-laying ceremony at the Marcos Monument following a Thanksgiving Mass at the Immaculate Conception Parish in Batac, attended by the First Family.

The President paid tribute to his father’s years in public service and reflected on the values and principles that he said continue to shape his commitment to serving Filipinos.

Article continues after this 

READ: Marcos honors late father: He left a legacy of service, sacrifice

The commemoration also included a “Natnateng” (Vegetables) Cook-off at the Imelda Cultural Center, featuring vegetable dishes from the province and celebrating Ilocos Norte’s agricultural traditions.

The event came two days before Marcos Jr.’s 69th birthday on Sept. 13./coa

World.title: Senate impeachment court claims impartiality in amici curiae selection
World.content:
The Senate impeachment court huddles. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court has maintained that it was impartial in picking the four retired Supreme Court (SC) justices that would serve as legal advisers on the issue of whether the voting threshold needed to convict or acquit Vice President Sara Duterte should be changed.

In an online press conference on Friday, impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol stressed that retired Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban, Reynato Puno and Hilario Davide, Jr., as well as retired Associate Justice Rodolfo Azcuna, were picked as amici curiae, or friends of the court, based on their credentials and known expertise on constitutional issues.

Puno served as chair of the Consultative Committee that reviewed the 1987 Constitution during the Duterte administration, while Davide and Azcuna were part of the 1986 Constitutional Commission that drafted the 1987 Constitution.

Article continues after this 

“That’s why they were chosen [because of their expertise], and also their known impartiality in their stance,” Tongol said.

READ: 4 retired SC justices giving views on `2/3′ conviction vote

These legal luminaries have also not yet publicly shared or discussed in media interviews or social media their respective positions on the issue, he added.

Both the defense and the prosecution were also consulted on the process and whether the parties have any questions by Presiding Officer Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero, said Tongol.

He, however, said that the impeachment court is considering adding more legal experts as it took into consideration public sentiments, including that only male legal experts, and no female justices, were invited.

Article continues after this 

READ: Senate impeach court eyes Sept. 23 ruling on votes to convict Duterte

“That is an ongoing process. Maybe this weekend, if ever there are developments on that, maybe more would be added (as amici curiae),” said Tongol.

Article continues after this 

The four retired justices are expected to provide their insights on Sept. 16 on the highly contentious voting issue as current rules require at least 16 votes from the 24 senator-judges to be able to secure a conviction of Duterte.

But four senators are unable to attend the trial: Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is in hiding amid a standing arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court; Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are detained on the nonbailable charge of plunder before the Sandiganbayan; and Loren Legarda, who is abroad on an extended medical leave.

The amici curiae for Duterte’s impeachment trial was appointed by Escudero, after Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo made an appeal last Tuesday to revisit the Presiding Officer’s initial ruling on the voting threshold.

Escudero maintained at the start of the impeachment trial that the court will maintain a 16-vote requirement to convict impeachable officials. However, Tulfo asked to revisit the ruling in lieu of three senators that have yet to attend a sinlge trial day due to legal battles.

World.title: 2 listed on manifest did not board ill-fated Palawan ferry
World.content:
Two people listed on the manifest of a ferry that caught fire on its way to Coron town on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, never boarded and are now struck off the missing list. PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD PHOTO

PUERTO PRINCESA CITY — Two people who were listed on the manifest of MV June Aster, which caught fire on its way to Coron town on Wednesday, never made it on board and are now struck off the missing list, according to Commodore Noemi Cayabyab, spokesperson of the Philippine Coast Guard, on Friday.

Search and rescue operations have since resumed for what is now 84 missing occupants of the ship currently stuck in a shallow portion of the sea near Calanhayuan Island in Coron town.

READ: Passenger ferry caught fire off Coron, Palawan

Article continues after this 

The new tally brings the total number of people aboard MV June Aster down to 115 passengers and 17 crew members. Responders have rescued 43 survivors and confirmed five fatalities.

The latest photos sent by PCG showed thick smoke still emerging from the ship, which still prevents search teams from boarding./coa

World.title: NBI tapped to probe flood control projects in Candaba, Pampanga
World.content:
Atty. Joey dela Cruz and Atty. Faye Singson, counsels for 14 residents from Candaba, Pampanga, along with former Candaba Mayor Jerry Pelayo, arrive at the National Bureau of Investigation-Organized and Transnational Crimes Division office on Friday to file a complaint seeking an investigation into alleged irregularities in flood control projects and the use of government funds involving entities supposedly linked to Candaba Mayor Rene Maglanque. INQUIRER / MARY JOY SALCEDO

MANILA, Philippines — Some citizens from Candaba, Pampanga, are requesting the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to look into alleged irregularities in flood control projects and the use of government funds involving entities supposedly linked to Candaba Mayor Rene Maglanque.

Atty. Faye Singson and Atty. Joey dela Cruz, counsel for the 14 residents who serve as the complainants, along with former Candaba Mayor Jerry Pelayo, arrived at the NBI’s Organized and Transnational Crimes Division office on Friday to file the complaint.

NBI TAPPED TO PROBE FLOOD CONTROL PROJECTS IN CANDABA, PAMPANGALOOK: Some citizens from Candaba, Pampanga, are requesting the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to investigate alleged irregularities in flood control projects and the use of government funds involving… pic.twitter.com/oxhoB5p2aU — Inquirer (@inquirerdotnet) September 11, 2026

The complainants specifically seek to probe alleged anomalies involving Sto. Cristo Construction & Trading and Globalcrete Builders, Inc., which supposedly secured P5.4 billion in contracts between 2022 and 2025.

Article continues after this 

Of these contracts, the P1.4 billion obtained by Sto. Cristo Construction & Trading was supposedly allocated solely for flood control projects in Candaba.

READ: NBI to file 30 more flood-control cases to DOJ, says Matibag

The complainants likewise questioned Sto. Cristo Construction & Trading’s alleged transfer of P753.3 million to Globalcrete Builders, Inc., which they believe is owned and registered under the name Maglanque.

READ: NBI probes P1.9B Davao flood projects given to just 1 contractor

Additionally, the complaint sought an investigation into MBB Global Properties Corporation, established in 2023.

Article continues after this 

The company is allegedly owned by Macy Monique Alarcon Maglangue, daughter of the incumbent Candaba mayor, and unnamed daughters of former Public Works Secretary Manny Bonoan and former Public Works Undersecretary Roberto Bernardo.

Mayor Maglanque has yet to issue a public statement regarding the complaint as of this writing. /jpv

World.title: From National SDGs to Regional Delivery: Central Asia’s Next Step
World.content:
Central Asia has entered a new phase of regional cooperation. The question is no longer simply whether the five countries can work together. Increasingly, it is whether growing political trust can be converted into practical institutions, shared measurements and tangible results for the people of the region.

The Sustainable Development Goals offer an important test.

Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan have each incorporated the 2030 Agenda into national development policies to varying degrees. Yet some of the region’s most difficult development challenges cannot be solved within national borders.

Water flows across them. Energy systems increasingly depend on regional balancing and trade. Climate change affects shared river basins, glaciers, pastures and ecosystems. Transport corridors only deliver their full economic value when they function across several countries. Air pollution, desertification and food security similarly have a regional dimension.

This creates a fundamental mismatch: many challenges are regional, while most mechanisms for implementing and measuring the SDGs remain national.

A foundation already exists

Central Asia is not starting from zero.

In 2021, the European Union and UNDP launched a Regional SDG Platform designed to work with governments and civil society in all five Central Asian states. The initiative supported knowledge exchange, policy analysis, monitoring and SDG financing. In 2024, a Regional SDG Monitoring Panel was launched to provide an integrated regional view of trends, policies, interlinkages, financing and data gaps.

Kazakhstan has played an important role in this process.

More significantly, Almaty is becoming home to the United Nations Regional Centre for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan. In August 2025, UN Secretary-General António Guterres and President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev witnessed the signing of the host country agreement. Guterres said the Centre could help translate stronger political relations in Central Asia into deeper economic integration.

The opportunity now is to turn that institutional foundation into measurable results.

Start with a limited number of shared priorities

Regional cooperation does not require Central Asian countries to create a second set of 17 SDGs or duplicate national institutions. A more realistic approach would be to identify a small number of issues where regional action clearly adds value.

Water and energy should be among the first.

Upstream and downstream interests have historically made this one of Central Asia’s most complicated policy areas. Climate change is making coordination increasingly unavoidable. Changes in glaciers and river flows affect agriculture, hydropower generation, ecosystems and drinking-water security across borders.

Instead of addressing water, energy and climate adaptation through separate policy tracks, countries could gradually develop shared indicators covering water efficiency, seasonal energy exchange, ecosystem resilience and climate risks.

Transport connectivity provides another opportunity. Governments understandably measure new roads, railways, border facilities and trade volumes nationally. But the real economic value of a corridor depends on the performance of the entire route.

Regional indicators could therefore measure border-crossing times, logistics reliability, digital customs interoperability and the environmental footprint of major corridors.

From data exchange to shared accountability

A regional approach also requires better data.

Central Asian governments already collect large volumes of statistics for national SDG monitoring. The challenge is not necessarily to create more indicators, but to make selected data comparable and useful for joint decision-making.

The existing regional SDG monitoring experience provides a starting point. The next step could be a compact regional dashboard focusing only on cross-border challenges. Governments, research institutions, civil society and international organizations could jointly review progress on a limited set of indicators each year.

This would not replace national reporting to the United Nations. It would complement it.

The difference is important. National reports ask: How is our country progressing? A regional mechanism would ask another question: Where can cooperation produce an outcome that no country can achieve alone?

The political moment is favorable

There is also a broader political reason to move now.

On 20 May 2026, the UN General Assembly adopted without a vote Resolution 80/260, “Strengthening regional cooperation and economic integration to ensure sustainable development in the Central Asian region.” The resolution encourages closer coordination among Central Asian states and calls on UN agencies, funds and programmes to align their activities with regional priorities.

This provides political legitimacy for moving from general commitments toward practical regional instruments.

The UN Regional Centre in Almaty could become an important platform for this work — not as a supranational institution, but as a neutral facilitator of data exchange, policy dialogue, expertise and joint initiatives.

Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, as the region’s two largest economies, have a particular opportunity to support this transition. But sustainable regionalism cannot be built around two countries alone. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are indispensable to water and energy cooperation; Turkmenistan is critical to connectivity, energy and engagement with Afghanistan.

The principle must therefore remain inclusive: five countries, shared ownership and practical benefits for all.

A Central Asian contribution to the global SDG debate

The implications could reach beyond the region.

The 2030 Agenda was designed around universal goals implemented primarily through national frameworks. Yet many of today’s development challenges — climate change, water scarcity, migration, energy transition, ecosystems and transport connectivity — are inherently transboundary.

Central Asia could help demonstrate how the gap between national commitments and regional realities can be narrowed.

The region does not need grand new structures. It needs a disciplined transition from dialogue to delivery: a few shared priorities, comparable indicators, regular review and joint projects where cooperation produces demonstrably better outcomes.

The political rapprochement of recent years has created an opportunity. The institutional foundations are beginning to emerge.

The next measure of Central Asian cooperation should therefore be not how often countries meet, but what they can achieve together.

The author is Jakhongir Isaev, the head of Department at the Center for Sustainable Development in Uzbekistan.

World.title: Kazakh Businesses to Trade Carbon Units on AIFC Exchange
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh businesses implementing environmental projects will be able to trade carbon units on the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) exchange under a planned agreement with the international carbon standard Verra, AIFC Product Director Zhanbolat Kakishev said at Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026.

“We will sign an agreement with the Verra standard. This will allow us to trade carbon units. Verra is one of the largest standards in this field. We will introduce it on our exchange, enabling entrepreneurs involved in environmental projects to trade carbon units directly on our exchange platform,” Kakishev said.

The agreement is expected to be signed during the AFD, taking place on Sept. 9-10.

The initiative is designed to expand access to the international carbon market for businesses implementing projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions.

Verra is an international nonprofit organization that develops standards for verifying greenhouse gas emission reductions and removals. Its Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) enables independently verified environmental projects to issue carbon units.

One carbon unit generally represents one metric ton of greenhouse gas emissions reduced or removed from the atmosphere, measured in carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e). Such units can then be traded with companies and other carbon market participants.

AFD participants also discussed Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop new asset classes and expand the country’s digital financial infrastructure, reflecting a broader push to modernize its capital markets.

AFD 2026 is held under the theme Delivering Impact. Capital in Action has attracted more than 8,000 registered participants, including representatives of major international investment companies and funds managing nearly $26 trillion in assets.

World.title: AFD 2026 Delivers New Agreements, Market Instruments for Regional Growth
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026: Delivering Impact. Capital in Action concluded with a series of agreements and new financial instruments to strengthen regional financial cooperation, sustainable finance, digital assets, aviation finance and access to capital.

Held on Sept. 9-10, the forum brought together 8,000 participants from 90 countries, including representatives of major global financial institutions and asset managers collectively managing more than $26 trillion. The forum also featured renowned Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen.

Expanding regional financial cooperation

Several agreements signed during the forum focused on regulatory cooperation and improving cross-border access to financial markets.

The Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA) signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the National Bank of Georgia on mutual access and recognition in financial services. The agreement establishes a framework for closer regulatory cooperation between the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and Georgian financial markets in selected areas.

AFSA also signed an MoU with the Croatian Financial Services Supervisory Agency (HANFA) to strengthen regulatory cooperation and further develop cooperation between the two authorities.

The agreements complement discussions held during the forum on reducing fragmentation between regional financial markets and facilitating cross-border capital flows.

The Astana International Exchange (AIX) and the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange (KSE) also agreed to strengthen cooperation and engagement between Kazakhstan’s and the Kyrgyz Republic’s capital markets.

New instruments for sustainable finance

A major development on the second day was AIX’s launch of trading in voluntary carbon credits verified under the international Verified Carbon Standard (VCS).

AIX became the first exchange in Central Asia to provide its own infrastructure for trading voluntary carbon credits. London-based Valor Carbon became the first supplier, with Standard International Market, an AIX broker and Trading Member, facilitating transactions.

The new exchange-based model is designed to provide transparent trading rules and market-based price discovery for carbon credits, creating an additional mechanism for climate projects in the region to access financing.

The initiative builds on the AIFC Carbon Platform and expands AIX’s environmental products, following the earlier introduction of I-REC renewable energy certificates.

The forum also advanced cooperation in sustainable finance through agreements involving the AIFC Green Finance Center, First Carbon Group, Green Investment Group and HYT-CAPITAL. The agreements aim to support sustainable projects, develop financial instruments and attract investment through capital markets in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

Aviation and digital assets

Aviation finance was another area where discussions moved toward practical cooperation. The AIFC and Development Bank of Kazakhstan agreed to cooperate on projects related to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

The forum also highlighted the development of Kazakhstan’s aviation finance ecosystem. Jupiter Jet completed its first aircraft leasing transaction with an American lessor with support from the AIFC Aviation Finance Hub.

Digital finance and tokenization featured prominently throughout AFD 2026. Tech Hub Ltd. and ōzen signed a framework cooperation agreement to develop a music royalty tokenization platform in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

Other agreements involving CodeCoin Tech Ltd., Delta DA Ltd. and Altyn Bank focused on cross-border financial services, fintech, asset management, trade finance and payment infrastructure.

From discussion to implementation

The agreements signed at AFD 2026 reflect the forum’s broader focus on turning investment opportunities into practical projects and market infrastructure.

The first day centered on sovereign and institutional capital, financial infrastructure, tokenization and the transformation of global finance. The program also included the launch of the AIFC Junior Mining Platform’s investor activities, with 23 early-stage mining projects presented to potential investors.

On the second day, the focus shifted further toward implementation – from carbon-credit trading and aviation finance to regional regulatory cooperation and new digital instruments.

As AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov said at the opening of the forum, competition for capital increasingly depends on the ability to transform opportunities into real projects and investments.

Against this backdrop, the agreements and market initiatives announced during AFD 2026 demonstrate the AIFC’s efforts to position Astana as a platform connecting international capital with investment opportunities in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia.

World.title: Dimash Calls for Investment, Infrastructure to Unlock Kazakhstan’s Creative Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh singer, composer and producer Dimash Qudaibergen called for greater investment, infrastructure and legal support for Kazakhstan’s creative industries during the opening ceremony of Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026 on Sept. 9.

AFD 2026 is a two-day event bringing together more than 5,500 participants from over 80 countries to discuss capital markets, investment, artificial intelligence, innovation, real-economy financing and cross-border capital.

While on stage, Qudaibergen performed “Aqerke,” “Stranger” and “Weekend,” as well as the traditional Kazakh kui “Adai” on dombra.

Following the performance, Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) Governor Renat Bekturov spoke with Qudaibergen about the potential of Kazakhstan’s creative economy, attracting investment to the sector, intellectual property protection and the challenges artists face when entering international markets.

Qudaibergen said the development of the creative industry requires not only investment, but also stronger legal protection for artists and mechanisms to connect creators with investors.

“Artists need legal protection and support from creative industry development funds. These funds can become a bridge between investors and new creative projects,” Qudaibergen said.

Bekturov noted that Kazakhstan’s creative sector brings together thousands of companies and more than 140,000 people, while its contribution to the economy remains relatively small, highlighting the need to develop the sector as a source of future growth.

When asked why investors should consider creative industries, Qudaibergen pointed to Kazakhstan’s culture, history and music as assets with strong international appeal.

“Our culture, our history and the music are truly unique, and that makes them interesting to an international audience,” he said, drawing on his experience of performing around the world.

Protecting creative independence

For Qudaibergen, attracting investment should not come at the expense of an artist’s independence or ownership of intellectual property.

He said the decision to share rights with investors or business partners is ultimately personal, but artists should understand the financial and contractual side of their profession before making such decisions.

“I choose the second option, because for me it is essential to keep both creative independence and ownership of my intellectual property,” he said.

Qudaibergen stressed that financial literacy is part of an artist’s professional responsibility, allowing creators to better understand contracts, finances and the business side of the industry.

“Education everywhere is very important,” he said, adding that understanding contracts, finances and the business side of the industry allows artists to make informed decisions and retain control over their work.

He also cited his own career as an example of how an artist can gradually move from performer to producer and entrepreneur.

Qudaibergen said he now works directly with business partners and operates his own label, established by his father, which promotes not only his work but also young artists.

His transition into production included an international vocal project on China’s Hunan TV, where he first gained international recognition through “I’m a Singer” show. Returning to the network as a producer, he said, gave him an opportunity to introduce other Kazakh talents to a global audience.

From Kazakh roots to global audiences

Qudaibergen said Kazakhstan’s cultural identity can become a competitive advantage internationally when traditional heritage is combined with contemporary approaches.

“Our uniqueness comes from combining respect for our roots with a desire to innovate,” he said. “We can make traditional things feel fresh and turn something authentic into a modern trend.”

During his tours, Qudaibergen has introduced audiences to musicians from his team and traditional Kazakh instruments, including dombra and kobyz. He said some international fans also became interested in Kazakhstan’s history, language and traditional music.

He also encouraged young Kazakh artists to remain connected to their identity while pursuing international careers.

“To become an international artist, you have to follow your own path, first of all. And then you need to believe in yourself,” he said.

He warned young artists against changing direction simply because of short-term financial opportunities.

“Professional career management means thinking long term,” he said. “You shouldn’t accept every offer just because it looks profitable today. You always have to remember the goal you are moving towards.”

Building a system for young talent

Qudaibergen said Kazakhstan’s creative sector needs a more systematic approach to developing talent, particularly in management, professional training, broadcasting and distribution.

He identified a shortage of qualified professionals as one of the industry’s key challenges, arguing that talented artists need more than opportunities to perform.

“We have not yet become a full-fledged industry with a clear system. So, we need to do our best to train professionals,” he said.

He also pointed to the limited presence of creative projects across television, radio and large-scale distribution platforms.

“The main task is to build professional infrastructure and create a clear, systematic path to international markets,” Qudaibergen said.

Qudaibergen said this was particularly important because young artists should not have to rely on chance encounters or simply hope that someone will discover them.

“This is exactly what I was missing when I started,” he said, recalling his own experience as a young artist from Aktobe who had little understanding of how to build an international career.

“Right now, it has become one more mission,” he said. “Young talents should grow inside a real creative development system, instead of simply hoping that one day they will get lucky and someone will invite them somewhere.”

Qudaibergen’s own career, from a young performer in Aktobe to an internationally recognized artist and producer, illustrates the potential of such opportunities. Reflecting on his journey, he emphasized that talent alone is not enough to build a lasting career.

“Hard work is also very important. It’s the most important thing,” he said. “When the universe turns to your side, you need to be ready.”

Qudaibergen is now preparing his new Dimensions world tour, continuing his international career while expanding his work as a producer and supporting young Kazakh artists.

World.title: AFD 2026: Creative Industry Pushes Investors to Rethink What Counts as Financial Asset
World.content:
ASTANA – What if a song, a game, a digital creator or a piece of intellectual property could be treated not only as a cultural product, but as an investable asset? For Kazakhstan’s emerging creative economy, that shift in thinking could be as important as the creative output itself.

The question was at the center of discussions on the second day of Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026, held on Sept. 10 and dedicated to creative industries as an asset class, moderated by David Tuganov, president of the Creative Industries Alliance of Qazaqstan (CIAQ), the panel brought together Aizatulla Hussein, founder of Õzen; Olzhas Akparov, CBDO of Cyber Temple; Julia Kushnir, head of business development for Eastern Europe and Central Asia at TikTok; and Askar Bilisbekov, CEO of Alem Capital Management Limited.

Tokenization of the song?

One of the clearest examples of that shift came from the music industry, where Õzen is working on what Hussein described as a new way to turn music intellectual property into a financial asset through blockchain-based tokenization.

“For the last seven years that we have been working in the music industry, our core business has been the distribution of music content in the digital space. But music is not simply entertainment. It is a full-fledged financial asset that can generate income over many years, and that income continues to grow,” Hussein said.

The concept is to tokenize music rights through smart contracts and allow investors to acquire a fractional economic interest in a song, with returns linked to the income generated by the underlying music.

“What we are doing now is tokenizing the music asset, the music intellectual property, through smart contracts. Now we give anyone the opportunity to come and buy a piece of this song, and when the income comes to the artist, proportionally to how many tokens they have acquired, they will receive those payments,” Hussein said.

The model, he said, could effectively create an internal marketplace for music, where investors can assess the performance and potential of individual compositions using data generated across digital platforms. Õzen’s model is still building the necessary legal and regulatory framework, with Hussein identifying jurisdiction as the key challenge rather than the technology itself.

“In principle, the technology is not a problem at all. These technologies have already been developed. The only serious thing that we need to implement correctly is the jurisdiction, how we can turn a contract into tokens,” he said, noting that the company hopes to launch pilot projects by the end of the year.

The move is significant because it changes the conversation around creative industries from one centered primarily on grants, promotion and audience growth to one centered on ownership, cash flows and investment returns.

Shift in investors’ mindset

Bilisbekov also emphasized this shift in investor thinking, noting that the main obstacle facing creative entrepreneurs in Kazakhstan is often not a lack of talent, but an insufficient understanding of how to present that talent as a business proposition.

Drawing a comparison with Hollywood’s film industry, he said investors have long understood that creative investments can be approached through venture capital strategies, where a number of projects are financed with the understanding that some will fail while a smaller number generate significant returns.

“In Hollywood, the principle was quite simple: invest in a large number of films, knowing and understanding that most of the films will fail,” Bilisbekov said.

He said similar venture-style approaches already finance creative projects globally, while Kazakhstan’s creative sector remains constrained by a fragmented market and a limited understanding of the investor relationship.

“In the creative industry in Kazakhstan and in our region, the attitude toward investors is always somewhat residual. Why? Because there is no understanding that an investor is, first of all, your partner,” he said.

For Bilisbekov, that means creative entrepreneurs also need to change how they themselves approach investment.

“We need to change our mindset,” he said, highlighting that creative founders must be able to understand the financial side of their businesses, communicate their models clearly and demonstrate that they can operate beyond the strength of an idea alone.

“One investor has never bought into a company simply because you are talented, simply because you have an idea,” he said.

From creativity to business value

The point is particularly relevant as the creative economy increasingly intersects with technology. TikTok, for example, is no longer simply a platform for entertainment, according to Kushnir, but part of Kazakhstan’s broader digital creative economy, giving creators, entrepreneurs and businesses direct access to audiences.

“The platform is part of Kazakhstan’s digital creative economy,” Kushnir said, emphasizing what she described as the democratization of creativity.

“Absolutely any person has all the tools and all the opportunities to interact with an audience,” she said, noting that creators do not necessarily need millions of followers or an established public profile to find an audience.

For businesses, that audience can translate into commercial value, with TikTok’s research with the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs showing that 80% of surveyed small and medium-sized businesses said the platform helps them attract new customers, 79% said it helps them retain customers, and around 70% said it helps them differentiate themselves from competitors. The next step, however, is converting reach and creativity into durable businesses and investable assets. That is where the convergence of creativity, technology and capital becomes particularly important.

Where AI meets creativity

Akparov described how artificial intelligence is already changing parts of game development, including early-stage concept work and the creation of visual references, while Bilisbekov said that Kazakhstan’s strongest competitive advantage may ultimately lie in its human capital.

“Our brains are absolutely competitive. There are simply a little bit more efforts needed in this direction. There will be more of these startups,” Bilisbekov said.

Hussein likewise pointed to a growing convergence between Kazakhstan’s technology and creative communities, arguing that the two sectors need to become less separate.

“IT people should come to creatives, and creatives should come to IT,” he said, describing them as two communities that have traditionally developed in parallel rather than together.

That convergence could become increasingly important as AI lowers some of the technical barriers to building digital products and puts greater value on ideas, storytelling, design and other forms of creative input.

For Kazakhstan, however, panelists suggested that the missing piece is still capital. Hussein noted that the country needs to create conditions for creative talent to develop into sustainable businesses, while Bilisbekov pointed to two priorities: dedicated programs for the creative industries and a deeper capital market.

“We don’t have, as far as I know, even a single acceleration program that has been launched for the creative industry. That is something that needs to be launched,” Bilisbekov said.

He also stressed the importance of developing Kazakhstan’s capital market more broadly, saying creative businesses need financing mechanisms that go beyond traditional business models.

“It is very important to develop the capital market. What we unfortunately lack today is exactly that,” he said.

That is perhaps the broader investment question emerging from Kazakhstan’s creative economy: not whether the country has talent, but whether it can build the financial, technological and regulatory infrastructure needed to turn that talent into assets that can be valued, financed and scaled.

The tokenization initiative being developed by Õzen offers one early example of what that could look like, moving music from a product consumed by an audience toward an asset in which an investor could potentially hold an economic interest.

For a country seeking to deepen its capital markets while developing a new generation of creative businesses, the shift may ultimately require both sides of the equation to rethink their roles: creatives need to become more financially literate, and investors need to become more comfortable assessing assets whose value may be built around intellectual property, audience, technology and cultural relevance rather than factories, equipment or conventional balance sheets.

World.title: ADCB Kazakhstan Plans to Triple Project Financing in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank plans to triple project financing in Kazakhstan over the next 18 months, from the current 2.5 trillion tenge (US$5.5 billion), as the bank expands its role in supporting the country’s real economy and infrastructure development.

The plans were discussed during a Sept. 9 meeting between Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Farooq Abdulrahman Al Marzooqi, Chairman of Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank Kazakhstan (ADCB Kazakhstan).

The meeting focused on expanding ADCB Group’s participation in projects in Kazakhstan, with particular attention to the development of the real sector and the modernization of digital infrastructure, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Bektenov highlighted Kazakhstan’s ongoing economic and institutional reforms to strengthen the country’s investment appeal. He also pointed to the growing role of the United Arab Emirates as an investment partner for Kazakhstan. UAE investments in the country have exceeded $7 billion over the past 20 years, with around $3 billion invested during the last two and a half years.

According to Bektenov, deeper involvement by ADCB Group could help Kazakhstan attract additional capital from the UAE and other Middle Eastern markets, while diversifying external sources of project financing.

Al Marzooqi highlighted the bank’s experience in Kazakhstan, including financing for energy and railway infrastructure, as well as projects in petrochemicals, transport and logistics.

Over the past 15 years, ADCB Kazakhstan has supported more than 100 business initiatives. Small and medium-sized enterprises account for around 90% of these projects.

ADCB explores energy financing opportunities

ADCB’s potential involvement in Kazakhstan’s energy projects was also discussed at a Sept. 10 meeting between Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov and an ADCB delegation led by Al Marzooqi.

The ministry outlined key investment priorities for the next three to five years, including the modernization of 77,500 kilometers of power grids, the addition of 8.4 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy capacity by 2035, and the development of gas processing facilities at major fields such as Kashagan and Karachaganak.

The talks also covered major value-added projects, including a 1.25-million-ton-per-year polyethylene complex, planned butadiene and alkylate production, and the expansion of oil refining capacity.

Kazakhstan proposed project financing, joint credit facilities and public-private partnerships as potential mechanisms for ADCB’s participation. Islamic financing was also highlighted, given the presence of ADCB Islamic in Kazakhstan.

The meeting follows growing UAE-Kazakhstan cooperation in the energy sector, including Masdar’s 1 gigawatt (GW) wind power project in the Zhambyl Region. ADCB said it was ready to further assess the projects presented by the Kazakh side.

The bank’s planned expansion comes as Kazakhstan seeks to mobilize greater private investment for infrastructure and economic diversification. The increased financing capacity is expected to support new projects across key sectors of the economy.

World.title: Rare-Earth Oxide Separation Facility Planned for Stepnogorsk
World.content:
ASTANA – Australian critical minerals company Lindian Resources and French rare-earth specialist Carester have agreed to advance plans for an 8,000-ton-per-year solvent extraction and rare-earth oxide separation facility in Stepnogorsk, Kazakhstan.

Under the agreement, Carester and Australian engineering company Tetra Tech Coffey will progress a definitive feasibility study (DFS), targeted for completion in the fourth quarter of 2026, reported Mining Technology on Sept. 3.

The facility is planned to produce separated rare-earth oxides, including neodymium and praseodymium, alongside a mixed heavy rare-earth compound containing dysprosium, terbium and yttrium.

The project will build on Lindian’s SARECO mixed rare-earth concentrate (MREC) processing facility in Stepnogorsk. Carester will provide process technology and engineering services and review the existing facility for potential optimization and upgrades.

The company’s integrated strategy links its Kangankunde rare-earths project in Malawi, where it plans to produce monazite concentrate, with downstream processing facilities in Kazakhstan.

The proposed solvent extraction facility is designed to receive SARECO product liquor solution and compatible third-party MREC. Lindian is also evaluating additional rare-earth feed sources in Kazakhstan.

The agreement includes a binding 10-year offtake arrangement, with two potential five-year extensions. Carester will purchase 70% of SEGH production and hold a right of first refusal over 70% of mixed heavy rare-earth carbonate produced at SARECO.

Carester will supply the heavy rare-earth products to its Caremag refinery in Lacq, France. Carester, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) and Iwatani Corporation are developing the refinery.

The Stepnogorsk facility is expected to benefit from existing power, gas, water, rail and reagent infrastructure, potentially providing cost advantages for the proposed expansion.

Lindian Executive Chairman Robert Martin said the agreement supports the company’s strategy of moving further downstream.

“The agreement with Carester represents another significant step in Lindian’s strategy to move further downstream to expand our markets and to capture more of the value from the rare earths that we produce,” Martin said.

The DFS is expected to be completed by the end of this year and will determine the next stage of development for the proposed facility.
