World.title: CPC Oil Loading Operations Resume After Drone Incident
World.content:
ASTANA – Oil loading operations at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal have resumed in normal mode after a Sept. 8 drone incident near the facility, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy said.

Following the incident, loading operations at Single Point Moorings (SPM) 2 and 3 were temporarily suspended.

The ministry said inspections of CPC’s cargo systems and tankers found no issues affecting the continuation of loading operations. No environmental impact was recorded.

“Following the necessary checks of the condition of CPC’s cargo systems and tankers, no issues affecting the further conduct of loading operations were identified. No environmental impact was recorded,” the ministry said.

Loading operations have since resumed and are currently operating normally.

The ministry also stressed that it imposed no restrictions on accepting oil from Kazakh shippers.

CPC remains a key export route for Kazakhstan’s crude, despite the country’s efforts to expand alternative transportation channels. As The Astana Times reported earlier, despite several disruptions from attacks on infrastructure, oil transportation into the CPC-K system increased 39% in January-August, while flows through several alternative routes also grew.

Experts have noted that disruptions to major export infrastructure create a strategic challenge for Kazakhstan. If the largest route is disrupted or becomes less available, the country cannot simply redirect all affected production elsewhere without hitting capacity, infrastructure and logistical constraints.

The latest developments therefore underscore the importance of maintaining reliable established export infrastructure while continuing to develop alternative routes.

World.title: Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Commission did not open proceedings against Pashinyan
World.content:
Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

The Corruption Prevention Commission refused to open administrative proceedings against Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. Commission members said the complaint contained no “obvious signs of violations of the code of conduct”.

Semyon Babayan, head of the human rights NGO Public Informant, had asked the commission to assess the prime minister’s alleged “violations of the code of conduct”.

“Pashinyan’s public rhetoric and the wording he often uses grossly violate the legally established integrity system and the ethical standards that public officials must follow,” the applicant said.

He presented the commission with 11 such examples. One of them was the word “immoral”, which the prime minister used to describe the Catholicos of All Armenians.

According to the human rights activist, “it insults the feelings of believers and violates the requirement for religious neutrality”.

However, the commission found that the wording remained within the permissible limits of freedom of expression.

For a long time, Nikol Pashinyan has demanded that Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II step down. He claims that the Catholicos has broken his vow of celibacy and has a daughter. The prime minister also believes that the Catholicos has links to foreign intelligence services and follows their orders. On 24 August, Nikol Pashinyan called the Catholicos “immoral” while speaking in parliament. He also referred to the Patriarch by his secular name, Ktrich Nersisyan. He has used this name for him since launching his campaign to reform the Church. In protest, opposition MPs banged on their desks every time the Catholicos’s name was mentioned. “Your Catholicos is immoral. If you are not bothered by the fact that the man who heads the Mother See is sexually active, then keep banging your desks as much as you like. There is no other way to have a child — even in the Church. There is only one way to have a child: sexual intercourse,” Pashinyan said.

Commission says the word “immoral” falls within the bounds of political speech

The commission commented on the use of the word “immoral” against the Catholicos, citing case law from the European Court of Human Rights. It stressed that political speech enjoys a broader scope of protection.

Commission members assessed the prime minister’s wording as falling within what is permissible in the context of political debate:

“The use of exaggeration, generalisations and even shocking or striking expressions is characteristic of political speech during political debates — in this case, a speech delivered from the parliamentary rostrum.”

They also noted that, according to the European Court of Human Rights, freedom of expression covers not only positive and favourable statements, but also those that may “offend, shock or disturb”.

The Corruption Prevention Commission therefore concluded that the prime minister’s statement should be considered in the broader context of political debate.

The decision also gives the meaning of the Armenian word “պիղծ”, which Pashinyan used, citing academician Eduard Aghayan’s Explanatory Dictionary of the Modern Armenian Language. It notes that the word primarily means “unclean, immoral, vicious”, while in a religious context it means “heretical, unacceptable, ungodly”.

As for the statement “your Patriarch is immoral”, commission members found no attack on the faith or a religious group. In their view, Pashinyan made an “assessment of the alleged conduct” of a specific member of the clergy:

“Pashinyan’s statement sought to criticise not the person, but a specific phenomenon — namely, the alleged violation of the vow of celibacy.”

The commission also stressed that the word “immoral” carries a negative connotation but “does not cross the line into vulgarity or profanity”. Its members also found no calls for violence or threats in Pashinyan’s speech.

According to the decision, the prime minister’s speech was “predominantly critical in nature, as is characteristic of political debate”.

What other violations did the human rights activist identify?

Semyon Babayan also told the commission about 10 other “serious violations” that he believes the prime minister had committed:

“Violation of the principle of separation of powers: a public statement that ‘there is no judge who would not do what I tell them to do’, which directly undermines the independence of the judiciary and trust in democratic institutions.

Use of offensive language: using crude, street-level rhetoric in public against opponents or citizens — conduct that is clearly incompatible with the ethics expected of a senior public official.

Unsubstantiated assessments and ‘back-of-the-envelope estimates’: arbitrarily citing percentages related to corruption and bribery, such as 70% or 100%, without referring to official or verified factual data.

Erosion of public trust: using threats and divisive rhetoric from a high state platform, which contributes to the spread of intolerance.

Threats to ‘smear [people] across the asphalt’: publicly calling for the use of force in a personalised and punitive manner, outside the framework of legal procedures.

The phrase ‘whimpering judges’: humiliating members of the judiciary and systematically discrediting the institution.

Statements that citizens would be ‘brought to their knees’ because of their political views: entrenching a culture of communication based on force and a commanding tone that is unbecoming of a statesman.

Segregation of fellow citizens by labelling them ‘persons of Armenian origin’: violating the principle of national unity and artificially dividing society.

Showing preferential treatment towards members of his own team: violating the principle of equal integrity standards for the sake of political expediency.

Erosion of the integrity and image of a public official: maintaining a marginal, sarcastic and aggressive tone in public debate, undermining the duty of a public official to set an example of appropriate conduct.”

The commission found no signs of an obvious violation in any of the examples cited.

Commission rejects case against Pashinyan

World.title: Property prices in Armenia rise again: new wave of emigration from Russia and other factors
World.content:
Armenia is seeing another wave of people relocating to the country, amid reports over the past two months of a possible mobilisation in Russia. As a result, both rents and property prices have risen again. On average, prices for rentals and properties for sale have increased by 20%.

At one point, prices were rising almost every day. This was evident from listings on popular online property sales and rental platforms. The biggest boom has been in the rental market. Activity is also increasing in cities near Yerevan, including Abovyan, Masis and Nor Hachn.

Most of those arriving are Armenians who had been living in Russia. They say they are moving to avoid being called up for military service and because of the uncertainty they have faced in recent months.

Amid the large influx, it has become difficult to find affordable and mid-range rental properties. This is also linked to students from the regions moving to the capital as the new academic year begins.

A Russian man found a job but cannot find a flat

Dmitry Popov arrived in Armenia with friends three weeks ago. They first stayed in Yerevan, then moved to Lori Province, where they found jobs in the towns of Alaverdi and Tumanyan.

He decided to stay in Yerevan, where he has acquaintances who offered him a place to stay. He has already found a job as a courier with one of Yerevan’s companies. He is now negotiating his pay with his employer. Meanwhile, Dmitry has been looking for a one- or two-bedroom flat in the outer districts of the capital. He cannot afford a place in the city centre because rents there are very high.

“At first, I was looking for a place for up to $500. Now I’m looking for one for $700. I still haven’t found anything because I need basic amenities — furniture and household appliances. Even when I find a flat with an average-quality renovation, it turns out there is no fridge, washing machine or comfortable sofa,” the young man explains.

He knows that the latest influx of migrants from Russia is largely driving the rise in prices.

After the initial influx and surge in prices during the first months of the Russia-Ukraine war, the property market began to stabilise. Prices fell slightly as many Russians returned home or moved to other countries. Now they have risen again.

“To be honest, I really like Yerevan. The city has its own rhythm, an interesting cultural scene, good food, friendly people and convenient public transport. I managed to find a job within a few days. Now I just need to find a flat. If I can’t find one in Yerevan, I’ll look in nearby towns. I’m asking local people how public transport works in the suburbs, what rental options are available and how lively those places are,” Dmitry says.

He says he did not have many options: he could either move to Yerevan or Tbilisi:

“I’ve visited both cities many times and had already been considering moving to one of them before the recent tensions in Russia. My friends who have lived in both cities recommended Yerevan, even though it is more expensive than Tbilisi. They said people in Yerevan are friendly, welcoming towards Russians and willing to help. They also said it would be easier to find a job here. By the way, they also suggested moving to other Armenian cities, such as Gyumri, Dilijan and Vanadzor.”

He says relatives in Russia call him to ask whether they should move to Armenia for the long term. He recommends it, although he also tells them about the problems.

He has already decided that if he manages to earn more in the future, he will buy a one-bedroom flat in Yerevan.

Factors affecting prices

Andranik Harutyunyan, director of Silver REA real estate agency, says apartment rents have risen by around 15% compared with last year. This is an average estimate, as prices vary significantly between different parts of the city and types of apartments.

The same applies to the property sales market. According to the estate agent, it is difficult to establish a single rate of price growth and compare it with last year’s figures:

“It is quite difficult to assess price changes in the primary market because developers sell apartments in residential complexes at different prices depending on the stage of construction. The secondary market is also seeing a noticeable increase in demand.”

Harutyunyan notes that members of the Armenian diaspora are showing greater interest in apartments on the secondary market. For them, buying property is a form of business investment. By renting out a property, they can earn a higher annual return than they would by keeping the same amount of money in a bank.

“Those who moved to Armenia after the Russia-Ukraine war began are also active. Some have been living here for about a year and have decided to settle permanently. Another group consists of people who had ties to Armenia in the past but have now decided to move their businesses and families here.

Interest is also being driven by the growing value placed on property assets in Armenia in recent years. As a result, demand for housing remains high in both the primary and secondary markets,” the real estate agency director says.

Apartment price trends by administrative district

According to data from the Cadastre Committee, property prices continued to rise across all of Yerevan’s administrative districts in the second quarter of 2026. However, the pace of growth varied. The biggest increases came in Nork-Marash, Shengavit and Ajapnyak.

Nork-Marash recorded the sharpest increase, with the average price reaching 553,000 drams ($1,527) per square metre. Compared with last year, this represents a 24% rise.

Apartment prices in Shengavit rose by around 19% over the same period, while prices in Ajapnyak increased by 16%. More construction and relatively affordable prices have helped drive demand in these districts.

Price changes were more moderate in other parts of the city. Growth has been relatively slow in the Small Centre and neighbouring Arabkir, largely because prices there were already high.

Overall, property prices in Yerevan continue to rise. However, the strongest growth is occurring in districts with development potential and relatively more affordable prices.

Property prices in Armenia rise again

World.title: How does Georgia’s parliament work? SJC analyses current legislative processes
World.content:
The Social Justice Center (SJC) analyses the work of Georgia’s 11th Parliament between 25 November 2024 and 26 June 2026. It notes that the parliament’s work has, on the one hand, undermined democratic institutions and rights and, on the other, expanded the executive branch’s discretionary powers and strengthened the centralisation of power.

The organisation’s director, Tamta Mikeladze, published the report’s main findings:

During this period, parliament adopted 276 legislative packages or initiatives. Almost half went through an accelerated procedure, while around 10% followed a simplified procedure. This means parliament adopted around 60% of legislative acts through accelerated or simplified procedures. The executive branch submitted more initiatives than parliament itself, showing that the legislative agenda was largely driven by government initiatives.

Almost half went through an accelerated procedure, while around 10% followed a simplified procedure. This means parliament adopted around 60% of legislative acts through accelerated or simplified procedures. The executive branch submitted more initiatives than parliament itself, showing that the legislative agenda was largely driven by government initiatives. During the same period, the parliament, which was almost entirely made up of members of the ruling Georgian Dream party, did not adopt a single opposition legislative initiative , including those submitted by the Gakharia for Georgia parliamentary party. After Gakharia for Georgia entered parliament, lawmakers formally opposed legislative initiatives in only 38 cases. In all other cases, they adopted the initiatives unanimously.

, including those submitted by the Gakharia for Georgia parliamentary party. After Gakharia for Georgia entered parliament, lawmakers formally opposed legislative initiatives in only 38 cases. In all other cases, they adopted the initiatives unanimously. The quality of the legislative process is also problematic. Explanatory notes generally did not indicate that broad consultations had taken place and often lacked relevant sectoral or comparative legal analysis. Of the 276 initiatives, local or international experts took part in only six cases, while just eight initiatives provided for the harmonisation of Georgian legislation with legal instruments of the Council of Europe, the EU or the UN.

Against this backdrop, the parliament’s work can be divided into several main areas:

● Restrictions on civil society and repressive controls – 7 legislative changes. Alongside the laws on “transparency of foreign influence” and “registration of foreign agents”, parliament amended the law on grants. These changes effectively placed civil society organisations under full state control and criminalised certain forms of their activity. Parliament also created an Agency for the Management of State Grants, restricted NGOs’ participation in state decision-making, tightened the rules for issuing and receiving grants, broadened the legal definition of a grant, and introduced new criminal and financial sanctions.

● Media and freedom of expression – 6 direct changes: rules on foreign funding changed, the Communications Commission gained wider powers, new requirements for broadcast content were introduced, coverage of court proceedings was restricted, and financial oversight mechanisms were strengthened.

● Five separate changes concerned freedom of assembly and expression, increasing administrative and criminal liability for actions related to protests.

● Public service – 8 changes. Institutional safeguards for civil servants were weakened, while political appointments and the discretion of senior officials gained greater importance. The Civil Service Bureau was abolished, and opportunities for employment under administrative contracts were expanded. At the same time, new financial benefits and mechanisms for obtaining permission to engage in certain activities were introduced, with access to them largely dependent on decisions by senior officials. This creates a risk of not only politicisation but also clientelist governance.

● Education and academia also became targets of centralisation. Changes adopted in 2025-2026 strengthened the government’s influence over university funding, student numbers, academic programmes, and the reorganisation and institutional structure of universities. The limited involvement of academics in the process points to a broader problem with academic freedom.

● Ideological and propaganda-related measures – 7 major legislative changes. These included the introduction of a new crime, “treason against the state”; the removal of the term “gender” from legislation; tougher drug policies; changes to labour and immigration rules for foreigners; and expanded mechanisms of state control. What these changes have in common is not only tougher policies in specific areas, but also the incorporation of political and ideological concepts into the legal framework.

It is also important to look not only at what parliament adopted, but at what it left off its agenda. During the reporting period, issues concerning the rights of children and prisoners, public procurement and corruption prevention, environmental protection and civil safety, healthcare, urban planning and construction, education, regional policy, agriculture and tourism were pushed into the background or postponed. As a result, parliament’s agenda was clearly dominated by restrictive and controlling legislation. At the same time, its positive legislative agenda, covering a broad range of public interests, was significantly weakened.

Tamta Mikeladze: “The parliament’s work is therefore, on the one hand, directed against democratic institutions and rights, while on the other, it strengthens the executive branch’s discretionary powers and centralisation.

The theoretical frameworks of ‘autocratic legalism’ and ‘sham law’ are important for describing this process. In such a system, a law may formally meet the technical requirements of a legal act, but it loses its primary function: limiting state power and reducing arbitrariness. The law no longer acts as a mechanism for constraining power. Instead, it becomes a tool for maintaining and consolidating power.

In short, Georgia’s process of autocratisation, after years of oscillating between hybrid democracy and hybrid authoritarianism, is now aggressively and systematically affecting the legal sphere itself for the first time. It is fundamentally changing the law’s substance and nature.

We still have no adequate understanding of how difficult it will be to rehabilitate the state, political system, legal system and society after the crisis and the authoritarian period that Georgian Dream has inflicted on them.”

On legislation in Georgia

World.title: Georgian blogger says Interior Ministry wants to punish him for insulting Russian propagandists
World.content:
Civil rights activist and blogger Tornike Razmadze says Georgia’s Interior Ministry has summoned him to court to impose a fine or administrative detention because he insulted Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov in response to their insults against Georgian King Erekle II.

Georgia’s recently established Hate Speech Unit at the Interior Ministry has accused Razmadze of violating Article 166, Part 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The provision covers swearing in a public place and carries a fine of 500 to 3,000 lari ($185–1,110) or administrative detention for up to 20 days.

According to the activist, the case concerns a video he posted several weeks ago in which Russian propagandists discussed Erekle II, calling him a “king who crawled on his knees”. Margarita Simonyan, in particular, claimed that King Erekle had begged the Russians for help “on his knees” and that modern Georgians would likewise get down on their knees and ask Russia to take them under its protection.

Tornike Razmadze explains that this was why he used obscene language against Simonyan and Solovyov — more precisely, against their mothers.

According to the blogger, Simonyan and Solovyov effectively insulted the ruling Georgian Dream party as well. What angers him most is that, instead of taking offence at the Russian propagandists, the government wants to punish the person who insulted them. Razmadze sees this message from the authorities as the most important aspect of the whole case.

The activist also appealed to Georgia’s Public Defender (Ombudsman):

“I am not asking you for protection or support. I have one simple request: record your position on the case opened against me. I simply want to hear your position.”

However, the Interior Ministry’s Hate Speech Unit said the case had nothing to do with kings or propagandists. It said Tornike Razmadze was accused of insulting Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze.

“Insulting comments on social media by citizen Tornike Razmadze and Anna Bdeyan directed at Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze were identified. Administrative proceedings have been launched against them under Articles 166 and 173,” the Interior Ministry said.

The blogger’s lawyer, Mikheil Zakareishvili, in turn, says the Interior Ministry deliberately added Article 173, which concerns insulting a public official, to the charges. He says the original reports did not contain such wording. The lawyer is convinced that the case was opened specifically because of the insults directed at Simonyan and Solovyov.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) considers the case against Razmadze another example of restrictions on freedom of expression. The association says prosecuting people over statements made on social media violates their fundamental constitutional rights and freedom of expression.

What is the Hate Speech Unit

The new Hate Speech Unit at Georgia’s Interior Ministry began operating on 1 June 2026. According to the ministry, its main task is to identify public statements that demean human dignity or are offensive and may constitute administrative offences.

Over the past three months, the unit has fined dozens of people. Vakhtang Sanaya, a journalist and presenter on Formula TV, became the first person to receive a two-week administrative detention sentence. Activist Giorgi Akhobadze also received a one-month detention sentence for a Facebook post.

Georgian blogger insults Simonyan

World.title: Russian Orthodox Church calls on pilgrims to ‘boycott’ New Athos Monastery in Abkhazia
World.content:
The Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) has called on pilgrims not to visit the New Athos Monastery in Abkhazia.

The ROC considers the monastery’s abbot, Father Dorotheus, a schismatic.

However, this did not stop Sergei Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff of the Russian presidential administration and the Kremlin’s point man for Abkhazia, from visiting the monastery.

The Moscow Patriarchate’s chancellor, Metropolitan Grigory, has sent a circular letter to all bishops of the Russian Orthodox Church warning that Russian pilgrims must not attend services at the New Athos Monastery. The services there are led by defrocked hieromonk Dorotheus (Dbar).

“We are concerned about cases in which Orthodox pilgrims from dioceses of the Russian Orthodox Church visit the New Athos Monastery and take part in services held there. Pilgrims often go to confession and receive communion there without knowing that they should not.

I ask you to take measures to ensure that pilgrims travelling to holy sites in Abkhazia with your blessing are always informed that they must not engage in prayer or Eucharistic communion with the monk Dorotheus. They should also be informed that the sacraments performed in schism have no spiritual grace,” Metropolitan Grigory wrote.

Archimandrite Dorotheus

Archimandrite Dorotheus heads the Holy Metropolis of Abkhazia, one of two unrecognised Orthodox churches operating in the republic. A graduate of Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and a doctor of theology, he is highly popular in Abkhaz society and well known in church circles.

His “rival” is Father Vissarion, who heads the Abkhazian Orthodox Church (AOC). He is the only serving Abkhaz cleric ordained by the Georgian Orthodox Church during the Soviet era. Despite its unrecognised status, the AOC enjoys the active support of the Russian Orthodox Church.

The ROC, by contrast, has opposed Archimandrite Dorotheus and officially defrocked him in 2023 for refusing to submit to its authority.

The Holy Metropolis of Abkhazia and the AOC have been engaged in a long-running and bitter conflict.

Father Vissarion has also addressed not Russian but Abkhaz believers, saying they should not take part in services at New Athos.

Father Dorotheus himself believes that the Moscow Patriarchate’s letter was prompted by Archpriest Nikolai Balashov, an adviser to Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Russia. According to Dorotheus, Balashov has consistently worked in the interests of the Georgian Orthodox Church for decades.

“Similar circulars have appeared repeatedly. Yet their authors stubbornly refuse to acknowledge the main point: pilgrims who visit the New Athos Monastery are not there ‘out of ignorance’. The overwhelming majority of them knowingly take part in the services I conduct.

These people know the church bureaucracy well and can see that it contains no spiritual truth — only political and administrative manipulation,” Father Dorotheus wrote on his social media page.

Dorotheus believes another factor also prompted the AOC leadership to step up its activity. On 28 August 2026, Abkhaz President Badra Gunba and Sergei Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff of the Russian presidential administration, made an unofficial visit to the New Athos Monastery.

According to Dorotheus, this was the first time since 2011 that such high-ranking officials had visited their monastery.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Boycott of the New Athos Monastery

World.title: Georgian ‘delegation’ delivers gifts to Russian unit fighting against Ukraine
World.content:
According to Russia’s RIA Novosti news agency, Georgian volunteers on a “humanitarian mission” in the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic delivered an icon of St George the Victorious, motorcycles and prayer rooms to a Russian unit named after St Gabriel Urgebadze and the Nevsky Brigade, which are fighting against Ukraine. Besik Danelia, a Georgian “public figure” who leads the volunteers, told the agency about the initiative.

The Georgian Orthodox Church strongly opposes the use of Archimandrite Gabriel Urgebadze’s name to justify or support military action. Archpriest Andria Jaghmaidze, head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s press service, said it was particularly unacceptable that some Russian Orthodox Church clergy had supported the initiative.

Father Gabriel (Urgebadze) was a Georgian Orthodox monk and archimandrite whom the Georgian Orthodox Church canonised as a saint. One of the best-known episodes of his life took place in 1965, during the Soviet era. During a 1 May demonstration, he publicly burned a huge portrait of Lenin. Authorities beat him severely, arrested him and sent him to a psychiatric hospital. Later, despite pressure and persecution from the authorities, he continued his church service. His life became associated with strict asceticism, helping others and the idea of love.

What is known about the unit named after Father Gabriel and Besik Danelia

In an interview with RIA Novosti, Besik Danelia said he had travelled to Donetsk to visit “brothers” who, according to him, “are defending their homeland on the front line”, and had brought them humanitarian aid.

Andrei Kramar, a representative of the de facto authorities in occupied Donetsk, also said that a “Georgian delegation” that openly supports Russia’s war had visited the region.

“A Georgian delegation came to us and brought humanitarian aid. They are doing this openly. They are proud to support and have chosen a side in the special military operation,” Kramar said.

Reports about the existence of a “Orthodox” unit named after Father Gabriel Urgebadze and made up of ethnic Georgians first emerged in January 2026.

Besik Danelia (right) in Donetsk. Photo: press service of Andrei Kramar, deputy chairman of the so-called DPR’s People’s Council

Besik Danelia was previously a member of Nino Burjanadze’s pro-Russian Democratic Movement – United Georgia party. He has also appeared on the Georgia Wave media platform, which is linked to Putin supporter Mamuka Pipia, where he echoed the Georgian Dream ruling party’s calls for an apology to Georgia’s occupied regions.

Georgian “delegation” in Donetsk

What the Georgian Patriarchate says

The Georgian Patriarchate says that using the name of Archimandrite Gabriel Urgebadze for a military unit is particularly incompatible with his legacy.

Archpriest Andria Jaghmaidze: “First of all, let us note that Orthodox people are dying on both sides of the Russia-Ukraine war. We watch this with deep pain in our hearts. We pray and ask the saints to intercede so that the Lord may grant peace to Ukraine, Russia and the whole world. And at such a time, without any consultation with the Georgian Orthodox Church or consideration of its position, we have unexpectedly encountered an unprecedented situation.

For us, it is categorically unacceptable to use the name of the Venerable Father Gabriel, an archimandrite, confessor and holy fool, for a military unit. The life and spiritual struggle of the saint were entirely devoted to faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and to preaching love and compassion for others.

It is also deeply disturbing that some clergy of the Russian Church support such an unacceptable use of the Venerable Father’s name.

It appears that the authors of this initiative are poorly acquainted with the life of Saint Gabriel. Against this background, this action appears to be a biased attempt to exploit the name of the Church.

The Georgian Orthodox Church distances itself from the use of the name of the Venerable Gabriel the Confessor and Holy Fool to justify or support military action.”

Gabriel Urgebadze unit

World.title: From ‘crown prince’ to prisoner: Irakli Garibashvili’s break with Georgia’s ruling party
World.content:
Irakli Garibashvili vs Georgian Dream

Georgia’s two-time former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili is currently in prison, from where he has openly challenged the authorities he himself represented for many years.

Over the past few weeks, he has published six letters accusing the Georgian government of persecution, blackmail and attempts to destroy his political future.

Garibashvili initially said the pressure against him had been exerted on the orders of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party. His criticism, however, later focused primarily on current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and another influential party figure, Mamuka Mdinaradze.

The confrontation is particularly unusual for a party that for many years appeared from the outside to be an entirely monolithic political organisation.

Irakli Garibashvili is far from an ordinary former official. For almost two decades, he was one of Bidzina Ivanishvili‘s closest and most trusted associates. When Ivanishvili stepped down as prime minister in 2013, he effectively installed the then 31-year-old Garibashvili as his successor.

Now Ivanishvili’s former chosen successor is writing from prison that the very system he once served has “stabbed him in the back”.

Garibashvili’s case is therefore no longer simply a criminal case involving a former prime minister. It has exposed a conflict within Georgian Dream and raised a broader question: is a new redistribution of power beginning within the ruling party?

From prime minister’s office to prison cell

Irakli Garibashvili’s career under Bidzina Ivanishvili’s wing began long before Georgian Dream came to power in 2012.

As early as 2011, Ivanishvili referred to Garibashvili as one of his closest advisers and aides.

Following Georgian Dream’s victory in the 2012 parliamentary election, Garibashvili became interior minister. A year later, Ivanishvili stepped down as prime minister and named Garibashvili as his successor.

Garibashvili consequently served his first term as Georgia’s prime minister from 2013 to 2015. He unexpectedly left government at the end of 2015, but returned in 2019 as defence minister. In 2021, he became prime minister for a second time.

During his second premiership, Garibashvili was one of Georgian Dream’s most hardline figures. He frequently clashed with the opposition, civil society and Western critics. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Garibashvili repeatedly echoed the government’s narrative about the threat of a “second front” being opened in Georgia and accused some Western figures of supporting the opposition.

In January 2024, he again stepped down as prime minister and was replaced by Irakli Kobakhidze. Garibashvili, meanwhile, became chairman of Georgian Dream. At the time, the party presented the change as a routine internal reshuffle.

In April 2025, Garibashvili announced that he was leaving politics altogether.

Several months later, a criminal investigation was launched against him.

How former prime minister ended up in prison

In October 2025, prosecutors charged Irakli Garibashvili with laundering a particularly large amount of illicit income.

According to investigators, the former prime minister provided false information in his asset declarations in an attempt to make illegally obtained income appear legitimate.

At the time, Garibashvili chose to remain silent and did not contest the case. On 12 January 2026, he pleaded guilty and reached a plea agreement with prosecutors. Under the deal, he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined 1m lari ($360,000). Two of his cars and $6.5m seized during a search of his home were also forfeited to the state.

After being taken into custody in the courtroom, Garibashvili was transferred directly to Penitentiary Establishment No 12 in the city of Rustavi.

Garibashvili later gave an almost sacred significance to his decision to remain silent. He now says that, at the time, he had consciously chosen not to confront the authorities.

Garibashvili and Ivanishvili: relationship spanning almost 20 years

Garibashvili worked in Ivanishvili’s circle even before Georgian Dream was founded. When Ivanishvili entered politics in 2011, Garibashvili was one of his closest associates. And, as noted above, in 2013 Ivanishvili handed him the leadership of the Georgian government.

Ivanishvili himself has often spoken about the early years of their personal relationship. In 2013, he recalled that Garibashvili had worked in the commercial department of one of his companies when Ivanishvili was buying a French-made helicopter. According to Ivanishvili, the young Garibashvili handled the negotiations with the French side so successfully that the sellers wanted to meet him in person.

In Georgian political circles, their relationship was widely seen as one between a patron and his political successor. Government opponents even described Garibashvili as Ivanishvili’s “obedient servant”, while Georgian media frequently portrayed him as a politician “groomed” by Ivanishvili and as being as close to him “as a son”.

Another episode also illustrates the hierarchical nature of their relationship.

In 2021, when Garibashvili was serving his second term as Georgia’s prime minister, a video recording of Bidzina Ivanishvili giving evidence in a Bermuda court was made public. The case concerned Ivanishvili’s legal dispute with Swiss bank Credit Suisse.

In court, Ivanishvili was asked what role Garibashvili had played in his financial affairs years earlier. Ivanishvili explained that Garibashvili had not been a financier and had mainly performed organisational tasks, such as arranging meetings, making phone calls and handling similar matters.

Asked, “So was he something like your secretary?”, Ivanishvili laughed and replied: “Call him whatever you like. Use whichever description you prefer.”

Following the release of the recording, political commentators highlighted the fact that Ivanishvili had twice appointed as the country’s prime minister a former subordinate whose earlier duties he had described in court in dismissive terms.

Ivanishvili mentioned in Garibashvili’s letter from prison

Against this backdrop, Garibashvili’s first public reference to Ivanishvili in a letter from prison, published on 17 August 2026, was particularly significant.

Garibashvili wrote that he had received an offer made on Ivanishvili’s instructions: to confess to another offence, this time a serious corruption crime. In return, he said he had been promised that the new charge would not add to his existing five-year prison sentence.

According to the former prime minister, the deal came with another condition: after his release from prison, he would not be allowed to return to politics.

Garibashvili said the authorities were seeking to ensure that he could not make a political comeback. In the same statement, he held Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream leadership personally responsible for his own safety and that of his family.

In his next letter, Garibashvili again referred to Ivanishvili, but this time in a markedly different tone.

He wrote that he had endured the authorities’ actions for many months because of his “20-year relationship with Bidzina Ivanishvili, immense love and respect for him, boundless gratitude and absolute loyalty to him“.

In subsequent letters, Garibashvili has sought gradually to shift the focus of the conflict away from Ivanishvili and towards the Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze tandem.

Some analysts believe Garibashvili is trying to avoid burning his remaining bridges with Ivanishvili and to persuade him that the real problem lies with the current prime minister and his circle.

Garibashvili, his wife Nunuka Tamazashvili and Bidzina Ivanishvili

Irakli Kobakhidze and Irakli Garibashvili

What changed after Garibashvili‘s letters

After 17 August, Garibashvili definitively broke his silence.

Several key allegations gradually emerged from his letters. He claims that the authorities deceived him, put pressure on members of his family, demanded that he confess to another corruption offence, and ultimately sought to eliminate any possibility of his return to politics.

Garibashvili also said that he had been given indications that his 75-year-old father could also be arrested.

Mamuka Mdinaradze rejected these allegations.

However, subsequent developments lent additional weight to Garibashvili’s claims.

On 24 August, prosecutors brought new charges against him.

This time, the case concerns the alleged receipt of a particularly large bribe, an offence punishable by between 11 and 15 years in prison if he is convicted.

According to prosecutors, Garibashvili received 750,000 lari ($275,735) through a scheme involving classified procurement contracts at the Defence Ministry. The investigation relies primarily on testimony from former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze and his alleged accomplice, Vasil Mkheidze.

Garibashvili has pleaded not guilty to the new charge.

The former prime minister says the proceedings are being used as a tool to exert political pressure on him.

Mdinaradze’s sudden departure

Meanwhile, against the backdrop of Garibashvili’s letters and his allegations against Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze, another significant development took place:

Mamuka Mdinaradze and Irakli Kobakhidze

Mamuka Mdinaradze, who for many years was one of Georgian Dream’s most influential figures and one of Kobakhidze’s closest political allies, announced that he was leaving the government and withdrawing from politics altogether.

In 2025, Mdinaradze was appointed head of the State Security Service, but remained in the post for only a short time. In July 2026, Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would become regional development minister in September and was expected to play a key role in overseeing regional policy.

However, on 27 August, Mdinaradze unexpectedly announced that he was not only stepping down from his ministerial post but leaving politics altogether.

Garibashvili linked the move to his letters.

“Mamuka Mdinaradze made such serious and grave mistakes in this case that they resulted not only in his removal from office, but also in his departure from politics,” the disgraced former prime minister wrote on 2 September in his fifth letter.

Mdinaradze himself presented his departure as a personal decision.

Why Garibashvili has become a problem for Kobakhidze

Garibashvili’s letters have raised questions about how much political influence the former prime minister retains while in prison. Some analysts believe Garibashvili still has supporters within Georgian Dream and that the authorities’ sharp response to his letters is evidence of his continuing political significance.

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili says Garibashvili realised that he enjoyed greater sympathy within Georgian Dream than Kobakhidze did, and that this encouraged him to continue resisting.

Kobakhidze, Zakareishvili argues, in turn discovered that “even Garibashvili sitting in prison is stronger than he is”.

One possible explanation for this assessment lies in the two men’s very different political backgrounds.

Garibashvili belongs to the first generation of the ruling party and has been part of Georgian Dream since its foundation. He was a member of Ivanishvili’s inner circle and built up strong political connections over the years, particularly in the regions.

Kobakhidze’s power, by contrast, is much more closely tied to the party apparatus and Ivanishvili’s direct backing.

Analyst Irakli Melashvili describes Garibashvili as a “symbolic figure” for supporters of the “old Georgian Dream”. In his assessment, the former prime minister was particularly close to the party’s conservative and pro-Russian electorate.

At the same time, Melashvili points to a fundamental contradiction: Garibashvili has now himself become a target of the system of which he was one of the principal architects and leaders for many years.

For that reason, his resistance cannot automatically be seen as a struggle for a democratic system.

“This is a struggle for his own survival, not for the public good,” Melashvili says.

Lazare Jorbenadze case and a new phase of confrontation

On 1 September, Garibashvili went a step further.

In another letter from prison, he demanded that the authorities provide answers about the circumstances surrounding the death of human rights activist Lazare Jorbenadze, who had publicly criticised Kobakhidze.

Garibashvili also wrote that questions remained unanswered about other cases of suicide which, he said, were linked to the period when the Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze group was in power.

Prosecutors subsequently questioned Garibashvili himself, as well as several other politicians and public figures. A prosecution service representative said Garibashvili had provided no information to substantiate claims that Jorbenadze may have been murdered.

Sixth letter: open confrontation with authorities

On 8 September, Garibashvili published his sixth letter.

He described the authorities’ response as a “ridiculous, repulsive and tragic masquerade” and said the questioning over the Jorbenadze case was an attempt to link him to the opposition United National Movement party.

Garibashvili also responded sarcastically to allegations in pro-government media that he had been acting in the interests of the “deep state” or France.

“I am lucky that I don’t know any other foreign languages, otherwise I would probably have been declared an agent of other countries as well,” he wrote.

He then addressed the authorities directly: “Stop these dirty political games against me!”

Garibashvili said he served neither the West nor the East, neither the North nor the South, and that his sole aim had been to serve Georgia.

He addressed parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili separately: “Shalva, this is not a legal process — this is ruthless political persecution!“

The letter ends with a message the former prime minister has repeatedly made in recent weeks:

“I am not fighting anyone — you yourselves stabbed me in the back… Now I am forced to defend myself and my family against this injustice and cruelty.”

‘Criminal’, ‘traitor’, ‘agent’: how party responded to former PM

Following Garibashvili’s fifth letter, Georgian Dream’s response became particularly harsh.

A man who twice served as prime minister for the party is now being described by his former allies as a “criminal” and a “traitor”.

A politician who for years himself used harsh rhetoric against government opponents has now become a target of the same system. The language being used against him will be familiar to the government’s critics: allegations of corruption, betrayal, serving the radical opposition and acting in the interests of foreign states.

Georgian Dream representatives say Garibashvili’s narrative has become indistinguishable from that of the “radical opposition”.

MP Gia Volski suggested that the former prime minister may have been led to believe that his struggle could help advance a “revolutionary process” in the country and that he could subsequently benefit from it politically.

Another MP, Dimitri Samkharadze, described Garibashvili as a “self-confessed criminal” and a traitor.

Meanwhile, pro-government television channels, citing Azerbaijani media, circulated allegations that Garibashvili had been acting in France’s interests in Georgia.

Current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also responded in exceptionally harsh terms.

He described his predecessor’s letters as “ridiculous and tragic”, saying Garibashvili had “sunk to the level of a blogger for some shady little newspaper”.

Georgian Dream secretary-general and Tbilisi mayor Kakha Kaladze, meanwhile, said it was regrettable to see his former ally in such a position, but publicly expressed his full support for Kobakhidze.

Ivanishvili remains silent

The key figure in the entire confrontation has so far remained largely out of public view.

Bidzina Ivanishvili has remained silent.

This is particularly notable because both sides in the conflict ultimately derived their political weight from his backing.

Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili sees one possible scenario in which Ivanishvili himself is managing the current process, with the ultimate aim of weakening Kobakhidze’s team.

Other analysts offer a more cautious interpretation: Ivanishvili is watching the confrontation unfold and will make a decision only when it becomes clear which figure is more useful for preserving his system.

David Zurabishvili, who supports this interpretation, says Ivanishvili has no permanent allies, only permanent interests. Accordingly, neither Garibashvili nor Kobakhidze is indispensable to him.

This explanation is also consistent with Georgian Dream’s history: prime ministers have changed repeatedly during the party’s time in power, while the centre of power has consistently remained with Ivanishvili.

Kobakhidze has no intention of stepping down

Against this backdrop, speculation is already mounting in Georgia over the possible resignation of Irakli Kobakhidze himself.

He has, however, dismissed the rumours.

Kobakhidze said journalists ask him “every three months” whether he is planning to step down as prime minister, adding that he expects to be asked the same question again in another three months.

More significant, however, was his explanation of what had happened within the government after he took office.

According to Kobakhidze, he and his team needed a year and five months to address what he described as “fundamental problems” that had accumulated within the system of government, acting on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s instructions.

Kobakhidze did not directly name Garibashvili in his remarks. The chronology, however, is clear: he was referring to problems that had accumulated in the system during his namesake’s tenure as prime minister.

Is Georgian Dream’s monolith beginning to crack?

Georgian Dream formally retains almost complete control over Georgia’s political system.

It dominates parliament, is seeking to ban several opposition groups, and many opposition leaders are in prison.

Yet it is under these circumstances that a conflict has erupted not between the government and the opposition, but between current and former leaders of the ruling establishment itself.

Giorgi Melashvili, head of the Europe-Georgia Institute, describes the situation as two parallel processes: on the one hand, the circle of decision-makers is narrowing and the system is becoming increasingly centralised; on the other, the Garibashvili case has exposed cracks in Georgian Dream’s internal monolith.

In his assessment, neither the opposition nor other former Georgian Dream figures have dealt the party a blow comparable to that inflicted by Garibashvili’s letters.

Gia Khukhashvili, meanwhile, describes the developments as a confrontation between two factions “at the royal court”. In his view, Ivanishvili remains the only person with the final say.

Much about these scenarios remains speculative, but the facts themselves already present a highly unusual picture:

Former PM behind bars: A two-time former prime minister is in prison, accusing the authorities of political persecution and his former allies of trying to destroy him and his family.

World.title: ‘Major cause for concern’: expert view on Armenian school students’ low level of knowledge
World.content:
Low knowledge levels among Armenian school students

School students in Armenia lag behind their peers in Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkey in terms of their level of knowledge. The comparison focuses in particular on 15-year-old students.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) conducted its annual study as part of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). Experts assessed students’ knowledge of mathematics and science, as well as their ability to analyse what they read.

The study included 760,000 15-year-old students from 91 countries. The results showed that the overall state of education around the world leaves much to be desired. However, experts in Armenia are particularly concerned about the situation in their own country. The education problems have also alarmed people far beyond the field’s specialist community.

Economist Tigran Jrbashyan sees the study’s results as a major cause for concern.

“This is no longer a problem for the education ministry. It is a question of Armenia’s economic security and long-term competitiveness,” he stressed.

Jrbashyan published several posts on his Facebook page, calling on the government to take immediate action. He proposes introducing a special regime in the education sector over the coming years.

Подробнее о результатах исследования, а также комментарий экономиста Тиграна Джрбашяна.

Results for students in Armenia and leading countries

According to the study, some cities in China lead the rankings for educational achievement, followed by Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan. The UK and Estonia also rank among the top 10.

Armenia’s results lag behind those of every other country in the region. Armenian school students scored below the OECD average in all areas covered by the study.

The average share of Armenian school students reaching the benchmark was

28% in science (OECD average — 74%),

28% in mathematics (OECD average — 65%),

19% in reading and the ability to analyse written text (OECD average — 67%).

Less than 1% of Armenian students achieved the highest level in mathematics, while the figure was even lower in science.

“And virtually none of the students demonstrated reading skills that would indicate an ability to understand lengthy texts, work with abstract or contradictory concepts, and distinguish facts from opinions,” Radio Azatutyun reports.

Comment

According to Tigran Jrbashyan, an economist and head of Ameriabank’s management consulting service, the PISA study assesses not so much what 15-year-olds know as their ability to apply their knowledge in practice: understanding texts, analysing information and solving problems.

“Among our 15-year-olds, 28% reach at least the minimum, Level 2 proficiency in mathematics. The figure is also 28% in science. In reading, however, only 19% reach this level. In other words, four out of five of our 15-year-olds do not even reach the basic level of functional reading literacy,” he said.

Meanwhile, according to the PISA study, 39% of teenagers in Georgia reach the basic level of reading literacy, compared with 36% in Kazakhstan and 35% in Azerbaijan.

The economist argues that no matter how much Armenia talks about its achievements in artificial intelligence and high technology, all its planned initiatives will remain unrealised projects without human capital.

“If Armenia ranks third from the bottom in problem-solving skills among 15-year-olds, our ambitions in AI and high technology cannot be limited to investment, equipment and infrastructure alone,” he explained.

Jrbashyan notes that Armenia has built, renovated and modernised schools in recent years. He considers this an unquestionable investment in the quality of education. At the same time, he says the country needs to change how it assesses the effectiveness of education policy.

In particular, he proposes assessing

how students’ reading skills and their mathematical and scientific knowledge have changed as a result of these investments;

whether the share of students who fail to reach the basic level has decreased;

whether the share of high-performing students has increased.

The analyst insists that, given the current situation, the government needs to

take immediate action to determine at which stage of the education system, and for what reasons, students lose ground;

set measurable targets for 2028 and 2031 and consistently work towards achieving them.

“The cost of inaction in the context of PISA is not simply a low ranking. It means lost economic growth and the loss of Armenia’s competitiveness for decades to come,” he stressed.

The expert believes the PISA 2025 results show that the scale of Armenia’s education problem has outgrown the pace of the government’s response. As a result, reforms carried out at the usual pace are no longer enough:

“I would propose declaring education an emergency national priority and introducing a special management regime for three to five years.”

Jrbashyan stresses that an emergency regime should mean not only faster decision-making and more resources, but also much greater accountability for results.

Moreover, he sees a need for national mobilisation on the issue. He believes education policy should not measure its success only through the next PISA study:

“We need to create a national system of regular assessment that will allow us to see every year where we are making progress and where we are not, and adjust policy accordingly.”

World.title: Uzbekistan and China step up gas cooperation with new joint projects
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. Uzbekistan and China discussed the implementation of joint projects and ways to strengthen long-term cooperation in the natural gas sector.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekneftegaz, following meeting between Chairman Abdugani Sanginov and Zhang Jiajhen, chairman of the Board of Directors of China’s Trans-Asia Gas Pipeline Company Limited (TAPLine).

According to the company, the meeting also highlighted the continued development of cooperation between Uzbekneftegaz and China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC).

The sides described TAPLine as a reliable, long-term partner within the framework of the Asia Trans Gas joint venture, which plays a role in their cooperation in the gas transportation sector.

Furthermore, the discussions covered the composition of the supervisory board of Asia Trans Gas and the alignment of its internal regulations with current legislation. The parties also considered an initiative to develop the joint venture as a “first-class company,” as well as ways to improve coordination and cooperation mechanisms between shareholders.

Moreover, the sides exchanged views on profit distribution and other issues related to the joint venture’s operations.

“Taking into account the current priorities, it is necessary to conduct an additional in-depth assessment of the economic efficiency, costs and implementation timelines of individual initiatives,” Sanginov said.

The Uzbekneftegaz chairman emphasized the need to carefully assess the commercial and operational implications of proposed initiatives before moving forward, according to the company.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the sides expressed readiness to further strengthen their existing partnership and continue dialogue on improving the efficiency of Asia Trans Gas and implementing mutually beneficial projects.

The talks underscore the continued role of Uzbekneftegaz’s cooperation with Chinese energy companies, including CNPC and TAPLine, in the development of joint projects and gas transportation infrastructure.

World.title: Kazakhstan's Tokayev appoints new ambassador to Georgia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has appointed Talgat Aduov as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Kazakhstan to Georgia.

This was announced in a statement by the press service of the Kazakh President.

“By orders of the Head of State, Talgat Aduov was appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Kazakhstan to Georgia.

Moorever, Malik Murzalin was appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Kazakhstan to Malaysia and relieved of his duties as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Kazakhstan to Georgia,” the statement said.

In addition, Bulat Sugurbayev was relieved of his positions as Ambassador of Kazakhstan to Malaysia and concurrently as Ambassador to Brunei Darussalam.

Talgat Aduov was born on March 20, 1976.

He served as Deputy Director of the branch of Turkuaz Telecom LLP in Almaty from 1998 to 2002.

From 2002 through 2006, Aduov worked as Third Secretary of the Investment Projects Monitoring Division of the Investment Committee of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kazakhstan and as Third Secretary of the Department of Asia, the Middle East and Africa of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kazakhstan.

From 2006 to 2007, he served as First Secretary, Adviser and Head of a Division at the Department of International Organizations and Multilateral Cooperation of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kazakhstan.

From 2007 to 2015, Aduov held positions as Expert, Senior Expert and Deputy Chief of Protocol of the President of Kazakhstan.

From 2015 to August 2016, he served as State Inspector of the Department of State Control and Organizational and Territorial Work of the Administration of the President of Kazakhstan.

From August 2016 to September 2017, Aduov was Deputy Chairman of the Management Board of NC KazAvtoZhol JSC.

From September 2017 to 2018, he served as Deputy Head of the Office of the Prime Minister of Kazakhstan.

In 2018, Aduov was First Vice President of Otandastar Foundation.

World.title: Tajikistan, Kuwait discuss further development of bilateral relations
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. Tajikistan and Kuwait discussed prospects for further developing bilateral relations and expanding mutually beneficial cooperation.

This was announced in a statement published by the Tajik MFA, following the meeting between Tajik Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Kuwait Khusrav Noziri and Emir of Kuwait Sheikh Meshal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah.

According to the Ministry in the course of the meeting, Tajik Ambassador presented credentials to Emir of Kuwait.

"At the beginning of the meeting, the Ambassador of Tajikistan conveyed greetings and a message from President of the Republic of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon to the Emir of the State of Kuwait, emphasizing that Tajikistan attaches great importance to bilateral relations with Kuwait and is interested in further expanding friendly ties and mutually beneficial cooperation with this country in all areas," the statement said.

In this context, the parties noted that the official visit of President of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon to the State of Kuwait on November 3-5, 2024, created the necessary prerequisites for further expanding the substance of bilateral relations and developing cooperation in various areas.

Following the meeting, the Emir of Kuwait conveyed his greetings and best wishes to President of the Republic of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon and wished the Ambassador of Tajikistan success in carrying out his new diplomatic mission.

Meanwhile, Tajikistan and Kuwait maintain diplomatic relations and cooperate through bilateral contacts and international platforms. The two countries have also held high-level exchanges aimed at developing cooperation across various areas of mutual interest.

World.title: Tokayev approves new regulations for Kazakhstan’s Security Council
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has approved regulations on the Security Council and its Office.

This was announced in a statement by the press service of the Kazakh President

Accordin to the press service, Tokayev signed a decree titled “On Certain Issues of the Office of the Security Council of the Republic of Kazakhstan and Amendments and Additions to Certain Acts of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan.”

“The decree approved the regulations on the Security Council and its Office, and also defined the powers of the Deputy Chairman of the Security Council of the Republic of Kazakhstan,” the statement said.

The tasks of the Security Council and its Office include a comprehensive analysis of global threats and challenges, as well as current aspects of the domestic situation.

The powers of the Deputy Chairman of the Security Council include organizing control over the unconditional and full implementation of acts and instructions issued by the Chairman of the Security Council, as well as decisions of the Security Council, including those adopted at operational meetings.

The Deputy Chairman will coordinate the activities of state bodies and organizations in implementing measures related to national security, the country's defense capability, legality and law and order.

The Deputy Chairman of the Security Council will also oversee issues related to information and cybersecurity, including the use of artificial intelligence, personal data protection, combating corruption and economic crime, and civil protection.

In addition, the Deputy Chairman of the Security Council will coordinate the activities of state bodies and organizations in implementing the above-mentioned measures and will conduct international cooperation.

The Deputy Chairman of the Security Council will also coordinate the activities of the Office of the Security Council.

The Office of the Security Council, as an independent state body, is directly subordinate and accountable to the Head of State.

The activities of the Office of the Security Council are aimed at strengthening and improving control over risks in the field of national security, ensuring the sustainability of public administration, providing institutional support, and implementing decisions of the Chairman of the Security Council and the Security Council of the Republic of Kazakhstan directly.

According to the presedential press service, the implementation of these tasks is aimed at strengthening the protection of the sovereignty and independence of the Republic of Kazakhstan, territorial integrity, national interests in the international arena, and the foundations of the constitutional order.
