World.title: Residents say they 'can't live without' firewood ahead of ban
World.content:
Residents in southern NSW who rely on firewood to heat their homes have banded together to protest against the end of a firewood permit program in two national parks.

The Riverina Domestic Firewood Program will end permanently in Murray Valley and Murrumbidgee Valley national parks when the collection season closes on October 30.

The program was introduced in 2010, after the parks were gazetted, so locals could still collect firewood for heating in a region with little access to natural gas.

The firewood program will end on October 30. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

On Friday, more than 100 people gathered in Deniliquin, calling on the state government to reverse the decision.

Jane Mathers, who lives on a property outside Tocumwal, relies heavily on firewood from the Murray Valley National Park to heat her home and cook food.

"I couldn't live without it, especially in the winter," she said.

" We can't afford the electricity; we are pensioners. "

Jane Mathers says she relies heavily on firewood. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

Mrs Mathers said, in addition to using firewood, each quarter her electricity cost about $1,000.

She said not having access to firewood would be a big blow to her husband and her.

"We can't afford to live on anything less than what we've got now," she said.

Mathoura resident Murray Dravitziki installed a fireplace two years ago.

"To buy the fireplace and have it installed was about $3,500," he said.

" Now we are just sort of up in the air as to where we go from here. "

The ABC understands there are no plans in place to reintroduce firewood collection in the two national parks following this season.

Decline in timber

The NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) said the collection program was ending due to the quality and quantity of wood available.

A decline in fallen timber on the forest floor is behind the decision to end the firewood program. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

In a statement to the ABC, an NPWS spokesperson said the program was placing significant pressure on the health and survival of native plants and animals.

"Fallen timber is a critical part of healthy forest ecosystems," the spokesperson said.

" It provides shelter, nesting sites, food sources and protection for a wide range of native Australian wildlife. "

Fallen timber provides shelter for a range of native Australian wildlife. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

The community can still source local firewood from state forests under the management of the Forestry Corporation of NSW and commercial operators.

Independent Member for Murray Helen Dalton, who organised the rally, is critical of the state government's decision.

"It's all very well and good for people to make decisions in Sydney but they are not the ones at the coalface," she said.

" Sydney and Canberra are telling us what to do and making our communities unliveable. "

Ms Dalton hopes a petition to reverse the decision will receive 10,000 signatures, so it can be tabled and debated in state parliament.

Fire risk concerns

Louise Burge lives just outside of Deniliquin, near the Murray Valley National Park.

She said the red gum forest's fire risk was terrifying.

Residents such as Louise Burge, who live near the national parks, are concerned about the fire risk. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato )

"Our biggest fear is the build-up of debris on the forest floor.

"Red gums have a lot of tree branch fall and that is what actually gets collected for firewood."

Edward River Council Mayor Ashley Hall said the decision could lead to catastrophic issues if there were fires in the future.

"I wouldn’t like to see the state government see that on their watch when these decisions are being made with zero consultation," he said.

"I think they need to cease this decision, come back to the community and have real good discussions with people on the ground."

The ABC contacted the office of the NSW Minister for Environment Penny Sharpe for comment but was directed to the NPWS instead.

The Rural Fire Service and Fire and Rescue NSW have also been approached for comment.

World.title: Search resumes for 80 missing in popular Philippines tourist spot
World.content:
The search for more than 80 people missing in the Philippines has resumed, but thick smoke has hampered rescue workers boarding the vessel.

More than 130 people were believed to be on board a ferry on Wednesday evening, local time, when fire broke out, quickly engulfing the boat in flames.

Richard Marceliano, one of the survivors, told GMA News that he saw a small amount of smoke that turned into a raging fire and spread through ​the ‌ferry within seconds.

He said he and other passengers spent nearly two hours floating in the sea before they were rescued.

The coast ⁠guard has deployed five vessels and ‌divers to the area, while army ‌rescue boats, fishermen and private resort owners continued to assist in the search that ‌began on Wednesday night.

At least 43 people have been rescued so far, according to the agency.

Coast guard spokeswoman Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said the number of missing stood at 84, after two people on the passenger list did not end up boarding the vessel.

The vessel was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pick-up truck and motorcycles.

Ferry MV June Aster after it caught fire off Palawan province. (Philippine Coast Guard)

The vessel, MV June Aster, had departed the capital of Manila just after 8pm local time and was expected to reach its destination of Coron around 6pm local time the next day.

Commodore Cayabyab said the coast guard received a distress call from the ferry's operator around 6:45pm local time near Coron, in the Palawan province, and launched a response within five minutes.

The burnt-out ferry is grounded near the town, known for its diving sites and island-hopping attractions.

Commodore Cayabyab said thick smoke had delayed rescue personnel from boarding the 53-metre boat to assess what happened.

"Our objective now is to enter the ship, to check the situation so we can assess the situation," she said on Thursday night.

Loading...

It is still unclear what caused the blaze.

A statement from ​the Maritime Industry ⁠Authority (MARINA), citing survivor accounts, said two successive explosions were heard from within the ship, which triggered the fire.

Commodore Cayabyab said one survivor believed it may have begun in the cargo hold.

"Everything happened in seconds," she said in a radio interview Friday.

"From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire, it spread very quickly," she said of survivors' accounts, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on life jackets.

"Most of the people we rescued were those who had been swimming away from the vessel."

Commodore Cayabyab said authorities were also still trying to confirm reports that foreigners were on board.

The ferry has run aground off the coast of Coron and is still smouldering from the fire that began on September 9. (AP: Philippine Coast Guard)

A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it was in contact with Philippine authorities to determine if any Australians were on board.

Commodore Cayabyab said, according to the vessel's records, it was built in 2002 and was certified to carry 306 passengers and 33 crew.

She said the vessel underwent a compliance inspection in March, which included checking that the correct number of life jackets were on board.

A spokesperson from the company that owns the ferry, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc, said it was fully cooperating with the investigation.

"We are working around the clock and have mobilised all available resources to manage this crisis," the company said in a statement.

"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for."

Reuters/AP/ABC/AFP

World.title: How two premierships in one year was the making of Isaiya Katoa
World.content:
In the four years since the remarkable season that forged Isaiya Katoa's first legend the Dolphins playmaker has proven time and again why he is the sort of player whose ascension was not expected but awaited.

On Saturday, Katoa will play in his first ever NRL semifinal when the Phins travel to Auckland to face the Warriors in the pick of the week one match-ups.

Katoa heads to New Zealand as the game's prince of playmakers amid a transformation from star of the future to star of the present.

It will be his first finals match of any kind since 2022, the season before his NRL debut and the year the limitless possibilities of his future revealed themselves.

Katoa has established himself as one of the top young halfbacks in the game. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

It began in the February, when Katoa signed with the Dolphins on his 18th birthday he already carried a mighty reputation among the league types who know about these things.

The hype around Katoa was enormous right from the jump, which doesn't feel like much of a burden now he's lived up to it but has crushed many a promising halfback before they could even get going.

With the Dolphins missing out on a host of big names for their inaugural season, they made a big bet that Katoa could become the star they need.

Given the lack of junior football over the past two seasons due to the pandemic that was no sure thing but Katoa showed his quality in that year's SG Ball competition, as he steered Penrith to the Under 19s grand final.

The Panthers were hardly a one-man band with future Parramatta hooker Ryley Smith and Warriors five-eighth Luke Hanson joining Katoa in the side, as did current Panthers dummy half Billy Scott.

The Windsor Wolves rake knew Katoa well by that point, having played against him growing up and with him at Patrician Brothers Blacktown.

"You could tell from a young age that he'd play NRL," said Scott.

"He was so mature, so calm and ahead of the game."

All of Katoa's poise didn't help in the early running as a Sydney Roosters containing Ethan Strange, Robert Toia, Solesi Foekti and Siua Wong ran out 20-0 leaders inside the first 25 minutes.

But Katoa laid on one try and helped create two more to claim man of the match honours as Penrith fought their way back to win 22-20 courtesy of a sideline conversion in the final seconds.

In the weeks that followed, the simmering tension between the Panthers and Dolphins over the latter landing Katoa came to a head.

He was excluded from the club's Jersey Flegg side for much of the season in a decision Penrith stressed was not personal, a claim which would eventually ring true.

After playing rugby, where he led Barker College to a Combined Associated Schools premiership win and occasional games back home for Glenmore Park Brumbies, Katoa was recalled by the Panthers, not for the Under 21s but straight into a reserve grade semifinal.

With Penrith's NRL side resting their entire starting side for the final round of the season, the reggies got the call up to the firsts and the kids had to step up to the seconds for the major preliminary final against North Sydney.

Alongside Isaiah Iongi and the Puru twins, in one of his first games against battle-hardened men, Katoa scored a try and set up two more amid a 22-14 win.

Then came another semifinal, a grand final qualifier in Jersey Flegg where the Roosters waited yet again.

NRL's unlikeliest blockbuster In a season bereft of quality, the Dolphins and the Warriors will meet in a marquee clash that doubles as the NRL's most unusual big game showdown.

In his first game with the side for the season, Katoa set up a try and kicked a field goal in a 27-22 victory.

Newcastle awaited in the grand final, as did an epic. The Knights were more than handy — Fletcher Sharpe lined up at fullback and Kurt Donoghoe a future partner-in-crime of Katoa's at the Phins, was at five-eighth.

Even though Katoa had been away from junior representative footy all season every Newcastle player knew what was in store.

"He was always one of the guns. You'd do a whole week of video pretty much just on him — which is still the same now," said Sharpe.

"He can be tricky to get a read on because he's got so many parts to his game."

Thomas Cant captained the Newcastle side at second row and despite having appeared in 38 NRL matches since he still calls this decider one of the hardest games he's ever played.

In the end it went to double extra time after the sides were locked at 18-all. Golden point beckoned and the two teams would play until there was a winner.

If you think that winner came from anyone but Katoa you haven't been paying attention.

"Honestly, my main memory is how good winning felt. We just stayed present and stayed in it. You get what you deserve, and if you put in the work it'll work out," said Scott, who again played alongside Katoa.

"He missed a few field goals in that game but even that's a credit to him — he stayed calm and when he needed to he nailed it."

All told, Katoa played six finals matches for Penrith that season across three different grades and won them all.

Just for good measure, he capped the season with a World Cup campaign with Tonga and his Test debut. He completed his HSC via correspondence during the tour and on return began life as a Dolphin.

Progress over the next three years was steady and over the last 18 months Katoa has fully blossomed.

The moment of Katoa's glory has seemingly arrived. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Unlike other young halves, who rely on their running game, all of Katoa's brilliance comes from between his ears and in his hands.

He is not a jack rabbit, but a craftsman with an artisanal touch and it was all there in those days with Penrith, clear as day through the grainy footage.

He holds the ball out in front, showing it this way and that. He delays his pass until the exact right moment when one defender has passed the point of no return and space must exist somewhere on his outside.

His poise, execution and inexplicable ability to make defenders sit on their heels and play with a desperate uncertainty because they don't know what's next is unmissable once you know what you're looking at.

Those talents have held up at every level since, becoming more finely honed until now when they will be battle-tested by a Warriors team who take no prisoners in front of more than 25,000 Kiwi screamers.

It will be a pressure unlike any Katoa has ever known and win or lose, there will be other days like this to come.

That has felt like his fate since Katoa's year of winning dangerously, which had an air of promise at the time but can now be retro-fitted into prologue, a mere taste of what was to come.

Before, Katoa was the son of a golden tomorrow and those days have now arrived and all those wins four years ago remain proof that while many are called, few are chosen.

World.title: 'Really scary': Residents seek clarity as gangland war becomes political
World.content:
A soundbite from a veteran detective has ignited a political war of words over gangland violence.

Assistant Police Commissioner Grant Taylor is no stranger to gun violence on Sydney's streets.

He was part of Taskforce Gain, set up more than 20 years ago to investigate a spate of shootings across Sydney's south west.

His comment was an attempt to contextualise the recent spate of shootings.

"It always looks like crime is out of control but when you look at it … we always have about eight organised crime murders a year, we've had six and then [Wednesday] night's made seven, we are basically on track [with] what we always have in regards to these murders," Assistant Commissioner Taylor told a press conference on Thursday.

" It's always going to be part and parcel to life in a big metropolis and this is no different. "

Grant Taylor says violent crime is "part and parcel" of living in a big city. (ABC News)

But it was a poor choice of words after three fatal shootings in just nine days.

NSW opposition leader Kellie Sloane seized on the comments, turning Sydney's tit for tat gangland war into a political issue.

"I do not accept that gangland murders are part of everyday life in our city. I do not accept that," she said on Thursday.

"The day we accept that this is normal is the day we have given in to organised crime. I will not give in to organised crime."

Kellie Sloane says gangland violence should not be normalised. (ABC News)

Boosted powers to target Sydney's gangsters, but police face a new problem They are the extraordinary powers the premier has promised to expand in a bid to combat gangland violence, but they face a major test in this era of organised crime.

The 2027 NSW state election is shaping up as a three-cornered contest between Labor, the Liberal-Nationals and One Nation.

Labor is hoping to gain enough seats to form a majority government while the Liberal-Nationals are hoping to retain as many of their current seats as possible.

One Labor insider, who asked to remain anonymous, suggested One Nation would likely try to politicise the issue of gun crime and said there was a degree of nervousness among MPs about the seats of Camden, Auburn, Penrith and Riverstone.

"I have no doubt they will probably try to, they always try, to seek fortune for themselves from the misfortune of others," they said.

'Really scary'

The eruption of gangland violence also has Western Sydney residents questioning the response of the government and NSW Police.

Rob from Condell Park, who did not want his surname used, said police had lost control of gun violence.

"I don't think they've got a leg to stand on, to be honest," he said.

"It looks like it's happening more and more frequently now. Gun laws don't work. I just think they've probably got to do a little bit more. Punishments aren't harsh enough."

Rob says police should be doing more to combat violent crime in Western Sydney. (ABC News)

Josie from Punchbowl, who did not want her surname published, said police should be tougher on gun crime.

"You just feel scared … I could just be walking innocently down the road with my daughter and then wrong place, wrong time," she said.

"You're hearing more and more of it and it's just really scary.

"I think they need to be tougher on the laws with shootings, obtaining guns and weapons and I think they need to enforce the law a bit more. You just can't go around shooting people in brazen daylight."

Peter Boutros from Greenacre said it was disheartening to hear senior police talking down the problem.

"I think it's insulating to be honest because we pride ourselves on being a good, safe country where our kids can run around the street and go to the park and play," he said.

"I don't remember this being the case 25 years ago when I was raised here as a kid."

Peter Boutros says violent crime has become more frequent over the years. (ABC News)

Election day looms

NSW Premier Chris Minns knows it could turn into a political headache and this week announced a suite of law reforms designed to stamp out the criminal networks.

"It's not normal, it's shocking, it's the kind of abject outside violence that we are not used to in our peaceful community and we shouldn't have to put up with it," he said on Thursday.

"I'd hate for anyone to believe that we're accepting of the status quo or we believe that it's normal or that it's acceptable or that we just have to turn a blind eye.

"I've seen with my own eyes NSW Police detectives put enormous resources into smashing these networks up and they do arrest the people responsible for it."

Chris Minns earlier this week announced another tranche of reforms to combat organised crime. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Labor insiders say it is too soon to predict what impact One Nation or the current string of gangland shootings will have on the March 13 state election.

But with just six months to go before the ballot boxes open, the pressure is on the government and police to stop the brazen and bloody attacks on Western Sydney streets.

World.title: Quick hits: NFL goes AFL, Jonas Brothers rock, and 100k fans see rare sight
World.content:
The NFL's first match in Australia lived up to the hype, with more than 100,000 fans packing the MCG to watch the San Francisco 49ers defeat the LA Rams.

There was more than just football on the field, with the Jonah Brothers rocking out at half-time and belting out one of the great Aussie anthems.

The NFL brought American flair to the MCG, but the game had a little AFL flavour.

Here are the quick hits from the historic season opener.

1. An anthem so nice he sang it twice

With the NFL playing its first ever match in Australia, it also meant that our national anthem was sung before an NFL game for the first time.

The honour of singing Advance Australia Fair was given to singer, and Commonwealth Games swimmer, Cody Simpson, and our man did us proud.

Simpson even gave the anthem a little twist at the end, this was a special occasion after all.

After completing the anthem, Simpson then sang the final two lines again, as planes flew overhead at the G.

2. A little AFL flavour at the 'G

Melbourne was getting a taste of America with the NFL.

The pageantry of pre-game, tailgates outside the MCG, and plenty of NFL fan fare.

But the NFL made sure to add some Australian flavour to its game as well.

Loading Instagram content

The first points of the match belonged to San Francisco 49ers kicker Eddy Pineiro, who kicked a 20-yard field goal in the first quarter.

Officials raise their arms in their air to signify a successful kick, but for this field goal, the action was a little different.

The officials extended their arms and made the same gesture for a goal in Aussie rules, a fitting touch for any game of footy played at the MCG.

3. 100,021 fans witness a rare sighting in the NFL

The NFL came to Australia with the intention of drawing a huge crowd, and putting on a spectacle.

That was achieved, and then some, with an official crowd of 100,021 packing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground. The official capacity of the MCG is 100,024, meaning the NFL was just three shy of claiming that every seat was filled on Friday.

And those 100,021 fans got to see something that most Americans never will: the centre catching a pass.

The centre is the player who snaps the ball between his legs to the quarterback at the start of the play.

The centre has two jobs:

Get the ball to the quarterback

Protect the quarterback or running back

But on a historic day in Melbourne, 49ers centre Jake Brendel became the hero of big men everywhere.

Midway through the second quarter, Brendel snapped the ball to quarterback Brock Purdy, and then protected his QB by blocking Rams defensive lineman Kobie Turner.

When Purdy threw his pass down the middle, Turner was able to jump in the air and get his hand to the ball.

As the ball hung in the air, threatening to be intercepted by the Rams, Brendel quickly reacted and caught the pass for a two-yard gain.

Frankly, it was a pity the MCG crowd did not get to see Brendel cut loose for a big run, but seeing him claim the first reception of his career was a moment that would not have been on any NFL bingo cards.

4. Jonas Brothers tribute to John Farnham

The superstars at the MCG on Friday were not restricted to footballers.

American pop rock band Jonas Brothers were the headline act at half-time.

The performance, albeit short, had all the the style and chorography of the half-time show at the Super Bowl.

And there was a nice touch to an Australian legend during the performance.

The American stars sang one of the great Aussie anthems, You're The Voice by John Farnham.

The capacity crowd at the MCG was in full voice for the famous song, a great nod to one of Australia's greatest artists.

5. Kittle wants a shoey, and to go home

There are few better personalities in the NFL than star San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle.

His interviews are always a highlight, especially after a 49ers win over their rivals in LA.

Following his side's impressive 27-7 win over the Rams at the MCG, Kittle gave a trademark interview with American broadcaster ESPN.

He was asked about the Australian tradition of a shoey, which the American star claimed he wanted to try.

"Are you trying to set me up to get in trouble?" he asked the reporter when quizzed on whether he would want to try a shoey.

"Wherever I can do one, I'm gonna try to find one in the stands."

Kittle finished off his interview in similarly entertaining style.

He said how much he was excited to leave Melbourne and head home, before appearing to make sure his comment did not come across like he, and his teammates, did not enjoy their week down under.

"We embraced going to Australia — 15-hour flight, we were here the whole week — it was a grind but we did it," he said.

"We'll see you guys back in America, I can't wait to go home. I did love Australia though, this place is awesome."

We loved having you George, bar the Rams fans here who have gone through a painful defeat.

World.title: Gliders return to world stage after missing last Paralympics
World.content:
Australia's women's wheelchair basketball team has returned to the world stage, two years on from missing qualification for the Paris Paralympics.

It has been a lean decade for the Gliders, once considered amongst the world's best, failing to qualify for the 2016 Paralympic Games as well.

But a new dawn appears to be breaking for the team, which, anchored by an experienced core and energised by an exciting group of tournament debutants, has begun its tilt at World Championship glory in Canada.

The Gliders have not competed in a major international tournament since the World Championships in 2023. (Supplied: Basketball Australia)

The tournament serves as an important stepping stone for the Gliders, with the side having already set the goal of a podium finish at the Brisbane 2032 Paralympics.

Meanwhile, Australia's men's side, the Rollers, are gunning for a third World Championship title, after missing the medals in Paris.

Taking the long way around

While the Gliders have been plotting their return to the top of the international game, China has emerged as a true powerhouse of women's wheelchair basketball, having medalled at the 2021 and 2024 Paralympics, as well as the 2022 World Championships.

So, a first-round tussle with the Asian powerhouse was always going to be a tough task for the Australians, and something of a baptism by fire for their three tournament debutants.

The Gliders went down by 11 points in their opener on Wednesday night, but it was a game of real promise for the Australians, according to emerging star Katelin Gunn.

"We haven't played as well as we have against China in quite a few years," Gunn told ABC Sport from camp in Ottawa.

The meet is Gunn's first major international tournament, but she has been in and around the Gliders' set-up since making her international debut in 2022.

Loading Instagram content

She was a member of the side that qualified for the tournament by the skin of its teeth late last year, triumphing in a gruelling repechage in Madrid after missing direct passage to the competition.

Head coach Jeremy Symot, who was appointed Gliders boss last year after a highly successful stint in the Australian domestic league, named the same 12-player squad for both the repechage and the World Championships.

The roster includes team legends Shelley Matheson and Sarah Vinci, who boast 40 years of international experience between them, as well as superstar centre Georgia Munro-Cook, fresh from her 3x3 bronze medal at the Commonwealth Games.

Gunn believes the squad is as strong as she has ever seen it, and that the shared experience of last November's repechage has pushed it to a new level.

"We took a lot of learnings from Spain and we will build more and more on them," Gunn said.

"In the few training sessions we've had together as a group, we have just connected more than ever."

Destination Brisbane

Munro-Cook captained the Gliders in their last Paralympic campaign in 2021. (supplied: Griffith University)

A 73-30 loss to Canada in their second game on Friday morning means that the Gliders now face an uphill battle to progress from Group A, with the Australians likely requiring handsome victories in their remaining pool matches.

But regardless of whether a knockout-round berth does prove elusive for the side in Ottawa, the tournament is a vital next step on the road to Brisbane 2032.

Gunn, who will be in her late 20s by the time of a potentially career-defining home Games, is aware it will take time for her team to reach its potential.

"It's all about building each game, each benchmark event, getting closer to where we want to be," she said.

"It's a slow process, but hopefully we'll be closer to where we want to be by the end of this competition."

World.title: When it's time to wash your pet's bed and how to do it
World.content:
Have you ever run a pet bed through the family washing machine and found your favourite jumper covered in hair after a later wash?

About 64 per cent of Australians live in a household with at least one pet — mostly dogs and cats — and most of them have their own comfy beds that can get pretty funky.

Our experts say it's generally OK to clean pets' bedding in your washing machine, but there are simple ways to make sure the bed, the machine and your clothes are not ruined in the process, as well as detergent considerations for your fur baby's comfort.

Cats self-clean, so their bedding can require less washing. (Unsplash)

Is it a hygiene problem?

While pet bedding can get quite dirty and smelly, associate professor Rietie Venter, who works on the traditional lands of Kaurna people at Adelaide University's School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Sciences, says running it through the home washing machine is low risk from a hygiene perspective.

Rietie Venter is Adelaide University's antimicrobial resistance lead with the School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Science. (Supplied: Rietie Venter)

"If you wash it separately [from your clothing], by itself, that should be absolutely fine," she says.

"If you have a heavy-shedding dog … you will have to remove the hair first, otherwise it just clogs up your machine."

Dr Venter says most of the oil, dirt, dead skin cells and microbes on the bedding go down the drain, so you're unlikely to pick up any problematic nasties if you wash your clothes in the same machine.

And while pets carry lots of microbes, she says when you cuddle them or allow them on your bed, you're exposed to the same germs anyway.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

How to wash pet bedding in a machine

Before putting pet bedding through your washing machine, Ngunnawal and Ngambri country/Canberra-based appliance repairer Tait Leaney agrees you should brush as much hair and debris off as possible.

Should you let your dog sleep in your bed? While there are several benefits to keeping our pets close at night, there are a few minor risks to consider.

He also recommends doing your own washing before your pet's.

And while it may be tempting to use scented washing products to cancel out odours, University of Sydney veterinary dermatology lecturer Tina Baxter urges pet owners to avoid them, particularly when laundering dog bedding.

"[Dogs'] noses prefer smells that are often quite off-putting for us," says Dr Baxter, who also works as a vet at the university's teaching hospital at Camden, on the traditional lands of the Dharawal, Gundungurra and Dharug peoples.

" When we make decisions around washing bedding in something that smells lovely to us, the dog may very strongly disagree. "

Dr Baxter recommends using enzymatic washing powders designed for humans that are "very mild" in smell.

Pet beds with removable shells can simplify the process, Dr Venter says, as the covers can be washed and dried regularly with ease.

But some beds can actually be put into the machine whole.

Our experts recommend low-fragrance washing detergents when cleaning pet beds. (Unsplash)

"Our dog … has one of those foam ones that you can just put in and … actually, it works quite well," Dr Venter says.

If you're washing a whole pet bed and you don't have a dryer, Dr Venter recommends doing it on a warm, sunny day with no rain, as the bedding needs to dry quickly so germs can't multiply in it while it is still wet.

In terms of what washing machine settings to use, Mr Leaney says it is best to follow the instructions on the bedding.

"As long as the pet bedding can withstand a hot wash, that's always going to be more hygienic," he says.

"But the hotter the wash … the harder it is on the [item being washed] and the less energy efficient it is."

Tina Baxter says cat and dog bedding generally only needs washing when it smells. (Pexels)

Will pet bedding damage my washing machine?

Putting your pet's bedding through the home washing machine is generally fine, Mr Leaney says.

But he has had one or two pet bed-related repair jobs during his time in the trade.

Tait Leaney is the director of a Canberra-based appliance repair business. (Supplied: Ginger Beard Repair Service)

"The main ones are … bedding with stuffing inside," he says.

"The washing machine will rip those up a little bit and then the stuffing ends up all through the machine."

However, if you follow the bedding's washing instructions, Mr Leaney says this scenario is unlikely.

When putting pet bedding through the dryer, as with human washing, it's important to clean the lint trap afterwards to avoid creating a fire hazard, particularly in older machines.

If you want to keep your washing machine sparkling between pet washes, Mr Leaney recommends wiping out any seals, throwing in two basic dishwasher tablets (yes, dishwasher tablets) and running a cleaning cycle (or the longest, hottest cycle you can), followed by an empty cycle to flush it.

If you've got big dogs or lots of pet bedding, he also warns not to overpack your machine, and says to check its capacity (usually in kilograms in the user guide), as it can become unbalanced, stop running, and leave you with a wet, smelly mess to deal with.

And for people who don't fancy sharing a washer with their pets, some laundromats have machines specifically for pet bedding.

Like humans, dogs can also be allergic to the dust mites that can accumulate in their bedding. (Unsplash)

How often should you wash your pet's bed?

If nobody in your family, including your pets, is immunocompromised or has allergies (for example, to dust mites, which are everywhere but can accumulate in bedding), Dr Baxter says dog bedding only needs washing "when it smells", but this will vary between animals.

She says the sniff test can also be applied to cat bedding.

"Cats are, by nature, fairly clean creatures," Dr Baxter says.

"It can probably sit there for some time without that causing any health problems."

World.title: 'The game is up': Aussie professor at centre of AI maths controversy speaks out
World.content:
Artificial intelligence has made the race to publish mathematical breakthroughs pointless, according to the Australian professor at the centre of a bitter dispute over a claimed solution to one of the world's most difficult unsolved mathematical problems.

"I think it's pointless. Like, I think the game is up," Melbourne-born Tristan Buckmaster told the ABC.

The New York University professor also warned Australia about the centralisation of resources into the hands of a small number of privately owned foreign companies, which were now publishing solutions to maths problems that had puzzled people for decades.

"Australia needs to think about protecting our own national interests in this world where the resources are so skewed," he said.

Professor Buckmaster said AI had become a crucial tool for research, but he had grave concerns about the recklessness of the companies building it as they competed for attention and commercial advantage.

"They have zero respect for the scientific community. I mean, it's appalling, honestly," he said.

Controversy as OpenAI claims solution to Navier Stokes problem The subject of the controversy may be extremely complex, but experts say it boils down to simple issues of trust and ethics.

This week, leading AI company OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven fiendishly difficult Millennium Prize problems that come with a US$1 million reward, using AI tools.

The moment of triumph for OpenAI and the artificial intelligence industry was sullied by accusations and criticism of the company's conduct by Professor Buckmaster.

He published a public statement this week accusing the AI company of trying to gazump him and his research partner Levent Alpöge, from OpenAI's rival Anthropic, after hearing they were close to solving the problem.

Professor Buckmaster also said the company offered to let write up their solution if he took his partner's name off the research.

Professor Buckmaster said he and Dr Alpöge had more research they could publish but questioned the point of racing ahead with it when AI could perform work that had previously occupied researchers for years.

He said there needed to be a discussion about how mathematics should operate in this new environment.

"What do we do about credit? What do we do about hiring? What do we do about PhDs?" he said.

Professor Buckmaster said some mathematicians had stopped publicly sharing what they were working on to avoid tipping off AI companies about their plans.

He has called on academics and people from OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepMind to discuss ground rules for how they worked together.

He said the companies' power carried responsibilities that went beyond competing to solve problems before their rivals.

Credit controversy

Professor Buckmaster and Dr Alpöge both used tools from OpenAI and Anthropic as they pursued solutions to mathematical problems about how fluids move.

After months of work, Professor Buckmaster became convinced the technology could make substantial contributions to the field of mathematics.

He said AI was like a "whole team of PhD students that don't need to eat and don't need to sleep".

Building on the work of mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, the pair found a solution to the Euler problem, a stepping stone to the Navier-Stokes problem.

Professor Buckmaster said he spent weeks checking and improving the "slop" proofs generated by AI.

OpenAI is best known for being the developer of ChatGPT. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

OpenAI then claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem. It said the company's researchers guided AI agents to come up with its own solution to the Euler problem and, then, Navier-Stokes.

The company said it began its effort after hearing rumours two Millennium Prize problems had been solved, later realising the rumours related to Professor Buckmaster and Dr Alpöge.

After hearing rumours that OpenAI had started to work on this, Professor Buckmaster said he contacted OpenAI to explain their work was a personal project and that the rumours had incorrectly identified the problem they had solved.

During calls between Professor Buckmaster and representatives from the company, Professor Buckmaster said OpenAI proposed he and Dr Alpöge publish their result before the company released its Navier-Stokes result.

He said another proposal would have involved him writing OpenAI's result under his name, acknowledging the company's model, but leaving out Dr Alpöge because he worked at Anthropic.

Professor Buckmaster said he refused because he believed it would be unethical to publish the research without acknowledging both the contributions of his partner.

Loading...

Time to 're-evaluate what math is'

OpenAI's lead researcher Sébastien Bubeck previously told The New York Times the offers were intended to help Professor Buckmaster, including by providing computing resources or allowing him to write up OpenAI's proof.

He acknowledged expressing not wanting to publish a paper with an Anthropic employee.

Professor Buckmaster questioned whether OpenAI's research had benefited from their unpublished work, which they had been using OpenAI's Codex tool to help write up.

The bigger, hungrier data centres set to escape looming restrictions Dozens of approved but yet-to-be-built AI data centre projects are expected to escape the federal government's proposed restrictions around energy and water use.

An OpenAI spokesperson denied that was the case.

"We can say categorically that it is impossible for Dr Buckmaster's Codex prompts over the last two months to have influenced the system in any way, including training," they told the ABC.

"In addition, since the completion of Navier-Stokes we have made substantial progress on another Millennium Prize problem. We are working through how to share these results thoughtfully."

For now, Professor Buckmaster said he wanted to finish existing work and support his PhD students and postdoctoral researchers, rather than chase another Millennium Prize.

"I think it's more important to re-evaluate what math is," he said.

World.title: ‘Lots of hugs’: Greens kiss and make up after internal fight
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalGreens ‘Lots of hugs’: Greens kiss and make up after internal fight Caitlin Fitzsimmons September 11, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Greens leader Larissa Waters says her leadership is secure and the party is ready for a broader fight on climate policy, despite the spectacle of three Greens senators crossing the floor to vote with the Nationals on a key vote on Thursday night. Long-serving South Australian Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young also said that Waters’ position as leader was safe. Waters told this masthead that no one in her party room or outside the party had raised concerns with her about her leadership, after the Greens took a position contrary to the urging of former leaders Bob Brown and Christine Milne. Senator Larissa Waters, leader of the Australian Greens, at Parliament House in Canberra. Alex Ellinghausen “I have a really respectful relationship with my colleagues, and that feeling’s mutual,” Waters said.



“No one loved coming to a different position on this issue, but everyone understands that people who’ve thought about it deeply can disagree on the method of getting to the same place. “This was Labor putting us in an impossible position by backtracking on a commitment to establish a national park and then demanding carbon credits for it. So we took a difficult decision, and it wasn’t an easy one to take.” The Greens under Waters’ leadership voted with Labor to allow state governments to earn carbon credits from protecting forest, which the NSW government wants to use for the Great Koala National Park and can also be used by other states. The Greens were wedged because they hold concerns about the role of carbon credits in allowing pollution to continue, but want to protect forests. The Australia Institute co-chief executive Richard Denniss, who was opposed to the carbon credits, had described it as “the Greens’ first major climate test in the Senate under leader Larissa Waters”. Waters rejected that it was a leadership test. “TAI can have their views, that’s fine. I don’t think he’s correct in this one, but that’s, you know, I don’t speak for them – I speak for the Greens.”



Waters said that the party engaged in “lots of discussions and lots of hugs”, ensuring disagreement was respectful and party unity survived. Waters was seen hugging Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer immediately after the vote in the Senate. Bleyer, who was sworn in only days earlier as a replacement for Peter Whish-Wilson, was one of the three who crossed the floor along with fellow Tasmanian Nick McKim and Western Australia’s Jordon Steele-John. At a time when One Nation is monstering the major parties in the polls and byelections, the Greens’ vote is holding steady on 12 per cent in this masthead’s Resolve Political Monitor. Waters said it was an uneven playing field. “Billionaires are paying Pauline Hanson to spread her lies,” she said. “It is not the fault of your neighbour, who might happen to be a migrant, that people’s lives are getting tougher, and she’s been helped out by billionaires and big corporations giving her wads of dough to fly around the country and spam billboards and pay for social media ads. But then when she comes into parliament, she votes for billionaires and corporate interests.”



Waters said the party would put this week’s vote behind them, and that she was excited about the fight ahead to secure improvements to the Safeguard Mechanism, Labor’s flagship climate policy that is under statutory review, while trying to knock out 40 per cent of the carbon credit market. More on this debate Pragmatism v Purity: Once again, the environmental movement is cleaved in two, with giants such as Bob Brown and Tim Flannery on different sides. Carbon credits for protecting public forests: The Greens have defied intense lobbying and voted against a Nationals motion to kill off the scheme. Civil war inside environmental movement: The fate of the Great Koala National Park hangs in the balance as a new carbon accounting method divides conservationists.



Carbon credits give states off-ramp for logging: The NSW may now fulfil its election promise to create the Great Koala National Park. Get to the heart of climate change and the environment.

World.title: Proposed bail laws set to land in centre of ongoing High Court fight
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Proposed bail laws set to land in centre of ongoing High Court fight Matt Dennien September 11, 2026 — 3:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland barristers have urged the state government to pause its proposed bail crackdown until a High Court challenge against similar elements of Northern Territory laws is decided. The Queensland Bar Association’s submission is one of more than 250 lodged for committee consideration of the Crisafulli LNP’s controversial “breach bail, go to jail” laws introduced last month. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli and Attorney-General Deb Frecklington speak to media after their election win in late 2024. Matt Dennien Several key organisations have raised concerns about the bill, its justification, the consequences of increased pressure on youth detention, prisons and police watchhouses, and further delays to court processes. Aimed at making it harder for people charged with specific offences while on bail to be released into the community, a mandatory 12-month minimum jail sentence will also apply to those guilty of the new offence.



The government has been gradually revealing parts of the proposed laws since it was first raised by LNP candidate – and now MP – for the Townsville seat of Hinchinbrook, Wade Chiesa, in November’s byelection. Public sentiment of the government’s hardline crime response has soured across the past year, despite the LNP’s suggestions its election promises to fix a crime crisis are starting to work. ABS data has shown victim numbers, a metric to which Premier David Crisafulli has tied his leadership, were already falling across the election year – and fell further across 2025. Bar association president Cate Heyworth-Smith KC, writing in the group’s submission to the parliamentary committee considering the bill, raised a series of concerns about the removal of judicial discretion and rules against double jeopardy.



Heyworth-Smith also said that the laws would provide less incentive for people to plead guilty, which would lead to more trials and more delays across the entire court system, and overcrowding issues in the detention system which would be “difficult to correct once they have begun”. Related Article Queensland government Qld’s ‘strongest bail laws in the country’ could reverse onus of proof While the government has insisted the laws are about deterring and punishing serious repeat offenders, she also laid out a hypothetical situation where a P-plate driver given bail for drink-driving was then caught up in the new bail regime for being only a passenger in a stolen car. “The resulting punishment would be seriously disproportionate to the offending behaviour,” Heyworth-Smith wrote. “These provisions do not merely create a risk of unjust outcomes, they ensure that unjust outcomes will occur.”



The association president also raised the High Court challenge against Northern Territory bail laws she said would appear to “transpose directly” to the new tougher bail test, a legal argument for which “the answer is not obvious, and the committee should not be told otherwise”. “The Association submits that the question is a real one, as is demonstrated by the referral of the matter to the Full Court of the High Court of Australia, and that the constitutional validity of such provisions will be illuminated by the decision,” Heyworth-Smith wrote. “The Association submits that the Committee should not report on the Bill before the High Court has delivered judgment.” Other submissions from the Crime and Corruption Commission warn about the risk of increased police misconduct through the treatment of people in overcrowded facilities, which the agency would actively monitor, and human rights overrides appeared to be inconsistent with the law. The Australian Workers Union and Queensland Police Union raised fears the laws would increase pressure on already crowded youth detention centres. The Queensland Law Society and National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Young People also urged the bill be rejected.



The Voice for Victims group said while supporting the government’s objective of strengthening community safety, success for victims was “measured by whether reforms reduce repeat offending”. Several submitters called for a review of the laws after a set period of time, or urged the release of government modelling around impacts on jails and watchhouses. The Queensland Human Rights Commission, in its first major foray into parliamentary process under leader Debbie Platz, called for the removal of mandatory minimum sentences and the new bail test from the bill. “While all offending is serious, the data does not indicate this form of offending is so prevalent, or increasing at such a rate, that it warrants an emergency response that overrides human rights,” she said. World.title: Dolphin calf found dead near Perth’s iconic Blue Boat House
World.content:
NationalWAMarine life Dolphin calf found dead near Perth’s iconic Blue Boat House Indigo Lemay-Conway September 11, 2026 — 3:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A dolphin calf has washed up on the foreshore next to the Blue Boat House in Crawley, sparking an urgent warning on fishing line responsibility. The young animal was found on Tuesday morning with deep cuts to its snout and notches on its dorsal fin – something the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions said was consistent with dolphin entanglement incidents. The dolphin calf was found next to the Blue Boat House in Nedlands. Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions While it isn’t confirmed, the DBCA believes the calf is Bindi Bindi, a three-month-old dolphin that was spotted in the Swan Canning Riverpark in August. “During a survey yesterday, we observed Bindi Bindi, a young dolphin calf, entangled in fishing line. Unfortunately, this is another case of a young calf becoming entangled in fishing line within the Swan Canning Riverpark,” the department said in a post to its social media last month.



“The line appears tightly wrapped around the calf’s mouth, cuts across the base of the dorsal fin and is also believed to extend around the pectoral fins. Editor's pick Homelessness ‘Where else are they supposed to go?’ Two-day deadline to clear Perth homeless camp sparks fierce backlash “Bindi Bindi was observed swimming slowly, with mum Click nearby. “At three months of age, Bindi Bindi is currently the youngest calf in the Swan Canning Riverpark dolphin community, making this a particularly concerning situation for both mother and calf. Bindi Bindi was last seen on August 24, still with fishing line wrapped around its body.



“Unfortunately, the complexity of the entanglement has ruled out simpler boat-based intervention,” DBCA said. In an updated post on Friday, the River Guardians (an arm of the DBCA) said they believed the dolphins to be the same. “Photographs of Bindi Bindi were compared with post-mortem images. Bindi Bindi was last sighted on August 24 despite extensive efforts to locate her. Based on these comparisons, the calf is believed to be Bindi Bindi,” the post said. “Although the scars and other identifying features are a close match, decomposition has affected some of these markers, so a definitive identification can’t be confirmed just yet. “While no fishing line was found on or near the calf when it was retrieved, evidence of entanglement can be lost over time as a carcass decomposes.”



DBCA Marine and Riverpark rangers retrieved the calf on Tuesday and transported it to Ellam Street, where Dr Delphine Chabanne from Murdoch University examined the animal. Editor's pick WA Parliament Rough sleepers to be moved away from Perth arms expo under new police powers “The next Dolphin Watch scientific vessel survey may help provide more clarity. If Click is observed without her calf and all other known calves are accounted for, it would strengthen the likelihood that the deceased dolphin is Bindi Bindi.” The department urged people to properly dispose of their fishing line and tackle to keep dolphins safe in the future. “Discarded fishing line can have devastating impacts on wildlife. If you’re fishing and see a dolphin nearby, reel in your line. Always take unwanted fishing line and tackle with you and dispose of it responsibly,” they said.



“Keep your distance. All vessels, including boats, kayaks, jet skis and stand-up paddleboards, must stay at least 100m from dolphins. People and dogs must stay at least 50m away. “If a dolphin approaches you, remain still and move away slowly when it is safe to do so.” If an injured dolphin is spotted, contact the Wildcare Helpline.

World.title: ‘He’s a magician’: Former Netanyahu adviser says he can win again
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict ‘He’s a magician’: Former Netanyahu adviser says he can win again Matthew Knott September 11, 2026 — 3:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Benjamin Netanyahu has a strong chance of winning next month’s Israeli elections despite underwhelming poll numbers and major political challenges, according to a former top adviser to the Israeli prime minister. Melbourne-born Mark Regev, a former senior adviser to Netanyahu and Israeli ambassador to the United Kingdom, said Netanyahu has proven his doubters wrong many times before and could remain Israel’s leader after the nation votes on October 27. “In Hebrew, he is known as a magician. He’s always pulling a rabbit out of his hat with politics. He’s only there for a long time because he keeps winning elections,” Regev said in an interview in Canberra. Benjamin Netanyahu is up for re-election in October and struggling in the polls. AP Regev said Netanyahu’s political career was widely thought to be over when he lost power in 1999 after a single term in office, yet returned to the prime ministership a decade later. Netanyahu also swiftly returned after losing power in 2021, returning in 2022.



Some analysts predicted Netanyahu’s career was over after the October 7 attacks of 2023 – the worst security failure in Israeli history – but he served out a full term and gradually improved his standing in opinion surveys. Related Article World elections ‘He’s been humiliated’: Israel’s strongman faces re-election jitters “It would be a mistake for the opposition to underrate his political capabilities,” said Regev, who also served as a spokesman for Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. While Netanyahu presided over the failure of October 7, Regev said he would argue that Israel was in a more secure position today than it was before the attacks. “Hamas is largely defeated. Hezbollah in Lebanon is largely defeated. In Iran, the monster is still there, but it’s been defanged,” he said.



The United Kingdom, France and Canada this week announced a ban on commercial activity with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which are considered illegal under international law, a move underlining Israel’s growing international isolation under Netanyahu. Australia did not join the push, but Foreign Minister Penny Wong has indicated more sanctions on Israel are on the way. Mark Regev said he expected an international “honeymoon” period if Netanyahu wins the elections. AP Significantly, US President Donald Trump reportedly did not try to talk UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham out of the policy when they discussed it, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave only a muted reaction. Trump and Netanyahu’s once-close relationship has been strained by their inability to defeat the hardline regime in Iran and Netanyahu’s refusal to commit to Trump’s Gaza peace plan.



An explosive report this week in Israeli newspaper Haaretz claimed that Netanyahu was personally alerted by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a large-scale offensive against Israel a week before October 7, but did not act on the warning. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu’s rivals call him ‘unfit’ for office after report he was warned of October 7 attack Netanyahu has branded the report an “absolute lie” and vowed to sue the newspaper. The UAE’s foreign ministry issued a statement that did not deny the report, saying: “When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities.” Four of Netanyahu’s main rivals issued a statement labelling him “unfit for office” and declaring they would work together to end his government.



Since 2022, Netanyahu has governed with the support of far-right and ultra-orthodox parties, including two senior ministers sanctioned by Australia for inciting violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. He said Netanyahu would likely seek to form a broader coalition government, including politicians to the left and right of his conservative Likud party, if it is possible after polling day. “I would think it’s in his interest to have a wider coalition, also a wider, larger majority in the Knesset [the Israeli parliament], which makes a government less susceptible to pressure from small elements,” he said. Netanyahu, who has been indicted for alleged war crimes by the International Criminal Court over Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza, vowed to establish a “broad national government” in June in an apparent bid to win back mainstream centre and centre-right voters ahead of the election. Regev said there would be a difference in style if Netanyahu loses the election, but he did not expect fundamental changes to Israel’s handing of key issues such as the West Bank and Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.



“I think if a new government was elected it might get a certain glow in the international community [but] the idea that another government is going to come in and suddenly take Israel in a 180 degree different direction is just not logical,” he said. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel targets UK in response to sanctions on settlements in West Bank Most Israelis do not believe there was a “partner for peace” on the Palestinian side, leading to the collapse in support for a two-state solution, he said. Most polls show former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party leading Netanyahu’s Likud, but also find neither the pro nor anti-Netanyahu blocs winning enough seats to form government. Mark Sofer, a former Israeli ambassador to Australia, told this masthead recently: “At this juncture, I cannot envisage a situation in which Netanyahu wins the next elections



“On the other hand, I can envisage a scenario in which the opposition doesn’t reach the 61 seats necessary to set up a government.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.
