World.title: In Dallas, a feisty Vance cements his status as Trump’s likely successor
World.content:
The vice president is showing that he too can deal in the kind of ugly, personal mud-slinging that Trump’s loyal audiences have delighted in for years.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dallas: A Republican TV  played on the big screen at the party’s midterm convention cast the upcoming election in stark, simple terms. “This is no longer simply Republican versus Democrat, or conservative versus liberal,” the baritone voiceover boomed. “Today the choice is unmistakable: extreme versus mainstream.” That will be the crux of the GOP message for the next seven or so weeks: radical, America-hating communists have taken over the Democratic Party, and the only salvation is Donald Trump and his sensible Republicans. Attendees celebrate at the conclusion of the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas. Bloomberg Vice President JD Vance leant into that framing when he took centre stage on Thursday night (US time) in Dallas, with a speech that was largely dedicated to attacking Democrats and spent little time on Republican achievements or promises for the future. He did not mention Trump’s extraordinary offer the previous evening – which Trump repeated on Thursday – of giving every American adult a $US5000 ($7000) “Trump Dividend” if the Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November. Rather, Vance focused on portraying the Democrats as “the party of hatred”. Like many of the speakers over the preceding five hours, the vice president targeted specific people, such as Senate candidate for Michigan Abdul El-Sayed, and Senate candidate for Texas James Talarico, whom Trump has branded “Tala-freako”.



Talarico has been a strong advocate for transgender people, including student athletes, though he has recently moderated some of his positions. Vance accused Talarico of being “obsessed with trans children” and even went as far as to imply, baselessly, that Talarico was a paedophile. “I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history,” he said. In normal times, a vice president might be expected to get his hands a little dirty during an election campaign: throwing bombs on behalf of a president who would rather stay a bit above the fray. Vice President JD Vance made it personal as he attacked Democrats for being a party of “hard-core hatred”. Bloomberg Trump, obviously, does not mind insulting his opponents. Vance, by following suit, is showing that he too can deal in the kind of ugly, personal mud-slinging that Trump’s loyal audiences have delighted in for years. Indeed, Vance’s most successful moment came when he was heckled by a protester in the stands waving the Mexican and Palestinian flags. The man was booed by the crowd (a person sitting near this correspondent shouted: “F--- Palestine”) and quickly escorted out by security. But Vance pounced. “My friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there – I’ll buy you the plane ticket,” he said to roars of applause and a lengthy “USA” chant.



Vance chuckled and added that this was the symbol of the far-left: “An idiot waving a Mexican flag, when he should be waving the flag of the United States of America.” The room went wild again. The vice president was also visibly angry when he brought up a taunt El-Sayed made about his wife, Usha, on social media. The Democrat had queried whether Vance would have been willing to introduce Usha, who is of Indian heritage, to his late grandfather, a white steelworker from Appalachia. For Vance, it was beyond the pale. “This is who the Democrats are now, my friends,” he said. “They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it.” A protester holds a Mexican flag as Vice President JD Vance speaks at the convention. AP Photo/Julio Cortez Eyes were on the vice president at this convention because after the midterms, the political conversation will start to turn to Trump’s successor. Vance is the obvious and leading candidate to become the next Republican nominee for president, though he is not without his detractors. If this was a quasi-audition, Vance certainly passed. At one point, after a woman yelled out “JD 48” – Vance to become the 48th president – the crowd cheered and began chanting: “48! 48!” Vance settled them down. “We gotta take care of business this November, then we’ll worry about what comes next,” he said.



Two events loomed large over the afternoon. Thursday was the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, and the eve of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks, in which nearly 3000 people were killed by Islamic extremists. It set the backdrop for several speakers to rail against Islamism and left-wing political violence. Texas senator Ted Cruz had the crowd on its feet several times as he condemned what he portrayed as a “red-green alliance” of communists and Islamists taking over the Democratic Party. “They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate capitalism, they hate the Constitution and they hate America,” he said. Trump greeting the audience. At one point, he made them recite a pledge to “the greatest president in the history of the United States”. AP Photo/Julio Cortez Texas senator Ted Cruz had the crowd on its feet several times as he condemned what he portrayed as a “red-green alliance” of communists and Islamists taking over the Democratic Party. AP Photo/Julio Cortez At one point, Cruz named several progressive Democrats and their associates, including New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, far-left podcaster Hasan Piker, El-Sayed and Talarico. “When people tell you who they are, believe them,” Cruz said. “When [far-left podcaster] Hasan Piker says America deserved 9/11, believe him.”



As he said it, a man in the crowd appeared to shout out “he should be shot”. He repeated the interjection each time Cruz mentioned another Democrat. El-Sayed was a constant target throughout the evening. Mike Rogers, a former Republican congressman who is running against El-Sayed for the Senate seat, accused his opponent of excusing or rationalising terrorism. When Lebanese-American man Ayman Ghazali rammed his car into the Temple Israel synagogue in Detroit in the name of Hezbollah earlier this year, El-Sayed said, “hurt people hurt people”. Ghazali had lost family members in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the previous week. A flag in honour of assassinated Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, who was killed exactly one year ago. Bloomberg Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan, was mentioned countless times. Bloomberg “They treat our country like it’s the villain,” Rogers told the Republican crowd in Dallas. “Terror is terror. Evil is evil ... You don’t sympathise with terrorists, you don’t sanitise extremism.” This was not just another Senate race, he added. “This election is about the soul of our country ... and it is about who you stand with when that American way of life is threatened.”

World.title: Hallelujah! This comic take on the creation of Handel’s Messiah hits just the right note
World.content:
The Greek Theatre, September 10, until September 19

The day before seeing Joyful Noise, I attended a funeral in an Anglican church for a dear friend who was an atheist, and the vicar handled the dichotomy with commendable wit and nuance. Georg Friedrich Händel, by contrast, was allowed precious little nuance by the Church of England when creating his Messiah, among the greatest artistic glorifications of their very own God. The bishops thought it blasphemous, and tried to have it banned.

US playwright Tim Slover’s 1998 play (now being adapted into a film starring Anthony Hopkins) creeps up on you as you adjust to a certain archness of tone mingling with comedy and high-stakes drama. And, at first, this Madeleine Stedman production (for Joining the Dots Theatre) struggled to hit exactly the right notes – not helped by nerves and variable projection. But then it settled, settled more, and steadily rose in confidence and quality, until one almost wanted to cry “Hallelujah!” – well before the story reached that bit.

The numerous intersecting plots of Joyful Noise are essentially historical. Iain Cox

The numerous intersecting plots are essentially historical, including soprano Susannah Cibber’s reputation being trashed by a case of adultery orchestrated by her abusive husband. Then there’s artistic bickering between Handel and his librettist, Charles Jennens, and between Cibber and rival soprano Kitty Clive; court wrangling between King George II and Bishop Egerton, and between the king and Handel; open warfare between Egerton and Handel. But the squabbles are all leavened with Slover’s fine line in humour.

Nicholas Papademetriou pitches his Handel perfectly, so the tetchiness and stubbornness are balanced by glimpses of warmth and wit, just as the jobbing composer’s pragmatism is balanced by intimations of a soaring creative spirit.

Madeleine Stedman’s direction includes many comic flourishes. Iain Cox

The ever-consistent Christopher Stollery brings presence and authority to King George, and effortlessly finds the truth in Slover’s sometimes heightened language. Angela Johnston is a riot as the cockney actor/singer Kitty, who enacts Desdemona’s death scene for Handel by way of audition, and who has the street cunning to manoeuvre her way to the top of a savagely competitive profession.

Matthew Abotomey stays just on the right side of overcooking Bishop Egerton’s manipulativeness, driven by a zeal to keep God locked in the cathedrals – far from the low places where operas and oratorios are performed. Mason Phoumirath’s Jennens is another zealot, determined that Messiah should be done his way rather than Handel’s, while also denying the House of Hanover as the realm’s legitimate royalty.

Laila Chesterman was initially too soft as the put-upon Susannah, but built her way into a performance that won our sympathy. Lloyd Allison-Smith (Handel’s secretary) and Alison Chambers (Handel’s biggest fan) also had their chances to shine in the smaller roles.

Stedman’s direction was replete with light comic flourishes, and it was just refreshing to see a play with no overt agenda. The fact that Christ was despised and rejected was what resonated with a worn-down Handel, and allowed him to converse with divinity.

World.title: He broke their heart, twice. But without Roger, the Warriors wouldn’t be here today
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 He broke their heart, twice. But without Roger, the Warriors wouldn’t be here today Dan Walsh September 11, 2026 — 3:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Roger broke my heart twice. He broke my heart when he went to rugby. And he broke my heart when he went and did his knee and couldn’t play for us again.” Warriors chief executive Cameron George could be singing a rugby league love song about Roger Tuivasa-Sheck – the magnetic, sexy-stepping, light-up-a-room, ever-so humble star who won’t play another game for the club after rupturing his ACL in late May. Roger Tuivasa-Sheck: a wonderful Warrior. NRL Imagery “Hands down, just one of the most special people I have ever met,” George adds. “The type of person you can only hope and pray comes along into your club.” The Warriors sold 26,000 tickets for Saturday’s final against the Dolphins in around 17 minutes. Win, and they’ll shift almost twice as many for a grand final qualifier at Eden Park in a fortnight. The smart money says they’ll do it in half the time.



Thirty-one years since they were born out of rugby league’s last great rush to expand and conquer, the Warriors are better placed than ever before to assume the true powerhouse status that has seemingly always been theirs for the taking, if only they could ever get their house in order long enough to do it. In their most recent rise, pivotal figures in the club’s history abound. From coach Andrew Webster and foundation halfback Stacey Jones to current owner Mark Robinson and retired attacking phenom Shaun Johnson. Warriors fans have good reason to be in full voice this year. Getty Tuivasa-Sheck looms as influential as any. “Because of what Roger did for this club and this team during the COVID-19, it won’t and can’t ever be forgotten,” George says.



“When we hit rock bottom in that period, his leadership, commitment and passion during that time was just phenomenal, and he kept the club together.” What the Warriors went through to ensure the NRL could resume on May 28, 2020, and stay afloat as a competition, has regularly and rightly been acknowledged in the years since. Tuivasa-Sheck boards the Warriors team bus in Newcastle and prepares to leave Australia, unsure when the NRL competition will resume, in 2020. NRL Imagery Players, coaches, staff and some, but by no means all, of their families relocated across the Tasman for the best part of three seasons – from May, 2020 to late-2022, when they played their first game on Kiwi soil in more than 1000 days. They lived out of suitcases, in isolation, and observed strict COVID protocols in half a dozen temporary accommodation set-ups across the Australian east coast.



Robinson, the insulation magnate who tipped millions of his own money into keeping the club afloat, and George both say another six months would have pushed the Warriors into withdrawing from the competition, which would have put the NRL in breach of its agreement to deliver broadcasters eight games per week and cost it $20 million. As Warriors captain in the 2020 and 2021 seasons, Tuivasa-Sheck was a rock for his homesick teammates as border confusion reigned, families struggled, losses stacked up and coach Stephen Kearney was sacked. George sums it up bluntly. “As a club, we lost so much of our identity as everything eventually wore us down.”



One poignant moment, from late August 2020, still stands out from a late-season win over the Bulldogs. Tuivasa-Sheck had spent almost four months away from his Auckland-based family at this point. A few days earlier, his youngest son had just started crawling, 2000 kilometres away. As he played the milestone video in the Accor Stadium dressing room, Tuivasa-Sheck offered a sad smile and admitted: “Oh man, I think about going home all the time … but I’m proud that I’m here. And my family is, too, sticking it out for the club.” ‘They stuck with us when we were struggling and in Australia. You’d like to think we’re paying them back.’ Roger Tuivasa-Sheck on the Warriors’ loyal fans Late in 2021, after a lengthy New Zealand border shutdown and almost two full seasons separated from his family, Tuivasa-Sheck did, eventually, go home. He gave up around $250,000 to move to rugby and pursue an All Blacks Test debut, breaking George’s heart in the process.



But when Tuivasa-Sheck’s return to the club in 2024 was sealed with “a handshake and a cuddle”, the Warriors were unrecognisable. “The club is just so different,” he says. “The biggest difference is Andrew Webster obviously, as coach. And the system he’s set up with Andrew McFadden [the club’s recruitment and pathways manager], it’s built for the long haul. That’s the best thing. Tuivasa-Sheck laps up the Warriors fanfare. Getty Images “All these young forwards you’re seeing like Leka [Halasima], Jacob Laban and Demetric [Vaimauga], they’re learning what it takes to play NRL from the ages of 14 and 16. I don’t think the Warriors have ever really had that before.” Those miserable COVID-19 years have given Tuivasa-Sheck, George and the Warriors a healthy perspective on what matters most now the sun is shining on them.



“I’ve had my time of sitting there and being disappointed by my knee injury, but that time is long gone,” says Tuivasa-Sheck, now 33 and off to Super League outfit Wakefield next year. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Immortal inspection: Attacking geniuses and game plans to win week one finals Andrew Johns League columnist “No one likes to look back at COVID, do they? But when you ask about those tough periods for the club and players, what I’m proudest of is how the fans are with us and enjoying these times now. “They deserve this success that’s coming, and I can confidently say there will be a lot of success in the future because of what the club is building. They stuck with us when we were struggling and in Australia. You’d like to think we’re paying them back.” Ask Tuivasa-Sheck who remains from his first Warriors stint, and he can only name a few players – hooker Wayde Egan, injured winger Dallin Watene-Zelezniak, centre Adam Pompey and playmaker Chanel Harris-Tavita. Robinson, George, Jones and McFadden are the most prominent among the staff and club bosses.



Such is the nature of modern professional sport. And when the Warriors were carrying a significantly heavier COVID-19 load than any other club, at times losing multiple homesick players per week, it’s hardly any surprise. “It’s crazy when you think about it that way – a whole NRL squad has been turned over in a couple of years, but the fan base has grown bigger than it’s ever been,” Tuivasa-Sheck says. The Warriors have invested significantly and soundly in what they offer fans on game day, and the club’s steady rise under Webster has helped sell out 41 of their 46 home fixtures since late 2022. “Absence makes the heart grow fonder,” George says.



If all was truly fair in love and rugby league, then Tuivasa-Sheck would be playing against the Dolphins on Saturday afternoon, not sidelined by a wretched ACL tear. But if the Warriors do go all the way, their talismanic former captain might break his boss’s heart for a third time – in the best, most deserving way.

World.title: ‘Lots of hugs’: Greens kiss and make up after internal fight
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalGreens ‘Lots of hugs’: Greens kiss and make up after internal fight Caitlin Fitzsimmons September 11, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Greens leader Larissa Waters says her leadership is secure and the party is ready for a broader fight on climate policy, despite the spectacle of three Greens senators crossing the floor to vote with the Nationals on a key vote on Thursday night. Long-serving South Australian Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young also said that Waters’ position as leader was safe. Waters told this masthead that no one in her party room or outside the party had raised concerns with her about her leadership, after the Greens took a position contrary to the urging of former leaders Bob Brown and Christine Milne. Senator Larissa Waters, leader of the Australian Greens, at Parliament House in Canberra. Alex Ellinghausen “I have a really respectful relationship with my colleagues, and that feeling’s mutual,” Waters said.



“No one loved coming to a different position on this issue, but everyone understands that people who’ve thought about it deeply can disagree on the method of getting to the same place. “This was Labor putting us in an impossible position by backtracking on a commitment to establish a national park and then demanding carbon credits for it. So we took a difficult decision, and it wasn’t an easy one to take.” The Greens under Waters’ leadership voted with Labor to allow state governments to earn carbon credits from protecting forest, which the NSW government wants to use for the Great Koala National Park and can also be used by other states. The Greens were wedged because they hold concerns about the role of carbon credits in allowing pollution to continue, but want to protect forests. The Australia Institute co-chief executive Richard Denniss, who was opposed to the carbon credits, had described it as “the Greens’ first major climate test in the Senate under leader Larissa Waters”. Waters rejected that it was a leadership test. “TAI can have their views, that’s fine. I don’t think he’s correct in this one, but that’s, you know, I don’t speak for them – I speak for the Greens.”



Waters said that the party engaged in “lots of discussions and lots of hugs”, ensuring disagreement was respectful and party unity survived. Waters was seen hugging Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer immediately after the vote in the Senate. Bleyer, who was sworn in only days earlier as a replacement for Peter Whish-Wilson, was one of the three who crossed the floor along with fellow Tasmanian Nick McKim and Western Australia’s Jordon Steele-John. At a time when One Nation is monstering the major parties in the polls and byelections, the Greens’ vote is holding steady on 12 per cent in this masthead’s Resolve Political Monitor. Waters said it was an uneven playing field. “Billionaires are paying Pauline Hanson to spread her lies,” she said. “It is not the fault of your neighbour, who might happen to be a migrant, that people’s lives are getting tougher, and she’s been helped out by billionaires and big corporations giving her wads of dough to fly around the country and spam billboards and pay for social media ads. But then when she comes into parliament, she votes for billionaires and corporate interests.”



Waters said the party would put this week’s vote behind them, and that she was excited about the fight ahead to secure improvements to the Safeguard Mechanism, Labor’s flagship climate policy that is under statutory review, while trying to knock out 40 per cent of the carbon credit market. More on this debate Pragmatism v Purity: Once again, the environmental movement is cleaved in two, with giants such as Bob Brown and Tim Flannery on different sides. Carbon credits for protecting public forests: The Greens have defied intense lobbying and voted against a Nationals motion to kill off the scheme. Civil war inside environmental movement: The fate of the Great Koala National Park hangs in the balance as a new carbon accounting method divides conservationists.



Carbon credits give states off-ramp for logging: The NSW may now fulfil its election promise to create the Great Koala National Park. Get to the heart of climate change and the environment.

World.title: Proposed bail laws set to land in centre of ongoing High Court fight
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Proposed bail laws set to land in centre of ongoing High Court fight Matt Dennien September 11, 2026 — 3:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland barristers have urged the state government to pause its proposed bail crackdown until a High Court challenge against similar elements of Northern Territory laws is decided. The Queensland Bar Association’s submission is one of more than 250 lodged for committee consideration of the Crisafulli LNP’s controversial “breach bail, go to jail” laws introduced last month. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli and Attorney-General Deb Frecklington speak to media after their election win in late 2024. Matt Dennien Several key organisations have raised concerns about the bill, its justification, the consequences of increased pressure on youth detention, prisons and police watchhouses, and further delays to court processes. Aimed at making it harder for people charged with specific offences while on bail to be released into the community, a mandatory 12-month minimum jail sentence will also apply to those guilty of the new offence.



The government has been gradually revealing parts of the proposed laws since it was first raised by LNP candidate – and now MP – for the Townsville seat of Hinchinbrook, Wade Chiesa, in November’s byelection. Public sentiment of the government’s hardline crime response has soured across the past year, despite the LNP’s suggestions its election promises to fix a crime crisis are starting to work. ABS data has shown victim numbers, a metric to which Premier David Crisafulli has tied his leadership, were already falling across the election year – and fell further across 2025. Bar association president Cate Heyworth-Smith KC, writing in the group’s submission to the parliamentary committee considering the bill, raised a series of concerns about the removal of judicial discretion and rules against double jeopardy.



Heyworth-Smith also said that the laws would provide less incentive for people to plead guilty, which would lead to more trials and more delays across the entire court system, and overcrowding issues in the detention system which would be “difficult to correct once they have begun”. Related Article Queensland government Qld’s ‘strongest bail laws in the country’ could reverse onus of proof While the government has insisted the laws are about deterring and punishing serious repeat offenders, she also laid out a hypothetical situation where a P-plate driver given bail for drink-driving was then caught up in the new bail regime for being only a passenger in a stolen car. “The resulting punishment would be seriously disproportionate to the offending behaviour,” Heyworth-Smith wrote. “These provisions do not merely create a risk of unjust outcomes, they ensure that unjust outcomes will occur.”



The association president also raised the High Court challenge against Northern Territory bail laws she said would appear to “transpose directly” to the new tougher bail test, a legal argument for which “the answer is not obvious, and the committee should not be told otherwise”. “The Association submits that the question is a real one, as is demonstrated by the referral of the matter to the Full Court of the High Court of Australia, and that the constitutional validity of such provisions will be illuminated by the decision,” Heyworth-Smith wrote. “The Association submits that the Committee should not report on the Bill before the High Court has delivered judgment.” Other submissions from the Crime and Corruption Commission warn about the risk of increased police misconduct through the treatment of people in overcrowded facilities, which the agency would actively monitor, and human rights overrides appeared to be inconsistent with the law. The Australian Workers Union and Queensland Police Union raised fears the laws would increase pressure on already crowded youth detention centres. The Queensland Law Society and National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Young People also urged the bill be rejected.



The Voice for Victims group said while supporting the government’s objective of strengthening community safety, success for victims was “measured by whether reforms reduce repeat offending”. Several submitters called for a review of the laws after a set period of time, or urged the release of government modelling around impacts on jails and watchhouses. The Queensland Human Rights Commission, in its first major foray into parliamentary process under leader Debbie Platz, called for the removal of mandatory minimum sentences and the new bail test from the bill. “While all offending is serious, the data does not indicate this form of offending is so prevalent, or increasing at such a rate, that it warrants an emergency response that overrides human rights,” she said. World.title: Dolphin calf found dead near Perth’s iconic Blue Boat House
World.content:
NationalWAMarine life Dolphin calf found dead near Perth’s iconic Blue Boat House Indigo Lemay-Conway September 11, 2026 — 3:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A dolphin calf has washed up on the foreshore next to the Blue Boat House in Crawley, sparking an urgent warning on fishing line responsibility. The young animal was found on Tuesday morning with deep cuts to its snout and notches on its dorsal fin – something the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions said was consistent with dolphin entanglement incidents. The dolphin calf was found next to the Blue Boat House in Nedlands. Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions While it isn’t confirmed, the DBCA believes the calf is Bindi Bindi, a three-month-old dolphin that was spotted in the Swan Canning Riverpark in August. “During a survey yesterday, we observed Bindi Bindi, a young dolphin calf, entangled in fishing line. Unfortunately, this is another case of a young calf becoming entangled in fishing line within the Swan Canning Riverpark,” the department said in a post to its social media last month.



“The line appears tightly wrapped around the calf’s mouth, cuts across the base of the dorsal fin and is also believed to extend around the pectoral fins. Editor's pick Homelessness ‘Where else are they supposed to go?’ Two-day deadline to clear Perth homeless camp sparks fierce backlash “Bindi Bindi was observed swimming slowly, with mum Click nearby. “At three months of age, Bindi Bindi is currently the youngest calf in the Swan Canning Riverpark dolphin community, making this a particularly concerning situation for both mother and calf. Bindi Bindi was last seen on August 24, still with fishing line wrapped around its body.



“Unfortunately, the complexity of the entanglement has ruled out simpler boat-based intervention,” DBCA said. In an updated post on Friday, the River Guardians (an arm of the DBCA) said they believed the dolphins to be the same. “Photographs of Bindi Bindi were compared with post-mortem images. Bindi Bindi was last sighted on August 24 despite extensive efforts to locate her. Based on these comparisons, the calf is believed to be Bindi Bindi,” the post said. “Although the scars and other identifying features are a close match, decomposition has affected some of these markers, so a definitive identification can’t be confirmed just yet. “While no fishing line was found on or near the calf when it was retrieved, evidence of entanglement can be lost over time as a carcass decomposes.”



DBCA Marine and Riverpark rangers retrieved the calf on Tuesday and transported it to Ellam Street, where Dr Delphine Chabanne from Murdoch University examined the animal. Editor's pick WA Parliament Rough sleepers to be moved away from Perth arms expo under new police powers “The next Dolphin Watch scientific vessel survey may help provide more clarity. If Click is observed without her calf and all other known calves are accounted for, it would strengthen the likelihood that the deceased dolphin is Bindi Bindi.” The department urged people to properly dispose of their fishing line and tackle to keep dolphins safe in the future. “Discarded fishing line can have devastating impacts on wildlife. If you’re fishing and see a dolphin nearby, reel in your line. Always take unwanted fishing line and tackle with you and dispose of it responsibly,” they said.



“Keep your distance. All vessels, including boats, kayaks, jet skis and stand-up paddleboards, must stay at least 100m from dolphins. People and dogs must stay at least 50m away. “If a dolphin approaches you, remain still and move away slowly when it is safe to do so.” If an injured dolphin is spotted, contact the Wildcare Helpline.

World.title: ‘He’s a magician’: Former Netanyahu adviser says he can win again
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict ‘He’s a magician’: Former Netanyahu adviser says he can win again Matthew Knott September 11, 2026 — 3:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Benjamin Netanyahu has a strong chance of winning next month’s Israeli elections despite underwhelming poll numbers and major political challenges, according to a former top adviser to the Israeli prime minister. Melbourne-born Mark Regev, a former senior adviser to Netanyahu and Israeli ambassador to the United Kingdom, said Netanyahu has proven his doubters wrong many times before and could remain Israel’s leader after the nation votes on October 27. “In Hebrew, he is known as a magician. He’s always pulling a rabbit out of his hat with politics. He’s only there for a long time because he keeps winning elections,” Regev said in an interview in Canberra. Benjamin Netanyahu is up for re-election in October and struggling in the polls. AP Regev said Netanyahu’s political career was widely thought to be over when he lost power in 1999 after a single term in office, yet returned to the prime ministership a decade later. Netanyahu also swiftly returned after losing power in 2021, returning in 2022.



Some analysts predicted Netanyahu’s career was over after the October 7 attacks of 2023 – the worst security failure in Israeli history – but he served out a full term and gradually improved his standing in opinion surveys. Related Article World elections ‘He’s been humiliated’: Israel’s strongman faces re-election jitters “It would be a mistake for the opposition to underrate his political capabilities,” said Regev, who also served as a spokesman for Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. While Netanyahu presided over the failure of October 7, Regev said he would argue that Israel was in a more secure position today than it was before the attacks. “Hamas is largely defeated. Hezbollah in Lebanon is largely defeated. In Iran, the monster is still there, but it’s been defanged,” he said.



The United Kingdom, France and Canada this week announced a ban on commercial activity with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which are considered illegal under international law, a move underlining Israel’s growing international isolation under Netanyahu. Australia did not join the push, but Foreign Minister Penny Wong has indicated more sanctions on Israel are on the way. Mark Regev said he expected an international “honeymoon” period if Netanyahu wins the elections. AP Significantly, US President Donald Trump reportedly did not try to talk UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham out of the policy when they discussed it, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave only a muted reaction. Trump and Netanyahu’s once-close relationship has been strained by their inability to defeat the hardline regime in Iran and Netanyahu’s refusal to commit to Trump’s Gaza peace plan.



An explosive report this week in Israeli newspaper Haaretz claimed that Netanyahu was personally alerted by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a large-scale offensive against Israel a week before October 7, but did not act on the warning. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu’s rivals call him ‘unfit’ for office after report he was warned of October 7 attack Netanyahu has branded the report an “absolute lie” and vowed to sue the newspaper. The UAE’s foreign ministry issued a statement that did not deny the report, saying: “When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities.” Four of Netanyahu’s main rivals issued a statement labelling him “unfit for office” and declaring they would work together to end his government.



Since 2022, Netanyahu has governed with the support of far-right and ultra-orthodox parties, including two senior ministers sanctioned by Australia for inciting violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. He said Netanyahu would likely seek to form a broader coalition government, including politicians to the left and right of his conservative Likud party, if it is possible after polling day. “I would think it’s in his interest to have a wider coalition, also a wider, larger majority in the Knesset [the Israeli parliament], which makes a government less susceptible to pressure from small elements,” he said. Netanyahu, who has been indicted for alleged war crimes by the International Criminal Court over Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza, vowed to establish a “broad national government” in June in an apparent bid to win back mainstream centre and centre-right voters ahead of the election. Regev said there would be a difference in style if Netanyahu loses the election, but he did not expect fundamental changes to Israel’s handing of key issues such as the West Bank and Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.



“I think if a new government was elected it might get a certain glow in the international community [but] the idea that another government is going to come in and suddenly take Israel in a 180 degree different direction is just not logical,” he said. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel targets UK in response to sanctions on settlements in West Bank Most Israelis do not believe there was a “partner for peace” on the Palestinian side, leading to the collapse in support for a two-state solution, he said. Most polls show former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party leading Netanyahu’s Likud, but also find neither the pro nor anti-Netanyahu blocs winning enough seats to form government. Mark Sofer, a former Israeli ambassador to Australia, told this masthead recently: “At this juncture, I cannot envisage a situation in which Netanyahu wins the next elections



“On the other hand, I can envisage a scenario in which the opposition doesn’t reach the 61 seats necessary to set up a government.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.
