World.title: In Dallas, a feisty Vance cements his status as Trump’s likely successor
World.content:
The vice president is showing that he too can deal in the kind of ugly, personal mud-slinging that Trump’s loyal audiences have delighted in for years.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dallas: A Republican TV  played on the big screen at the party’s midterm convention cast the upcoming election in stark, simple terms. “This is no longer simply Republican versus Democrat, or conservative versus liberal,” the baritone voiceover boomed. “Today the choice is unmistakable: extreme versus mainstream.” That will be the crux of the GOP message for the next seven or so weeks: radical, America-hating communists have taken over the Democratic Party, and the only salvation is Donald Trump and his sensible Republicans. Attendees celebrate at the conclusion of the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas. Bloomberg Vice President JD Vance leant into that framing when he took centre stage on Thursday night (US time) in Dallas, with a speech that was largely dedicated to attacking Democrats and spent little time on Republican achievements or promises for the future. He did not mention Trump’s extraordinary offer the previous evening – which Trump repeated on Thursday – of giving every American adult a $US5000 ($7000) “Trump Dividend” if the Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November. Rather, Vance focused on portraying the Democrats as “the party of hatred”. Like many of the speakers over the preceding five hours, the vice president targeted specific people, such as Senate candidate for Michigan Abdul El-Sayed, and Senate candidate for Texas James Talarico, whom Trump has branded “Tala-freako”.



Talarico has been a strong advocate for transgender people, including student athletes, though he has recently moderated some of his positions. Vance accused Talarico of being “obsessed with trans children” and even went as far as to imply, baselessly, that Talarico was a paedophile. “I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history,” he said. In normal times, a vice president might be expected to get his hands a little dirty during an election campaign: throwing bombs on behalf of a president who would rather stay a bit above the fray. Vice President JD Vance made it personal as he attacked Democrats for being a party of “hard-core hatred”. Bloomberg Trump, obviously, does not mind insulting his opponents. Vance, by following suit, is showing that he too can deal in the kind of ugly, personal mud-slinging that Trump’s loyal audiences have delighted in for years. Indeed, Vance’s most successful moment came when he was heckled by a protester in the stands waving the Mexican and Palestinian flags. The man was booed by the crowd (a person sitting near this correspondent shouted: “F--- Palestine”) and quickly escorted out by security. But Vance pounced. “My friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there – I’ll buy you the plane ticket,” he said to roars of applause and a lengthy “USA” chant.



Vance chuckled and added that this was the symbol of the far-left: “An idiot waving a Mexican flag, when he should be waving the flag of the United States of America.” The room went wild again. The vice president was also visibly angry when he brought up a taunt El-Sayed made about his wife, Usha, on social media. The Democrat had queried whether Vance would have been willing to introduce Usha, who is of Indian heritage, to his late grandfather, a white steelworker from Appalachia. For Vance, it was beyond the pale. “This is who the Democrats are now, my friends,” he said. “They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it.” A protester holds a Mexican flag as Vice President JD Vance speaks at the convention. AP Photo/Julio Cortez Eyes were on the vice president at this convention because after the midterms, the political conversation will start to turn to Trump’s successor. Vance is the obvious and leading candidate to become the next Republican nominee for president, though he is not without his detractors. If this was a quasi-audition, Vance certainly passed. At one point, after a woman yelled out “JD 48” – Vance to become the 48th president – the crowd cheered and began chanting: “48! 48!” Vance settled them down. “We gotta take care of business this November, then we’ll worry about what comes next,” he said.



Two events loomed large over the afternoon. Thursday was the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, and the eve of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks, in which nearly 3000 people were killed by Islamic extremists. It set the backdrop for several speakers to rail against Islamism and left-wing political violence. Texas senator Ted Cruz had the crowd on its feet several times as he condemned what he portrayed as a “red-green alliance” of communists and Islamists taking over the Democratic Party. “They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate capitalism, they hate the Constitution and they hate America,” he said. Trump greeting the audience. At one point, he made them recite a pledge to “the greatest president in the history of the United States”. AP Photo/Julio Cortez Texas senator Ted Cruz had the crowd on its feet several times as he condemned what he portrayed as a “red-green alliance” of communists and Islamists taking over the Democratic Party. AP Photo/Julio Cortez At one point, Cruz named several progressive Democrats and their associates, including New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, far-left podcaster Hasan Piker, El-Sayed and Talarico. “When people tell you who they are, believe them,” Cruz said. “When [far-left podcaster] Hasan Piker says America deserved 9/11, believe him.”



As he said it, a man in the crowd appeared to shout out “he should be shot”. He repeated the interjection each time Cruz mentioned another Democrat. El-Sayed was a constant target throughout the evening. Mike Rogers, a former Republican congressman who is running against El-Sayed for the Senate seat, accused his opponent of excusing or rationalising terrorism. When Lebanese-American man Ayman Ghazali rammed his car into the Temple Israel synagogue in Detroit in the name of Hezbollah earlier this year, El-Sayed said, “hurt people hurt people”. Ghazali had lost family members in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the previous week. A flag in honour of assassinated Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, who was killed exactly one year ago. Bloomberg Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for US Senate from Michigan, was mentioned countless times. Bloomberg “They treat our country like it’s the villain,” Rogers told the Republican crowd in Dallas. “Terror is terror. Evil is evil ... You don’t sympathise with terrorists, you don’t sanitise extremism.” This was not just another Senate race, he added. “This election is about the soul of our country ... and it is about who you stand with when that American way of life is threatened.”

World.title: Hallelujah! This comic take on the creation of Handel’s Messiah hits just the right note
World.content:
The Greek Theatre, September 10, until September 19

The day before seeing Joyful Noise, I attended a funeral in an Anglican church for a dear friend who was an atheist, and the vicar handled the dichotomy with commendable wit and nuance. Georg Friedrich Händel, by contrast, was allowed precious little nuance by the Church of England when creating his Messiah, among the greatest artistic glorifications of their very own God. The bishops thought it blasphemous, and tried to have it banned.

US playwright Tim Slover’s 1998 play (now being adapted into a film starring Anthony Hopkins) creeps up on you as you adjust to a certain archness of tone mingling with comedy and high-stakes drama. And, at first, this Madeleine Stedman production (for Joining the Dots Theatre) struggled to hit exactly the right notes – not helped by nerves and variable projection. But then it settled, settled more, and steadily rose in confidence and quality, until one almost wanted to cry “Hallelujah!” – well before the story reached that bit.

The numerous intersecting plots of Joyful Noise are essentially historical. Iain Cox

The numerous intersecting plots are essentially historical, including soprano Susannah Cibber’s reputation being trashed by a case of adultery orchestrated by her abusive husband. Then there’s artistic bickering between Handel and his librettist, Charles Jennens, and between Cibber and rival soprano Kitty Clive; court wrangling between King George II and Bishop Egerton, and between the king and Handel; open warfare between Egerton and Handel. But the squabbles are all leavened with Slover’s fine line in humour.

Nicholas Papademetriou pitches his Handel perfectly, so the tetchiness and stubbornness are balanced by glimpses of warmth and wit, just as the jobbing composer’s pragmatism is balanced by intimations of a soaring creative spirit.

Madeleine Stedman’s direction includes many comic flourishes. Iain Cox

The ever-consistent Christopher Stollery brings presence and authority to King George, and effortlessly finds the truth in Slover’s sometimes heightened language. Angela Johnston is a riot as the cockney actor/singer Kitty, who enacts Desdemona’s death scene for Handel by way of audition, and who has the street cunning to manoeuvre her way to the top of a savagely competitive profession.

Matthew Abotomey stays just on the right side of overcooking Bishop Egerton’s manipulativeness, driven by a zeal to keep God locked in the cathedrals – far from the low places where operas and oratorios are performed. Mason Phoumirath’s Jennens is another zealot, determined that Messiah should be done his way rather than Handel’s, while also denying the House of Hanover as the realm’s legitimate royalty.

Laila Chesterman was initially too soft as the put-upon Susannah, but built her way into a performance that won our sympathy. Lloyd Allison-Smith (Handel’s secretary) and Alison Chambers (Handel’s biggest fan) also had their chances to shine in the smaller roles.

Stedman’s direction was replete with light comic flourishes, and it was just refreshing to see a play with no overt agenda. The fact that Christ was despised and rejected was what resonated with a worn-down Handel, and allowed him to converse with divinity.

World.title: He broke their heart, twice. But without Roger, the Warriors wouldn’t be here today
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 He broke their heart, twice. But without Roger, the Warriors wouldn’t be here today Dan Walsh September 11, 2026 — 3:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Roger broke my heart twice. He broke my heart when he went to rugby. And he broke my heart when he went and did his knee and couldn’t play for us again.” Warriors chief executive Cameron George could be singing a rugby league love song about Roger Tuivasa-Sheck – the magnetic, sexy-stepping, light-up-a-room, ever-so humble star who won’t play another game for the club after rupturing his ACL in late May. Roger Tuivasa-Sheck: a wonderful Warrior. NRL Imagery “Hands down, just one of the most special people I have ever met,” George adds. “The type of person you can only hope and pray comes along into your club.” The Warriors sold 26,000 tickets for Saturday’s final against the Dolphins in around 17 minutes. Win, and they’ll shift almost twice as many for a grand final qualifier at Eden Park in a fortnight. The smart money says they’ll do it in half the time.



Thirty-one years since they were born out of rugby league’s last great rush to expand and conquer, the Warriors are better placed than ever before to assume the true powerhouse status that has seemingly always been theirs for the taking, if only they could ever get their house in order long enough to do it. In their most recent rise, pivotal figures in the club’s history abound. From coach Andrew Webster and foundation halfback Stacey Jones to current owner Mark Robinson and retired attacking phenom Shaun Johnson. Warriors fans have good reason to be in full voice this year. Getty Tuivasa-Sheck looms as influential as any. “Because of what Roger did for this club and this team during the COVID-19, it won’t and can’t ever be forgotten,” George says.



“When we hit rock bottom in that period, his leadership, commitment and passion during that time was just phenomenal, and he kept the club together.” What the Warriors went through to ensure the NRL could resume on May 28, 2020, and stay afloat as a competition, has regularly and rightly been acknowledged in the years since. Tuivasa-Sheck boards the Warriors team bus in Newcastle and prepares to leave Australia, unsure when the NRL competition will resume, in 2020. NRL Imagery Players, coaches, staff and some, but by no means all, of their families relocated across the Tasman for the best part of three seasons – from May, 2020 to late-2022, when they played their first game on Kiwi soil in more than 1000 days. They lived out of suitcases, in isolation, and observed strict COVID protocols in half a dozen temporary accommodation set-ups across the Australian east coast.



Robinson, the insulation magnate who tipped millions of his own money into keeping the club afloat, and George both say another six months would have pushed the Warriors into withdrawing from the competition, which would have put the NRL in breach of its agreement to deliver broadcasters eight games per week and cost it $20 million. As Warriors captain in the 2020 and 2021 seasons, Tuivasa-Sheck was a rock for his homesick teammates as border confusion reigned, families struggled, losses stacked up and coach Stephen Kearney was sacked. George sums it up bluntly. “As a club, we lost so much of our identity as everything eventually wore us down.”



One poignant moment, from late August 2020, still stands out from a late-season win over the Bulldogs. Tuivasa-Sheck had spent almost four months away from his Auckland-based family at this point. A few days earlier, his youngest son had just started crawling, 2000 kilometres away. As he played the milestone video in the Accor Stadium dressing room, Tuivasa-Sheck offered a sad smile and admitted: “Oh man, I think about going home all the time … but I’m proud that I’m here. And my family is, too, sticking it out for the club.” ‘They stuck with us when we were struggling and in Australia. You’d like to think we’re paying them back.’ Roger Tuivasa-Sheck on the Warriors’ loyal fans Late in 2021, after a lengthy New Zealand border shutdown and almost two full seasons separated from his family, Tuivasa-Sheck did, eventually, go home. He gave up around $250,000 to move to rugby and pursue an All Blacks Test debut, breaking George’s heart in the process.



But when Tuivasa-Sheck’s return to the club in 2024 was sealed with “a handshake and a cuddle”, the Warriors were unrecognisable. “The club is just so different,” he says. “The biggest difference is Andrew Webster obviously, as coach. And the system he’s set up with Andrew McFadden [the club’s recruitment and pathways manager], it’s built for the long haul. That’s the best thing. Tuivasa-Sheck laps up the Warriors fanfare. Getty Images “All these young forwards you’re seeing like Leka [Halasima], Jacob Laban and Demetric [Vaimauga], they’re learning what it takes to play NRL from the ages of 14 and 16. I don’t think the Warriors have ever really had that before.” Those miserable COVID-19 years have given Tuivasa-Sheck, George and the Warriors a healthy perspective on what matters most now the sun is shining on them.



“I’ve had my time of sitting there and being disappointed by my knee injury, but that time is long gone,” says Tuivasa-Sheck, now 33 and off to Super League outfit Wakefield next year. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Immortal inspection: Attacking geniuses and game plans to win week one finals Andrew Johns League columnist “No one likes to look back at COVID, do they? But when you ask about those tough periods for the club and players, what I’m proudest of is how the fans are with us and enjoying these times now. “They deserve this success that’s coming, and I can confidently say there will be a lot of success in the future because of what the club is building. They stuck with us when we were struggling and in Australia. You’d like to think we’re paying them back.” Ask Tuivasa-Sheck who remains from his first Warriors stint, and he can only name a few players – hooker Wayde Egan, injured winger Dallin Watene-Zelezniak, centre Adam Pompey and playmaker Chanel Harris-Tavita. Robinson, George, Jones and McFadden are the most prominent among the staff and club bosses.



Such is the nature of modern professional sport. And when the Warriors were carrying a significantly heavier COVID-19 load than any other club, at times losing multiple homesick players per week, it’s hardly any surprise. “It’s crazy when you think about it that way – a whole NRL squad has been turned over in a couple of years, but the fan base has grown bigger than it’s ever been,” Tuivasa-Sheck says. The Warriors have invested significantly and soundly in what they offer fans on game day, and the club’s steady rise under Webster has helped sell out 41 of their 46 home fixtures since late 2022. “Absence makes the heart grow fonder,” George says.



If all was truly fair in love and rugby league, then Tuivasa-Sheck would be playing against the Dolphins on Saturday afternoon, not sidelined by a wretched ACL tear. But if the Warriors do go all the way, their talismanic former captain might break his boss’s heart for a third time – in the best, most deserving way.

World.title: Outdoors schemes funded to help fight youth crime
World.content:
Outdoors programmes combatting youth crime Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Is sport the answer to cutting youth crime and re-offending by tamariki?

This week, the government announced it's giving almost $2.5 million to six community sport and outdoor programmes as part of the government's wider goal to reduce serious and persistent youth offending by 15 percent by 2030.

Whenua Iti Outdoors in Tasman is getting $450,000 of funding over two years

Mark Bruce-Miller told Checkpoint on Friday it will make an "enormous difference".

"Sport and active recreation allows young people the opportunity to connect in social settings, to get out and connect to the natural world and develop skills that are quite hard to develop in and around classroom settings."

He said it was possible schemes like this keep youth out of trouble.

"We all know that when we feel more connected and we feel more confident and we feel safer and more confident, we're less likely to perhaps go down some of the negative pathways that some people choose."

Whenua Iti Outdoors' funding will go towards a new project in Buller's Kawatiri region for 10- to 14-year-olds, Bruce-Miller said.

"At that young age, they're unlikely themselves to be getting into too much trouble. But there may be some risk factors within their lives, within the community that are identified by teachers or on social services or whanau that would allow them to enter into the program and come alongside positive role models active in the outdoors across two years."

He said they would get to try mountain biking, kayaking, paddle-boarding, campfire cooking and "having face-to-face experiences with their peers in team outdoor settings".

Minister for Sport and Recreation Mark Mitchell said the funding was part of the Government's plan to reduce youth offending.

"It is about backing community led solutions and giving young people positive pathways which help prevent them from entering or re-entering the youth justice system."

It was not clear yet if Whenua Iti's programme would take place during or outside of school time.

"We're fortunate enough to work with many - 5000 - young people every year across Aotearoa, and often young people who aren't excelling in more conventional education environments.

"To be able to show them that they can succeed, that they can be confident, that they can be great team players, it's just a normal experience. It's why we do what we do."

World.title: Orthopaedic Surgeon hopes $300m HNZ funding will ease growing waitlists
World.content:
Huge waitlists for orthopaedic surgery Nine To Noon Download MP3 10m

A North Shore orthopaedic surgeon says funding to reduce surgery wait lists has not been "as smooth running" as they had hoped.

Orthopaedic Association President-elect Edward Yee told Nine to Noon that Health New Zealand last month announced funding of $300 million over six years with private hospitals to try reduce wait lists.

"We've been trying to work with Health New Zealand to make this a lot more transparent... we believe it's a good initiative and hopefully it will make a big difference for our communities."

He said there was some variability across the country, with some centres doing better than others and that has further added to the complexity of rolling out the funding.

"It hasn't been smooth running I guess partly because not every centre has the same capabilities."

He said to his knowledge contracts had gone out to private hospitals who had tended the costs for effective operations but was not too sure it was all hospitals.

"I don't know how close the finances are, but not all hospitals, I understand, have been able to secure a tender from the government."

With an ageing population and medical advancements that allow for more operations, increased wait times have been a growing concern for the orthopaedic department.

Yee said on the North Shore, they had around 2300 people currently on the waitlist with a catchment of half a million people.

He said they worked primarily on insourcing for surgery but with the recent spike in illnesses they are looking to outsource.

"With the late surge and respiratory illnesses and flus, a lot of those beds have been taken up with ill people, so it has curtailed our usual elective output.

"We are hoping that we will get some outsourcing done."

He said the source of waitlists being so long across the whole country came down to generations of poor investments by several governments.

"Everything from staff, infrastructure and even IT. I mean, without the complete team, you can't really run an effective hospital."

Delays in ACC have recently been flagged as an added strain onto the system.

Yee said the wait time for ACC approvals or disapprovals has been getting longer.

"I have noticed recently there has been longer delays in getting this through, and some of them were pretty obvious injuries as well."

In June of this year Dr Alex Malone, chair of the Orthopaedic Association (NZOA)'s ACC liaison committee, also raised the issue of growing wait times for ACC approvals.

Malone had said numbers provided at the time to the NZOA by ACC showed the average time taken to approve surgery had gone up from 10 days in 2025 to 18 days this April - an 80 percent increase.

"It's frustrating for the patients who have further delays to their treatment and rehabilitation, longer time off work," Malone said.

ACC's Phil Riley, head of service operations, confirmed the data it had recently provided to the Orthopaedic Association showed there had been some recent periods of higher demand that led to a decline in timeliness of decision-making, but that this was improving.

Andy Windsor, Health NZ's national director of procurement and supply chain, said Health NZ had five health targets to support the delivery of better health outcomes.

One was shorter wait times for treatment with 95 percent of patients waiting less than four months for elective treatment and outsourcing treatment to private hospitals was helping achieve that.

"Health NZ has run a secondary procurement process to establish longer-term contracts with private surgical providers to undertake planned procedures and support the delivery of equitable, timely, safe and high-quality surgical care."

Three providers had contracts for the delivery of orthopaedic surgical services, he said.

The contracts began on July 1, 2026 and would run until June 30, 2029, with a single three-year right of renewal through to June 30, 2032.

They covered orthopaedic procedures, including total hip replacements, total knee replacements and partial knee replacements.

The total maximum whole-of-life value of the three contracts was $298.4 million over six years, with a total annualised volume of 3222 procedures. Information relating to individual provider contract values and volumes was commercially sensitive, he said.

World.title: Ellerslie homicide: Gear for camping or murder? Defence probes Poon's purchases
World.content:
The lawyer for a man accused of double murder has pointed blame at the other man there on the night of the killings.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li is on trial in the High Court at Auckland. He is accused of murdering Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife Mei Han Chong in 2023, which he denies.

He has also denied plotting to kill his former landlord with a man he met in church, Shu Man Poon.

Poon has been giving evidence in Li's trial and has faced questions on Friday morning from Li's lawyer, Paul Dacre KC.

The defence lawyer turned the narrative around on Poon, claiming it was he who murdered the couple in their Ellerslie home.

Poon last year pleaded guilty to his role in the killings, but earlier in his evidence said it was Li alone who shot the Kwoks with an air-pistol and stomped on them as they lay on the floor.

He told jurors that Li then struck Kwok with a sharpened tomahawk, before he did the same.

"Do you think Mr Li was responsible for you killing Mr and Mrs Kwok?" Dacre asked.

"Yes," Poon replied, with the help of an interpreter.

"I'm going to suggest that you are responsible for your actions, do you agree?" said Dacre.

Poon did.

"And that you, and you alone are to blame for your actions, do you accept that?" Dacre asked.

"Not accept," Poon said.

Dacre asked about military-style boots Li had bought for Poon.

Poon said when they left the Kwoks' house, his boots were covered in blood.

"Was the cause of the blood on your boots because you had been stomping on Mrs Kwok?" Dacre said.

"No," Poon replied.

The court delved into Poon's background, coming to New Zealand as a 13-year-old, his training to be a nurse, and his work as an Armourguard security guard.

He said he had suffered from mental health issues since the death of his father, and was being medicated.

Poon was asked about his martial arts background, something the court had earlier heard both men were passionate about.

He said he had been appointed as a junior martial arts coach, practising Pak-Mei.

"Are you skilled at martial arts?" Dacre asked.

"No," Poon said.

"Did you give the impression to other people including the [church leaders] that you were a master in martial arts?" Dacre asked.

"I let them know who I really was."

Dacre asked who that was.

"Now I'm just only a most shameful senior, that's all," Poon said.

Dacre asked about a number of purchases Li had made for Poon.

Poon had racked up a $7000 debt to Li through online shopping, while he was receiving ACC payments for an ankle injury.

Li had loaned Poon money to buy the tomahawk that would later be used in the Kwok killings because he wanted to go camping, Poon said.

"Are you suggesting, Mr Poon, that that is a camping tomahawk?" Dacre asked.

"For chopping wood and breaking for the fire," Poon replied.

They also bought two pairs of night-vision goggles, also for camping Poon said, as well as a glass-cutter and coffee frother.

"Do you think in all these circumstances that you were taking advantage of Mr Li, to buy these items knowing that you couldn't pay him back?" Dacre asked.

"At that time under ACC, I haven't got more than enough money to pay him back, but once I get back to work I already told him that I would pay him back weekly," Poon said.

Poon had bought an air-pistol through a buy now, pay later scheme, as well as an air-rifle, machete and BB gun, he told the court.

He was asked by Dacre why he would buy the weapons.

"I love shooting while I was young, but I knew that I would never be allowed to shoot on any living beings, that's why I purchased, like, an aluminium box that can sit the target board on it for target shooting," Poon said.

Dacre asked about Poon's relationship with Li after the pair met at the Amazing Grace Christian Church.

Poon considered himself Li's 'big brother', something heard throughout his evidence.

"Were you sort of suggesting that you were acting as a sort of moral compass for Mr Li?" Dacre asked.

"I would not say it's a moral leader, but like an adviser."

Poon said he was setting a moral example for Li.

Dacre took Poon through the events of his arrest in Hamilton, and asked why he spoke to police following his guilty pleas.

"I'm willing to speak the truth," he said.

Dacre asked if he saw any advantage in speaking to police. Poon said it wasn't on his mind.

It was then Dacre threw another accusation at Poon - that the reason he was giving evidence was to assist his chances for a reduced sentence in the Court of Appeal. Poon said he never thought that far ahead.

"Are you suggesting to this court today that you've never thought about the issue that giving evidence may assist your appeal," Dacre asked.

"No," Poon said.

Poon said that moment was the first time he had connected the two actions.

The defence asked questions about the plot to murder Li's former landlord.

Poon denied ever agreeing to kill Li's landlord or taking steps to do so, saying he never intended to cause her any harm. He said he was there in his capacity as Li's 'big brother' and to try to stop him going through with the plan.

Dacre asked why Poon didn't stop Li when they went to his former landlord's property. with a plan to murder her.

"You know the difference between right and wrong, you know the difference between legal and illegal," he said, with Poon agreeing.

"Why won't you take responsibility for going around to that address?"

Poon had a number of times said he did not remember details about the plot.

"If somebody talks or makes a suggestion to anybody in this courtroom that they should join in a kidnapping and torturing of somebody, people would remember whether they agreed or didn't agree to that proposition," Dacre said.

Poon said he did not remember.

Dacre asked Poon about his interview with police following his arrest.

Poon at the time had told police he wasn't confident where Mei Han Chong's body was, as it too dark to see and he couldn't remember.

Jurors heard on Thursday the pair had put Chong's body in the back of the Kwok's blue Kia, and driven it to Kereru Grove in Greenhithe to dispose of it.

"Did you know, on the morning of the 10th of November 2023, the name of the road where Mrs Kwok's body was dumped," Dacre asked.

Poon said yes.

"You knew where the body was, you knew that the police wanted to find the body, (...) you knew that Mr Kwok wanted to find his mother, and you told the police that you didn't know where the body was, is that correct?" Dacre said.

"Yes," Poon said.

"So, you lied to the police?" Dacre asked.

Poon again replied yes.

But later in the day, Dacre conceded Poon had circled part of a map given to him by police later in the interview, showing where the body was dumped.

He had also told police it was Kereru 'reserve', Dacre said.

"You knew the name Kereru from the beginning, and it was four hours later that you told them," he said.

"At that time from the arrest to the interview, my mind, my emotion was under a very, very high stress and afraid, and scared," Poon said.

"From that time, I was trying to bring back myself back in one piece."

Poon had also told police the last place he had seen the Kwok's car.

Dacre asked a similar line of questions about the stolen licence plates, used to mask the identity of Poon's car.

He asked who's idea it was to steal the plates, Poon said it was Li's.

Dacre turned to the statement Poon gave police after his guilty pleas, where he had told officers it was his idea.

"Your answer, 'mine', in brackets 'my idea,'" Dacre said.

He asked if Poon said that and if it was true.

"That was incorrect," Poon said, adding it was a mistake.

Dacre took Poon through more evidence, including a list of body disposal sites.

It read - Head Mission Bay, Body Greehithe and opposite to coronation Rd, Leg Takapuna Lake Pupuke, Organs Birkenhead Wharf.

"Is that the document that you typed up?" Dacre asked.

Poon replied that he did not remember.

He then drew Poon's attention to messages he had sent about an injury to Li's ankle.

Poon said Li had injured it stomping on the Kwok's, but messages between the two indicated Li had injured it slipping on a path.

Poon had already told the court that story was cover for the night of the killings.

"This whole section is just an excuse for giving him a chance to apply for ACC for extra money," Poon said.

"Are you seriously suggesting to the court that after the murder of Mr and Mrs Kwok, you and Mr Li were involved in a conversation that might lead to a false ACC claim?" Dacre asked

Poon said that was correct.

Dacre put forward that Li's account of the injury was the true one, and that Poon was lying.

"What I'm suggesting to you, if you tell the truth that that conversation is an honest conversation between the two of you, that makes a lot of what you've said to this court a lie," Dacre said.

World.title: NRL: Warriors scalpers' demands for $500 a ticket slammed as a 'kick in the teeth'
World.content:
Wahs fans rucked off as scalpers profit

Fans furious as tickets being re-sold for hundreds more Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

It's gutting, gross, a kick in the teeth and against the culture of the Wahs.

That's what fans are saying about tickets for Saturday's qualifying clash against the Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium, which sold out in minutes.

Not long afterwards, ticket listings began appearing on Trade Me and other online marketplaces, with some sellers asking hundreds of dollars more than what they paid.

One listing offered four tickets in the Eastern Stand for a buy-now price of $1200, describing them as "arguably the best seats in the house."

Another seller was asking $500 for two tickets in the uncovered South Stand - seats which cost $25 for an adult during the regular season and $45 during the play-offs.

Super-fan Woody Materoa said it was gutting. He jumped online for tickets but didn't make it on to the site in time.

"We're quite big fans of the Warriors and to sort of see people getting tickets that are not even going to attend the game is pretty crap."

They were planning to fly up from Blenheim to watch the game.

"There's always going to be somewhere that's going to take advantage of that sort of stuff but yes you know, they're trying to make money, whereas we just want to watch the game."

Materoa said something should be done to stop this from happening again.

"It's supposed to be a game that's enjoyed by all Kiwis, you know, especially called 'New Zealand Warriors'. So I think they do need to take action," fellow fan Paul Natac said.

He's been a Wahs fan since 1995, when he was just 13 years old.

"They really made it accessible for people who are vulnerable, you know, where a little bit of joy of watching rugby league helps them. The Warriors have done a really good job at $10 tickets sometimes over the season, and then all of a sudden originally $44 tickets are being sold over a hundred bucks, 200, 300 even. Some of them are $500 per ticket."

Natac missed out on securing tickets in both the pre-sale and general release and had considered buying marked-up tickets.

"I can afford it, so shall I just buy it? And at the end of the day I just kind of calmed down and went, at the end of the day, I'll just be promoting this behaviour for the next game."

Sports commentator Sam Ackerman said scalping wasn't in the spirit of the Wahs culture.

"The members who appear to be doing it, that's a kick in the teeth because they are part of that experience and they know exactly what that investment emotionally means."

He said it's hard to digest.

"People have bought more than they want for the purpose of on-selling, not just on-selling for a bit, on-selling for ridiculous profits as well. And it means that there's been conversations of having to tell kids who idolise these players, who go along to all the games, being part of that journey, that they can't go."

He also believed something needed to change.

"This is a club and a sport that has been embraced by all socioeconomic communities. This is a sport, a competition, a team for the people. And some people have decided to take that out of their hands."

Consumer spokesperson Jessica Walker. Supplied / Consumer NZ

Consumer spokesperson Jessica Walker said there's no law that prevents people from purchasing tickets and reselling them at a higher price.

"Which is obviously really disappointing for people who are looking for tickets to any major event and find that they can't because they have been snapped up by people looking to make a profit on them."

The one exception to the rule was events covered by the Major Events Management Act 2007, which applied to major events that were deemed to provide a substantial benefit to the country.

The Warriors game did not qualify.

"We really urge people to be aware that if you are buying a resold ticket, you need to look out for terms and conditions from the official seller that if they know a ticket has been resold, then they don't have to honour it.

"Another thing to be aware of is if you buy a resold ticket and then the event is cancelled. The official ticket agent is likely to refund the original purchaser. So then it would be on you as the person that bought the resold tickets to chase the person who originally purchased the ticket to get a refund."

She said while best practice was to stick to official ticket sellers or to buy off people you know, if you're going to buy a resold ticket - at least use your card.

"Because if things go wrong, you can approach your bank to try and ask for something called a charge back."

Walker said it's something Consumer thought the Government needed to clamp down on.

"It is not fair that people are priced out of being able to go and see things that they want to see, but a sporting event, a gig, a concert, festival, it should be equitable and we need to have better protection. So they were not at the mercy of people who do buy them all up and then inflate the cost significantly."

World.title: 'I need to get back to Barbara': Willie Jackson challenged on Labour's capital gains tax policy
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins says senior MP Willie Jackson should have been clearer when answering questions on the party's capital gains tax (CGT) policy.

Appearing on the Ryan Bridge TODAY panel alongside National's Paul Goldsmith on Friday morning, Jackson said National was lying about Labour's capital gains tax, while National says Jackson has only created more confusion.

Both National and Labour are claiming victory after the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) partially upheld a complaint against a National Party attack ad, and told the party not to use it again in its current form.

On Wednesday, the ASA said National's allegation that KiwiSaver would be "hit" by Labour's CGT would "mislead or confuse consumers" and was a breach of the principle of truthful representation.

Labour has maintained KiwiSaver is exempt from its CGT proposal, which is designed to cover commercial property and residential investment property only.

Some small businesses would be affected by the tax if they sold, but Labour's argument is that the majority of small businesses lease their buildings, so would not be subject to the tax.

Furthermore, small businesses wanting to sell their premises and move into a larger property would be exempt.

National intended to appeal the ASA decision, saying because some KiwiSaver funds invest in commercial property they would be affected by the CGT if those commercial properties were sold.

It also pointed to the ASA's decision not to uphold a complaint against National's claim that small businesses would be affected.

Labour, meanwhile, has said the ASA ruling meant National had been "caught out" and was running a "campaign of lies".

On Friday morning, Goldsmith said Labour would need to "get the shredder out" while Jackson said National were "liars," not only for their CGT comments but the "nine new taxes" accusations as well.

"They're putting billboards up. They're talking about nine taxes - it's one tax. It's called capital gains. Alright? It's very clear. Stop the lies," Jackson said.

But when it came to questions on the specifics of the capital gains tax, Jackson deferred to Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds.

Jackson was asked if the CGT would apply if a business which owned their premises sold that property, and if KiwiSaver funds invested in companies with properties would also be affected if those properties were sold.

Barbara Edmonds. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"I need to get back to Barbara on this," he said. "I don't think so. I need to do a check with Barbara.

"I'm not the finance spokesman, for goodness sake. We've got one tax, it's called capital gains tax. That's it."

He was again pushed for an answer on whether KiwiSaver funds invested in a company would be affected by the CGT if that company sold its property.

"I'll give you the answer: no," Jackson replied.

Goldsmith said Jackson was "totally wrong", to which Jackson said "let's find out from Barbara Edmonds".

'Chaotic and confused'

National campaign chair Simeon Brown said Jackson had created more confusion about Labour's policy.

Simeon Brown. RNZ / Nick Monro

"If Labour is this chaotic and confused just talking about its capital gains tax, imagine what the implementation would be like," he said.

"National has been pointing out for months that Labour's capital gains tax will affect many businesses when they sell their property, and a recent Advertising Standards Authority ruling supports this."

Speaking to the Bay of Plenty Times in Tauranga on Friday, Hipkins said he had spoken to Jackson and conveyed to him that he "should have just been upfront and clear" about what the policy was.

"I think he was being combative, which Willie can sometimes be. But in doing that, he should have been clearer that our policy is actually very simple.

"If a business owns a property that is sold, and they sell the property as part of a sale of a business, only the sale of the property is where capital gains tax applies. It does not apply to the sale of businesses per se. But it may apply to a commercial premises that's owned by a business."

World.title: Dunedin councillor Benedict Ong trespassed from the University of Otago
World.content:
Controversial Dunedin councillor Benedict Ong has been trespassed from the University of Otago grounds and premises following student complaints about inappropriate and unwanted behaviour.

The Otago University Students' Association confirmed plans to trespass Ong from its premises on 2 September and urged the university to ban him from the campus.

Ong claimed that student concerns were false and malicious attacks in a social media post that included a photo of him on campus with tape over his mouth.

The university confirmed Ong has been served a notice of trespass on 11 September after it considered complaints from students and has discussions with them.

Ong was no stranger to controversy, after being asked to resign by his colleagues for breaching the council's code of conduct in March and a suspension from all committees and subcommittees for nine months following another conduct complaint in May.

On 10 September Ong shared text messages he said were from university proctor Dave Scott, with the first saying Scott had been tasked with serving Ong documents on behalf of the university and the association.

According to the shared messages, Scott wanted to hand the documents to Ong discreetly and asked where they could meet before the councillor requested a public statement, saying he believed it was a "wrongful ban".

The third message said Scott preferred not to present the documents at his workplace or ask police to serve them.

In the post, Ong asked them to be served outside the Dunedin Public Art Gallery before an extraordinary council meeting on 11 September.

Speaking to media outside the gallery, he confirmed he had not been served yet, but expected to be.

He refused to take responsibility, saying his actions did not provoke the trespass and claimed complaints about his behaviour at a campus protest were politically motivated.

He called for video footage from the protest to be released - which the university said, in a letter Ong posted on social media, validated reports that two students asked him to move and appeared uncomfortable when he refused to do so.

On 3 September, the university invited Ong to respond to the proposed trespass notice and gave him until 3pm 7 September to respond, in the letter.

In response, Ong said he believed a deadline was inappropriate because he was elected by the Dunedin community "which has generationally subsidised our oldest University".

In the letter, university registrar Dr David Clark told Ong the association had reported two incidents at a campus protest alleging that his physical proximity or contact was unwanted and he had refused to move when asked by two students.

Clark also noted that Ong had taken photos at student flat parties and posted on social media about being near the St David Street building at 3am and at Ubar late at night.

"Your behaviour towards students on campus within these contexts has led to them reporting that they feel uncomfortable and unsafe," he said.

The association said the complaints had come from a variety of students this year and there were concerns he was interacting with students who were vulnerable because they had been drinking, Clark said.

Possible options raised included a trespass notice covering all university grounds and premises or limiting access to specific premises, dates, times or purposes.

Ong has continued to claim the allegations were false, his visits to Ubar were well documented on his social media accounts and "student supporters" had asked to take photos with him.

The university confirmed it did not intend to make any further statements to help protect the privacy of students.

World.title: ACT and NZ First pitch tighter immigration controls, others warn against anti-immigration policies
World.content:
With ACT and New Zealand First pitching tighter controls on immigration, National, Labour and the Greens are warning against populist anti-immigration policies.

Party leaders and spokespeople were giving speeches at the annual Immigration Conference in Auckland on Friday.

New Zealand First's Winston Peters launched more than a dozen proposals - almost all of which would curb or restrict migration.

Labour's Phil Twyford also came prepared, proposing a mix of policies including a citizenship pathway for children born to undocumented parents, a longer permanent residency process, and a review of the financial criteria for parent visas.

However, he spent much of his speech decrying a "dumpster fire" of right-wing populists demonising migrants and refugees.

National's Erica Stanford, who is the current minister, said she did not support ACT's proposal to abolish permanent resident visas.

While some permanent residents could apply for citizenship, it would force those whose country of origin did not allow dual-passport holders to make a "heartbreaking" choice.

"Our permanent resident visa provides certainty and stability for people who have demonstrated a commitment to New Zealand. It also provides that competitive advantage ... to attract skilled workers," she said.

She also criticised the New Zealand First and Green amnesty for Pacific overstayer policies, saying such approaches "do not work".

"What they do fuel is the next generation of overstayers who think if they wait long enough they will have a pathway to residence or a valid visa."

Stanford told reporters National and NZ First were "very aligned" on immigration but parties proposing to seriously restrict immigration needed to explain who would be turned away, with nearly half of primary applications based on partnership visas and nearly as many on filling skills shortages.

"It is a real juxtaposition to say 'we want the best people', but then 'we're also going to restrict the numbers' ... they're proposing saying 'well if you're here illegally we'll give you some kind of amnesty', those two things are the polar opposite: 'if you're doing the wrong thing, welcome, but if you are people we just really need, well we're going to restrict your right to residence'."

She would not express concern, however, saying many parties "announce a range of policies that never actually make it through coalition negotiations. So it would be wrong of me to say I'm concerned about anything because we have to wait and see".

Greens spokesperson Ricardo Menendez March also criticised parties that would conflate New Zealand's challenges with immigration.

"In our country we face a huge amount of challenges: we have an infrastructure deficit, an ageing population, we have low wages compared to other comparable nations, we have a tax system that overtaxes work while it doesn't really want to touch wealth.

"None of these issues were caused by migrant workers, and none of these issues will be addressed by throwing dog whistles on getting tough on immigration, or extending the time that it takes for someone to become a permanent residency."

Governments trying to change residency requirements to meet labour demand, he said, ignored the reality that it was people who affected and who had often already put down roots.

The Greens' "settled residency pathway" policy would provide a pathway to residency for those who had been living in New Zealand for five years.

The party would also end 12-month stand-down periods requiring workers to leave the country between visas, and allow migrant workers to change jobs.

March defended the Greens' amnesty proposal, saying migrants often had no ties to the countries they were being deported to.

"[New Zealand has] around 20,000 or so overstayers in this country, and a regularisation programme won't add significant infrastructure pressures considering the people are already here, many of them are already working, many of them are already paying tax."

Parmjeet Parmar for the ACT Party talked up removing any ballot system for the parent resident visas and instead having a queue, and clarified that removing the permanent residence category would not stop migrants from settling in New Zealand.

"People will be able to stay here indefinitely, but there is going to be a physical presence test ... people will have to show that they have been here in New Zealand for 730 days, which is two years, in [any given period of] five years."

She said the policy was very similar to Australia and Canada's approach, warning that the immigration system was being "abused".

"I have heard many, many cases where people have gained permanent residency, but then have left New Zealand and haven't come back for very, very long time. I've also heard cases where people are coming back when they need our free or subsidised education system, or they need healthcare here to New Zealand.

ACT has also been pushing for stronger deportation laws, and Parmar highlighted the party's plan to establish a dedicated overstayer enforcement unit inside Immigration NZ.

"If somebody works illegally the lawful migrant who paid the fee and met the requirements is being undercut. If an employer exploits workers every responsible employer is forced to compete against someone who has decided the rules do not matter.

World.title: New Zealand First unveils plans for dramatic overhaul of immigration system
World.content:
New Zealand First is wanting to make sweeping changes to the country's immigration laws.

The party unveiled over a dozen new policies on Friday ahead of November's general election.

NZ First policies

Restrict birthright citizenship, so only the children of citizens are automatically entitled to New Zealand citizenship at birth

Double qualifying periods for attaining citizenship or permanent residence, from five to 10 years

Increase application fees for citizenship and permanent residence "to reflect its value and to better fund the wider immigration system"

Prevent asylum seekers who have applied for a work visa while in New Zealand from being eligible

Prevent asylum seekers from using temporary work rights while their claim is being assessed

Make all visa holders ineligible from claiming jobseeker, accommodation supplement, or any other benefits during their first 10 years

Deport overstayers who have been in New Zealand illegally, and prevent them from ever being able to apply for another New Zealand visa

Give Pacific Island overstayers two years to apply to remain in New Zealand legally on a valid visa

Student Visa holders would not have automatic work rights after completion of their studies, and would be required to leave the country before being able to apply for another visa

Citizens would be prioritised for social housing

A 30-year population plan to coordinate immigration, housing and infrastructure planning

Hold a referendum on capping resident visas at 20,000 a year

The proposed resident visa cap would require infrastructure to exist or be fully funded and scheduled for delivery before major population growth could occur.

Councils would also have more freedom in planning, a move that would appear to override some of the settings in the reforms to the Resource Management Act progressed by the coalition this term.

Speaking at the annual Immigration Conference in Auckland on Friday, NZ First leader Winston Peters said population growth should not outpace an ability to build the country.

"New Zealand First will substantially reduce non-essential immigration and restore the principle that immigration is a privilege, not a right," he said.

"New Zealand is more than an economy. It is a nation with its own history, institutions and way of life. Immigration policy should strengthen social cohesion and encourage integration into a shared national community."

He rallied against what he said was "unfettered immigration being used as a crutch for the economy and the failing workforce that's planning for our people that's going on".

He said when NZ First was in government with Labour immigration had been cut back.

"In the same way, it is happening in the UK, Europe, USA and more recently in Australia ... in 2021, when we were no longer part of the government, the Labour government's feet became totally off the brakes."

He said National and ACT had said "nothing about it at all" until "just seven weeks out from the next election".

National and ACT in 2023 both campaigned on streamlining the immigration system to target high-skilled workers.

Peters said it would be "imperative" for NZ First to hold the Immigration portfolio "to ensure the oversight, control and reform of the immigration system".

"We need immigration to New Zealand. We always have. It has been an essential part of our history, and the first people that came to this country, namely the Māori, were immigrants themselves - otherwise where is this famous place called Hawaiki that we came from?

"This should be smart, controlled immigration policy, bringing in immigrants who we need, not who need us.

"Other politicians perversely say diversity is strength, to shut you down, but it is not. Unity is strength, not diversity."

The immigration spokespeople for National, Labour and the Greens all criticised calls to restrict immigration.

National's Erica Stanford said parties doing so needed to explain who would be turned away - with nearly half of primary applications based on partnership visas, and nearly as many again on filling skills shortages.

Labour's Phil Twyford said New Zealand could not follow Europe and the United States "down a path of division and scapegoating" and needed to maintain sensible, pro-immigration policies while holding onto public confidence.

World.title: 49ers ransack 'Rams House' in epic Melbourne NFL show
World.content:
The Melbourne Cricket Ground is bathed in sunshine on a September's day as thousands of fans stream in from all corners.

Fans of one team in red jerseys and the other in blue and gold take your mind back to the Sydney-West Coast AFL grand finals from two decades ago.

Atmospheres such as this is usually only reserved for the likes of the AFL grand final or the Boxing Day Test, but it is very quickly apparent that this is bigger than both.

It is a Friday morning, and despite it being a sunny September day, the AFL is nowhere to be seen because the National Football League is in town.

49ers cap Aussie week with win The San Francisco 49ers have claimed a commanding win at the MCG, beating the LA Rams 27-7 in the NFL's historic first match in Australia.

If NFL commissioner Roger Goodell had any fears about how the league would be able to fill a 100,000-seat stadium on a Friday morning, scenes from hours before the game would have had him resting easy.

Hours before the game begins, the fact that it was early in the morning did not stop hundreds of fans from getting stuck into drinks at the Pullman Hotel across the road from the MCG, with the positive vibes no doubt welcomed by the same venue recently in the news for all the wrong reasons.

On the drive to the MCG, NFL merchandise stuck out like a sore thumb before the historic venue was even within eyesight.

Melburnians are proud of their city's reputation as a sporting hub and they were not going to miss this opportunity to show up and show out.

NFL MVP Matthew Stafford had his work cut out for him at the MCG. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

If you were not familiar with the history of the LA Rams and the San Francisco 49ers, this is no ho-hum game of football. These two teams do not like each other.

After making their way through the organised security booths in the Yarra Park precinct, a set-up which meant there were no lengthy queues you'd usually associate with an event of this magnitude, fans wasted little time before slinging barbs between each other.

A group of four Rams fans from Los Angeles described their visit to Australia for the game as "a trip of a lifetime" as they proudly proclaimed the MCG to be "Rams House" for the day.

With these two teams bitter rivals it is unusual to see fans from the different sides fraternising, but that is exactly what one couple travelling from the US has done. The husband, Jamie, is a 49ers fan and the wife, Carmen, is a Rams fan.

"Typically, hanging out is forbidden in those places, so we thought if we come here it would be okay," Jamie said pre-game.

However, the fandom wasn't solely Americans making sojourns Down Under either, with the chance to watch a NFL game in real life a rich reward to Aussie fans who usually toil through all hours of the night just to catch a glimpse of their favourite teams in action.

One such fan, Zac, got into American football through his father who had spent some time in Buffalo, and therefore became a tortured Bills fan.

Zac did not follow in his father's footsteps and instead followed the Philadelphia Eagles. He was overjoyed at getting a fist pump from Eagles icon Nick Foles who was in Melbourne covering the game for Netflix.

"It's so weird watching a game at 3am and your team scores and you can't make any noise in your living room because your entire family is asleep," he said.

"So it's just you and your cat watching the TV going, 'F**k yeah.'"

Cody Simpson ran through the last two lines of the anthem an extra time. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

He described the experience of watching a regular season NFL game in Melbourne as "surreal".

"You're absolutely jazzed and your adrenaline is high, and then half an hour later you've got to get up for work on a Monday morning," he said.

As the pre-game festivities got underway there was a real juxtaposition of Australian and American culture.

Indigenous dancers performed a Welcome to Country dance with American breakdancers doing their thing in close proximity.

The juxtaposition of the two cultures was never more evident than when the Shane Warne Stand sign being flanked by LED advertising boards showing the Stars and Stripes from the American flag during Infinity Song's rendition of The Star Spangled Banner.

There was just one thing the fans from the two nations agreed upon: booing former Collingwood president Eddie McGuire as he ran out for the coin toss alongside Australian artist G-Flip.

Fans were given masks to form the flags in the stands. (ABC Sport: Chris De Silva)

Despite the clash being nominally a Rams home game there was no secret as to who dominated the stands as Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, the 2025 league MVP, was roundly booed as he ran out with his team amid blue and yellow smoke.

With all the festivities going on it was easy to forget that there was an actual football game to be played. And with the smell of the smoke still in the air, we finally got things underway.

The Rams, who were roundly criticised for not flying to Australia earlier ahead of the game, sleepwalked their way through much of the first quarter until Stafford linked up with star receiver Puka Nacua, who tip-toed his way along the sideline for some solid yardage.

Nacua's run meant that teammate Kyren Williams was able to run into the end zone in the opening moments of the second quarter for the historic first-ever NFL touchdown on Australian soil.

Williams's name will be mentioned in trivia competitions in pubs all around Australia for decades to come.

FIFO Rams may have lost the battle for hearts and minds Ahead of the NFL's debut at the MCG the San Francisco 49ers have embraced Australia and been embraced right back. But have the LA Rams missed an opportunity to throw their arms around the locals?

Despite this being a game between two California-based teams, NFL fans from all corners evidently found their way to the MCG, with just about all of the NFL's 32 franchises represented in some form in the stands.

As the Rams mariachi band came out during the quarter-time break, three fans wearing a Sam Darnold jersey, a Dak Prescott jersey and a Joe Montana jersey broke out into a salsa.

While much is made of American sport's half-time shows, the entertainment began well before the Jonas Brothers took centre stage.

Along with the mariachi band there was a separate band with a small stage set up near the usual AFL interchange benches, breaking into varying covers of classic hits such as Bryan Adams's Summer of 69.

The Jonas Brothers put on the half-time show. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

With NFL games taking over three hours of actual time there is an emphasis on keeping the fans engaged throughout, especially during stoppages.

Fans were asked to vote for which song they wanted to sing in unison and unpredictably picked Daryl Braithwaite's Horses, which might as well be Australia's other national anthem at this point.

As 100,021 fans later broke out into a passionate rendition of Horses there was something indescribably magical about it.

With the big show in town, Australia's footy stars that usually aren't able to get a moment of breathing room in Melbourne were able to slip into relative obscurity.

A current and former St Kilda cohort of Rowan Marshall, Jack Steele and Luke Dunstan were packed in among fans sitting in the fourth tier of the MCG, all decked out in Rams gear.

Despite proclamations of the MCG being Rams House, the home side gradually found themselves in trouble after Williams's opening touchdown.

An incredible goal-line stop from the 49ers defence denied a Stafford tush-push at the very end of the third quarter.

It was the kind of stop you would expect from the Rams's star-studded defence of Myles Garrett and the recently unretired Aaron Donald, and it became very obvious that this would not be the day the Rams would remember fondly.

A touchdown from Deebo Samuel sent the 49ers into raptures once again and the underdogs had claimed a dream start to their season, downing their more-favoured rivals 27-7 despite a 12,640-kilometre road trip.

The 49ers had arrived and well and truly ransacked Rams House and run away with the chocolates.

The NFL came, it saw, and it well and truly conquered Melbourne.

World.title: Sydney Roosters claim NRLW minor premiership after another perfect season
World.content:
The Bulldogs have flirted with the biggest upset in NRLW history before the undefeated Roosters charged home in the final 20 minutes for a 42-12 win at the Sydney Football Stadium.

Entering last night's game in Sydney with just three wins all year and having conceded 178 points in four consecutive losses, the Bulldogs led until the 52nd minute, only to run out of steam with strike centre Monica Tagoai in the sin bin.

While they were far from their best, it was a 26th consecutive regular-season win for master coach John Strange's Roosters side, who remain on track to reclaim the premiership they lost to the Broncos last year, with their only loss in round five of 2024.

The Roosters will now enjoy the bye afforded to the top two teams in week one of the six-team finals format.

Despite being huge underdogs, the visitors had the early ascendancy, and it took almost 12 minutes before Otesa Pule crossed for the Roosters to get the scoreboard ticking.

It did not take long after that for Corban Baxter to slip a gem of a pass to Jessica Sergis, who ran 40 metres to score her competition-leading 15th try of the season.

Just when it looked like the floodgates would open, the Bulldogs worked their way back down the field, and Tagoai powered her way over to bring her side within four points with 10 minutes left in the half.

Seven minutes later, the Dogs' five-eighth Andie Robinson flew high over Baxter to pluck a pinpoint Tayla Preston bomb from the air and touch down.

With Preston's conversion, they were surprise 12-10 leaders at the break, leaving the shortest-priced favourites in NRLW history shell-shocked.

To make matters worse for the Roosters, Baxter left the field at half-time for a head injury assessment and failed to return after the interval.

The Bulldogs stayed on top for the opening 13 minutes of the second stanza, before Tagoai was sin-binned by referee Karra-Lee Nolan for a hip-drop.

Five minutes later, Isabelle Kelly, starting in her 50th game as captain of the Roosters, tore through the middle of the Dogs' defence and found prop Millie Elliott in support for the competition leaders to reclaim the lead.

Taina Naividi was next over the stripe and Canterbury's dream was over.

More tries followed to Pule, Mia Woods, Sergis and Jocelyn Kelleher for a final score that somewhat flattered the minor premiers.

Despite the loss, it was a brave effort from the Bulldogs and coach Brayden Wiliame, in his final game at the helm before Mark O'Meley takes the reins in 2027.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
